text:
On the IRGC's View of the Conflict

Iran's behavior after the first 40 days of the US-Israeli war of aggression has been perplexing at times.

Why - after the first 2 week Pakistani backed ceasefire - are they rejecting multiple offramps?

Do they want actually want more war?

I'm referring to the IRGC as a monolith here, which is an oversimplification (though there does seem to be a overall consensus on most the points listed below).

I do believe there is a real divergence among Iranian leadership between parts who do not want continued war (primarily because their job is running the economy & country and the war makes this extremely challenging) and elements in the armed forces who prioritize their long term worldview over anything else. Of course there are some IRGC people in the former category & some elected people in the latter, but that goes beyond the scope of this post.

The perspective of the dominant faction in Iranian leadership (which I will just call the IRGC going forward) of the current conflict can be summarized with the following five points:
 
1 - This War is Existential 

The  fundamental asymmetry in this war is that the US and Israel do not have the type of skin in the game that Iran does. If they do not get what they want, it won't be pleasant, but the stakes are not comparable to what Iran faces.

The IRGC view is that what is at stake here is not just some uranium, control over a waterway, or the Islamic Republic, but Iran's sovereignty (which includes  control over oil & ability to make weapons) and even its territorial integrity. Out of all of these five points, I find this one to be the most rational.

The existential nature of the conflict means they are willing to take extreme measures and risks that they wouldn't under less dire circumstances. 

Conversely, the conflict is not existential for the other side. This means that no matter how motivated their leaders are, they will be averse towards taking extreme risks in the same matter.

2 - The Conflict Didn't Start In February

 This war is the just the latest chapter in a larger conflict that was triggered by the October 7 2023 attacks (which were done without Iran's permission or knowledge). 

This conflict started in Iran's periphery, but eventually led to the dismantlement of a great deal of its regional network (the weakening of Hezbollah & fall of the Assad regime). While Iran initially did not want to get involved directly, the sequence of events that started on the April 1 2024 attack on its consulate in Damascus pulled it in anyway & eventually led to full war on the Iranian homeland.

Until February 2026, this conflict was primarily characterized by Iran's retreats and Israel's advances.

Saddam's fate offers a lesson to Iran. The US was not able to overthrow him in one go. But rather they had an initial war, followed by a decade of sanctions, uprisings, and a no fly zone, and only then the final blow.

As such, on and off conflict with the US in which the other side periodically "mows the lawn" until they are out of breath and then starts again a year or two later is also seen as an existential threat.

Furthermore, Iran's experiences in the 2010s and bitter failure of the JCPOA (in which from Iran's perspective it made compromises upfront and the US cheated and pulled out of) have convinced the IRGC that a continuation of the same diplomacy-threats cycle is foolish (I disagree with this point).

Iran offering compromises in the same manner will not satisfy the other side, but rather ensure the cycle continues. The only way to break this cycle is through the battlefield.

3 - This is the Decisive Battle

The key turning point was the United States and Israel choosing to launch a second war less than one year after the first one. 

Many people attribute Iran's more aggressive stance to Khamenei's death and the empowering of a new generation of hardliners. There is some truth to this, but the bigger factor in my view is simply that previous methods failed to prevent a new war.

Trying to compromise, relying on regional mediation, and exercising strategic patience to stay out neither stopped the first war in June 2025, nor the subsequent one in February 2026 (nor should it be forgotten the Pezeshkian government genuinely tried to reach a diplomatic settlement to avoid UN snapback sanctions between these two wars & the Europeans played hardball). All of these only made the other side view Iran as weak and strengthened their appetite for conflict.

Iran took the first available opportunity to end the 12 Day War (there were some theatrics with what time the ceasefire ended, but it ultimately took the offer). Today that is viewed as a mistake and something that emboldened the other side.

Everything since the meek response to the assassination of Qassem Soleimani up to February 2026 is viewed by the IRGC as major blunders. 

Trump and Netenyahu's decision to start a new war fully convinced Iranian leadership that any weakness would mean more pain in the long run. The Americans made the decision to start the war, but they would not be able to choose when and on what terms to end it.

While Iran has seen many blows in the past few years, it is not currently in a Saddam 2003 situation. If there will be a decisive round - now it is the time to do it. 

Thus the IRGC views this war not only as a war of defense against a powerful enemy - but the decisive war that will shape the region for decades. 

People focusing too closely on things like the US midterm elections or short term fluctuations of the markets are at risk of missing the forest for the trees - these might play a small role in Iran's calculations, but right now it's convinced that it in the next few months it can favorably change the balance of power in the region for the next 25 years. That's the real prize.

The only parallel to this in the modern history of these sides would be the Summer 2006 Lebanon War (this led to a dramatic expansion of Iran's Axis and stopped Israel from attacking Hezbollah for almost two decades).

If this war doesn't end with a decisive blow to the other side then even if it stops the conflict for a few months or years, the existential threat is still present and the previous cycle continues.

The IRGC is not under the delusion they can impose a total and complete defeat on the US army, but they want the sting to be so painful that it causes a permanent change in their calculations and this will not happen again.

4 - This is a Zero Sum Conflict

Putting this all together, the IRGC has concluded this is a zero sum conflict. There will be a winner and a loser. There is no compromise possible.

This is quite different than Iran's behavior with the West before this. The entire premise of the JCPOA was that it would be a win-win scenario for all sides. Similarly, the Pezeshkian administration tried to convince the US (before the 12 Day War) that they could get a win-win by normalizing relations with Iran and investing there.

It's unclear exactly what this faction defines victory as, but it seems to center around three points: 

- The complete withdraw of the US from Iran's neighborhood including closing down bases

- Iran gaining complete control over the Strait of Hormoz. This is interpreted in a maximalist sense, it isn't just a return to the pre-war status quo while ensuring Iran can export oil, but rather that every ship coming in and every ship going out needs Iran's explicit permission (the toll is a secondary issue, the control is what matters). 

- A complete end to the war on all fronts (thus ending the conflict and the cycle, not just this war).

I believe the first and third point are somewhat achievable. It's pretty clear the US can't defend its bases from Iranian attacks. Equipment and soldiers on the south cost of the Persian Gulf are increasingly turning into liabilities (we already see a significant withdraw to Jordan and Israel)

I have a lot of skepticism about the second point. It seems to be quite the stretch to think Iran can achieve this. 

This particular point doesn't appear to be just a few rogue generals though ... not returning to the pre-war status quo is one of the few clear cut things that one sees in Mojtaba Khamenei's statements. 

I suspect one reason for this is that it is viewed as a major source of leverage that would guarantee sanctions relief actually happens (rather than being subject to the whim of US Congress and pen of the POTUS). It would also be a very concrete Iranian win and US loss.

Thus, the IRGC is open to an end to the conflict - if Iran gains a clear cut victory. In the case of the MoU, this meant maximalist control over the Strait. When the US wasn't willing to concede on that then they decided the MoU wasn't worth it and fired on the ships traveling without Iran's permission.

In my view this is extremely risky. By removing the option for compromise then the other side may become far more aggressive than it would have otherwise, conclude it has no other choice, and respond to Iran with very extreme measures.

American's military outposts in the Middle East may be at risk, but its homeland is quite safe. However it is Iran's infrastructure and homeland who are at risk of annihilation if the bet goes wrong. 

5 - This is a Battle of Wills

The IRGC views Iran's core weapon not as drones or missiles but willpower. The key is to simply be stubborn enough and stay committed long enough so the other side moves onto something else.

And because this is existential for Iran but not the other side, they are likely to get distracted by some other crisis or adventure, but Iran cannot afford to.

It would be negligent not to mention here that while for the average Iranian citizen the war has brought nothing but agony and extreme difficulty - this doesn't impact the IRGC's will. They believe the struggle is worth it. What matters to them is their ability and willingness to keep fighting, not the views of the general population.

Of course what is unsaid here is that the US has a far greater ability to escalate and inflict pain than Iran does. Most importantly it has a mass nuclear arsenal. 

While I do not think it is likely they use nuclear weapons at this point, if things get to the point where Iran refuses to give concessions and the global economy is actually on the abyss of a meltdown, I think the temptation will exist. And Iran has no answer for that escalation.

Unaccounted Factors

The framework presented above goes a long way in explaining Iran's current assessment of the conflict, why it behaves the way it does, and why even if Trump wants to find a way out of the war, Iran won't necessarily give him that.

I've also highlighted why I believe this is extremely risky and in my view has a high risk of overplaying Iran's hand.

I do concede that it is possible they have some sort of capability that I am unaware of that would change the balance of power & make what I view as unwise decisions as less risky.

No I don't think they have some crazy super weapon that no one has ever discovered or are technologically on par with the United States. But nonetheless there are some things that could be strategic game changers.

I tried to think about what such capabilities would be and came up with the following:

a - Tunnels (likely)

It is quite possible that the IRGC has a network of tunnels that are far deeper and more extensive than anyone imagines. 

Keep in mind the Israel was quite surprised by the extent of Hamas's tunnels in Gaza. That was by a militia that ruled over a few cities that have been under complete siege since 2007.

In contrast Iran is a nation state with very advanced capabilities. It's not particularly speculative to think that they have something underground far beyond what we think. And which goes deep enough that they cannot be destroyed with airstrikes.

They may have some level of advanced manufacturing capabilities to keep the missile and drone programs going (in addition to storage which we know is underground). You can't make everything underground, but a big part of the process could move there. As well as things like protecting remaining political figures. 

If advanced enough this would mean that even with very extreme bombings of the surface (which would result in unimaginable suffering for the ordinary person), they would still be able to continue building, moving around, and launching missiles and drones to disrupt the Strait and hit US forces in the area.

b - Nuclear Weapon (maybe)

It's also possible that the weaponization effort is far more advanced than expected and somewhere deep under the earth (other than a certain mountain near Natanz) there are advanced centrifuges spinning trying to get past the finish line.

If the capability exists to create an advanced enough nuclear weapon that can be put on a miniaturized warhead within weeks, then that could change things significantly.

If such a program exists, I doubt any of the elected government is aware of it. 

There are many reasons to be skeptical of this and I view it as a maybe and not likely. But if there were a time to make a rush for the bomb, this would be it.

c - Next Generation Missiles (less likely)

It is also possible Iran has some missile capability that has not yet been unveiled and is being saved for later down the escalation ladder. 

This would relate to a leap ahead in accuracy and range. For example something that could reliably hit American bases in mainland Europe or Diego Garcia.

I'm fairly skeptical of this, but if it existed this would also change the situation.

Conclusion

Put together, this all means that Iran will be far less willing to compromise than ever before & is less likely to accept offers that it would previously be satisfied with.

Ending the war alone is likely not enough. The entirety of the government is united in thinking that at minimum, some kind of economic relief from the noose of sanctions is needed. But, as discussed above, there is a powerful faction that demands far more than this. And this faction appears to have the upper hand at the moment.

text:
BTS kicks off Metlife Day 1 with exciting soundcheck 💜

BTS brought the excitement to MetLife Stadium early on Saturday, August 1, as RM, Jin, Suga, J-Hope, Jimin, V and Jung Kook took the stage for their Day 1 soundcheck. VIP attendees quickly shared excited reports and brief glimpses from inside the venue, while the group tested its live setup ahead of the evening concert.

Wow, it never fails to amaze me how liberals will take a hit piece from a biased source and run with it. You never even looked into it. The State was protecting the child. 

Paxton’s office offered the deal after a hung jury and after the victim refused to testify again. They did not want to force the child to go through it again. 

Adam Hoffman, a former Waco attorney, was charged with continuous sexual abuse of a young child — a first-degree felony that can carry 25 years to life. The alleged abuse of his son’s friend lasted years, beginning when the boy was about 7. McLennan County DA Josh Tetens recused because Hoffman had consulted him before Tetens was elected, so the Attorney General’s office took the case. 
The 2025 trial ended 7–5 for conviction. A retrial was possible, but prosecutors said they had no path to a felony conviction without the child’s live testimony. About 10 months later they offered a plea: drop the felony, plead to two Class A misdemeanors (indecent assault and displaying harmful material to a minor), and initially recommend essentially one day (time served). Because the written admission did not specify the victim’s age, Texas sex-offender registration was not triggered. 
Visiting Judge Roy Sparkman refused the one-day proposal (“One day. Seriously?”), then raised it to 30 days plus surrender of Hoffman’s law license, then to 60 days after the mother said 30 days was “not enough.” Hoffman served about 29 days and was released for good behavior. He later moved to Nebraska, where he is required to register. 

The reason is: hung jury + victim unwilling to testify again + no other way to prove the felony. The office chose a guaranteed misdemeanor conviction and some punishment over a high-risk retrial that would force the child back on the stand.

BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Friday, August 28, 1959, Braniff International Airways welcomed the delivery of its fourth beautiful new Lockheed L-188 Electra four-engine prop-jet-powered airliner. Ship N9704C landed at Dallas Love Field and taxied to the Braniff Operations and Maintenance Base on the east side of the airport. Braniff would fly a total of ten Electras, nine new and one leased, between 1959 and 1969. The big Braniff Electra Jet was painted in the 1959 Red and Blue Electra Jet Color Scheme.

Assistant Chief Pilot Captain Cotton Safrit piloted the big plush Electra from the Lockheed Electra Plant located at the Lockheed Air Terminal at Burbank Airport, California. At the time of the arrival of Ship N9704C, four additional new aircraft were scheduled for delivery through January 1960. The aircraft included Ship N9705C, slated to arrive in September 1959, followed by Ships N9706C and N9707C in October and Ship N9708C in November and followed by Ship N9709C in January 1960. Braniff was offered a tenth Electra, which was an L-188A model that was scheduled for delivery to Capital Airlines. However, Capital did not take up the order and it was delivery to Braniff in October 1962, which was the last new Braniff Electra delivery.

With the loss of a BAC One-11 Fastback Jet, Ship N1553, at Falls City, Nebraska, in August 1966, the company was in need of additional capacity. To fill this need, Braniff leased an Electra from Frederick B. Ayer and Associates, which was registered as N16816. The aircraft became the first Electra to be painted in the 1965 Alexander Girard Solid Color Scheme. The Electra was especially attractive in the Turquoise Solid Color Scheme with White Wings, Engines and Vertical Tail with Alexander Girard Sky Font and BI Tail Logo in Black.

Ship N9704C was scheduled to go into regularly scheduled Braniff service four days after its delivery on September 1, 1959. Effective on that date, new Electra service was scheduled to begin between Dallas Love Field and Washington National Airport. In addition, service increased to three round trips daily between Love Field and New York/Newark Airport. The big Electra would also begin replacing Douglas DC-7C El Dorados over the same route operating as Flights 10, 7, 542 and 543.

However, a new DC-7C El Dorado nonstop flight began September 1, between Dallas and Washington DC. The new flight departed Dallas shortly after 9AM and arrived at National Airport at just before 330PM, while the return nonstop flight departed Washington DC at 5PM and arrived in Dallas at just after 7PM in the evening.

By 1965, the big Electras and new BAC One-11 The New Jets would replace all of Braniff legendary Douglas DC-7C El Dorado fleet. Just a year later, the last Douglas DC-6 El Conquistador flight was flown leaving only the twin-engine Convairs as Braniff’s sole piston-powered airliners in service. However, in late summer 1967, with the arrival of the magnificent new Douglas DC-8-62 Intercontinental Jet, the last Convair were retired making Braniff an all jet-powered airline. The Electra fleet was also retried just two years later in April 1969, which brought Braniff International fully into the pure jet age.

@CryptoLawyerz maybe 12 apostles 🤷🏻‍♀️

Why 12 specifically?
No one recorded a precise, rational reason. Later commentators offered two overlapping explanations:
•  Symbolism. Twelve was a number of completeness in a Christian society: 12 apostles, 12 tribes of Israel, 12 months. Sir Edward Coke said the law “delighteth herself in the number of twelve” because it appears in Holy Writ.
•  Practical size. It was large enough to feel like a representative slice of the community and to make a unanimous verdict carry weight, yet small enough to deliberate. Early juries also had to swear from personal knowledge of the facts; 12 oaths in one direction decided the case.
The U.S. Supreme Court in Williams v. Florida (1970) called the exact number 12 “a historical accident, unrelated to the great purposes which gave rise to the jury” and “wholly without significance except to mystics.” That decision allowed states to use six-person juries in many cases. Many serious criminal trials still use 12 because of tradition, perceived legitimacy, and research suggesting larger groups recall evidence better, are less easily dominated by one personality, and better reflect the community. https://t.co/zhGZLNzrJj 
So “peers” originally meant ordinary people of similar standing from the same locality, and 12 became the conventional size of that group. It is custom more than constitutional command.

How Many Fascist Cronies Can One Republican Have?
Georgia Senate candidate Mike Collins seems determined to answer that question.
Jeet Heer
US Senate candidate Mike Collins speaks during an election-night watch party after winning the Republican nomination, Tuesday, June 16, 2026, in Jackson, Ga.

US Senate candidate Mike Collins speaks during an election-night watch party after winning the Republican nomination, Tuesday, June 16, 2026, in Jackson, Georgia.(Colin Hubbard / AP)

Not for the first time, Republican Georgia congressman and Senate nominee Mike Collins is having to fend off questions about a former staffer’s florid public embrace of racism. On Thursday, The Washington Post reported that “a former staffer for Representative Mike Collins (R-Georgia) shared images in June and July on his X account of a swastika and one that depicts himself in Ku Klux Klan robes.” 

The former staffer in question is 24-year-old Mike Parra, who worked as an intern for Collins as well as a contractor for a pro-Collins leadership PAC. Parra says he was merely being “satirical,” and that he is not really a white supremacist. But he has also described himself as a “twink fascist,” used anti-Black slurs, and said he thinks “the white race contributes more to the world,” which most people would recognize as the core belief of white supremacists.

This article has been made free to read. Keeping it that way isn't.
Donate

Since Parra no longer works for Collins, his racist posts might seem a minor matter. But this is not the first such scandal involving Collins and his staff—not by a long shot.

As The Washington Post sums up:

    A number of people in Collins’s orbit have been accused of having ties to white nationalists or of making racist or antisemitic comments, and the congressman’s own social media presence has also drawn scrutiny….

    Collins, a trucking executive, has faced scrutiny over his own social media feed, where he has shared posts that were called racist and antisemitic, allegations he has denied….

    In July, Collins replaced his…chief of staff Kip Talley after Slate reported on his participation in a group chat that included Nick Fuentes and Richard Spencer, both of whom are white supremacists and antisemites….

    CNN reported in July that Collins’s son-in-law, David Alan Scheer II, has shared Nazi imagery online.…

    In May, another Collins ex-staffer, William Paul, confronted Rep. Mike Lawler (R-New York) at a bar, hurling antisemitic insults at him…

Having one racist crony may be regarded as a misfortune. Having several should make even the most naïve investigator suspicious.

Aside from these incidents of racism and antisemitism from various confederates, Collins also fired another staffer, Brandon Phillips, for a vile post mocking the attempted suicide of the wife of a rival political consultant. The viciousness of that post shares an affinity with the racist trolling that Collins and his associates have often indulged in.

It’s a mistake to see this nastiness and bigotry as having no wider importance beyond the individuals concerned. Rather, they reflect a political fact that extends beyond Collins: Over the past 10 years, racist invective has become one of the main ways that the GOP activates its base and courts younger voters. It was not by chance that figures like Parra and Phillips worked for Collins. Rather, their passion for outré violations of common decency were what made them desirable employees—until they went too far and had to be disavowed.

In 2017, in the wake of the infamous Unite the Right march in Charlottesville, Virginia, the journalist Alex Pareene wrote a remarkably prophetic essay for Splinter arguing that the alt-right racist provocateurs who attended the rally were the future of the GOP. Pareene noted:

    Racial resentment has been a driving force behind College Republican recruitment for years, but at this point it’s really all they have left to offer. In the age of President Donald Trump, what inspires a young person not merely to be conservative or vote Republican, but to get active in organized Republican politics? Do you think it’s a fervent belief that Paul Ryan knows the optimal tax policy to spur economic growth? Or do you think it’s more likely to be something else?

Pareene ended his essay by naming one rally attendee:

    These future Republican elected officials could easily look very much like rally attendee Nicholas Fuentes, a Boston University student until his decision this week to leave the school. He didn’t appear to be a formal member of any young Republican organizations, but he was a self-described Republican. In interviews, he denies being a white supremacist. On Facebook, after the rally, he wrote: “The rootless transnational elite knows that a tidal wave of white identity is coming.”

In 2017, Fuentes was, to borrow a Bob Dylan phrase, a complete unknown, a college dropout with some local notoriety for his racist provocations. But he would shortly become one of the most popular streamers on the far right, infamous for his repeated Holocaust denial and praise of Nazism. Both Trump and his vice president JD Vance have been diligent about cultivating the hard-core racists in their coalition, including Fuentes, who infamously dined with Trump and Kanye West at Mar-a-Lago in 2022.

We’re now a decade into Trump’s takeover of the GOP. It ill-behoves us at this late date to be shocked by the fact that a Trump acolyte like Mike Collins has said bigoted things, has bigoted family members, and has repeatedly hired bigots for his staff. Collins does all this because this is how you succeed in GOP politics.

Jeet Heer

Jeet Heer is a national affairs correspondent for The Nation and host of the weekly Nation podcast, The Time of Monsters. He also pens the monthly column “Morbid Symptoms.” The author of In Love with Art: Francoise Mouly’s Adventures in Comics with Art Spiegelman (2013) and Sweet Lechery: Reviews, Essays and Profiles (2014), Heer has written for numerous publications, including The New Yorker, The Paris Review, Virginia Quarterly Review, The American Prospect, The Guardian, The New Republic, and The Boston Globe.

🇺🇸🇨🇦 A patriotic Canadian and I have a good dialogue on U.S.- Canada trade relations plus some Asian nations. 

The Buick part is right. The conclusion is not.

Enclave is Michigan. Envista and Encore GX are Korea. Envision is China. Trax and Trailblazer are Korea too. That is GM’s cheap-crossover map. It is not proof Washington somehow forgot Asia.

China already sits under stacked 301 and 232 duties. Average rates on Chinese goods are still in the mid-30s tariff-wise. That is why the next Envision leaves Shanghai for Kansas in 2028.

Korea took the 25% auto tariff, then bought a 15% cap in the U.S.–Korea trade agreement. Canada did not need that cap. It already had the better offer: USMCA content rules that can cut the effective 232 hit toward 12.5%, and lower still if more of the vehicle is U.S.-made. Canadian vehicles stayed in the 232 band. Listed Canadian goods now also face the 50% Section 338 tariffs after the August talks collapsed.

That is why walking away after a deal was on the table last Tuesday makes no economic sense for Canada.

May I remind you that USMCA is not dead. It is on annual review. Energy, potash, and qualifying North American content were carved out of parts of the new list on purpose. Cars and steel were not. That is industrial policy aimed at the next retooling cycle, and Buick’s next move has already been announced.

What is the best university in the USA, notwithstanding a branded university?

FUFU
When you look beyond famous brand names like Harvard or Stanford, the title of best university in the United States often belongs to premier public research institutions like the University of California, Berkeley or the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor.  UC Berkeley is widely considered the top public university in the nation and frequently outperforms elite private schools in global research impact, engineering, computer science, and social sciences. It offers world-class faculty and groundbreaking innovation without relying purely on private status or prestige.  University of Michigan is another top contender because almost all of its academic programs rank in the top ten nationally, offering unmatched breadth across medicine, business, law, engineering, and the arts.  For students focused on technology and high career outcomes, Georgia Institute of Technology provides world-renowned engineering programs and one of the highest returns on investment in the country at a lower tuition cost.  If your priority is pure undergraduate teaching, top liberal arts institutions like Williams College or Amherst College often provide a superior personal education compared to large, famous research universities.  Ultimately, the best university depends on your specific goals, but UC Berkeley leads the nation when balancing raw academic power, research impact, and value beyond simple brand prestige.

text:
Bisate Lodge: Where Luxury Meets Conservation in Rwanda🇷🇼

Nestled on the edge of Volcanoes National Park in northwestern Rwanda, Bisate Lodge is one of the country’s most remarkable luxury safari destinations. Surrounded by the dramatic Virunga Mountains, the lodge offers visitors an extraordinary combination of comfort, nature, wildlife, and conservation.

Bisate is particularly famous for its proximity to Rwanda’s mountain gorillas. For travelers visiting the region to experience gorilla trekking, the lodge provides an ideal base from which to explore the forested slopes of Volcanoes National Park and encounter one of Africa’s most endangered and fascinating animals.

The lodge itself blends contemporary luxury with traditional Rwandan architectural influences. Its distinctive, rounded villas are designed to reflect the cultural character of Rwanda while providing guests with spectacular views of the surrounding volcanic landscape. Inside, natural materials, warm furnishings, and large windows create a peaceful atmosphere that complements the wilderness outside.

What makes Bisate especially meaningful is its commitment to conservation. The lodge has been involved in restoring degraded land through reforestation, helping to expand native forest habitat and create a healthier ecosystem for wildlife. Guests can become part of these efforts through activities such as tree planting and guided experiences that highlight Rwanda’s remarkable biodiversity.
Beyond gorilla trekking, visitors can enjoy birdwatching, nature walks, cultural experiences, and opportunities to learn about the communities and conservation initiatives surrounding Volcanoes National Park.

Bisate Lodge represents a different kind of luxury, one that is deeply connected to the landscape. It demonstrates how tourism can contribute to protecting nature while creating memorable experiences for travelers.

In the heart of Rwanda’s volcanic highlands, Bisate offers more than a beautiful place to stay. It offers an opportunity to experience the wilderness, discover Rwanda’s rich culture, and become part of a story of conservation and hope.

text:
#OnThisDay August 29, 1905: Flames Over Flathead.

Newspapers reported that forest fires were burning through the heavily wooded country surrounding Flathead Lake in northwestern Montana. A dispatch originating in Butte stated that approximately 1,000 acres had already burned and that settlers in the affected region were becoming alarmed. Although the surviving report offered few details concerning the precise location, ignition source, or suppression effort, the fire occurred at an important moment in the environmental and administrative history of the Flathead region. It coincided with rapid settlement, expanding commercial use of western Montana's forests, and the creation of a new federal system for managing the nation's forest reserves.

The Flathead Valley contained one of Montana's richest forest environments. Botanist Harry Nichols Whitford, whose major study The Forests of the Flathead Valley, Montana appeared in 1905, documented extensive forests composed of species including western larch, Douglas fir, lodgepole pine, ponderosa pine, Engelmann spruce, and other conifers. His field observations also demonstrated that wildfire was already a defining ecological force. Whitford observed that scarcely any section of the territory he examined had escaped burning to some degree. Some fires remained at the surface and scarred standing trees, while others produced much greater changes in forest composition and structure. His work provides unusually direct scientific evidence of the fire-shaped landscape that existed when the August 1905 fires were reported.

The fires also occurred during a period of rapid economic development. Kalispell had emerged as the principal commercial center of the Flathead Valley following its founding in 1891. Logging operations expanded as settlement increased and transportation links improved. The John O'Brien Lumber Company established a large mill at Somers on Flathead Lake in 1900, with an annual capacity estimated at approximately forty million board feet. Logs reached the mill through a combination of river drives, lake towing, and railroad transportation. Another mill on the Stillwater River increased its daily production to approximately 70,000 board feet by 1905. Forests therefore represented both a dominant feature of the local environment and a major economic resource.

The institutional setting of the August fires was equally significant. Congress had passed the Forest Reserve Act in 1891, and President Grover Cleveland established the Lewis and Clarke Forest Reserve in 1897. That reserve originally included large portions of what later became the Flathead National Forest and Glacier National Park. Early federal forest administration remained limited. Supervisors worked across immense areas with few roads, trails, ranger stations, communications systems, or employees. Their duties included guarding federal forests against illegal timber cutting and fire while administering public uses of the land.

The year 1905 marked a fundamental change. Congress transferred responsibility for the federal forest reserves from the Department of the Interior's General Land Office to the Department of Agriculture, and the Forest Service was created under Chief Forester Gifford Pinchot. In the Flathead region, administrative changes followed quickly. Page S. Bunker became supervisor after the removal of his predecessor, and Flathead Forest Reserve headquarters moved to Kalispell later in 1905. The headquarters occupied a single room in the Conrad Bank Building for ten dollars per month, including heat. These modest arrangements demonstrate how limited federal infrastructure remained when the August fires threatened the area.

Montana's state fire-protection system was likewise still developing. Territorial and early state laws prohibited destructive burning, and in 1901 Montana enacted legislation intended to prevent fires from spreading from railroad rights-of-way into forest lands. State records later estimated that railroad locomotives caused 65 percent of Montana forest fires at that time. This statistic demonstrates the importance of railroad-generated fires statewide, but no surviving evidence cited here establishes a railroad as the cause of the August 1905 Flathead fires. Montana did not establish an Office of State Firewarden until 1907 or an Office of State Forester until 1909.

The August 29 fires therefore document an important transitional period. Northwestern Montana possessed extensive commercial forests and growing settlements, yet organized wildfire suppression remained rudimentary. Roads, telephone systems, ranger stations, firefighting organizations, and coordinated state-federal protection would expand during subsequent years. The catastrophic fires of 1910 would later accelerate that transformation dramatically. The comparatively small 1905 Flathead episode survives as evidence of the conditions that preceded those reforms: expanding settlement and timber use existed beside immense forest landscapes in which fire remained both common and difficult for public authorities to control.

text:
Remembering Hurricane Katrina: 21 years on

On 29 August 2005, Hurricane Katrina came ashore on the Louisiana and Mississippi coast. The levees protecting New Orleans gave way, roughly 80 percent of the city went under water, and more than 1,800 people lost their lives. At over US$125 billion in damage, it remains the costliest tropical cyclone on record.

Today Cynoptec pauses to remember the people of the Gulf Coast, the families who never recovered what was lost, and the emergency crews who worked through the worst of it.

Katrina’s track was forecast well. The warnings came days ahead. But days is all the conventional system can offer, and for a city of half a million people, a fragile levee network and an evacuation plan that assumed everyone had a car, days was not enough.

That gap is the reason Cynoptec exists.

Our vision is to forecast the conditions that produce events like Katrina not days out, but months out, and in time, years out. The Cynoptec Climate Model tracks the physical cycles that load the atmosphere and ocean for extreme seasons, so that councils, insurers, agribusiness and emergency managers can plan, fund and build before the system forms, not after it is named.

A warning measured in months changes what is possible. Levees get reinforced. Stock is moved. Insurance is repriced. Evacuation routes are tested when the sun is still shining.

Twenty one years on, the best way to honour Katrina is to make sure the next one is seen coming from much further away.

text:
Ecclesiastes 3-4 & Psalm 80 | August 29th | 2026 Global Bible Journey

Experience the Word of God in a new, immersive way.

It’s About Growth, Not a Checklist

As we continue through August 2026, remember that this journey is about genuine spiritual growth, not just "checking a box" for the day. Our goal is to let these scriptures transform our perspective and our priorities. If you missed a few days or are just joining us for the first time—don’t worry! Just jump right in with us today. The path to growth is always open, and there is no "behind" in this study.

Today’s Reading

In Ecclesiastes 3–4, the Preacher reflects on the appointed rhythms of life in a fallen world, opening with the timeless poem that "for everything there is a season, and a time for every matter under heaven." He acknowledges that God has set eternity in the human heart, yet observes the painful realities of oppression, envy, and isolation under the sun—famously highlighting the value of companionship and community by declaring that "two are better than one" and "a threefold cord is not quickly broken." Turning to the book of Psalms, Psalm 80 offers an earnest communal prayer calling upon the Shepherd of Israel to restore His people. Drawing upon the rich imagery of Israel as a transplanted vine from Egypt now facing destruction, Asaph repeatedly cries out the heartfelt refrain: "Restore us, O God; cause Your face to shine, and we shall be saved." This video is designed to help you focus on the text without distraction, featuring modern visuals and a clear, read-along experience.

Join the Global Community

This project is an outreach of the Richmond Church of Christ in Kentucky, connecting brothers and sisters from across the globe—including our communities in Nigeria, India, and South Africa. While our videos are "text-first," our teaching and discussions reflect the views we espouse at our local congregation.

Read With Us—Don't read alone!

Join our private Facebook group to discuss today's reading, share prayer requests, and connect with our global family: https://t.co/fM9NqMCwFZ

Producer’s Tip: Customize Your Speed

We produce these videos at a moderate pace to allow for reflection. If you prefer to read faster or slower, click the Settings (Gear Icon) on this video player, select "Playback Speed," and adjust it to your liking (0.75x to slow down, or 1.25x to 1.5x to speed up).

Subscribe to stay with us for all 365 days of 2026!

Med Venezuela under OFAC-sektorssanktioner enligt två presidentdekret är den juridiska ramen för detta avtal oklar, förvänta snabba åtgärder från finansdepartementet för att skapa undantagslicenser eller en bredare sanktionsomstrukturering. Guld föll -2,3 procent och silver -3,4 procent idag, i linje med minskad efterfrågan på säker hamn potentiellt kopplad till signaler om energiförsörjningsexpansion. Skyfallsvarningar aktiva i San Antonio/Bexar County (Texas) och fortsatta översvämningsvarningar längs Illinois River. FEMA-katastrofdeklarationer förblir aktiva i Indiana (översvämningar) och flera delstater för skogsbrand. Arméns riktad energi-lasersystem engagerade framgångsrikt fientliga drönare vid södra gränsen, första bekräftade operativa användningen.

EUROPA
Islands EU-folkomröstning pågår idag; ett "ja"-resultat skulle återstarta en vilande anslutningsprocess och skulle kunna påverka bredare EU-utvidgningspolitik inklusive Ukraina, Moldavien och västra Balkan. Natos övning Saber Junction 26 fortsätter i Tyskland, testar integration av drönarkrigföring. Rysk statsmedia TASS lyfter fram tusentals demonstranter i Washington mot Trumps politik. Kung Harald av Norge har avlidit; Trump uttryckte kondoleanser.

MELLANÖSTERN
Iranstödda PMF-fraktioner i Irak planerar enligt uppgift attacker mot Saudiarabien som svar på de saudisk-amerikanska attackerna mot PMF-högkvarteret den 29 juli, bör behandlas som ett trovärdigt hot som kräver bevakning givet källan (OSINTWarfare flaggade Al-Arabiyas historik av felaktighet). Somalisk piratvåg direkt kopplad till spridningseffekter från USA-Iran-kriget. Hangarfartygshållning: CVN-77 (Bush) i Arabiska havet, CVN-72 (Lincoln) i Indiska oceanen, framskjuten närvaro upprätthållen. Resevarningar på nivå 3 för Qatar, Kuwait och Bahrain.

AFRIKA
Situationen i Niamey, Niger kräver akut bevakning, skottlossning och explosioner över huvudstaden kan indikera ett försök till motkupp eller inomjunta-våld. Ebolan i DR Kongo förblir kontinentens allvarligaste folkhälsonödsituation; internetavbrott i DR Kongo (IODA-kritisk varning, pågående 7 dagar) komplicerar insatssamordningen. Internetstörningar pågår även i Kap Verde och Togo. FN:s säkerhetsråd sammankallade om Haiti efter Kenscoff-massakern på 47-plus civila.

ASIEN-STILLAHAVSOMRÅDET
Bangladesh höll nyligen ett presidentval (20 augusti). Ett amerikanskt militärflygplan (anropssignal COL360) spåras över södra Australien på höjd, vilket antyder rutinmässig ISR-verksamhet. Kinas JL-3 SLBM-test i öppet hav (juli, OSINT-bekräftat) förblir en central strategisk signal. Övningen Pahlawan Warrior 26 mellan amerikanska och bruneiska styrkor nyligen avslutad.

MARKNADSIMPLIKATIONER

Venezuela-oljeavtalet (65 miljarder fat): baisseartat för råolja om levererbart; WTI knappt rörligt (-0,1 procent), marknaderna skeptiska till kortsiktig påverkan givet sanktionskomplexiteten.

📉 Guld -2,3 procent, silver -3,4 procent: rotation bort från säkra tillgångar; kan återspegla optimism kring Venezuela-avtalet eller kortsiktig vinsthemtagning.

📈 S&P +0,47 procent, Nasdaq +1,04 procent: risk-on-ton; Fear & Greed på 68 (girighet).

📉 Russell 2000 -1,1 procent: småbolagsunderprestation, divergens värd att bevaka för signaler om avmattad tillväxt.

DXY +0,52 procent, EUR/USD -0,58 procent: dollarn stärks, delvis driven av energi-/geopolitiskt förtroende.

Polymarket: 53,5 procent ingen Fed-räntesänkning i september: marknaderna nästan delade inför septembers FOMC, volatilitetsrisk kring mötet 15–16 september.

Ebolaeskaleringen (PHEIC) i DR Kongo: risk för afrikanska aktiemarknader och störning av försörjningskedjan för DR Kongos mineraler (kobolt, koltan).

Instabiliteten i Niger: riskpremie i Västafrika förhöjd; potentiell störning av uranförsörjning (Niger är en central global leverantör).

INDIKATORER ATT BEVAKA

Niger/Niamey: bekräftelse av karaktären på dagens skottlossning och explosioner, motkuppförsök, inomjunta-konflikt eller militant attack. Niger levererar cirka 5 procent av global uranproduktion; långvarig instabilitet har implikationer för kärnbränsle.

Venezuela-oljeavtalets juridiska struktur: bevaka akuta OFAC-licensutfärdanden eller ändringar av presidentdekret under de kommande 48 timmarna som skulle signalera att avtalet har en verklig genomförandeväg snarare än att vara ett politiskt tillkännagivande.

Islands EU-folkomröstningsresultat: omröstningen stänger idag. Ett "ja"-utfall utlöser bredare EU-utvidgningsmomentum och stärker den transatlantiska demokratiska blocksignalen.

text:
A wistful Dave's Car ID Service today as we bid farewell to America's universally beloved singing angel, Dolly Parton. I was moved as everyone was by her passing, but I didn't have quite the right words to express it. So may I present for you her life in cars, my most sincere expression of tribute and admiration.

I think this may be the earliest photo of Dolly with an automobile, and one that is important in understanding her life story arc. First, the car: a 1953 Cadillac. The man fender-sitting on it with Dolly is her uncle, Bill Owens, and presuming she is about 7-8 years old here the car is fairly brand new.

Dolly did grow up rather impoverished in rural Tennessee, and you can imagine when Uncle Bill dropped by in his flashy Cadillac for a visit it was quite an event. And Uncle Bill became an important influence and mentor for Dolly. 

Bill Owens performed as "Little Billy Earl with the Spit Curl" in the early 1950s, a sort of proto-rockabilly, but settled into a long career as a Nashville songwriter with over 800 songs to his credit.

He also was the man who taught Dolly to play the guitar at around 8 years old. And by the time she was 10, he recognized she had so much talent that he arranged for her to perform on the Cas Walker Farm & Home Hour radio program from Knoxville, her first broadcast performance. When Dolly was 13, he helped arrange her debut performance on The Grand Ole Opry, where she was introduced by Johnny Cash. And brought the house down, with 3 encores.

When she was in high school, she became one of Uncle Bill's songwriting partners before branching out with her own solo songwriting. After finishing high school she moved to Nashville, where she and Uncle Bill were both signed as songwriters for Combine Music. They cowrote three 1966 top 10 country hits - "Put It Off Till Tomorrow" and "The Company You Keep" for Bo Phillips, and "Fuel To the Flame" for Skeeter Davis.

Dolly and Uncle Bill teamed to write many songs, and he wrote several for her and her duet partner Porter Wagner, before she ascended to superstardom. In his later years Uncle Bill was a frequent performer at Dollywood.

ANGELS ON THE WAY 

Oprah Winfrey’s first opportunity on television came in 1973, when she was just 19 years old. Chris Clark, then the News Director at Nashville’s CBS station in Tennessee, gave her that opportunity.

In our quest to move forward in life, God often places angels on our way.

To Oprah, Chris Clark was her angel.

I often say, it is better to prepare and not have opportunities than to have opportunities come your way and find you unprepared.

Preparation is important because when an opportunity comes and you miss it, you may never get that same opportunity again.

Everyone has an angel who will show up at one point or another. The question is: How prepared are you to take advantage of what your angel offers?

I remember when I was Senior Boys Prefect and SRC Zone 5 President of the Greater Accra SRC in 1998. I had six schools under my jurisdiction: St. John’s Grammar, Achimota School, PRESEC, WASS, GHANATA, and Osu Doku Senior High School.

Even as a young student leader, I was sleeping in a kiosk at Kotobabi, Accra, opposite the Police Station.

Despite those challenges, I remained prepared to learn, serve, and make a difference.

Then came my angel.

I was adopted by the Village of Hope Orphanage, which took me off the streets, gave me a home, paid my accumulated school fees at St. John’s Grammar and supported me through the University of Ghana. I made sure to take full advantage of the opportunity I had been given.

After the University of Ghana 🇬🇭, I did my National Service at the Orphanage in Gomoa Fetteh. It was there that I met the man I affectionately call “Grandpa Don Barnett.” He was an Elder at the Oklahoma Church of Christ in Edmond, and he supported me through Law School until I was called to the Bar in 2010.

I can talk about several Judges and Senior Lawyers who became mentors and, in many ways, angels in my life.

When I first entered Parliament as an opposition MP, I saw and faced many difficult things. But I was blessed to have colleagues who supported me in my work, including Hon. Haruna Iddrisu, Hon. Muntaka Mubarak, Hon. Governs Kwame Agbodza, Hon. Ibrahim Jaja, Hon. Afenyo Markin, and Hon. Patrick Boamah.

In the 8th Parliament, despite the 137-137 situation between the two sides and one Independent Member, I introduced 19 Private Members’ Bills as a first-time MP. Three of these eventually became law, including the legislation that abolished the death penalty under Act 29.

Finally, I recall how the Right Honourable Speaker, Alban Sumana Kingsford Bagbin, took a personal interest in my work and supported me to succeed on many of these fronts.

Looking back, I can clearly see the hand of God through the many angels He placed on my path.

God will always put angels in our way when we genuinely desire to serve, grow, and make an impact on the lives of others.

But remember this:

Anytime you look around and do not find an angel, YOU MUST BECOME THE ANGEL TO OTHERS. 

Someone is waiting for the opportunity, encouragement, support, mentorship, or helping hand that only you can provide.

Be prepared.
Be available.
Be someone's angel.

KEEP MOVING FORWARD. 🙏🏾🇬🇭

Trump vows legal order to break up 'nasty monopoly' in food processing

U.S. President ​Donald Trump on Friday said he was preparing a legal order to allow farmers and ranchers to be given the right to ‌process their own food aimed at breaking what he called "a nasty monopoly" among the nation's top processors.

Trump did not name a particular food or industry in his post on Truth Social but said he was "authorizing legal documents to be drawn" quickly.

Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins posted on X that there would be "big announcements" related to beef processing beginning on Monday, including expanding ranchers' ​ability to sell across state lines, added support for smaller meat processors and rescinding "outdated guidance."

Earlier this week, Trump said on the Glenn Beck program ​that he would look into whether there are too many beef processing plant regulations.

Beck, who owns a ranch, suggested to Trump ⁠that Department of Agriculture regulations were impeding ranchers from processing their own animals, leaving them to rely on the nation's highly consolidated meat processing industry.

Four companies ​control about 85% of U.S. meat processing: Cargill [RIC:RIC:CARG.UL]; Tyson Foods (TSN.N), opens new tab, JBS USA [RIC:RIC:JBS.UL] and National Beef Packing Co [RIC:RIC:NBEEF.UL].

The companies did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

White House spokeswoman ​Anna Kelly said, "The administration is drafting several policy actions to further support those who feed the world."

Trump's move comes as consumers continue to face rising grocery prices ahead of November's midterm election.

CONSOLIDATION FIGHT
Meat is inspected by the USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service, which posts inspectors at meat processing plants to ensure products meet federal standards. Ranchers are generally prohibited by federal food ​safety laws from selling meat from animals they have slaughtered and processed themselves, with some exceptions.

Farm and ranch groups have argued for years that consolidation in the ​meat processing sector has made it difficult for small producers to stay afloat because there are not many companies competing to buy their cattle and they must transport their animals ‌to USDA-inspected ⁠meat processing plants, sometimes at a high cost.

The Meat Institute, which represents meatpacking companies, said food safety could be at risk if more ranchers process their own meat.

"Allowing uninspected meat to be sold to unwitting consumers is the wrong approach, and risks undermining this country’s reputation for producing the safest meat products in the world," the group said. “If the goal is to lower beef prices for American families, lowering food safety standards is the wrong response."

The National Cattlemen’s Beef Association, which represents ​ranchers, said it supports creating more ​opportunities for small beef processors and ⁠eliminating unnecessary regulations but warned Trump against weakening meat inspection standards.

David Anderson, agricultural economist at Texas A&M University, said that he did not think that Trump's plan would have a significant impact on competition in the beef industry.

"The numbers on that ​would be so small," he said of on-farm slaughter. "That really doesn't change the bigger broader market at all."

The administration ​of former President Joe ⁠Biden attempted to tackle consolidation in meatpacking in part through rules to promote competition and fairer pay for chicken farmers, which the Trump administration has indicated it will rescind.

Both the Biden and Trump administrations have steered funds towards supporting smaller meat processors, in an attempt to offer more options to ranchers.

Trump's move comes as the nation's meat processing sector ⁠grapples with ​a 75-year trough in supply as rising cattle costs outpace gains from soaring prices.

Trump also announced ​last week that more ground beef could be imported into the United States without tariffs. The Justice Department has also said it is investigating whether meatpacking companies were illegally driving up consumer beef prices.

Pope Leo XIV[a] (born Robert Francis Prevost,[b] pronounced /ˈpriːvoʊst/ PREE-vohst;[3][c] September 14, 1955) is the head of the Catholic Church and sovereign of Vatican City.

Born in Chicago in the United States, Prevost became a friar in the Order of Saint Augustine in 1977 and was ordained as a priest in 1982. He earned a Doctor of Canon Law (JCD) degree in 1987 from the Pontifical University of St. Thomas Aquinas in Rome. His service includes extensive missionary work in Peru in the 1980s and 1990s, during which he worked as a parish pastor, diocesan official, seminary teacher, and administrator. Elected prior general of the Order of Saint Augustine, he was based in Rome from 2001 to 2013, and traveled extensively as part of this work, including to the order's many provinces and missions around the world. He then returned to Peru as Bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, and became a Peruvian citizen. In 2023, Pope Francis appointed him prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops in Rome, and president of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America. Upon his return to Rome, Prevost was made a cardinal.

As a cardinal, Prevost emphasized synodality, missionary dialogue, and engagement with social and technological challenges. He has also addressed issues such as climate change, international migration, church governance, and human rights. Prevost's election in the 2025 conclave was unexpected by observers; he was a dark horse candidate, with Vatican insiders believing the prospect of a pope from the United States to be unrealistic given its status as a superpower. He is the first pope to have been born in the United States, and the first to be a citizen of Peru. He is also the first pope from the Order of Saint Augustine. Following the precedent of Pope Leo XIII, who developed modern Catholic social teaching amid the tumult of the Second Industrial Revolution, Prevost chose the papal name Leo XIV—both to echo Leo XIII's concern for workers and fairness, and as a response to the challenges of a new industrial revolution and artificial intelligence.

As pope, Leo has consistently opposed armed conflict and nationalism while advocating for the rights of immigrants. He has introduced new warnings about the use of artificial intelligence technology. Leo has affirmed the teachings of his predecessors, including social teachings and the climate policy of Pope Francis. He has consistently pointed to the teachings of the Second Vatican Council as the "guiding star" of the church. In 2026, he confronted the second Écône consecrations, which resulted in renewed excommunications and schism with the Society of St. Pius X.

Credit from @beingliberal  -  Dolly Parton: A Shot in the Arm for Public Health
Dolly Parton did more than receive the Moderna COVID-19 vaccine in 2021—she helped make its development possible. Her $1 million donation to Vanderbilt University Medical Center supported research that contributed to the vaccine’s development, turning her generosity into a lasting contribution to public health.

When Parton eventually received her vaccination, she used the moment to encourage others to follow her example.
“I’m old enough to get it, and I’m smart enough to get it,” she said. “I’m dead serious about the vaccine. I think we all want to get back to normal, whatever that is—and that would be a great shot in the arm, wouldn’t it?”

True to her personality, Parton delivered the message with humor and music, adapting the refrain of her classic song “Jolene” into a playful vaccination appeal:
“Vaccine, vaccine, vaccine, vaccine. I’m begging of you, please don’t hesitate.”

Her decision was especially notable because she had previously said she did not want to be vaccinated ahead of other Americans simply because she had donated money to the research. “I don’t want it to look like I’m jumping the line just because I donated money,” she told the Associated Press.
Parton’s example combined philanthropy, humility and public advocacy. She helped fund research, waited her turn and then used her enormous public platform to promote vaccination—an unusually effective form of civic leadership during a public-health crisis.

Her vaccination also came as President Joe Biden said the United States would have enough coronavirus vaccine doses for every adult by the end of May, two months earlier than previously expected. Against that backdrop, Parton’s 2021 message offered a simple appeal: trust the science, get vaccinated and help the country move forward.  -  https://t.co/b5l5O9fCTD

    This ruling reaffirms a fundamental American principle that the government cannot deport people simply because it dislikes their political views. Students do not surrender their constitutional rights at the classroom door, and international students do not surrender their freedom of expression when they come to study in the United States. Criticizing the policies of a foreign government, including the genocidal government of Israel, is protected political speech.

The lawsuit was brought by the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE) in August 2025 on behalf of The Stanford Daily, Stanford University’s student newspaper, and an anonymous female plaintiff. The newspaper argued that student reporters on visas refrained from covering pro-Palestinian protests on campus out of fear of being deported, while the Jane Doe was a noncitizen who had spoken out on behalf of Palestine and now was worried about government retaliation.

“The reporters in our newsroom shouldn’t have to fear that writing a story will result in their deportation. Today’s victory means they won’t have to,” the paper’s editor-in-chief George Porteous wrote on social media on Friday.

In particular, the lawsuit challenged two provisions of the Immigration and Nationality Act that Secretary of State Marco Rubio used to justify seeking the deportations of Khalil, Columbia student Moshen Mahdawi, and Tufts University student Rümeysa Öztürk. The first allows the secretary of state to deport a noncitizen for speech if the secretary “personally determines” the speech “compromises a compelling foreign policy interest.” The second allows the secretary to revoke visas entirely at their own discretion.

FIRE said the decision was the “first in the country to squarely rule on the constitutionality of these statutes” and that it would “reverberate in similar proceedings around the country.”

“In America, free speech doesn’t just belong to the people who say things the government agrees with,” FIRE attorney Conor Fitzpatrick said in a statement Friday. “Today’s ruling proves that free speech isn’t a privilege, but the inalienable right of every man, woman, and child.”

text:
Dear Professor 

The Illusion of Conventional Pomp and the Necessity of Strategic Hardness for the Netherlands
​Contemporary Dutch defense debates are dominated by a costly and fundamental misconception. While The Hague pours billions of euros into building up conventional armed forces—training extra military personnel and procuring heavy hardware—it completely ignores the naked reality of modern power politics. In a world where nuclear weapons are the ultimate geopolitical instrument, expanding traditional armies changes nothing whatsoever about the security balance for a country like the Netherlands. It is time for the Netherlands to drop the fantasy world of outdated alliances and conventional saber-rattling and face hard facts.
​The Powerlessness of the Dutch Conventional Mass
​Anyone who objectively studies strategic relations understands that classical ground warfare loses its decisive significance the moment the nuclear threshold comes into view. A large-scale conflict between nuclear superpowers will never limit itself to a conventional exchange of infantry and armored divisions. For the Netherlands, with its open geography and densely populated territory, additional tanks or brigades are nothing more than stage props in an advanced diversionary maneuver on a strategic level.
​The current focus on massive conventional build-up primarily serves a political purpose: acting as a symbolic "tripwire" in the hope that allies will feel morally obligated to intervene. But that brings the Netherlands directly to the next fatal weakness of the current system: the absolute unreliability of the foreign umbrella.
​The Bankruptcy of Allied Security for the Netherlands
​The idea that a friendly power would risk its own capital and population to defend the Netherlands is a dangerous illusion. The laws of sovereign power politics dictate that in times of existential crisis, a country always chooses self-preservation. The notion that France or the United Kingdom would launch a strategic nuclear retaliation—risking complete obliteration by Russia—for the security of The Hague is completely unrealistic.
​When push comes to shove, an ally will guard its own borders and leave the Netherlands out in the cold. Any Dutch state that outsources its ultimate security to good intentions or the political whims of Washington, Paris, or London will find itself defenseless and abandoned at the decisive moment. Article provisions and mutual assistance treaties turn out to be merely fragile pieces of paper in times of need.
​Towards a Realistic Reassessment of Dutch Security
​The conclusion flowing from this is as clear as it is controversial for the established political order in The Hague: true security cannot be leased for the Netherlands, nor can it be obtained through borrowed guarantees. As long as the country wishes to survive on the edge of the blade in a fundamentally unpredictable world, it will have to keep control of the ultimate deterrence entirely in its own hands. Dependence on foreign nuclear weapons—whether it concerns US storage on Volkel or the theoretical protection of other European powers—is synonymous with total strategic vulnerability for the Netherlands.
​Openly breaking through decades-old dogmas regarding non-proliferation and blind trust in NATO meets with diplomatic resistance and political discomfort in the House of Representatives. Yet the core of this analysis cuts right through all bureaucratic caution. Whoever in the Netherlands realizes that traditional military build-up stands powerless on a strategic level against nuclear powers must dare to recognize that the current course offers false security. True autonomy requires a radical break with yesterday's illusions and a sober, uncompromising focus on self-reliance for the Dutch nation.

When governments—past and present—have nothing meaningful to offer, people naturally start looking for alternatives. The problem is that many people aren’t educated about the consequences of those alternatives. Socialism becomes attractive when the existing system repeatedly fails people: “Everything will be free!” sounds wonderful when you’re drowning in debt and losing faith in your government. But there is no such thing as free. Somebody always pays for it, and eventually that bill comes due.

Democrats understand the frustration and are playing the political game to win elections—and frankly, they might succeed. Americans are drowning in personal debt, the country itself is drowning in debt, we’re spending enormous amounts of money and attention on conflicts overseas, and millions of people feel like nobody in Washington is actually fighting for them. So when somebody comes along promising a completely different system, of course people are willing to experiment. When the status quo looks terrible, almost anything new can sound great.

Maybe one positive consequence of all this will be the emergence of a real third party. I would love to see conservatives return to old-school capitalist principles while separating themselves from the Republican Party as we currently know it. Democrats are already experiencing their own political realignment, and, as usual, they seem much less afraid than Republicans to blow up their old establishment when they think it isn’t working.

I don’t have much faith in our current version of democracy, and God forbid we ever embrace socialism or communism. But maybe this political earthquake teaches people a few things: nothing is actually free; the era of politicians staying in power until they practically die in office needs to end; and Americans should demand that their government put American interests first. And if voters on both the left and right are increasingly rejecting AIPAC’s influence over American politics, then maybe we’ll finally have a serious conversation about how much influence any foreign country or foreign-policy lobby should have over our government.

Something has to replace the political system people are losing faith in. I just hope what replaces it is more freedom, accountability and genuine competition—not another ideology selling “free” solutions with a very expensive price tag.

text:
Ummm…calm down…I have to admit, I’m enjoying watching some of my friends suddenly discover their deep, almost sacred reverence for historic names now that Donald Trump has renamed Lake Ontario “Lake America.”

Where was this passionate defense of tradition when we spent the last decade playing cultural Mad Libs with names?

The Cleveland Indians became the Guardians.

The Washington Redskins became the Commanders.

Aunt Jemima was evicted from the breakfast table and replaced by Pearl Milling Company.

Uncle Ben got demoted to Ben’s Original.

The Native American woman disappeared from Land O’Lakes butter.

Eskimo Pie became Edy’s Pie.

The Dixie Chicks became The Chicks.

Lady Antebellum became Lady A.

Universities and real-estate professionals started replacing “master bedroom” with “primary bedroom.”

Computer programmers began retiring “master/slave” terminology.

Schools, streets, statues and buildings bearing the names of historical figures were renamed by the hundreds.

Then there were the military bases.

Fort Bragg became Fort Liberty.

Fort Hood became Fort Cavazos.

Fort Benning became Fort Moore.

Fort Polk became Fort Johnson.

Fort Lee became Fort Gregg-Adams.

Fort Gordon became Fort Eisenhower.

Fort Rucker became Fort Novosel.

Fort Pickett became Fort Barfoot.

Fort A.P. Hill became Fort Walker.

We even watched Mount McKinley become Denali.

Meanwhile, our vocabulary got its own remodeling job. “Mothers” sometimes became birthing people, “pregnant women” became pregnant people, and “breastfeeding” acquired the alternative chestfeeding in some institutional language.

And Columbus Day? Plenty of cities, states and institutions decided Indigenous Peoples’ Day was preferable.

For years the message was: Names matter. Words matter. Language evolves. Old names can be changed when society decides another name better reflects its values. If you're offended by the change, get over it.

Okay.

Apparently there was an asterisk:

This principle remains valid until Donald Trump names something.

Suddenly the people who spent a decade redecorating the dictionary have chained themselves to the furniture.

Personally, I think Lake America is mostly political theater, and pretty funny political theater at that. Canada is perfectly free to keep calling it Lake Ontario. Nobody is confiscating their maps.

But after watching everything from pancake syrup to Army installations get renamed in the name of cultural sensitivity, I simply cannot work up the appropriate level of outrage over a lake.

So to my friends who are losing sleep over Lake America, I offer the same compassionate advice conservatives received during the Great Renaming:

Language changes. Names evolve. Try to keep up. 😎

text:
No. It is not "the fault" of French or Quebec.  
The failure of the trade negotiations at the end of August 2026 between Canada and the United States is multifactorial. Language and culture were a sticking point, but not the only one, and both sides tell different versions.

What Ottawa says.  
Mark Carney explained that he ended the talks because the United States had "asked too much" and offered too little, with last-minute changes. He explicitly cited, among the red lines, "the protection of the French language and our culture." In Quebec, Christine Fréchette supported this: identity and language are not negotiable.

The points raised by the Americans included:  
bilingual / French labelling (Bill 96 and display rules);  
the "discoverability" of French-language content on streaming platforms (Netflix, etc.);  
the financial contribution obligations of American broadcasters to Canadian/Quebec content.

For Canada, these are fundamental rights, not "trade irritants" that can be conceded.  
What the United States says.  
Jamieson Greer (Trade Representative) and Donald Trump denied that French was a red line. Greer said that discoverability had been "emphasised" but that it was "the last thing" that would have derailed a good agreement.

Trump called Carney's assertion a lie and stated that he likes French Canadians. American officials also suggested that Carney had politicised the issue with elections approaching (federal by-elections and Quebec election in October).

Other heavy topics weighed in: heavy trucks and the auto sector, tariff levels, supply management (milk, important in Quebec), American alcohol, and the overall reliability of the agreement after last-minute back-and-forths.

In summary.  
French did not "derail" the deal on its own. It is a recurring trade irritant for Washington (labeling costs, content rules), but Ottawa and Quebec consider it non-negotiable. Blaming "the French and Quebec" ignores the other concessions demanded, the tariffs already imposed, and the fact that Canada chose to protect linguistic and cultural policies rather than accept what it deemed a bad deal.

The two accounts are not fully reconcilable based on public statements. The negotiations simply revealed that priorities were not aligned.

🇷🇺🇪🇪🇱🇹🇱🇻⚡ Russia may be considering one of the most dangerous gambles imaginable — a LIMITED attack on NATO followed by NUCLEAR BLACKMAIL.
The scenario now being discussed is terrifyingly simple.
Russian forces make a rapid incursion across the border and seize a relatively small piece of Estonia, Latvia or Lithuania.
Then Moscow stops.
And Putin tells NATO:
“We only took this territory. If you launch a major counterattack, Russia will use tactical nuclear weapons against NATO military targets in Europe.”
Then comes the REAL objective.
Negotiations.
The Kremlin could offer to withdraw from the captured NATO territory in exchange for enormous political concessions: recognition of Russia’s territorial conquests in Ukraine, an end to Western military assistance to Kyiv and the reduction or removal of NATO forces from the Baltic states.
The entire gamble would depend on ONE calculation:
That Washington, Berlin, Paris and London would be unwilling to risk nuclear war over “a few border villages.”
Basically — take a small piece of NATO territory, threaten nuclear escalation, frighten the West and then trade that territory for Ukraine.
There is no solid public evidence that such a detailed operational plan has actually been approved by the Russian General Staff.
But the threat of Russia attempting a limited operation against NATO is being taken seriously enough that CIA Director John Ratcliffe secretly flew to Moscow on August 25.
According to multiple reports citing people familiar with the mission, Ratcliffe warned Russia against attacking NATO — with particular concern about Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
The message was essentially impossible to misunderstand:
DO NOT TEST NATO.
The Kremlin confirmed Ratcliffe’s visit and his meetings with Russian intelligence officials, although Putin did not personally meet him.
Trump publicly downplayed the trip as “semi-routine” and later said he was not worried that Russia would attack NATO.
But you don’t secretly send the DIRECTOR OF THE CIA to Moscow because absolutely nothing is happening.
The last publicly known visit by a CIA director to Moscow before this one was William Burns in November 2021.
He went there to warn Putin about Ukraine.
Three months later, Russia invaded.
Maybe this time Moscow will listen.
Because attacking Ukraine was one thing.
Testing Article 5 of NATO is something completely different.
And one miscalculation could start the biggest war Europe has seen since 1945. 🇺🇦🇪🇺🇺🇸

🛏️ Makeshift apartment: Timothy Walters, 36, a longtime head custodian at Hackett Middle School in Albany, moved into a storage room on the fourth floor above the auditorium around October. He brought in beds, furniture and a mini-fridge, effectively turning the space into a studio apartment. 

👨‍👧‍👦 His children stayed there: Walters had custody of his four children on some weekends and acknowledged bringing them into the school after hours. He said the extra beds were partly needed for those visits. 

🎥 How he was caught: School officials discovered the arrangement in late April while reviewing security footage as part of a separate investigation into alleged fraudulent overtime claims by other custodial employees. The footage showed Walters apparently remaining in the building around the clock. 

💰 Financial hardship: Walters said he had been struggling with housing costs and child-support obligations. He had reportedly been earning about $80,000 including overtime in 2025, but said he still couldn't secure affordable housing. 

🚪 Suspension and resignation: The Albany City School District suspended Walters and considered terminating him. He ultimately resigned effective June 23 after 17 years working for the district. He was not accused of participating in the separate overtime fraud investigation. 

⚖️ Trespassing case dropped: Police initially investigated Walters for allegedly trespassing in the school, but the charges were later dropped. He has said he knew living there was wrong but felt he had few alternatives. 

🤝 Community support: Walters is currently staying with an uncle and reportedly has received two job offers. His sister also launched a GoFundMe campaign to help him secure housing.

It’s easy to get caught up measuring our lives by checklists, titles, and milestones. Pope Leo offered a profound reminder on identity and worth: our value doesn’t stem from our abilities, achievements, successes, or failures, nor from our wealth or status. We are solely a gift from God—first and foremost human beings, not human doings.

Holding onto that perspective makes the blessings and creative milestones feel all the sweeter, while keeping life grounded in what truly matters.

It's been seven years since I faced significant mental health challenges with bipolar disorder and made the decision to step away from traditional work. I have been in therapy every Saturday since December and have made amazing progress. Thanks to the steady grace and support of family and friends, I can honestly say I am doing better today than at any other point in my adult life. I share this because removing the lingering stigma around mental health matters deeply to me. If you are navigating a difficult season, reaching out for support isn't weakness—it's genuine courage.

Taking time to heal has made room for so much joy in everyday routines. Most days you’ll find me spinning additions to my growing vinyl collection, diving into Xbox and Switch 2 sessions, or pairing epic audiobooks with sci-fi art to finally conquer my reading backlog.

Creatively and fraternally, this past season has brought moments I could have only dreamed of:

Music Across the Globe: I partnered with Elastic Stage in London to bring nine Align Orion records to physical vinyl across 90+ countries. My digital music has also been streamed in over 147 countries.

Literary Milestones: Having my book, Moonlight Bridge, added to the historic library archive at the House of the Temple in Washington, D.C. is a dream come true. Moonlight Bridge also reached #35 in Spiritual Growth on the Kindle Store, and my ebook Portals debuted as a #1 new release in Philosophy.

Fraternal Fellowship: I am celebrating almost 12 years as a Master Mason, deepening my connection with the inspiring leadership across Wisconsin Freemasonry, and giving back to a community that continually lifts me up. I’m a significantly better man as a result of my time in Freemasonry and I’m determined to leave our phenomenal fraternity better than I found it.

Thank you to everyone who listens to the music, reads the books, and checks in along the way. I’m deeply grateful for where the path has led, and even more thankful for the community sharing the journey with me.
