text:
Here Is What The Covid "Measures" Cost Me 

In late October 2019, I published Chelsea’s New Beginning.

I found an illustrator who fit the series exactly as I had imagined it—most importantly, someone who gave Chelsea a face that will define her for years to come.

I chose the self-publishing route because if this book series was going to become my primary source of income, receiving most of the royalties was a no-brainer. What was even more important was keeping all the rights, so I would always have the final say over my project. With traditional publishing, you don’t get that. The publisher or agency takes most of the profit and the rights, and they can hand them off to whoever they want. That’s why so many authors hate film adaptations of their work.

I wasn’t going to go that route.

The downside, of course, is that you’re on your own when it comes to marketing—making sure people even know your book exists, let alone want to buy it.

The self-publishing package I purchased came with a “marketing kit,” and I didn’t realize until it was too late that it was completely insufficient. It was just bookmarks, postcards, and business cards.

Meanwhile, I was trying to do everything that actually matters, such as:

get press releases out

get my book into bookstores and libraries

read to children at schools and daycares

When I went back to the self-publishing company’s website to look for real marketing support, they did offer services—but all of them were far outside my budget.

And I desperately needed the services they offered if I was ever going to break free from spending all my time working just to survive… watching my life go by without me… instead of building the life I actually wanted—pursuing my passions and helping other people do the same.

But there was no way I could afford them with my current job situation.

At the time, I was working three jobs, and after paying bills, I always had barely anything left over.

At the same time, it was extremely important for me to get back into acting and singing—my original career path before college. But I still didn’t have the foundational training in place that would have made an impact on directors. I was already 30–31 years old. Most of my experience had been in high school shows, with only two community theater productions.

I couldn’t afford to audition.

I couldn’t afford to rehearse.

And working multiple jobs meant I was working evenings—exactly when most rehearsals take place.
I hadn’t been in a stage show since 2014.
And I wouldn’t be in one again until 2024.

And that gap wasn’t by choice.

All of that was already bad enough.

Because this wasn’t starting from zero.

I had already been held back for years—pulled into government assistance programs for disabled individuals that are actually wired to limit you instead of helping you grow.

At the same time, I was discouraged, belittled, and shamed for having dreams and ambitions by my own mother—who had no interest in helping me get to a place where I could fund those ambitions myself without sacrificing basic living expenses, and worse.

Starting in early 2020, the fear-driven media frenzy started spreading into my workplaces.

At first, I mentally brushed off the warnings about the coronavirus. I had heard the same kind of messaging before with things like bird flu and swine flu. People who practiced basic health hygiene were fine. To me, those events were nothing more than psyops, and I already believed the government was more than capable of manufacturing viruses and illnesses.

But I never expected what came next.

I never expected them to actually shut the country down and stop people from living their lives over this.

I was also isolated at the time.

I wasn’t connected to many like-minded people or local members of the health freedom movement. I had never been taught how to network, and I didn’t have the time or resources to build those connections. So I didn’t see this coming.

And when my workplaces started requiring masks, I was completely unprepared.

At that point, I needed the money.

I was already behind on debts I had taken on just to move out of my mother’s basement. I wasn’t educated or equipped enough to stand up for my rights. I didn’t have a circle of like-minded people to support me.

I wasn’t even at my baseline for survival.

So I wore the masks.

Not because I agreed with it.

Because I had to if I wanted to have my bills paid, food in my stomach, and gas in my car.

And the masks were hell.

I was breathing warm air back into my lungs all day. Human beings are built to breathe in cool, fresh air—not recycle what they just exhaled.

My managers and supervisors didn’t care what it was doing to me. If I took it off for even a moment, they would throw fits.

If I had already reached financial freedom—if I had been in a position of strength—I would have told those employers exactly where they could shove their masks.

I would have fought back.

I would have led charges for others to fight back.

Because I already knew there were major problems with the systems in place—systems designed to limit and harm people like me.

Years earlier, I had already made a promise to myself: if I ever had the resources, I would fight to dismantle those systems and push back against that kind of control.

And that was before this covid nonsense even started.

It was only going to get worse.

In May 2020, I was working two jobs—returning shopping carts at one, and working as a security officer at another.

I was outside returning carts and stepped inside briefly—nowhere near anyone—with my mask off.

I was sent home.

And later, I was fired.

Two months later, in mid-July 2020, it happened again.

I had my mask off while I was on break—again, nowhere near anyone.

More than 6 feet away from the nearest person.

An account manager walked in, saw me without it, and immediately threw a fit.

She followed me to my car and demanded my badge.

Around that time, my mother was in contact with a holistic doctor.

I went to that doctor, got examined, and obtained a note explaining why I should not be wearing a mask.

The security company had actually asked me to provide that documentation after the earlier incident.

I did what they asked.

But when I gave them the doctor’s note, they refused to honor it.

From childhood into my mid-20s, I was placed on Social Security income—with my mother as my payee receiving the funds herself.

That system was used as a weapon.

It kept me from building independence as efficiently, fully, and freely as I should have been able to.

In 2015—three years after I graduated college—Social Security told me there was an overpayment generated (despite me never receiving a cent of that money) and I had to cut my work hours if I wanted to keep receiving benefits.

At first, I complied.

Then, after several months, I rejected it.

Because I could see exactly what it was doing:

It was keeping me from living my life the way I was meant to.

My mother enabled that system.

Eventually, I was able to meet with a lawyer through Kansas Legal Services.

We spent months working through my overpayment case, and when it finally went before a judge in late 2018, it was dismissed with very little resistance.

Fast forward to mid-2020.

After losing two jobs over mask requirements, I was pushed back into the same system.

My mother urged me to reapply for Social Security disability benefits because I could no longer trust employers not to violate my rights or my bodily autonomy.

I should never have had to choose between breathing properly and earning a paycheck.

I was approved for disability benefits, with the difference now being that I was receiving the money myself this time.

But even then, nothing was straightforward.

When my mother and I asked how much I could earn monthly without losing benefits, the agent refused to give us a clear answer. We had to ask multiple times—four, if I remember correctly—before he finally mumbled:

“$2000.”

I was also approved for unemployment.

Shortly after that, I was hired at a dog daycare.

Before I was even hired, I told this new employer clearly:

I could not wear a mask for health-related reasons.

They said that was fine.

For about five months—from August 2020 to January 2021—I had both that job and disability benefits.

For the first four months, everything was fine.

No enforcement.

No pressure.

No issues.

Then it changed.

Management started making it a problem.
They refused to take my documentation seriously.

They tried to intimidate me into wearing a mask after I had already said no.
They rejected:

my doctor’s note

medical exemptions

religious exemptions
Everything.

Eventually, I was fired.

Over the phone.

The same week—

I lost my disability benefits.

Just like that, I had no income.

No way to pay for:

rent

my car

insurance

internet

phone

food

gas

Nothing.

I had already gone through a major low point in 2018.

Now, in the first half of 2021, I was pushed into another one.

After spending most of my adult life trying to get things on track by myself—trying to build a life I actually wanted—I was once again knocked back down.

Still missing opportunities.

Still unable to afford the training and resources I needed to move forward.

Still being forced to watch my life go by without me despite my efforts to turn things around.

I spent months fighting to get my disability back.

It had turned out that the amount was lower than what that agent had told both me and my mother.

And I wasn’t even close to making $2000 a month at the dog daycare job I had been working.

But with Social Security, there’s no accountability for mistakes they made. If they mess up, you pay the consequences. Not them.

Eventually, around June or July 2021, I was approved again for disability.

I was also approved again for unemployment—because it was proven that my employer knew about my medical situation before hiring me, and still fired me anyway despite the documentation I had provided.

Months later, the covid vaccine was rolled out.

I had predicted earlier that this was a setup for a new vaccine.

People were harmed by it.

Many have died.

There are documentaries covering this. There are alternative sources and public health freedom voices speaking out. There is footage of people collapsing after normal, everyday activity.

I was never given the opportunity to say no to the vaccine.

I was fired three times over the mask first.

But if I had been?

I would have been even stronger.

More forceful.

More ferocious in saying no.

Because my siblings and I were already damaged from childhood vaccines. Any vaccine at that point was a hell-no for me.

And through all of this, I’ve spent the last five years trying to build my platform and resources.

Trying to establish myself as a children’s book author.

Trying to raise awareness for my Chelsea series so I could fund future books and expand the message—especially tying it into autism.

I’ve had people who want to support me.

But most people in my corner can only support me in limited ways.
And the reality is:
A financial breakthrough—whether that’s upper five figures or six—would allow me to do far more. Not just for myself, but for others who are being harmed and don’t have the resources to fight back.

Because what I’m building now goes beyond Chelsea.

Nathan’s Universe is even bigger.

I’m trying to get my story, my cause, and my mission in front of the right people—the people who already care, who already understand, and who are ready to support something meaningful.
Because once I reach financial freedom, I won’t just be rebuilding my own life—

I’ll be in a position to actually push back.

To fight.

To make real progress for people who have been put in situations like mine.

And I plan to do this when they roll out the next scam-demic.

I know I’m not the only one this happened to.

Many people have experienced far worse than I have because of the covid tyranny.

And this is exactly why I’ve started building a space for people who have lived through this—to connect, to share, and to not feel like they’re the only ones.

This is part of a much bigger mission I’m building right now.

Because people should not have to go through this alone.

No one should ever have to choose between making a living and keeping their bodily autonomy—whether that means breathing fresh oxygen or having (unknown) toxic substances injected into their immune system.

If that’s something you want to be part of, you can find the link in the comments:

Show up in person with your passport, your birth certificate, and—if you changed your name—a third document to prove you didn't fake the first two. Election worker makes a mistake? 5 years in federal prison.
Who wrote it? Heritage Foundation and a Koch-funded think tank. Who funded the push? Elon Musk ($1M), Michael Flynn's PAC ($50K), and the same dark-money network that grades the senators who vote for it. Who gets paid? Document vendors, banks, and consultants.
Who pays—on every level:
• 21 million eligible citizens blocked from registering because they don't have a passport or birth certificate on hand
• Election workers facing felony charges for honest mistakes, in a job that's already hemorrhaging staff
• Taxpayers footing the bill for new verification infrastructure while the bill offers zero federal funding to help states
• Married women who changed their names—now need a third document to bridge the gap
• Small-dollar GOP donors sending $25 to "stop the steal" while billionaires collect the PAC money
The Heritage Foundation's own database found ~100 cases of non-citizen voting in 40+ years out of 1.3 billion votes cast. Kansas proved the model: 0.002% fraud, 12% of eligible citizens blocked.
This isn't election integrity. It's a poll tax with extra steps, written by billionaires, sold by grifters, and paid for by you—four times over.

text:
New York City's government grocery stores are a disaster waiting to happen

Government-run grocery stores claiming to offer a 30% discount below typical retail prices will lead to empty shelves and demands for more money to be spent on the self-inflicted problem.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has announced a city-owned grocery store program offering a "core basket" of essential items: fresh produce, meat, seafood, cheese, milk and bread. The plan is to sell the goods at 30% below typical retail prices, once a month, at five city-run locations.

Ezra Levant walked through the economics of the Democratic Socialist's plan on Tuesday's episode of The Ezra Levant Show.

The first problem is the math, given grocery store margins run at about 1-2% and meaning there is no 30% fat to cut.

"Why didn't the boys at Walmart think of that first?" Ezra asked. The answer is in Mamdani's own policy document, which Ezra read in full. The city will provide free real estate, cover rent and property taxes, fund the initial buildout, and then offer additional subsidies to push prices below cost.

"The taxpayer will fund the gap," Ezra said. "That's how you get 30% cheaper food. Someone else pays for it."

The second problem is a matter of basic economics.

Price, Ezra explained, is how markets ration scarce goods against unlimited demand. Remove the price signal and rationing happens another way — lineups, sellouts, insider skimming, and resellers.

He pointed to Boris Yeltsin's famous unscheduled stop at an American grocery store in 1989, where the sheer abundance and absence of lineups was a genuine shock to a man who had lived his entire life under Soviet central planning.

"He said even the Supreme Leader of the Soviet Union didn't have such variety and choice," Ezra said. "His aides later said it was the final light bulb moment where he abandoned Communism." That same grocery store model is what Mamdani is proposing to replace.

The third problem is precedent.

Ezra played footage from Kansas City, Missouri, where a city-subsidized grocery store — launched with similar promises and millions in public investment — was filmed last year with nearly empty shelves, a rotten smell at the entrance, and no hot food or deli.

"There was a time this store was on life support," a local community leader said in the footage. "I can tell you today it's damn near dead." The city's response was to say it would support "long-term viability based on normal revenues."

Ezra also pointed to the competitive damage the program will do to the thousands of independent bodegas — corner stores run largely by new immigrants — that make up much of New York's neighbourhood food retail. "The taxpaying bodega owner is financing his own competition," he remarked.

Mamdani's first store is not expected to open until late 2029. The announced capital cost is already $70 million — a figure Ezra said will inevitably double.

"Everything's going to be over budget," he said, and the results will be just as poor as the Kansas City grocery store.

"The shelves will be empty because they're being priced for political reasons, not economic ones. And of course, the answer will be we just need more money. More central planning."

Wishing the city's residents good luck in dealing with Mayor Mamdani's plan, Ezra said "New Yorkers are about to get a billion-dollar education in supply and demand."

"New Yorkers are about to get a billion-dollar education in supply and demand," Ezra said. "Good luck to you guys."

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

On this day in 1777, a 19-year-old French aristocrat named Marie-Joseph Paul Yves Roch Gilbert du Motier—better known as the Marquis de Lafayette—walked into the chambers of the Second Continental Congress in Philadelphia and changed the course of the American Revolution. Born into immense wealth and military tradition, Lafayette had already defied his king, his family, and the British navy to reach these shores. He had purchased his own ship, slipped out of France in disguise, and crossed the Atlantic at his own expense, driven by a burning belief in the American cause of liberty.

Congress was wary. Foreign officers had been flooding in, many seeking rank, glory, and pay. Lafayette was different. He asked for nothing in return—no salary, no pension, no guaranteed command. He simply offered his sword, his fortune, and his life. Moved by his zeal, his illustrious family connections in France, and the clear value of such a high-profile volunteer to the struggling young republic, Congress acted. On July 31 they commissioned him a major general in the Continental Army—without pay.

The rank was intended as largely honorary at first. Lafayette had almost no battlefield experience and spoke little English. But the young man refused to be a figurehead. Within days he met George Washington, and the two formed one of the most remarkable friendships in American history. Washington, childless and burdened by the weight of the war, found in the eager Frenchman something of a son. Lafayette soon proved himself under fire at Brandywine, where he was wounded while helping rally the American lines. He would go on to fight at Monmouth, lead troops in Virginia, and play a decisive role in the campaign that ended at Yorktown.

What began as a bold gesture by a teenage nobleman became one of the great partnerships of the Revolution. Lafayette’s arrival signaled to Europe that the American cause was worthy of serious attention. His later efforts in France helped secure the critical alliance and the ships and troops that made independence possible. He asked for no reward beyond the chance to fight for liberty—and in doing so, he earned a permanent place in the story of the United States.

A TYPICAL DAY FOR GHOST MITCH 

by Satire Lady

   Ghost Mitch reports for work every morning with his pockets stuffed with cash. He even has extra pockets on his favorite pair of footy pajamas, so there’s a lot of cash. He still isn’t entirely certain why.

  The first thing he does is turn the thermostat down to negative forty seven.  They can wear a sweater. 

He reaches into his pocket.
Pulls out a thick wad of bills.
He offers it to a Senate page.
The money vanishes before it reaches the kid’s hand. Ghost Mitch studies his empty fingers. Looks into the empty pocket.
Keeps walking.

    His ears peek up, hears Chick. “Chuck your stories are getting shorter,” he says, just to hear Chuck object. 

  After every filibuster Ghost Mitch hollered Attaboy! and made the lights flash, 

  A senator passes wearing a particularly nice watch.  Ghost Mitch reaches into another pocket.Another enormous wad of cash. He points at the watch. The senator never notices. Halfway through the offer…
The money quietly evaporates.

Ghost Mitch checks his own watch.
Moves on.

Someone says,
“Kentucky.”
Ghost Mitch briefly materializes.
Checks his watch. Wanders past gavel, replaces gavel with wooden spoon then he slides across the room on the soles of his footy pajama and drifts past Rand Paul’s office. The stapler is right where it belongs. Ghost Mitch puts the stapler in the trash can .

  Ted Cruz walks by and Ghost Mitch takes a moment to blow in his ear. Mr Cruz then suddenly pauses in the middle of a sentence.

He can’t explain why.  But it gave him the heebie jeebies. 

Ghost Mitch keeps floating.
Chuck Grassley is speaking.
Ghost Mitch quietly positions himself behind him.
Slowly.
Encouragingly.

“Keep going, son.”

Nobody sees the nod but Chuck smells aWarner  butter candy and a hint of Vicks 

Deceased Mitch floats again behind Rand who then absentmindedly smooths his hair.
He isn’t sure why.

Ghost Mitch continues down the hallway.
He reaches toward a Senate voting station.

Discovered unwritten rule, no pulse no in-person vote.  Electronic only for our deceased members,  Ghost Mitch looks at the machine for a moment.
Moves on.
By afternoon he’s carefully sneaking toward Rand Paul’s desk…

…as though invisibility wasn’t already enough.
A Capitol Police officer walks by.
Ghost Mitch instinctively ducks behind a marble column.

The officer keeps walking.

Ghost Mitch waits a few more seconds anyway.

Then he remembers.

He’s dead.

He quietly resumes sneaking. 👻

text:
Every scientist Bill Nye respected told him the same thing.

Do not do this. You cannot win a debate against someone who does not accept evidence as the basis for changing their mind. You will give them exactly what they want — a platform, a credential, the appearance of a genuine scientific controversy where none exists. Going will make things worse.

It was January 2014. Ken Ham, founder of the Creation Museum in Petersburg, Kentucky, had issued a public challenge. Ham's museum was a twenty-seven-million-dollar facility built on the premise that the Earth was created approximately six thousand years ago, that dinosaurs and humans had coexisted, and that the Grand Canyon had formed during Noah's flood. Ham wanted to debate whether creationism was a viable model of origins in the modern scientific era.

Nye understood the argument against going. He had heard it clearly and from people he trusted.

He also thought about the children attending that museum. He thought about the young people being taught that accepting evolution meant rejecting God, that choosing science meant abandoning faith, that geological evidence was a kind of conspiracy against believers. If he did not show up, those children would hear only one side of the conversation.

On February 4, 2014, Bill Nye walked into the Creation Museum in his trademark bow tie.

Nine hundred people filled the hall. Tickets had sold out in two minutes. Another 750,000 computers were logged into the livestream. Church groups gathered in fellowship halls across the country. Homeschool families sat around laptops. By conservative estimates, nearly three million people watched.

This was not a neutral venue. It was Ham's museum, Ham's audience, Ham's territory. Nye knew it and went anyway.

Ham spoke first, with confidence and warmth and the kind of absolute certainty that comes from a position that does not consider itself subject to revision. He showed slides of credentialed scientists who accepted creationism. He proposed a distinction between what he called observational science — things measurable in the present — and historical science — interpretations of the past. We can agree about the technology that put a rover on Mars, he said, but we can disagree about how Mars came to exist. He framed the debate as a matter of freedom, arguing that scientists who believed in creation were silenced and marginalized for their views.

Then Nye stood up.

He did not mock. He did not attack faith directly. He did not call anyone stupid.

He asked questions and presented observations.

He pointed to starlight. Billions of stars are more than six thousand light-years away. We can see them with telescopes, and their light has been traveling toward us for billions of years. If the universe is only six thousand years old, how do we account for light that has been in transit longer than the universe has existed?

He showed photographs of rock formations — layer upon layer of sediment turned to stone, uplifted, eroded away, then covered by new layers. He explained what geology tells us about how long these processes take and asked what would need to be true for hundreds of feet of solid rock to form, erode, and be redeposited in the span of a single year.

He talked about the fossil record — not simply that fossils exist, but the specific pattern of where they appear. Simple organisms in older rock, complex organisms in younger rock, consistently, across hundreds of millions of catalogued specimens worldwide.

"We have never found a single rabbit fossil in Precambrian rock," Nye said. "Not one. That is exactly what we would expect if species evolved over time. It would be impossible if all animals were created simultaneously."

Ham had answers ready for each of these — that God could have created light already in transit, that catastrophic flood conditions can accelerate geological processes, that radiocarbon dating is unreliable because we cannot verify that decay rates have been constant throughout history.

The most clarifying moment came during the question-and-answer period.

Someone in the audience asked both men the same question: what would change your mind?

Ham's answer was direct. Nothing. He was a Christian. The Bible was the word of God. That was his starting point and it would not change.

Nye's answer was equally direct. Evidence. Show him one verified example that contradicted the evolutionary model, and scientists worldwide would need to reconsider everything.

The audience did not boo. They did not leave. They listened.

Afterward, in interviews outside the hall, something emerged that was quieter and more significant than the debate itself. Young evangelical students described sitting between two worlds — raised in one framework, encountering another in classrooms and on science programs, told by their communities that accepting one meant rejecting the other. Several said the debate had not changed their beliefs but had given them something they had not quite had before: permission to hold questions without immediately resolving them into apostasy.

Nye's presence on that stage — calm, specific, willing to be the only scientist in a room full of people who disagreed with him — offered something to those young people that a refusal to show up could not have offered. It showed them that evidence-based inquiry and genuine respect for the people asking questions can exist in the same room at the same time.

The debate did not convert Ken Ham. His ministry continues. The museum still operates and draws visitors from across the country.

But the video of that evening has accumulated tens of millions of views in the decade since. It is shown in science classrooms. It has sparked conversations about whether faith and scientific inquiry must necessarily be enemies, or whether the framing that presents them as a binary choice is itself the problem.

Nye did not win by defeating his opponent. Ham's position remained unchanged at the end of the evening. What Nye did was show up in hostile territory and refuse to be anything other than precise, patient, and genuinely engaged with the people watching — including the ones who arrived certain they disagreed with everything he had to say.

Sometimes that is enough.

Somewhere, a teenager raised to believe that accepting evolution meant abandoning God watches Bill Nye calmly explain ice cores and starlight and the fossil record. And arrives at the quiet, private realization that perhaps the choice being presented to them is not the only one available.

That teenager did not appear in any headline. Their name will not be in any record. But they were in the room, or watching a screen, and something shifted.

That was the point of going.

Has there ever been a conversation you were advised not to have — that turned out to matter more than the people warning you away from it had understood?

He told his students to go to the windows.
Get out. Jump if you have to.
Then Liviu Librescu walked to the classroom door and pressed his body against it.
He was 76 years old. He weighed 140 lbs 
The gunman was in the hallway.
It was April 16, 2007. A Monday morning. Solid mechanics class at Virginia Tech, Room 204. Twenty-two students, most of them 19 or 20 years old.
At 9:45 AM, gunshots echoed through Norris Hall. Room by room, the shooter was working his way down the corridor.
Liviu heard it. He understood immediately.
He had survived the Holocaust. He had survived a labor camp. He had spent decades living under Communist oppression. He knew exactly what evil sounded like.
He told his students to escape through the windows. Second floor - it was a drop, but they'd survive. Then he walked to the door and held it shut with his body.
The shooter tried to force it open. It wouldn't move.
He fired through the door. Wood splintered. Bullets came through.
Liviu stayed.
Behind him, students were climbing out the windows. Dropping to the ground. Running. One by one, all twenty-two of them got out.
The shooter kept firing through the door.
Liviu held it shut until every student was safe.
Then the bullets killed him.
When police arrived, they found his body at the door.
All but one of his students survived. Not one was injured.
Liviu Librescu was born on August 18, 1930, in Ploiești, Romania.
He was Jewish. In 1941, when he was eleven years old, Romanian authorities sent him and his family to a labor camp. His father died there. Liviu survived. When the war ended, he was fifteen.
He went back to school. Studied engineering. Earned a doctorate from the University of Bucharest.
But Communist Romania had no interest in allowing a Jewish intellectual to succeed. He was blocked from academic positions. Passed over for jobs he deserved. He applied to emigrate. The government kept refusing.
Finally, in 1978 when Liviu was 48 years old Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin personally intervened. Romania let him go.
He had spent most of his adult life trapped in a country that didn't want him.
In Israel, he taught at Tel Aviv University. Published over 300 papers. Became an international expert in aeroelasticity - the science of how air flows over aircraft wings.
In 1985, Virginia Tech offered him a position. He moved to Blacksburg, Virginia. He taught there for 22 years. His students loved him - demanding but kind, high standards, genuine care.
He was still teaching full-time at 76. Still publishing research. Still showing up every Monday morning for solid mechanics.
April 16 was the first day of Passover - the Jewish holiday celebrating liberation from slavery and oppression.
Liviu Librescu died on the day his tradition sets aside to celebrate freedom.
He spent his entire life escaping death and oppression by luck, by persistence, by the intervention of others. And on his last morning, he chose to stand at a door so that twenty-two young people could have the future he had fought so hard to reach.
He could have run. He could have hidden. He could have climbed out a window with his students.
He chose to stay.
The Virginia Tech shooting killed 32 people that day - the deadliest school shooting in American history at the time.
Room 204 had zero casualties.
Because a 76-year-old Holocaust survivor held a door with his body until every student behind him was gone.
His funeral was held in Israel. Students from Virginia Tech flew across the ocean to honor him. The Israeli government awarded him the Star of David Medal posthumously. Virginia Tech named a scholarship in his memory.
His son said his father died the way he lived - protecting others.
A man who survived everything evil threw at him for 76 years.
On his last day, he made sure 22 kids survived too.
Professor Liviu Librescu.August 18, 1930 - April 16, 2007.
Holocaust survivor. Labor camp survivor.
302 published papers. 22 years at Virginia Tech.22 students out the window.
He held the door

text:
From my libertarian perspective, Elon Musk is one of the most important entrepreneurs of our time, but not someone I follow uncritically. I admire much of what he has achieved, while firmly disagreeing with some of his recent political choices.

I strongly support Musk’s relentless drive to challenge entrenched interests through innovation rather than bureaucracy. SpaceX demonstrated that private enterprise could outperform government monopolies in space. Tesla forced an entire automotive industry to innovate. Starlink has shown how decentralized private infrastructure can often deliver where governments fail. These successes reflect a core libertarian principle: free individuals operating in competitive markets solve problems more effectively than centralized planning.

I also share Musk’s commitment to free speech. Liberal democracies have increasingly embraced censorship through governments, regulators and digital platforms acting in concert. Defending the right to express unpopular opinions is essential to a free society. Freedom of speech exists precisely to protect dissent, not merely opinions that enjoy political approval.

I also strongly support initiatives such as DOGE and the use of artificial intelligence to reduce the size and cost of government. AI offers an unprecedented opportunity to detect fraud, expose corruption, eliminate duplicate payments, audit procurement, identify waste and make public spending transparent. The objective should never be to create more surveillance of citizens, but more accountability of governments. If technology can help dismantle bloated bureaucracies while strengthening due process and individual rights, libertarians should embrace it enthusiastically.

Where I part company with Musk is his growing support for anti free market nationalist and ethno-populist movements in parts of Europe. Libertarianism begins with the individual, not the nation, ethnicity or collective identity. People should be judged by their actions, their character and their respect for the rights of others, never by immutable characteristics such as race, ancestry, religion or country of birth. The moment politics starts dividing people into competing tribes, liberty gives way to collectivism.

I am equally sceptical of protectionism and economic nationalism. Free trade has lifted billions out of poverty, increased prosperity and reduced conflict between nations. Closing markets, favouring domestic industries through political power or treating peaceful immigrants as collective threats undermines the very openness that made free societies successful.

Ultimately, my admiration for Elon Musk lies in his entrepreneurial courage, his willingness to challenge bureaucratic orthodoxy and his defence of open debate. My disagreement lies in my firm belief that liberty is universal. It cannot be reserved for particular nations, cultures or ethnic groups. 

A genuinely free society protects every peaceful individual equally, relies on voluntary cooperation instead of political tribalism and measures people by what they do, not by who they are. That remains the essence of the libertarian tradition.

text:
V interesting post which distinguishes 
There are those who view their investments as art and those who view their investments as inventory!

In the context of managing money under a formal mandate, this distinction becomes far more practical than philosophical.

When your job is to consistently deliver returns and alpha for unit holders - the mindset has to tilt towards inventory management. In Indian MF industry this becomes relevant as consistency is the mandate. Investors redeem on underperformance, distributors move assets, and as fund manager you don’t have liberty for “waiting for the story to play out.” The product has to work across cycles with acceptable tracking error, liquidity, and risk parameters. That reality forces objectivity. Saying this from personal experience

The art-collector approach searches for exceptional businesses, develops deep conviction, and is prepared to hold through long periods of underperformance if the thesis remains intact. There is genuine beauty in that method when it works. But it sits uncomfortably with the requirements of most equity mandates in India — particularly diversified products where the expectation is relatively consistent relative performance rather than occasional spectacular absolute returns followed by long droughts.

The inventory approach treats every position as capital temporarily deployed to generate excess return. Positions exist to contribute to the portfolio’s expected risk-adjusted return. When that contribution declines relative to available alternatives, the capital is reallocated. Holding period is a function of edge and opportunity cost, not affection for the business.

Neither approach is pure. Most of us operate somewhere in between. But when consistency of alpha delivery is the explicit job description, the inventory lens becomes more useful than the art-collector lens.

A supermarket manager does not fall in love with any particular SKU. He constantly evaluates margin, velocity, space utilisation and customer demand. Capital in a mutual fund portfolio is the same scarce resource. Every rupee allocated to one name is a rupee not available for another. At every rebalance the question is simple: does this name still offer a better expected contribution after costs, liquidity and risk than the next best available alternative?

This does not mean one abandons fundamental analysis. Far from it. Solid process-driven portfolio construction still requires understanding of business quality, competitive position, earnings power and valuation. The difference is that these inputs are used to estimate expected return and risk rather than to form emotional attachment. Once the expected edge is quantified (even if imperfectly), the position becomes inventory to be managed rather than a painting to be admired.

The psychological difficulty remains real. We are trained to say “I believe in this company.” Under a mandate the more useful statement is closer to “this security currently offers a higher expected risk-adjusted return than the alternatives available to me after realistic implementation costs.” The second formulation is colder, but it is also more aligned with the job of delivering consistent alpha.

Objectivity of this kind sits comfortably within a solid fundamental and process-driven approach. It does not require abandoning bottom-up research. It simply requires that the research feed a disciplined capital-allocation process rather than an emotional ownership process. Defective inventory is still rejected. The process remains selective. It is simply selective on expected contribution to the portfolio rather than on. The objective is not to love the merchandise. It is to maximise the return generated by every unit of capital allocated to that shelf, rebalance after rebalance, while staying inside the risk and liquidity boundaries of the product.

The art is still in the process. The inventory management is how the process stays honest with the mandate.

text:
Euzebe Virdine is photographed here moments before his execution on August 8, 1924. Convicted of multiple murders in Louisiana, his final request was to have his photograph taken on the gallows.

Virdine was a farm laborer from St. Landry Parish who was convicted of murdering several people during robberies in the early 1920s. Nicknamed the "axe murderer" by newspapers, he was sentenced to death by hanging after being found guilty.

Just before his execution in Opelousas, Louisiana, Virdine made an unusual request: he asked for a photograph to be taken with the noose already around his neck. Officials granted the request, creating one of the most haunting execution photographs in American history.

By the 1920s, public executions had largely ended in the United States, but executions were still witnessed by officials, journalists, and invited spectators. Images like this are exceptionally rare and offer a stark glimpse into how capital punishment was carried out a century ago.

Louisiana used hanging as its primary method of execution until 1941, when it adopted the electric chair. The state's final execution by hanging took place that same year, ending a practice that had been used for generations.

text:
August 1, September 24 Nuestra Señora de las Mercedes (Our Lady of Mercy), Barcelona, Spain.
1214 - 1218
.
The Blessed Virgin appeared to Saint Peter Nolasco, to his confessor, Raymund of Pennafort, and to King James of Aragon, and through these three men established a work of the redemption of captives. She desired the establishment of the Mercedarian religious order. (derives from the Spanish word for mercy - merced) Its members would seek to free Christian captives and offer themselves, if necessary, as an exchange.
.
Timeline
.
1189
.
Saint Peter Nolasco is born at Mas-des-Saintes-Puelles, near Castelnaudary, Languedoc, France.
.
1214
.
At the age of twenty-five he took a vow of chastity and signed over his vast estates to the Church.
.
August 1, 1218
.
The Blessed Virgin appeared to Saint Peter, to his confessor, Raymund of Pennafort, and to the king, and through these three men established a work of the redemption of captives. She desired the establishment of the Mercedarian religious order. (derives from the Spanish word for mercy - merced) Its members would seek to free Christian captives and offer themselves, if necessary, as an exchange. The complete name of this order is: Order of the Blessed Virgin Mary for the Ransom of Captives (OdeM).
.
August 10, 1218
.
The king went to the cathedral for a Mass celebrated by the bishop of Barcelona. Saint Raymund went up into the pulpit and narrated his vision. The king sought the blessing of the bishop for the plan, and the bishop bestowed the habit on Saint Peter and two others, who vowed to give themselves as a hostage if necessary.
.
Jan 17, 1235
.
The Order was legally constituted at Barcelona by King James of Aragon was established in Spain and later approved by Gregory IX under the name of Our Lady of Mercy. St. Peter was the first superior, with the title of Commander-General; he also filled the office of Ransomer, a title given to the monk sent into the lands subject to the Moors to arrange for the ransom of prisoners.
.
1249
.
St. Peter resigned his superiorship; he was succeeded by Guillaume Le Bas.
.
Dec 25, 1258
.
St. Peter dies.
.
April 4, 1615
.
A feast day was instituted and observed on September 24th, first in the Mercedarian Order, then everywhere in Spain and France.
.
Sept 30, 1628
.
Pope Urban VIII canonized St. Peter Nolasco
.
1687
.
A plague of locusts was banished from Barcelona through the intercession of the Virgin of Mercy, and the miracle has been celebrated ever since – with Barcelona's biggest and noisiest of festivals.
.
Feb 22, 1696
.
The feast day (Sept 24) was finally extended to the entire Church by Innocent XII.
.
1730
.
Our Lady of Ransom was proclaimed "Patroness of the Peruvian Lands" and in 1823 "Patroness of the Armies of the Republic."
.
Sept 24, 1921
.
On the first centennial of the nation's independence, the image was solemnly crowned and received the title of "Grand Marshall of Peru" on the Feast of Our Lady of Mercy, since then declared a national holiday, when every year the army renders homage to her high military rank.
.
The name for the Marian commemoration on September 24 was changed to 'Our Lady of Mercy' after Vatican II.
.
In early August of 1218, St. Peter Nolasco, St. Raymund of Penafort, and James, King of Aragon, each had a vision of the Virgin Mary asking them to found a religious order devoted to freeing Christian captives from the Muslims, who still held much of Spain. The Order of the Blessed Virgin Mary of Mercy grew quickly, collecting alms for ransom and sometimes offering themselves in exchange for prisoners. The statue of the Mother of God of Mercy in Barcelona (right) dates from the 1300s. She became the city's patron saint after saving it from a plague of locusts in 1687. Before the counter-reformation, the Mercedarian Order celebrated the feast of Our Lady of Ransom on August 1, the date when she showed St. Peter Nolasco their white habit. The Vatican changed the date to September 24 when it extended the feast to the entire Church in 1696. Since Vatican II, Catholic observance of Our Lady of Mercy's day is limited to places and organizations that claim her as patron. Meanwhile, the Mercedarians have changed their mission to teaching and chaplaincy, and the Barcelona soccer team visits the Basilica of La Mercè after victories in thanks for her help. Her fiesta in Barcelona is a spectacular sequence of processions, dances, music, games, and fireworks. (Information from "Festa de la Mare de Déu de la Mercè," Arquebisbat de Barcelona,
.
Description
.
She is dressed all in white: over her long tunic she wears a scapular with the shield of the order imprinted breast high. A cloak covers her shoulders and her long hair is veiled by a fine lace mantilla. Some images have her standing, with the child in her arms, or carrying two bags of coins for use in ransoming Christians imprisoned by Moors. In yet others he is shown with her arms extended showing a royal scepter in her right hand and in the left some open chains, a symbol of liberation.
.
Approval
.
No formal investigation was performed by the Church to confirm this apparition. The Order of Mercedarians was approved by Gregory IX under the name of Our Lady of Mercy. A feast day was instituted and observed on September 24th, first in this Order of Our Lady, then everywhere in Spain and France. It was finally extended to the entire Church by Innocent XII.

text:
Deeply saddened and angered by the direction of the Church of England under Archbishop of Canterbury Sarah Mullally. She is committing much-needed Church funds,£100 million, to Africa under the banner of slavery “reparations,” even though no living member of the Church bears any responsibility for the transatlantic slave trade. Current parishioners and clergy are not the perpetrators of historical sins committed centuries ago.
British Christians and religious figures were among the first and most determined abolitionists. Figures driven by their faith helped end the trade and free the enslaved. To now treat the Church as if it must perpetually atone by transferring scarce resources ignores that proud record of moral leadership.
This is destroying the Church from within. How can ordinary people be expected to keep donating when money is being given away wholesale like this? Many congregations are already struggling to maintain buildings, pay clergy, and support local ministry. If this continues, the Church of England itself may not survive in any recognisable form.
Why is the institution centring woke causes and pandering to Marxist-derived theories such as critical race theory and gender ideology, instead of centring the Gospel, the person of Jesus Christ, and the historic faith? The Church’s mission is Christianity—not the latest progressive political fashions. As the late Anne Widdecombe once observed of the Church of England, “For years I’ve been disillusioned by the Church of England compromising on everything.” She left because it was following society rather than leading it—and that same pattern of institutional self-flagellation, of teaching us to be ashamed of our heritage, continues today.
It is heartbreaking to watch yet another once-proud British institution being hollowed out and undermined at the very time when Christianity is desperately needed to fill the spiritual and moral void in our society. We need hope, not endless atonement and division. King Charles, as Supreme Governor of the Church of England, has done little to restore faith in it, despite the clear need for a confident, Christ-centred Church that can offer genuine hope to the nation in these uncertain times.

text:
Timeline Cleanse

M1 Carbine

The M1 Carbine is a lightweight, semi-automatic carbine developed for the U.S. military during World War II. It was designed as a compact, easy-to-carry weapon for support troops, officers, and specialists who needed more firepower than a pistol but didn’t require a full-sized battle rifle like the M1 Garand.

In the late 19330’s, the U.S. Army sought a lighter alternative to the heavier M1 Garand for rear-echelon troops, artillery crews, vehicle operators, and others who found the full sized rifle cumbersome. 

Winchester developed the design with contributions related to David Marshall “Carbine” Williams’ short-stroke gas piston concept.

Production ran primarily from 1942 to 1945, with over 6.1 million units made during WWII—more than any other U.S. small arm of the war.

Key Specifications
•  Cartridge: .30 Carbine (7.62×33mm)
•  Action: Gas-operated, short-stroke piston, rotating bolt
•  Weight: About 5.2 lb (2.4 kg) unloaded; roughly 5.8 lb loaded with sling
•  Overall length: 35.6 inches (900 mm)
•  Barrel length: 17.75–18 inches (451–457 mm)
•  Magazine: Detachable box (standard 15-round; later 30-round)
•  Muzzle velocity: Approximately 1,990 fps with a 110-grain bullet
•  Muzzle energy: Around 960–970 ft-lbs (about the same energy at 100 yards as the muzzle energy of a .357 Magnum).
•  Effective range: Generally considered 200–300 yards
•  Rate of fire: 60–70 aimed rounds per minute (semi-auto)
The .30 Carbine sits between typical pistol and full-power rifle cartridges in power. It offers more energy and range than handgun rounds (significantly outperforming 9mm or .45 ACP from a carbine-length barrel).

Major Variants
•  M1: Standard fixed-stock semi-automatic version (by far the most common).
•  M1A1: Paratrooper model with a folding wire stock and leather cheek pad (produced only by Inland).
•  M2: Selective-fire (semi/full-auto) version introduced later in the war and used more in Korea; cyclic rate around 650–750 rpm.
•  M3: Infrared night-vision equipped variant (limited numbers, based on the M2).

Ten primary contractors built them during WWII. Inland Division of General Motors was by far the largest (over 2.6 million). Others included Winchester, Underwood, Saginaw (GM), National Postal Meter, Quality Hardware, IBM, Standard Products, Irwin-Pedersen, and Rock-Ola. Parts were designed to be interchangeable, and many carbines were later arsenal-refurbished with mixed parts.

Widely issued in WWII across all theaters. It saw extensive use in Korea and limited use in Vietnam (especially by South Vietnamese forces and some U.S. units early on). It was also supplied to allies and used by police/military forces postwar. Many were sold as surplus on the civilian market - especially through the Civilian Marksmenship Program (CMP).

Today, a serviceable M1 Carbine can sell for $1800.00 on up. Original NOS magazines, which used to sell 3/$5.00 now sell for $50 a $70 each. While original partially heat treated contract magazines are considered reliable for self defense (replacing the spring is recommended after 70’years of storage) aftermarket magazines are not. KCI (South Korea) are considered the most reliable after market magazines, especially in 30 round configurations.

Barrel wear on an original M1 Carbine is typically minimal unless abused. New springs are typically recommended. These rifles run cleaner than gas impingement (AR) designs and are much easier to clean after a range day. 

Soft point ammo is reliable in original equipment and is an excellent choice for home defense.

These rifles are low recoil, accurate, light and generally a pleasure to shoot.

text:
Fix It Friday: Prior Authorization Next Steps

There is momentum in Congress right now for Medicare Advantage prior authorization reform. The House Ways and Means Committee advanced H.R. 3514, the Improving Seniors' Timely Access to Care Act, on July 15 with a substitute amendment, alongside its Senate companion, S.1816, from Senators Warner and Marshall. The bill would require Medicare Advantage plans to build electronic prior authorization systems, meet real-time decision standards for routinely approved services, and publicly report denial rates and processing times. It is worth noting that a version of this bill has been introduced in nearly every Congress since 2019 with broad bipartisan support and still has not reached the President's desk, so no independent physician should treat its passage as settled.

Whether this particular bill becomes the vehicle or not, the standard it should be measured against already exists and CMS built it. WISeR bars its contractors from writing new coverage criteria and ties every determination to existing statutory and regulatory coverage policy. It guarantees a real peer-to-peer review with a clinician on every denial. And as of July 6, it now includes a gold-card exemption for physicians with a 90 percent affirmation rate. Medicare Advantage plans have never been required to do any of that.

Physicians should be telling CMS and their members of Congress, through whatever legislation is moving, comment letters on Medicare Advantage rulemaking, or direct advocacy, that this is the floor: coverage criteria tied to existing National and Local Coverage Determinations rather than proprietary standards, a genuine same-specialty peer-to-peer review before any denial is finalized, and a gold-card pathway for physicians with demonstrated track records. CMS proved this is operationally possible in six states in six months. There is no remaining excuse for Medicare Advantage plans to offer physicians less.

Separately, Congress should let WISeR's own FY2027 funding stand rather than adopt the House Appropriations rider blocking it. The physicians operating under this model today have more real protections than they have ever had under Medicare Advantage. The fix is not to tear that down. It is to make every plan build the same thing.

text:
#OnThisDay in 1986 Roller Blade macaroni slid into video stores. During the second Dark Ages of the near future where everyone wears inline skates, Doctor Sacticoy and the Samurai Devils need a magic crystal to take over what's left of the world, and only Mother Speed and the Bod Sisters of The Cosmic Order of Roller Blade stand in their way. Normally these horribly habited nuns spend their time healing others with their mystical switch blades, but when a threat arises, they strip to their skivvies and use their knives for less charitable purposes. With the time for charity passed, Sister Sharon Cross, with some timely help from lawmen Marshall Goodman and the Roller Patrol, leads her order to battle. This direct-to-video cheapie is in no way as enjoyable as director Donald G. Jackson’s other post-apocalyptic opus, Hell Comes to Frogtown, but it's got… something. Maybe it's the world he builds which, like Surf Nazis Must Die, is bizarre and stupid, but somehow still feels real.

Is it just me, or do you also get the feeling The Cosmic Order of Roller Blade is not officially sanctioned by the Church? I mean, the Church doesn’t micromanage every religious order, nor should it, but the Catechism does have a few things to say regarding nuns and sisters in general. “Religious life derives from the mystery of the Church. It is a gift she has received from her Lord, a gift she offers as a stable way of life to the faithful called by God to profess the counsels. Thus, the Church can both show forth Christ and acknowledge herself to be the Savior's bride… Religious life in its various forms is called to signify the very charity of God in the language of our time.” Now, this all gets expressed in any number of ways by the various religious orders out there, but I'm willing to bet that none of the officially approved orders are running around in thongs and knifing people. Not yet, anyway.

text:
Who is Callum Marshall?

🇬🇧 Name: Callum Marshall
🎂 Age: 21 (Born 28 November 2004)
📍 Position: Centre-Forward (can also play as a winger)
🦶 Preferred foot: Left 

Callum Marshall is a Northern Ireland international striker known for his intelligent movement, work rate and finishing. He made his name in West Ham's academy before gaining senior experience in England and Germany. 

Career path

🟦 Bangor Rangers (Youth)

Marshall began playing football with Bangor Rangers before moving to one of Northern Ireland's biggest academies. 

🟢 Glentoran Academy

He continued his development at Glentoran, where his goalscoring ability attracted interest from rival clubs. 

🔵 Linfield Academy & First Team (–2022)

Marshall joined Linfield's academy and made his senior debut at just 16. He scored on his first senior start in the Northern Ireland Football League Cup before earning a move to England. 

⚒️ West Ham United (2022–2026)

West Ham signed him in January 2022. Marshall became one of the standout players in the academy, helping the Hammers win the 2023 FA Youth Cup and the U18 Premier League South. He also made three competitive first-team appearances. 

🟡⚪ West Bromwich Albion (Loan, 2024)

His first senior loan in England was short, with limited opportunities before returning to West Ham.

Under a mile of Antarctica’s ice there is a landscape frozen in time….

Deep beneath the East Antarctic ice sheet, scientists have uncovered a vast, ancient landscape the size of Maryland that has remained untouched for 34 million years.

In a remarkable discovery within the Wilkes Land region, researchers have used satellite observations and ice-penetrating radar to map a hidden prehistoric world buried under more than a mile of ice. This 12,000-square-mile terrain features massive highland blocks and valleys nearly 4,000 feet deep, carved by ancient rivers long before the continent froze over. Scientists believe this region once enjoyed a much warmer climate, likely supporting lush forests and diverse life forms before it was sealed away from sunlight tens of millions of years ago.

What makes this find particularly significant is its pristine condition. While most glaciers erode the land beneath them as they shift, the ice in this specific area has remained exceptionally cold and slow-moving, preserving the landscape as a geological time capsule. This stability provides a rare opportunity for future exploration; researchers are now planning to drill through the ice to collect ancient soil samples. These organic materials could offer critical clues about Earth’s past climate and the historical formation of the Antarctic ice sheet, revealing secrets hidden in a world we are only beginning to understand.

source: Jamieson, S. S. R., Ross, N., Paxman, G. J. G., et al. (2023). A preserved fluvial landscape beneath the East Antarctic Ice Sheet. Nature Communications.

Did you actually read the bill yourself? Why do you ask questions like that without sharing the pros and cons? Or in this case, just a con.  Do you work for the people, or the lobby and the donors like the rest of them? 
Let's talk about what the SAVE America Act actually does, who built it, and who cashes the checks.
THE FINE PRINT:
To register to vote in a federal election, you would need to hand over documentary proof of U.S. citizenship in person. A passport works. So does a military ID with your service record. A Real ID works—but only if your state bothered to mark citizenship on it, and only five states do that. A driver's license? Only if you also bring your birth certificate. Changed your name after marriage? Your birth certificate won't match your license, so you need a third document to bridge the gap. Tens of millions of married women just got added to the paperwork maze.
Want to register by mail? Banned. Online? Banned. Same-day registration at the polls? Banned unless you have a passport or birth certificate in your pocket that day. States must also purge their voter rolls using federal databases that the Social Security Administration admits are outdated "snapshots in time."
THE TRAP FOR ELECTION WORKERS:
If an official registers a voter without the exact right stack of papers—even if the voter is a citizen, even if it was an honest mistake—that official faces up to five years in federal prison. The bill also lets any private citizen sue election officials for not complying. States are already bleeding election workers. This turns the job into a felony risk.
THE PRICE TAG:
The Senate version offers zero federal dollars to help states build this new verification system. The House's scaled-back version dangles $10 billion in incentives—nearly double everything Congress has spent on election administration since 2002 combined.
THE AUTHORS:
This isn't grassroots legislation. The policy framework was drafted by the Heritage Foundation and the Texas Public Policy Foundation—a dark-money think tank that took $5 million from the Charles Koch Foundation and $7.4 million from Stand Together Trust. Heritage Action, the political arm, then made the SAVE Act a key vote on its congressional scorecard. They write the bill. They grade the vote. They keep the senators in line.
THE PROFITEERS:
• Document-verification vendors—the bill creates a federal mandate for ID-authentication software and poll-book systems.
• Banks and financial institutions—the bill requires "documentary proof" that banks are positioned to certify. Senators who chair Finance and Banking committees (Crapo, Paul) oversee the industries that would handle that certification.
• Dark-money shops—Heritage, TPPF, Americans for Prosperity. They manufacture the crisis, sell the solution, and harvest the donations.
• PAC operators—Scott Presler's Early Vote Action raised nearly $3 million, mostly from Elon Musk ($1 million) and Michael Flynn's PAC. It went to fundraising firms and media consultants, not voter registration.
THE VICTIMS:
• 21 million eligible citizens who don't have a passport or birth certificate on hand—veterans, students, elderly, rural residents, people of color, married women. Confirmed by the Brennan Center, VoteRiders, and University of Maryland.
• Election workers—now facing felony charges for clerical errors.
• Taxpayers—states must pay for new infrastructure with no federal help.
• Small-dollar donors—sending $25 to "stop the steal" while billionaires collect the PAC money.
THE FUNDERS:
• Koch network: $12 million+ into TPPF and affiliated groups.
• Elon Musk: $1 million to Presler's panic-amplification PAC.
• Michael Flynn's PAC: $50,000 to Presler.
• Heritage Foundation / Heritage Action: The bill's architect and the scorecard enforcer.
• Americans for Prosperity: Koch's street-level activation arm.

text:
Years ago I went to an adult summer camp. It was in late August of 2016 and it was hosted by this indie music blog that was quite popular within the Brooklyn scene.

At the time, my brother was living in this unbelievable Loft in Greenpoint and was hosting SoFar Sounds  concerts regularly, which were extremely popular.

The guy throwing the summer camp festival invited me because he wanted a connection at my brother’s place- I guess he wanted to host his own concert there or something. So he gave me two discounted tickets to this long weekend in Western Massachusetts.

It was the summer I was 25 years old and I was dating a girl out of my league. I was constantly spending more on her than I should have been and by the end of the summer she was expecting a vacation. I had just started my business and was barely making ends meet, but I knew if I wanted to keep her around I was going to have to come up with something.

Now I had the perfect thing to offer; adult summer camp. Surprisingly, she was pleased with this.

I explained to her what it was and she was excited about the whole thing, but was not about to stay in a cabin with 10 other strangers. She said she would go if we could camp out in a tent instead of staying in the bunks.

I called the guy hosting the event and he said it wouldn’t be a problem.

I found an old tent in my parents attic and watched a few youtube videos on how to set it up.

We made the four drive to the festival, which was called Welcome Campers, and got there just as these busses filled with Brooklyn hipsters were showing up. It was like Indie music heaven. Free IPAs, tons of artisanal food trucks, angsty folk bands playing and a crowd that ranged from Reddit engineers to baristas.

We checked in, and when we were assigned a cabin  I told the lady that we had been granted the right to sleep in a tent. She shrugged and suggested we pitch the tent up on the soccer field.

So we did. I hauled the tent, our suitcases and sleeping bags up to the soccer field and set it up perfectly. I remember the look in my girls eyes. It was the first time I think I truly impressed her. I was imaging what she would look like in a wedding gown and for the first time that whole summer thought she actually might be the one.

We set our sleeping bags up and then went down to the water to partake in the festivities.

It was amazing. We lounged out on this large tube on the lake and listened to this indie band play through their set. At the end we were handed a tall can of craft beer and were meeting a bunch of friendly, cool people.

And then a voice came on the loud speaker…

“Will the couple who pitched their tent on the field please report to center campus.”

We looked at each other. Did we just hear what we think we did? But then it came again.

“Will the couple who pitched their tent on the field please report to center campus.”

So we went and met with a park ranger who was an older, overweight man with grey hair and a trucker hat and a bush of hair coming out of his ears.

He greeted me and asked if I was the young man with the tent on the soccer field. I told him that I was and he told me in a very matter of fact way that I was going to have to take it down.

I explained that I was given permission to have the tent by the guy throwing the festival and he once again told me that I was going to have to take the tent down.

I asked him why and he told me that there had been a bear sighting earlier and they couldn’t take any chances. He explained the liability and assured me that we wouldn’t want to be bear food.

I looked at my girl and saw all the excitement drained from her face. Every point that I had won with her was erased and I knew this was about to turn ugly.

“Hey man,” I said to the park Ranger, “Can I talk to you over there?” and pointed to a spot out of ears reach from the others.

Listen, I said, “We have to sleep in that tent tonight. What’s it gonna cost to keep it up?”

He asked if was bribing him. He said “I don’t care if you hand me all the money in the world. You’re not sleeping in that tent tonight.”

“Well then where are we going to sleep?”

“In the bunks, like everybody else.”

I looked at my girl, who was super skinny, like fashion model skinny, And beautiful in a kind of sickly way. Like an acquired taste. The definition of heroine chic. She looked way more appropriate on the streets of New York City. Up here in the country she looked kind of sickly and unnatural.

I looked the Park Ranger dead in the eyes and said “She can’t sleep in the bunks with everybody else?”

“Well why not?”

To this day I can’t believe that I said this. It was the worst possible excuse in the world... 

I told him to look at her. I said, “She has a disease. A wildly contagious disease. Trust me, it would not be good if she slept in a bunk with others. I don't know what would happen to the others campers but it would not be pretty." 

"She has a contagious disease?" The Ranger asked me. 

"Yes," I said.

"Well then can I ask you something...?"

"Go right ahead."

"What the hell are you doing sleeping with her?" 

Good question, I said and then told him that I had been vaccinated and was now immune to her illness. 

He shook his head and said "Well you're not sleeping in the bunks, I'll tell you that." 

To me, this read as victory. I went over to my girl, who was panicking and uneasy and assured that we were alright. We were going to sleep in that tent tonight.

"Really? What you say to him." 

"Let's just say I told him I wasn't taking no for an answer. My girl wants to sleep in a tent. My girl is going to sleep in a tent." 

She looked at me like I was her hero. All the excitement came back to her and a rush of happiness overwhelmed us both. We went up to the tent , right around dusk and were in the process of getting comfortable. 

I very rarely got laid in this relationship and it seemed like this was going to be a lucky night. Up until... 

Two golf carts rolled up to the tent. It was the park ranger with these women that had a type of hazmat plastic mask over their faces. 

They spoke through a megaphone and asked us to get out of the tent.

I got out and saw them and  knew immediately what was happening. 

"There she is, that's the one with the disease."  The park ranger said pointing to my girlfriend. 

My girl looked at me, confused as all hell. "What's happening?" 

"What disease do you have?" One of the ladies asked.

"What disease do I have?" 

And that's when I knew I had to come clean. 

"She doesn't have a disease!" I said.

"You said she has a disease." 

"I know. I was lying."

"What the fuck did you tell him?" My girl said. 

"I know. I said that she has a disease. It was a lie. I made it up. I said it so we could sleep in the tent." 

"You made up that I have a disease? What the fuck is wrong with you. Are you retarded?" 

She was turning blood mad. SO mad I had never seen her like this. The nurses and the ranger just kind of stopped and watched her lay into me. 

"Out of all the fucking things you could have told him. You told him I have a fucking disease. I can't fucking believe this." 

"Just to be clear ma'am, you don't have a disease?" 

"No." 

"Okay, we'll let you work this out."  They said, and drove the carts away. 

I was now alone with my girl again, and a moment of silence passed. I went to put my arm around her and she backed away. 

"Take me home." She said. And we began the four hour drive back to New York. In silence...

text:
People defend #LindsayClancy but stayed silent about #LatarshaSanders :

Latarsha Sanders was found guilty of first-degree murder (not NGRI) primarily because the jury rejected her insanity defense after key medical evidence of her severe mental illness was excluded from the trial, and the prosecution successfully framed her as “evil” and malingering rather than psychotic. ￼
In February 2018 in Brockton, Massachusetts, Sanders (then in her 40s) fatally stabbed her sons Marlon (Edson) Brito, 8, and La’son Brito, 5, dozens of times in what she later described to police in delusional terms involving “voodoo,” “rituals,” “the bad people,” and efforts to “fix them up” afterward. She had been exhibiting escalating paranoia, conspiracy theories (e.g., Illuminati), and erratic/aggressive behavior in the preceding days. She was later diagnosed with schizophrenia (paranoid type) or related psychotic disorders that clinicians said had gone largely untreated for decades; a prosecution-hired forensic psychologist also found schizophrenia symptoms and that it was “highly likely” she was symptomatic around the time of the killings (though the Commonwealth did not call that expert). ￼
Under Massachusetts law, a defendant is not criminally responsible (NGRI) if, due to mental disease or defect, they lacked substantial capacity to appreciate the wrongfulness of their conduct or to conform their conduct to the requirements of the law. The prosecution bears the burden of proving criminal responsibility beyond a reasonable doubt. A successful NGRI finding leads to commitment to a psychiatric facility (potentially long-term), not release. ￼
At her 2022 Plymouth Superior Court trial, the defense (attorney Elliot Levine) presented a clinical neuropsychologist (Thomas Deters) who concluded after extensive evaluation that Sanders was in a “very severe psychotic state” and not criminally responsible. The prosecution (Assistant DA Amanda Fowle, under DA Timothy J. Cruz) offered no competing mental-health expert. Instead, Fowle argued Sanders was “evil,” “selfish,” and “playing the crazy card”; pointed to her post-killing statements/blaming of others, partial cleanup, and behavior as evidence she knew what she was doing; and cited a 2016 notebook entry about writing a book and money as purported motive for fame/profit. Graphic crime-scene evidence was emphasized. ￼
Critically, the trial judge excluded substantial medical records (including prison and hospital diagnoses of schizophrenia-spectrum disorders, observations of hallucinations/paranoia, and treatment history) that the defense sought to introduce. Prosecutors successfully argued these were largely post-offense, involved hearsay, or were otherwise inadmissible/irrelevant. This left the jury without much of the documented clinical picture of her longstanding and acute illness. The jury deliberated roughly four hours and convicted her of two counts of first-degree murder (mandatory life without parole) plus witness intimidation. ￼
Sanders’ current attorney has appealed to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, arguing the exclusion of the medical evidence violated her right to present a complete defense and that prosecutorial tactics (including character attacks, mischaracterizations, and speculation such as a “Law & Order” influence theory not in evidence) constituted misconduct
