text:
The Leo Frank Trial: Mary Phagan Murdered Within Hour After Dinner

The Atlanta Constitution,

Saturday, 2nd August 1913,

PAGE 1, COLUMN 1.

DR. H. F. HARRIS GIVES STARTLING EVIDENCE ABOUT TIME OF MURDER

Wound on Eye of Girl Victim of Pencil Factory Crime
Looked as if It Came From Blow of Fist, Secretary of State Board of Health Tells the Jurymen.

WHILE ON THE STAND DR. HARRIS COLLAPSES FROM RECENT ILLNESS

Frequent Clashes Take Place During Testimony of N. V. Darley, Assistant Superintendent of National Pencil Factory, Over the Alleged Nervousness of Frank.

Within three-quarters of an hour after she had eaten her frugal breakfast of cabbage and bread, Mary Phagan was dead.

This startling fact was brought out at Friday's session of the Leo M. Frank trial, when Dr. Roy Harris, secretary of the state board of health, took the stand to tell of the post-mortem examination he performed on the body of the child.

The time of the murder has always been a mooted question. When Dr. Harris made his declaration and exhibited a small bottle containing particles of cabbage, which had been taken from the stomach and which had not had time to digest, a thrill went through the court room.

Crowd on the Qui Vive.

As soon as Dr. Harris entered the court room during the afternoon session, the crowd seemed to sense the dramatic situation which was to follow.

It was pretty generally known that Dr. Harris had made an examination, but the result of this examination was not known.

When he came into the room, carrying a small physician's satchel and looking slightly pale from a three days' illness, all eyes were turned toward him.

What would he testify to? This was the question each asked his neighbor.

Dr. Harris briefly told of his medical experience and then proceeded to explain the details of his examination of the dead girl's body.

Cabbage Found In Stomach.

He stated that he had found in the stomach of the girl particles of undigested cabbage and he exhibited a bottle containing them. He said in reply to a direct question that the condition of the cabbage showed she had met her death within a half to three-quarters of an hour after she had eaten this food. He also displayed a bottle of fluid taken an hour afterward from the stomach of a man who had eaten cabbage and bread. None of the cabbage was visible.

Dr. Harris was emphatic in his statement that Mary Phagan must have met her death from one-half to an hour after she had eaten.

He also described the wound on the dead girl's head, and said she must have been struck an upward blow. The blow on the eye, he said, looked as if it had been inflicted by a person's fist.

Commenting on the general condition of her body he said he could not tell whether she had been outraged, but there were evidences of violence indicating it.

Dr. Harris had been on the stand but a few moments when he was taken with a fainting spell and was compelled to leave the stand. The defense did not have an opportunity to cross-question him. In fact, Solicitor Dorsey had not finished the direct examination when he left the room. He will resume his testimony as soon as his physical condition will permit.

The state expressed satisfaction at the testimony of Dr. Harris, and Mr. Dorsey was particularly pleased. Speaking of the turn of affairs he said:

"It is perfectly plain sailing from now on. We have a mass of evidence and it is only a question of knitting it together"

Mrs. Coleman's Testimony.

As soon as Dr. Harris had made his startling statement in regard to the time of Mary Phagan's death, the minds of those in the court room reverted to the testimony of her mother, Mrs. J. W. Coleman, who, earlier in the week, had told of the little girl having eaten cabbage for breakfast the morning before she was killed.

Frequent Clashes Occur.

Frequent clashes took place between opposing counsel during the testimony of N. V. Darley, assistant superintendent of the National Pencil factory. The point at issue was the nervousness of Frank on the morning following the murder. Darley testified that Frank was very nervous. On cross-examination he said he had seen him equally as nervous on two other occasions.

During the introduction of the time slips as evidence, Frank appeared to lose the calm which has been his marked characteristic during the trial. In fact, the long hours in court seem to be telling on him.

Albert Mc Knight, husband of Minola Mc Knight, and who made a sensational affidavit and afterward retracted it, and who cooks for the Franks, testified that on the day of the murder he was in the Frank kitchen; that he saw Frank come in the dining room, but did not see him eat anything. He stated Frank spent several minutes in the room at the sideboard and then left the house, taking a car at Pulliam street and Georgia avenue.

Luther Rosser riddled Mc Knight's testimony and endeavored to show it was impossible for him to have seen from the kitchen into the dining room.

"What is your position with the company?"

"I am general superintendent and director of the company."

"How long have you held that position?"

"In Atlanta I have held that position since August 10, 1908. My place of business is at 37 to 41 South Forsyth street."

"About how many employees have you there?"

"About 107 in that plant?"

"Male or females?"

"Mixed. I guess there are a few more girls than boys."

"On Saturday, April 26, I will get you to state if that was a holiday with your company?"

"Yes, sir, it was a holiday. The factory was shut down."

Several People in Building.
"Who was in that building during the day?"

"Well, there were several people who come in during the morning."

"Was anyone in the office with you up to noon?"

"Yes, sir, the office boy and a stenographer."

"What time did they leave?"

"About 12 or a little after."

"Have you a day watchman there?"

"Yes, sir."

"Was he on duty at 12 o'clock?"

"No, sir, he left shortly before."

"Who came in after the stenographer and the office boy left?"

"This little girl, Mary Phagan, but at the time I didn't know that was her name. She came in between 12:05 and 12.10, maybe 12:07, to get her pay envelope, her salary."

Frank Pays Mary Phagan.

"You paid her?"

"Yes, sir, and she went out of the office."

"What office was you in at that time?"

"In the inner office at my desk, the furtherest office to the left from the main office."

"Could you see the direction she went in when she left?"

"No, sir, it was impossible."

"What was your impression?"

"My impression was she just walked away; I didn't pay any particular attention."

"Do you keep the door locked downstairs?"

"I didn't that morning, because the mail was coming in. I locked it at 1:10 when I went to dinner."

"Was anyone else in that building?"

"Yes, sir, Arthur White and Harry Denham. They were working on the machinery, doing repair work, working on the top floor of the building, which is the fourth floor, about the middle of the building, but a little more to the rear."

"What kind of work were they doing?"

"They were tightening up the belts; they are not machinists, one is a foreman in one department and the other is an assistant in another, and Denham was just assisting White, and Mrs. White, the wife of Arthur White, was also in the building. She left about 1 o'clock. I went up there and told them I was going to dinner, and they had to get out; and they said they had not finished, and I said 'How long will it take?' and they said until some time in the afternoon; and then I said, 'Mrs. White, you will have to go, for I am going to lock these boys in here.'"

Door Was Locked.

"Can anyone from the inside open those doors?"

"They can open the outside door, but not the inside door, which I locked."

"In going in the outside door, is there any way by which anyone could go in the basement from the front?"

"Yes, sir; through the trap-door."

"They would not necessarily have to go up the steps?"

"No, sir; they couldn't get up there if I was out."

"You locked the outer door?"

"What time did you get back?"

"At 3 o'clock, maybe two or three minutes before, and I went to the office and took off my coat and then went upstairs to tell those boys I was back; and I couldn't find them at first, they were back in the dipping room, in the rear, and I said, 'Are you ready?' and they said, 'We are just ready;' and I said, 'All right, ring out when you go down, to let me know when you go out;' and they rang out, and Arthur White come in the office and said, 'Mr. Frank, loan me $2.' and I said, 'What's the matter? We just paid off,' and he said, 'My wife robbed me,' and I gave him $2 and he walked away, and the two of them walked out."

Newt Lee Arrives.

"And you locked the doors behind them?"

"I locked the outer door, when I am in there, there is no need of locking the inner door. There was only one person I was looking for to come in, and that was the night-watchman."

"What time did he get there?"

"I saw him twenty minutes to 4."

"Had you previously arranged for him to get there?"

"Yes, sir. On Friday night I told him, after he got his money. I gave him the keys and I said, 'You had better come around early tomorrow, because I may go to the ball game;' and he came early because of that fact. I told him to be there by 4 o'clock, and he came twenty minutes to 4. I figured I would leave about 1, and would not come back; but it was so cold I didn't want to risk catching cold, and I came back to the factory as I usually do. He came in, and I said, 'Newt, you are early,' and he said, 'Yes, sir;' and he had a bag of bananas with him, and he offered me a banana; I didn't see them, but he offered me one, and I guess he had them. We have told him, once he gets in that building never to go out. I told him he could go out; he got there so early, and I was going to be there. He came back about four minutes to 6; the reason I know that, I was putting the clock slips in, and the clock was right in front of me. I said, 'I will be ready in a minute,' and he went downstairs, and I came to the office and put on my coat and hat and followed him and went out."

Saw Newt and Gantt Talking.
"Did you see anybody with him as you went out?"

"Yes, sir; talking to him was J. M. Gantt a man I had fired about two weeks previous."

"Did you have any talk with Gantt?"

"Newt told me he wanted to go up to get a pair of shoes he left while he was working there, and Gantt said to me, 'Newt don't want me to go up,' and he said, 'you can go with me, Mr. Frank,' and I said 'that's all right, go with him, Newt,' and I went on home, and I got home about 6:25."

"Is there anything else that happened that afternoon?"

"No, sir; that's all I know."

"You don't know what time Gantt come down after he went up?"

"Oh, no; I saw him go in and I locked the door after him, but I didn't try them."

"Did you ask Newt?"

"Yes, sir. I telephoned him. I tried to telephone him when I got home. He punches the clock at half hour intervals, and the clock and the phone is in the office, and didn't get an answer, and at 7 o'clock I called him and asked him if Gantt got his shoes, and he said yes he got them, and I said is everything all right, and he said yes, and the next thing I knew they called me at 7:30 the next morning."

Did Lee Let People In?

"Do you know whether your watchman, at any time, has been in the habit of letting people in there, any time?"

"No, sir."

"Have you ever heard of it?"

"No, sir."

"Did you ever have any trouble with any watchman about such as that?"

"No, sir."

"Do you know whether any of your employees go there at night?"

"Yes, sir. Gantt did when he was working there; he had a key and sometimes he would have some work left over. I never have seen him go out until I go out; I go out and come back, but he has come back before I left, but that is part of his duty."

"Did you take a bath yesterday or Saturday night?"

"Yes, sir Saturday night at home."

"Did you change your clothes?"

"Yes, sir."

"The clothes that you changed are at home?"

"Yes, sir; and this is the suit of clothes I was wearing Saturday. After I left the shop I went to Jacobs' Pharmacy and bought a box of candy for my wife, and got home about 6:25."

PAGE 1, COLUMN 3

Witnesses Called to Stand to Testify Against Frank
Photos by Francis E. Price. Staff Photographer.

From left to right: Mrs. George W. Jefferson, who was a witness on Thursday morning; R. P. Barrett, who testified to finding Mary Phagan's pay envelope and strands of her hair, and Mrs. Maggie White, who told of seeing strange negro in pencil factory on afternoon of crime.

PAGE 2, COLUMN 2

Frequent and Angry Clashes Between Attorneys Mark the Hearing of Darley's Testimony

N. V. Darley, mechanical head of the National Pencil factory and directly in charge of the Georgia Cedar company, an adjunct concern, was put on the stand by the state, after Mrs. White had finished.

"How long have you been with the company, and are you still employed there?" asked Solicitor Dorsey.

"I've been there about five years, and am still employed there."

"Who is your immediate superior?"

"I consider Sig Montag my immediate superior," he replied.

"What is your relation to Frank?"

"We are co-laborers, on an equal basis."

"With whom do you more often come into contact?"

"With Frank."

"Did you see Frank on Saturday, April 26?"

"Yes."

"What time did you leave the factory that morning?"

"About 9:40."

"When did you next see Frank?"

"About 8:20 Sunday morning, at the factory."

"Was Frank there when you got there?"

"No; he came up just as I got there."

"What were you doing there?"

"Mrs. Frank had called me up and told me all. Mr. Frank had asked her to tell me to go to the factory."

Rosser objected to the witness telling anything Mrs. Frank had told him, and, despite the solicitor's statement that it had already been proved that Frank had asked his wife to call up Darley, Judge Roan ruled out his statements about what the wife had said.

Noticed Frank's Nervousness.
"Did you notice Frank as you got there?"

"Yes."

"What did you observe about him?"

"Nothing at first."

"Well, what, if anything, later?"

"When we started to go to the basement I noticed his nervousness."

"Describe it."

"Well, he started to lower the elevator, and as he reached for the rope his hands trembled, and then when he started to nail up the back door of the basement later his hands trimbled again, and I took the hammer and nailed up the door myself."

"What, if anything, did Frank say to you?"

"When we started to nail up the back door he made some remark about his clothes, and pulled off his coat."

"Did he say anything about coffee?"

"Not then."

Why Frank Wanted Coffee.
"Well, what did he say at any time that morning about coffee?"

"At the station house he told me he had been rushed away from home without any breakfast and carried into a dark room, where they turned the light on and showed him the dead girl, and that he was nervous and wanted some coffee."

"What did he say breakfast would do for him?"

"He said breakfast would keep him from being nervous."

"Did he get any breakfast?"

"I don't know; I left him at 10 o'clock."

"Did you see Newt Lee at the time you saw Frank in the factory?"

"Yes."

"Was Lee nervous or composed?"

The solicitor fired the above question at the witness as though seeking to show the jury that the man he charged with being guilty was nervous when at the scene of the crime, and the innocent man was not.

"Lee seemed thoroughly composed," answered the witness.

"What was said in the basement?"

"Something was said about the staple and Frank said that it would have been easy for anyone to have pulled out the staple. The staple looked to me like it had been pulled out before," the witness said.

"Did Frank suggest that the murder had occurred in the basement?"

"Yes."

"Repeat his words."

"I can't repeat the exact words, but I know he suggested that."

"Did he say anything later about being nervous or not?"

"Monday afternoon he said that if he had had some breakfast that morning he would not have been so nervous."

"What brought up the talk?"

"I don't remember what or who brought it up."

"How often did Frank try to explain his nervousness?"

"Twice."

"On what subject did Frank seem to dwell the most, the murder or his nervousness?"

Rosser Offers Objection.

Rosser entered a strong objection to this question, claiming that the witness was not qualified to testify about it. Judge Roan ruled that it could not be asked in that form.

"Well how often did he talk about the murder?"

"On numerous occasions."

"How much of Frank's body was shaking?"

"His hands."

The solicitor then produced a former affidavit made by Darley, in which the man had said Frank was shaking all over.

After he had looked at it, Darley reiterated his statement that only Frank's hands were trembling.

"It's too much to say that a man's whole body is trembling; you can't well tell," he continued.

"When were his hands trembling?"

"As we started to go down the elevator to the basement he reached for the rope and both hands trembled," and here the witness held up both his own hands and shook them violently.

Two Members of Jury
Photo by Francis E. Price. Staff Photographer.

On the left F. V. L. Smith, and on the right Beder Townsend.

"Could Frank have nailed up the back door?"

"I think so."

"What did you swear about this in your affidavit?" asked the solicitor, but the witness held out that he thought Frank could have nailed the door.

"How did Frank look that Sunday morning?"

"Pale."

"Can you say or not if Frank was upset and why in either case?"

Rosser Takes Dig at Dorsey.

"The witness can't testify in regard to 'upset,'" roared Attorney Rosser; "if he'd been in the courtroom all the week, though, and had watched the solicitor he would know what the word means."

"I don't see why we can't use the good old Anglo-Saxon word, 'upset,' instead of having to use 'nervous,'" the solicitor objected, and after an argument the court ruled that "upset" was just as much allowable as the Latin derivative.

"Well, was Frank upset?" continued the solicitor.

"I can't say that he was."

"Look here at what you said in your affidavit!" yelled the solicitor, apparently thoroughly exasperated.

Attorney Rosser declared that the solicitor had no right to talk in such a manner as to indicate to the jury what the witness had said in a former affidavit which had not been placed in evidence and went on to say that Frank's actions on that morning had shown that he was not thoroughly upset. Before he and the solicitor finished arguing the affair had almost developed into regular argument as to whether or not Frank was upset, rather than in contesting about the witness using the word.

"Well, on that Sunday morning was Frank thoroughly done-up?" asked the solicitor, seemingly determined to get down to plain, old Anglo-Saxon in preference to the Latin derivative, "nervous."

"What in the world does 'done-up' mean?" objected Reuben Arnold, Mr. Rosser's partner in the case. "It may mean in bed, for all I know," he added.

The court, however, held that "done-up" might come into the case and take its stand by the side of "upset" and that it was for the jury to determine what was meant when a witness used either of the words.

Frank "Partially Done-up."

Darley then declared that Frank was "partially done-up" on that Sunday morning that the body was discovered.

"Give your reasons for saying he was partially done-up," said Mr. Dorsey.

"Well, he did some things that a man entirely unstrung could not have done," said Darley.

"Unstrung" was a new word and when it came into the trial spectators expected Attorney Rosser to ask for its credentials, but he let it in without a murmur.

"Did Frank sit steadily on your knees in the auto ride to the station?" asked the solicitor.

"No, he was trembling and shaking."

"Did you see Lee?"

"Yes."

"What was his demeanor?"

"He was composed."

Mr. Rosser objected to the question about Lee, and Dorsey withdrew it.

"Did you attend to any business Monday?" the solicitor then asked.

"Yes"

"Did you see the financial sheet Sunday?"

"Yes."

"Who called your attention to sheet No. 28?"

"Frank."

"What did he say?"

"He said something about it."

"What time was it?"

"Between 8:20 and 9:45."

"Did J. M. Gantt ever come to the factory after he was discharged?"

"Yes."

"Did you see Frank examine the financial sheet?"

"Yes, he handed it to me."

"When did Haas, the insurance agent, come to the plant?"

"On Monday or Tuesday in May."

"What was done after his visit?"

"The plant was cleaned up in a general way."

"Did you clean up the first floor?"

"Yes, it was cleaned on May 3."

Bludgeon Produced in Court.

Mr. Dorsey then asked the defense to produce the bludgeon which it is claimed was found later in May near the elevator. They produced it.

"Did you see this club found?" Mr. Dorsey asked, sending it clattering down on the floor between the witness and the jury box.

"No."

"Was the finding of the club subsequent to the cleaning up?"

"Yes."

"Did you see anything on the rear of the office floor near the ladies' dressing room Monday after the murder?"

"Yes, blood," replied the witness.

"Who called your attention to the blood?" asked Attorney Arnold.

"Barnett and Quinn."

Arnold Cross-Questions.

"How many strands of hair did Barrett show you?" asked Mr. Arnold, who here took up the cross-examination which before this Attorney Rosser had always conducted.

"When I first saw them they were wound around a lever, and there seemed to be six or eight in all," said the witness.

"Wasn't it difficult to tell their color?"

"Yes."

"Barrett did most of the discovering, didn't he?"

"Yes."

"Isn't he mono-maniac on the subject of the crime; buys all the papers and keeps constant watch on the case?"

"Barrett claims to have discovered the blood spots, doesn't he?"

Mr. Dorsey also got this question ruled out.

"When you first saw the blood spots, who pointed them out to you?"

"Quinn, Barrett and others."

"Were they hidden by white spots?"

"Partially; not completely."

"In other words, the man who attempted to hide the spots left the spots and the attempt to hide them revealed," said Mr. Arnold.

"It looked that way," replied the witness.

"Did Barrett tell you he was working for the rewards?"

Mr. Dorsey objected to this question, and was sustained by Judge Roan.

"Did you ever see any blood around Mary Phagan's machine?"

"No."

"Did you see Barrett find the pay envelope?"

"No. I was at the other plant."

"What did most of the employees do with their pay envelopes?"

"Tear them and take out the money."

"By looking at this envelope can you tell whether it ever had any money in it?"

"No, there are no indications by which one can tell."

"Don't you find such envelopes all over the factory?"

"Yes, even in the metal room."

"Liable to find them anywhere, aren't you?"

"Yes."

"Nothing more common than pay envelopes?"

"No."

"Were you present when Frank ran his finger down the time slip?"

"Yes."

Fails to Identify Time Slip.

Mr. Arnold then showed the witness the time slip which the defense claims is the one taken out of the clock that Sunday morning by Frank.

"Is this the one?" the attorney asked.

"I can't say that it is, they are all alike."

"Did you notice the absence of punches on it?"

"No."

At this juncture M. Johenning, one of the jurors, stated that he desired some information about these time slips, and he and the witness exam

FREQUENT CLASHES BETWEEN ATTORNEYS

Continued From Page Two.

🚨 RIPPLE IS QUIETLY BUILDING A FINANCIAL OPERATING SYSTEM FOR GOVERNMENTS AND BANKS

PAYMENTS. CUSTODY. STABLECOINS. TOKENIZATION.

BUT WHERE DOES XRP ACTUALLY FIT?
For years, Ripple was described mainly as a faster alternative for cross-border payments.

That description is now incomplete.

By August 2026, Ripple’s strategy has expanded across four critical layers:

▪️ Payments
▪️ Digital-asset custody
▪️ Stablecoin infrastructure
▪️ Tokenization
This is no longer a single-product story.
It is an attempt to connect legacy banking, regulated digital assets, public blockchains, and real-time settlement through one institutional technology stack.

🏦 1. CONNECTING BLOCKCHAIN TO CORE BANKING

In January 2026, DXC Technology announced that it would integrate Ripple’s custody and payments technology with its Hogan core-banking platform.

Hogan supports more than 300 million deposit accounts and approximately $5 trillion in deposits worldwide.

That does not mean $5 trillion has moved onto blockchain.

It means banks operating on this infrastructure may gain a pathway to offer programmable payments, tokenization, custody, and digital-asset transfers without replacing their mission-critical core systems.

That bridge between legacy banking and on-chain finance could be one of Ripple’s most important partnerships yet.

🌍 2. BANKS AND FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ARE BUILDING DIFFERENT PIECES

Ripple’s recent institutional expansion includes:

▪️ Kbank in South Korea deploying Ripple Custody wallet infrastructure for institutional digital assets.

▪️ Kyobo Life Insurance exploring near-real-time settlement of tokenized government bonds.

▪️ SBI Group officially launching RLUSD in Japan through SBI VC Trade in June 2026.

▪️ Convera combining its global FX and commercial-payment network with Ripple’s stablecoin settlement infrastructure.

▪️ Absa Bank introducing institutional digital-asset custody in South Africa—not ODL, as sometimes incorrectly reported.

▪️ AMINA Bank adopting Ripple Payments for near-real-time cross-border transactions.

▪️ Mastercard, WebBank, and Gemini exploring RLUSD settlement on the XRP Ledger for card-payment flows.

Each partnership addresses a different layer of the future financial system.

Some move value.
Some hold value.
Some tokenize value.
Some settle value.

🏛️ 3. GOVERNMENTS AND CENTRAL BANKS ARE TESTING THE TECHNOLOGY

Ripple has publicly announced or participated in digital-currency initiatives involving Georgia, Palau, Montenegro, Bhutan, Hong Kong, and Colombia.

The National Bank of Georgia selected Ripple as the technology partner for its Digital Lari pilot.

The Central Bank of Montenegro signed an agreement with Ripple to develop a digital-currency strategy and controlled pilot.

Palau tested a USD-backed government stablecoin on the XRP Ledger with government employees and selected merchants.

Ripple also participated in Hong Kong’s e-HKD pilot programme.

But these distinctions matter:

These are mostly pilots, research programmes, or controlled experiments—not nationwide CBDC deployments.

Ripple previously said it was discussing CBDC technology with more than 20 countries. That does not mean 20 central banks have launched currencies using Ripple.

⚡ 4. WHERE DOES XRP ACTUALLY FIT?

This is the question every XRP holder should ask.

Not every Ripple partnership uses XRP.

Ripple Custody can secure many different digital assets.

CBDC platforms may operate without XRP as a bridge asset.

RLUSD can settle transactions on XRPL without XRP being the principal transferred asset.

Every XRPL transaction uses a tiny amount of XRP as a network fee—but that is not the same as large-scale institutional demand for XRP liquidity.

The clearest confirmed institutional XRP use case remains cross-border liquidity.

SBI Remit has explicitly used XRP as a bridge currency for remittances from Japan to the Philippines, Vietnam, and Indonesia.

In that model:

Local currency enters.
XRP bridges the value.
Destination currency exits.

The transfer can settle without maintaining large pre-funded accounts in every destination market.

That is where XRP’s original design becomes economically meaningful.

💡 THE BIGGER PICTURE

Ripple does not appear to be forcing every partner to use XRP.

Instead, it is building an ecosystem in which banks and institutions can enter through custody, payments, stablecoins, wallets, or tokenization.

Once those rails exist, XRP becomes one available liquidity instrument within a much larger financial network.

That strategy may be slower than the hype cycle wants—but potentially more durable.

Payments move value.
Custody protects value.
Tokenization represents value.
Stablecoins stabilize value.
XRP can bridge value.

Ripple is assembling every layer.

The real XRP question is no longer:

“How many partnerships has Ripple announced?”

It is:

“How much real institutional liquidity will ultimately flow through XRP?”

Infrastructure creates possibility.

Usage creates demand.

Scale creates value.

text:
Mary Phagan Case the Southern Trial of the Century: You Are There

Leo Frank Juror’s Life One Grand, Sweet Song....Not

Atlanta Georgian

August 2nd, 1913

O. B. Keeler.

The juror's life is not unmixed with care.

Look him over next time you attend the Frank trial. Size up his little job. Weigh his responsibility. Consider his problems.

And then, if seeking employment, go out and sign a contract to make little ones out of big ones.

It's a more satisfactory way of earning $2 a day.

The juror's business is to collect evidence by the earful, sift the same, separate the true from the false, and make it into a verdict as between the Stat[e] of Georgia and Leo Frank.

On the face of it, the plan is beautifully simple.

But the beauty is only skin deep.

You are reckoning without the lawyers.

Here Entereth the Lawyer.

The simple-minded layman—and that rating includes the juror—starts out with the idea that the business of a lawyer is to extract evidence from the witness in available form for proper consideration by the juror.

It speedily develops that the full intent of counsel is to prevent the witness from unburdening himself in any way whatsoever. The more expensive the counsel, the less information the opposition will be able to wheedle out of its star performers.

The method of blocking is objective—that is, it is by means of objections. It appears that our system of jurisprudence takes cognizance of the juror as a mere babe in arms, not fit to assimilate the strong meat of evidence straight.

How the Juror Is Spared.

So he is sedulously raised on the bottle.

Mr. Dorsey (for example) has a witness by whom he is aching to show that Leo Frank was nervous the morning he was apprised of the tragedy. Mr. Rosser and Mr. Arnold are equally positive that the witness is not competent to judge if Mr. Frank was nervous. Also they are quite sure that the bottle-fed juror is utterly incapable of deciding if the witness is competent to decide if Mr. Frank was nervous.

They do not intend that the juror shall endanger his delicate thinking apparatus by grappling with any such abstruse problem.

So they fix it up this way.

Witness: "He insisted on having some coffee."

Mr. Rosser: "I object to the use of the word ‘insisted.' It manifestly is a conclusion of the witness, and as such has no place in the evidence. I ask that the word be ruled out."

Objections Fix the Fact.

And the court orders it ruled out, thereby fixing the circumstance firmly in the mind of the juror. And then Mr. Dorsey twists the query around and gets the witness to state that Frank asked for coffee twice at his house and once at the factory.

Just why that arrangement suits the defense bet[t]er than the simple proposition that Frank insisted on the coffee is not entirely plain—to the layman.

But it seems that the juror is to be shielded from any breath of anything not bearing strictly on the guilt or innocence of the accused.

Specific and accurate information being thus at a premium, the juror probably is amazed when Mr. Rosser, vibrating with grief and indignation, protects against Detective Scott reading from some notes he made while working directly on the case.

The court also is shocked, but permits Mr. Scott to "refresh his memory" by means of the notes and then retail the product of such refreshment by word of mouth.

This is agreeable to Mr. Rosser and the court, but when Mr. Dorsey offers further to refresh Mr. Scott's somewhat wilted recollection, Mr. Rosser intimates at the top of a robust voice that such a thing shall be accomplished only over his (Mr. Rosser's) inanimate form.

And that promptly affords the bottle-fed juror some more evidence to ponder.

Mr. Dorsey insists it is his right to "lead" the witness.

The witness demands to know if he is suspected of holding back.

Mr. Dorsey declares he has been trapped by the witness, and Mr. Rosser appends the somewhat doubtful comment that Frank Hooper is a wise man.

Here Are More Problems.

Now, add this to the problems of the troubled juror:

Is Mr. Scott balking?

If so, has Mr. Dorsey the right to hold an ear of corn in front of him?

Has Mr. Dorsey been trapped?

And, in view of the foregoing, is or it not Mr. Hooper a wise a man?

Other problems for the exercise of the Frank juror on the side, as it were, would include the following:

Should Mr. Dorsey be permitted to examine a witness without interruption by Mr. Rosser?

Should Mr. Rosser be permitted to object?

If so, should Mr. Dorsey scowl while Mr. Rosser is objecting?

Does Mr. Rosser consider whisky a good remedy for indigestion?

Would He Hide Evidence?

Would anybody think that Mr. Rosser would have anything to do with suppressing evidence, except in the regular and approved objective method prescribed by law?

Is Mr. Scott a trained sleuth?

And one more thing that tends to lend an acrobatic cast to the mental processes of the Frank juror.

Once in a while—not very often, it's true—but once in a while something gets by Mr. Rosser and Mr. Arnold. The witness may be quick on the trigger. Or Mr. Dorsey may manage to frog up a subtle query with a joker in it.

And after the storm of objection has thundered itself out and Mr. Rosser is mopping the sings of honest toil from his brow, and Mr. Dorsey is wearing an expression similar to that of a cat that knows all about what happened to the canary—why, then the court orders the stenographer to strike out the answer.

And the obliging juror is instructed to forget it.

Yes?

Would You Forget it, Too?

Just suppose that you, being an honest and hard-working juror, trying in an honest and hard-working way to extract a morsel of real information from a jungle of cross-questions and crabbed answers and objections and oratory and recrimination—suppose that the honest and hard-working witness should beat 'em to it for once, and disgorge something really interesting.

And then suppose the judge should tell you to wipe it right off your mental slate, and not remember it, or consider it, or thinks about it any more forever.

You would do it, would you not?

Neither would we.

The juror's life is not unmixed with care.

Specific and accurate information being thus at a premium, the juror probably is amazed when Mr. Rosser, vibrating with grief and indignation, protests against Detective Scott reading from some notes he made while working directly on the case.

The court also is shocked, but permits Mr. Scott to "refresh his memory" by means of the notes and then retail the product of such refreshment by word of mouth.

This is agreeable to Mr. Rosser and the court, but when Mr. Dorsey offers further to refresh Mr. Scott's somewhat wilted recollection, Mr. Rosser intimates at the top of a robust voice that such a thing shall be accomplished only over his (Mr. Rosser's) inanimate form.

And that promptly affords the bottle-fed juror some more evidence to ponder.

Mr. Dorsey insists it is his right to "lead" the witness.

The witness demands to know if he is suspected of holding back.

Mr. Dorsey declares he has been trapped by the witness, and Mr. Rosser appends the somewhat doubtful comment that Frank Hooper is a wise man.

Here Are More Problems.

Now, add this to the problems of the troubled juror:

Is Mr. Scott balking?

If so, has Mr. Dorsey the right to hold an ear of corn in front of him?

Has Mr. Dorsey been trapped?

And, in view of the foregoing, is or is it not Mr. Hooper a wise man?

Other problems for the exercise of the Frank juror on the side, as it were, would include the following:

Should Mr. Dorsey be permitted to examine a witness without interruption by Mr. Rosser?

Should Mr. Rosser be permitted to object?

If so, should Mr. Dorsey scowl while Mr. Rosser is objecting?

Does Mr. Rosser consider whisky a good remedy for indigestion?

Would He Hide Evidence?

Would anybody think that Mr. Rosser would have anything to do with suppressing evidence, except in the regular and approved objective method prescribed by law?

Is Mr. Scott a trained sleuth?

And one more thing that tends to lend an acrobatic cast to the mental processes of the Frank juror.

Once in a while not very often, it's true but once in a while something gets by Mr. Rosser and Mr. Arnold. The witness may be quick on the trigger. Or Mr. Dorsey may manage to frog up a subtle query with a joker in it.

And after the storm of objection has thundered itself out and Mr. Rosser is mopping the signs of honest toil from his brow, and Mr. Dorsey is wearing an expression similar to that of a cat that knows all about what happened to the canary why, then the court orders the stenographer to strike out the answer.

And the obliging juror is instructed to forget it.

Yes?

Would You Forget it, Too?

Just suppose that you, being an honest and hard-working juror, trying in an honest and hard-working way to extract a morsel of real information from a jungle of cross-questions and crabbed answers and objections and oratory and recrimination suppose that the honest and hard-working witness should beat 'em to it for once, and disgorge something really interesting.

And then suppose the judge should tell you to wipe it right off your mental slate, and not remember it, or consider it, or think about it any more forever.

You would do it, would you not?

Neither would we.

The juror's life is not unmixed with care.

PAGE 51, COLUMN 3

BRILLIANT LEGAL WARRIORS WHO ARE BATTLING FOR FRANK

These two men are recognized as champions of the Atlanta bar.

LUTHER Z. ROSSER. REUBEN ARNOLD.

BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Thursday, August 2, 1979, Braniff International inaugurated the carrier's first Boeing 747 service from the US Mainland to South America. Three Latin American destinations received Braniff Jumbo Jet service, including Buenos Aires, Argentina; Bogota, Colombia and Santiago, Chile.
Four weeks earlier, Braniff International inaugurated Boeing 747 service from Los Angeles to Hong Kong with intermediate stops at Honolulu, Hawaii, and Guam Island.

Braniff, since the 1960's, had sought to link the Pacific Rim and Far East to South America via the US Mainland. With the addition of the new Boeing 747 service from Los Angeles International Airport to the three South America airports Braniff successfully linked the Orient with single-plane service. Passengers could now fly from Hong Kong to Buenos Aires and Santiago without change of plane and in one day's time. Connecting service was available from the Far East to Bogota via Los Angeles.

Braniff's initial Boeing 747 schedule featured two weekly roundtrips from Los Angeles to Santiago, Chile, and Buenos Aires, Argentina. A single weekly Boeing 747 roundtrip flight operated from Los Angeles to Bogota, Colombia. Boeing 747 schedules to South America were increased as new Jumbo Jets were delivered. Braniff operated six Boeing 747s at the time of the inaugural service to the three Latin American destinations and reported seven more on order. Boeing 747 service was already offered on Braniff's routes across the Pacific and the Atlantic.

With the addition of Boeing 747 single-plane service between Asia/Pacific and The Far East and Latin America, Braniff's strong initial load factors over the Los Angeles to Hong Kong route, were further boosted with the new LAD link. However, the unprecedented rise in fuel during 1979 and worsening economic in the US and around the world began reducing not only leisure travel but critical business travel as well. In the first half of 1980 specifically, Braniff as well as other international carriers began suffering losses on routes that were operated with big jets that just a year earlier could operate half-empty and still breakeven or in Braniff's case make a significant profit.

In addition to the new LAD 747 service, America's favorite airline that Ended the Plain Jane and the Plain Plane, also announced that it had received authority from the Civil Aeronautics Board to serve Caracas and Maracaibo, Venezuela. Braniff intended to serve the two destinations via the Houston Gateway over a Houston to New Orleans then Maracaibo and Caracas routing with Boeing 727-200 Stretch Jets.

MISSTEPS PERFECTING the SHUTTERBUG STRUT

--Not your everyday Historical Fiction
Excerpt-Chapter 6: Mandatory Palestine, 1927

Gazing into the Mediterranean horizon, Alexandra sought her escape. She had spent a healthy part of the last six weeks frolicking the salty seas—from the beaches of the Portuguese Algarve to those of the Greek Islands—exercising a type of Polynesian ocean worship she had sampled in Hawaii. The waves had been middling, but time in the sun had left her skin nicely bronzed. Haifa provided ideal conditions for bodysurfing. The ankle waders found interest in her antics. Some offered applause, while others gawked as if she were a rumbustious sea creature that kept washing ashore.
--There was one dogged frowner: a thickset woman with golden curls spilling out of her bathing cap, who, if raised in Japan, would have been trained in the art of the Sumo. Now she stood waiting with two police officers, pointing.
--Alexandra was unsure of her offense, awash in a strange land and knowing few of its rules. Her Jantzen swimsuit clung to her lithe frame modestly. Perhaps it struck blasphemously to display wet hair in the ancient Holy Land. She jumped bashful waves that broke close to shore and ducked under the churning lather of those so forceful they collapsed under their weight out to sea. Having the patience to corral the ideal wave proved key, and likely her only chance, short of swimming for Cyprus, to avoid arrest.

BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Thursday, August 2, 1973, Braniff International President and Chief Operating Officer Charles Edward Acker detailed the superb progress that had been made in marketing the Airline’s travel education division to the general public. The memo released to all Braniff employees noted that, "Braniff Education Systems, Inc., has had a rapid and encouraging growth and acceptance since it began operations as Braniff International Airline Career Academy in May 1971.

On February 2, 1972 (state of Nevada corporate filing date), Braniff International formed a new subsidiary called Braniff Education Systems, Inc., to offer its industry-leading airline training to the public. Braniff's Airline Career Academy, located at 8001 Lemmon Avenue on the east side of Dallas Love Field, would house the new BESI training facility.

Braniff Chairman of the Board of Directors Harding L. Lawrence announced the proposed facility that would offer vocational training and educational programs to the general public. Lawrence noted that Braniff Education Systems would initially concentrate on training younger men and women for a career in the aviation and travel industry. The new school would be accommodated by expanding the company's Airline Career Academy that was opened in 1971.

The Airline Career Academy was opened to train students for airline ticketing and reservations agent careers and the new entity would also train its new students for these highly marketable positions. In addition, the syllabus would be expanded to include training for ramp services, electronics, flight, sales, and maintenance. In the near future, courses would also be expanded for training in language training, hotel careers training and personal development. Once Braniff Education Systems, Inc., was formed and then merged into the Airline’s holding company, Braniff International Corporation, in 1973, the Airline Career Academy and BESI functions were also merged into one educational entity.

Mr. Acker further noted in his memo of August 2, that, “All Braniff International personnel can support training programs with pride and should contribute to our effort of making Braniff Education Systems a world lead in the field of vocational-trade training.” He continued, “Due to the immediate acceptance in the industry and the initial success of our Reservations/Ticketing-Sales school (Airline Career Academy), we established on January 28, 1972, a fully-owned subsidiary known as Braniff Education Systems, Inc.”

The officers of Braniff Education Systems, at the time of the memorandum, were as follows:

Harding L. Lawrence - Chairman of the Board
Charles Edward Acker - President
Edward W. Lang - Vice President
Tom Coulter - Treasurer
Jay Jackson - Secretary

When Airline Career Academy was founded in 1971, there were only three employees. As of August 2, 1973, Braniff Education Systems, Inc., employed 60 full-time employees. The company also had sales offices in Dallas, Ft. Worth, Houston, San Antonio, Oklahoma City, Tulsa, Kansas City, Seattle, Chicago, Los Angeles and Miami, with offices scheduled to open in New Orleans, Atlanta, Minneapolis, Detroit, Denver, Portland San Francisco, Omaha and Tampa. Clearly, the company set up its sales offices in Braniff cities and oftentimes leased space from Braniff International.
The company offered the following airline and non-airline courses at three Dallas locations, one in Ft. Worth and one at Lima, Peru:

Reservations/Ticketing Sales - Dallas Love Field
Ground Operations - Dallas Love Field
Flight Engineer - Dallas Love Field
ATR Type Rating Boeing 727, 707 and McDonnell Douglas DC-8 - Dallas Love Field
Flight Attendant - Love Field and Lima Callao Airport, Peru
Persuasive Salesmanship - Dallas Love Field
Airframe and Powerplant - Ft. Worth Meacham Field
Aviation Maintenance Review Course - Ft. Worth Meacham Field
Auto Mechanics - 2956 Reward Lane, Dallas
Welding - 2956 Reward Lane, Dallas
Air Conditioning - 2956 Reward Lane, Dallas

In a span of two years, BESI, had established itself as a significant leader in the education travel industry. A superb reputation had been built quickly based on the high value of the Braniff International name. Also, the school marketed itself as an entity that was significantly different from most independent vocational trade schools. Mr. Acker stated in his memo that the following points easily propelled Braniff Educations Systems above the rest:

Sales Representative were salaried

Interviews were conducted in BESI offices

Nine out of 21 Sales Representatives were previous BESI graduates

Fourteen BESI employees were graduates of various courses

Personnel involved in supervising and instructing the courses average 7 years of airline or related experience

Average student age was 22

Less than 25 percent of graduates were employed by Braniff International
Two BESI employees had more than 20 years of service with Braniff International
Eight employees had worked for Braniff International prior to joining BESI
School standards, including refund policies, were designed for the student’s benefit.
BESI policies were more strict than those required by the Texas Education Agency, which approved all BESI courses

Over 20 airline personnel had enrolled in Braniff Education Systems courses and many airline personnel, including Braniff International employees had sons and daughters enrolled

Mr. Acker asked that all Braniff employees promote BESI to their friends, family and any other prospective students that they might know. Braniff Education Systems, continued in operation as BESI but under two different trade names until 2007. Today, the entity is once again owned by Braniff Airways, Incorporated.

text:
CLEAN AND SOBER.
The real moral of this story is that you need to understand who your real friends really are. If your friends don’t in some way make your life better and they don't lift you up and if they are constantly leading you astray taking advantage of you in some form of fashion. Then those are not your real friends they are nothing more than fake ass fair weather friends who want to do nothing more than manipulate, mooch off you and are nothing more than a bunch of disgusting freeloaders. Those are not your friends. You can’t buy friendship or love. That comes from the heart and there is no price tag or performative behavior that you can place on for something like that.

Introduction.
When I was a high-school and college kid I had a brief but spectacularly messy fling with drugs and alcohol. Eventually the universe (and a couple of concerned adults) suggested I might want to try something different like an intervention at the hospital to take me to drug rehab. So I went to treatment, and I’ve been clean and sober ever since.
Flash back with me.
Austin, Texas. The sticky summertime after my sophomore year at the University of Texas. I’m sitting in a fluorescent-lit conference room that smells faintly of industrial carpet and last week’s coffee. Fold-up chairs have been arranged in a giant, slightly wobbly circle. In the middle of it all stands our counselor for the day: a woman whose name is CindyLou Gilmore. (I still don’t know if that was her real name or an alias designed to keep the atmosphere light.)
CindyLou rises, claps her hands once for attention, and beams at us like she’s about to announce free pizza.
“Okay, everybody! Welcome to our first group therapy session together. I’m CindyLou, and I’ll be your counselor for this not so merry little adventure that you are about to go on right now. Every single one of you seated here today knows exactly why you’re here. You’re here because your substance-abuse problems got a little… too performative to say the least. The kind of performative behavior that made you dangerous to yourselves and, on occasion, to innocent bystanders. If that weren’t true, you’d be somewhere far more fun right now—probably still outdoors, soaking up the Texas sun.
“Now, let’s get one thing straight: substance abuse is a disease. Not a moral failing, not a character defect, no just a garden-variety disease—its right up there with cancer, diabetes, or even heart disease. Know on thing, you’ve got this. We’re here to help you treat it. Simple as that.”
She pauses for dramatic effect, then gestures toward the back of the room. A guy who looks like he might have been a roadie for rock band in a former life stands up holding a cardboard box the size of a small refrigerator. Inside are spiral notebooks and a small forest of cheap ballpoint pens. He begins circulating, solemnly handing one of each to every person in the circle as if we were about to sit for the SATs of sobriety.
And that, ladies and gentlemen, is how my official journey into recovery began: in a circle of metal chairs, under the watchful eye of Cindyloo Gilmore, armed with a brand-new notebook and the faint hope that this whole “disease” thing might actually work.
Cindyloo goes on. I want you to write down what it is that you have done that got you on the path to your substance abuse issues that you are facing today.

Cut to senior year of high school.

I’m seventeen, staying the weekend at the Rojas house in the Kern neighborhood of El Paso, right up against the mountain. Mom and Dad are in the middle of splitting up after twenty-six years of marriage, and home has become a war zone, so I escape here whenever I can. The Rojas have been close family friends for years; my brother will eventually marry one of their daughters (though that won’t last).
Downstairs I’m alone on the bottom bunk. Upstairs, Marlysue and Arnoldito are asleep near their parents (both EPISD teachers). Andrianna, the hot varsity cheerleader, is off camping in Ruidoso with her quarterback boyfriend. Misty and Alexander are already at UT Austin—Misty living with my older brother, Alexander on a full ride that will one day lead him to Los Alamos as a nuclear physicist .
That’s when Marco, twenty-five, slips in the front door and heads downstairs. College hadn’t worked out for him 2 years at UTEP and he couldn’t cut it; he’s now an assistant chef at a local spot (and will later cook his way through Austin, New York, and Seattle, ending up with a wife, three kids, and five grandkids). He sees me, grins, and says, “Hey Brendan, staying with us again this weekend?”
“Yeah. Mom and Dad are going through a pretty nasty divorce. Things are toxic at home, so Mom dropped me off.”
“No problem. Your a member of the family. Glad you’re here.”
He reaches into the nightstand, pulls out a joint, lights it, and holds it out. “Ever tried any of this?”
“No. Never.”
“Here—take a couple hits.”
I do. Two or three deep ones. Then it hits: bubbly, floating, pure cloud-nine. Reality softens at the edges. Everything looks… different. Weee. This is fun.
The rest of the story unspooled from there. My parents finished the divorce. Mom (choir teacher at Coronado High) left for three months to care for my dying grandfather at MD Anderson; I stayed home with our nanny Julia, then moved in with Uncle George across town, visiting on weekends. Dad, who had been El Paso’s DA (including the big Chagra cases), took a job as chief federal prosecutor in San Antonio, later he became a federal judge, remarried, and eventually retired to our family vacation home in Cloudcroft. He died years later in a Las Cruces nursing home from COVID complications after a heart attack.
But that night on the bottom bunk? That was the first spark.
Cut to:
Lunchtime at Coronado High. The parking lot is a sea of cars and teenagers peeling off toward every fast-food joint within a five-mile radius.
That’s when I spot Billy Sharpington—the guy who can get you anything. Concert tickets? UTEP basketball? Sun Bowl seats? Billy’s your man. He is basically Mike Damone from Fast Times at Ridgemont High, only with a better car. He’s leaning against the hood of his Trans Am, right-hand man and erstwhile bodyguard Rick Forrestal beside him. Rick is the all-city running back who once dashed ninety yards for the last minute winning touchdown against Eastwood in the big cross town rivalry game. He was pretty good. I should know—I played against him on JV.
I walk up, make the universal “you got any weed?” gesture, and say, “Hey dude, I hear you’re the one who can hook me up.”
Billy laughs. “I’m your man.” He opens the passenger door, folds the seat forward, and says, “Hop in. Join me in my office.” He tosses the keys to Rick. “You’re driving. Take us around for a bit.”
We cruise to the Der Wienerschnitzel drive-through. Rick orders three chili dogs and fries, hands them out, and we roll around the neighborhood munching while Billy digs into a leather satchel, lights a joint, and passes it back. We take turns puffing away, floating higher with every turn of the tires.
Just before we pull back into the school lot, Billy hands me a lid of marijuana. “Free sample. You know where to find me.”
I did. I spent the better part of my senior year buying dime bags from him on a regular basis.

CUT TO A FEW MONTHS LATER
Senior trip. Downtown Union train Station. The entire senior class is milling around, waiting for the Amtrak to Disneyland. This will be my third visit: once as a bratty seven-year-old (my older brother was not thrilled to babysit with me in the backseat of the car on the way out there), once again at thirteen on a family trip that also hit SeaWorld, and now this.
My buddies and I already rolled up stoned to the gills, beers circulating in the car, and we’ve got enough weed in our carry-ons to last the weekend. On the train the porters quietly sell us miniature bottles of booze when no one’s looking. Couples Hooking abound. I get properly drunk, pass out, and wake up sometime in the middle of the night to the unmistakable sounds of a couple in the seats in front of me having a very enthusiastic good time making love. I roll over and go back to sleep.
We stumble off the train in L.A. and head straight into the park on a tour bus—still high, still buzzed, and hung over. Disneyland on that particular wavelength is a completely different planet. Space Mountain becomes an absolute fever dream. I stagger off the ride, still spinning, and look up to see a cluster of little kids posing for pictures with Cinderella and Mickey Mouse for mom and dad.
My stomach chooses that exact moment to revolt. I lurch to the nearest trash can and unload everything—barf, barf, more barf—right in front of the photo op. The parents spin their kids away in horror. One of them stage-whispers, “Don’t look at that man, he’s sick.”
A total different experience from the previous trips.
(The next time I’d return, at twenty-two for a Xerox interview at their regional office in Costa Mesa, the magic was gone. I’d simply outgrown the place. I was very bored it just wasn’t the same. The allure of Disneyland had gone)
Graduation was the following week. The week after that my grandma packed me off on a six-week tour of Europe—partly to give my mother breathing room while she recovered from the divorce. I spent most of those six weeks gloriously drunk on Austrian, British, and German beer, plus whatever French and Italian wine I could find.
CUT TO FRESHMAN YEAR AT UT AUSTIN
Freshman mixer night in the giant Student Union ballroom. Free punch flowing, the whole class circulating, and onstage: Christopher Cross and Joe “King” Carrasco tearing it up live.
From across the room I lock eyes on a five-foot-three (maybe four) brunette who is, in a word, lethal. Drop dead gorgeous. I gather what little courage the punch has given me, walk over, and say hello. She says hello back. We just… click.
Her name is Monica. Business major, theater junkie, and—poor girl—about to spend the next two years of her life with me.
Austin is a college party town that will eat you alive if you let it. I immediately fell in with the wrong crowd, chasing approval from people who were never really my friends. Their alpha male was a guy we will politely call Keith Brain-turd. Every Friday or Saturday night the phone would ring:
“Hey Brendan, cool band tonight. Let’s hoist some brews and blow a few doobies.”
And off I’d go, leaving Monica behind or waiting.
One night she dragged me to a show at Bass Concert Hall. I showed up late, still drunk and stoned, and nodded off twice during the performance. When the curtain fell she stood up without a word and stormed out. We had a full-scale parking-lot war.
Then came spring break Monica and I went to Cancun. Bars, clubs, the usual. I got stoned with some guys, Monica fell asleep back at the hotel, and I decided a solo beach stroll sounded brilliant. Next thing I know I’m face-down in the sand. Memory gets fuzzy, but two Penn State girls in bikinis somehow enter the picture. I have vague memories of rolling on the beach with hot naked girls tossing and rolling in the pounding surf. That is all I can remember.
I wake up at 6:30 a.m. wearing only a shirt. My pants and shoes are bobbing in the surf ten yards out. I am not going in after them.
I start the walk of shame back to the hotel. A crew of local construction workers waiting for their ride spots me, pants-less, and loses it. “¡Loco gringo!” they howl.
In a moment of pure genius I yank two leafy branches from the hotel landscaping and hold them strategically front and back. I stroll up to the front desk like this is completely normal, explain I’ve lost my key, and the clerk (who recognizes me) hands one over a key without blinking.
I walk into the room. Monica sits up in bed. She takes in the full bush-branch ensemble.
I offer my carefully prepared excuse: “Fell asleep on the beach. The tide just… took my pants.”
She stares at me, equal parts furious and exhausted.
“Yeah right, Brendan. What was her name? Was it the girl from Carlos ’n Charlie’s last night? Do you love her? Or do you love me? Because this shit is getting really old, and if I didn’t love you so much I’d have kicked you to the curb a long time ago. I just… I can’t take it anymore.”
Then she buries her face in the pillow and starts to cry. I have seen this act of the play before. She always says this, but it is always performative. She comes back to me in the end.

THE SHIT HITS THE FAN
End of sophomore year at UT. Somehow my grades are still decent despite the nonstop partying, drinking, drugging, and cheating on Monica. I’m sitting in my apartment trying to decompress when she stops by earlier that day.
“My parents and my two little sisters are driving up from Houston,” she says. “They want to meet you and take us to dinner at the Nighthawk Steakhouse. Dress up and don’t be late. Seven-thirty. And just so you know, I’m not staying for summer session this year. I’m going home to lifeguard at the country club like always. I’ll come up when I can, or you can come down.”
I tell her I’ll be there.
Not thirty minutes after she leaves, there’s a knock. Keith Brain-turd and a couple of his usual drug-worm buddies. They pile into the living room. Keith immediately rolls a joint; I grab a six-pack from the fridge everybody cracks them open. In minutes we’re all high and buzzing.
End-of-year bash at Robert Millington’s place tonight,” Keith says between hits. “You remember him—the Wall Street guy who buys rounds for everybody? Loaded as hell. Big house up on the hill overlooking Town Lake. I say “He went to UT didn’t he?” Keith says “Yep and he is now a big shot on Wall Street. Making money hand over fist. He is totally loaded like you wouldn’t believe. A true master of the universe. Every time he’s in town I hook him up with whatever he needs. Tonight there’s going to be weed, blow, Everclear punch, jello shots, the works. And hot women flying in from New York, L.A., even some European flight attendants. Guaranteed action. I promise you are going to score with some hot women tonight”
“I can’t,” I say. “I’m supposed to meet Monica’s family at 7:30.”
Keith waves it off. “Hell with Monica. She’ll forgive you. We’ll get you there on time—or I’ll drive you to the steakhouse myself if you’re late. C’mon. Tonight’s the party of the year.”
I cave.
We roll up to the mansion around about six. DJ spinning by the pool, booze everywhere, gorgeous women already in bikinis. Robert greets us at the door like we’re royalty. Within minutes a model named Jillian (not her real name) hands me a glass of champagne and a joint of Maui Wowie. Someone else appears with a silver tray of coke lines. I take a couple of hits up the nose. After that everything turns into a Technicolor blur—naked people in the pool, random hookups everywhere, music pounding.
Next thing I know it’s morning and I’m face-down on the neighbor’s front lawn with a massive black eye that I can’t explain. Keys and wallet still in my pocket, thank God. I stagger to my car and drive home, crash hard.
Two hours later: bang-bang-bang on the door. Its Monica.
She takes one look at the black eye and erupts. “You stupid bastard. You stood me up again. My mother warned me about you and I didn’t listen. Well, now I’m listening now. This is the last time you’ll ever see me. I’m done. She then screams at me even louder and says you dirty piece of shit asshole! I hate you! I hate you!”
She turns and walks away. I don’t even try to argue. She’d left before and always come back. Not this time. This time would be totally different.
The next day I go to her apartment. Her roommate opens the door, looks me up and down, I ask if Monica is there and says, “She left for Houston yesterday. Told me if you showed up to call the police. So if I were you, asshole, I’d leave before I dial 911.” Door slam.
I call her Houston number. She answers, hears my voice, and hangs up.
That’s when it finally sinks in. I’d let my dirty rotten drug-worm friends and the life of partying cost me the one person who actually loved me. The weight of it is crushing. I feel suicidal—like the only way off this ride is to end it. I can’t believe that I let my party friends play me and manipulate me like they did. I now have a huge monkey on my back and I don’t know what to do. I just can’t get it of my back or make it go away. Out of my I am desperation I feel totally hopeless. I just want to die. So I call 911 and tell them exactly that.
Half an hour later two cops and a social worker show at my door. They take me to the hospital for observation. A couple of days of talking to doctors, psychologists, and social workers pass in a fog. Then one morning a doctor, a nurse, and two security guards appear. They escort me downstairs to a conference room.
Almost my entire family is waiting—Mom, Dad (divorced for years but both there), and a bunch of the people and the friends who still actually cared about me. They sit me down and stage an intervention. For an hour they tell me, calmly and clearly, that I have a serious problem and that I need help.
Then the nylon restraints go on, and they take me straight to rehab.
Officially for the record.
I have been totally clean and sober ever since which to me is a badge of honor that I wear proudly like a soldier who was decorated for bravery in combat does.

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

On this day in 1964, the Gulf of Tonkin incident began—an event that would dramatically expand America’s role in Vietnam.

On the afternoon of August 2, the destroyer USS Maddox was on an intelligence patrol in international waters when three North Vietnamese torpedo boats attacked. The Maddox opened fire with her 5-inch guns as the boats closed and launched torpedoes. Carrier aircraft from the USS Ticonderoga joined the fight. One boat was left dead in the water; the others fled damaged. The Maddox took only a single machine-gun bullet.

Two nights later, under heavy weather and darkness, the Maddox and USS Turner Joy reported a second attack. Radar contacts and sonar reports of torpedo wakes filled the night. The ships zigzagged and poured hundreds of rounds into the darkness. Yet even as the engagement unfolded, Captain John Herrick sent a flash message that still echoes:

“Review of action makes many reported contacts and torpedoes fired appear doubtful. Freak weather effects on radar and overeager sonarmen may have accounted for many reports. No actual visual sightings by MADDOX. Suggest complete evaluation before any further action taken.”

Washington did not wait. That same night President Lyndon Johnson told the nation:

“Renewed hostile actions against United States ships on the high seas in the Gulf of Tonkin have today required me to order the military forces of the United States to take action in reply… Repeated acts of violence against the Armed Forces of the United States must be met not only with alert defense, but with positive reply.”

He ordered airstrikes on North Vietnamese patrol boat bases. Within days Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, giving the President authority “to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack against the forces of the United States and to prevent further aggression.”

The first clash was real. The second almost certainly never happened—a deadly mix of weather, radar ghosts, and the fog of war. Yet that incomplete information became the legal foundation for a war that would cost more than 58,000 American lives.

History rarely offers clean lessons. This one demands we remember both the courage of the men on those destroyers and the speed with which uncertainty can commit a nation to years of costly struggle.

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

One hundred and fifty years ago today—August 2, 1876—the American West lost one of its most magnetic, dangerous, and unforgettable figures in a single, sudden second.

James Butler “Wild Bill” Hickok sat at a poker table in Nuttal & Mann’s Saloon No. 10 in the muddy, gold-crazed town of Deadwood, Dakota Territory. The room smelled of whiskey, sweat, tobacco, and cheap perfume. Outside, the Black Hills boomtown roared with miners, gamblers, prostitutes, and dreamers chasing fortune. Inside, Wild Bill—tall, long-haired, sharp-eyed, and already a living legend—was trying to win a few dollars the only way he still knew how.

He had been a Civil War scout, a Union spy, a stagecoach driver, a buffalo hunter, a lawman who cleaned up the streets of Abilene and Hays City with a pair of ivory-handled Colts, and a showman who briefly toured with Buffalo Bill Cody. By the summer of 1876, the frontier was closing and the old gunfighter was nearly broke. Deadwood’s gold camps offered one last chance at easy money around the card tables.

That afternoon he drew the worst seat in the house. His usual caution failed him. For once, he sat with his back to the door and the open room. He was holding a strong hand—two black aces and two black eights—when a small-time gambler and drifter named Jack McCall stepped up behind him. Without a word, McCall raised a single-action .45 revolver and fired one shot into the back of Hickok’s head at near point-blank range.

Wild Bill never had time to turn. He slumped forward onto the table, cards still in his fingers. Those four cards—aces and eights—became instantly and forever known as the “dead man’s hand.” The fifth card has been lost to history, argued over ever since.

Chaos erupted. McCall tried to flee, waving his gun and shouting that he had avenged his brother. A miners’ court quickly assembled, found him not guilty in a farce of a trial, and set him free. Weeks later, authorities rearrested him. This time the verdict was different. Jack McCall was hanged in Yankton on March 1, 1877—the first man legally executed in the Dakota Territory.

Hickok’s body was first buried in Deadwood’s original cemetery under a simple wooden marker. Years later, as the town grew and the old burial ground was moved, his remains were transferred to Mount Moriah Cemetery. There he still rests, high on a hill overlooking the gulch that once pulsed with gold fever and gun smoke. Visitors still come to stand at the grave of the man who helped invent the myth of the Western gunfighter.

On this August morning in 1876, the cards were dealt, the shot was fired, and a chapter of the American frontier closed forever. Wild Bill Hickok lived hard, fought harder, and died the way the stories always seemed to demand—at a poker table, with a bullet in the back, and legend already waiting to claim him.

As of early August 2026, Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-KY), 84, remains absent from the Senate after roughly seven weeks of 'recovery'.

Timeline and Official Account
On June 14, 2026, emergency responders were called to McConnell’s Washington, D.C., residence. Reports and 911 audio indicated an unconscious person and CPR in progress related to a possible cardiac event (identity not officially confirmed by his office at the time).

His office initially offered only minimal statements confirming hospitalization and recovery.

On July 12–13, McConnell's office broke the silence with a statement and a photo of himself in a hospital bed (with a newspaper for date verification) alongside his wife, Elaine Chao. 

He said he had taken a fall at home, was briefly unconscious, developed mild pneumonia while hospitalized, underwent tests, suffered no broken bones or concussion, and had been moved to a rehabilitation facility. 

He expressed intent to return and finish his term.

On July 27, his office and the Office of the Attending Physician released a further update (with a new photo dated July 26). 

He was said to be undergoing intense physical therapy, was not yet medically cleared for a full schedule, would miss that week’s Senate work ahead of the August recess, and would skip the traditional Fancy Farm political picnic in Kentucky. 

It was reiterated that he was working to return and appreciated well wishes.

Current Status
McConnell has missed a substantial number of Senate votes and remains away from public duties and events. 

Speculation and criticism have continued over the limited information released, his prolonged absence, and fitness for office. 

Prank “missing person” posters describing the senator in mocking terms have appeared around Washington, D.C.

We ask again, is Mitch McConnell alive?

text:
THE DIGITAL EURO IS COMING HERE’S EVERYTHING YOU NEED TO KNOW 🚨

Europe is building its own central bank digital currency (CBDC). Not a private stablecoin. Not crypto.  Actual public money issued by the ECB, available to every citizen and business in the euro area. Here’s the full, unfiltered breakdown with timelines, countries, features, risks, and sources.

Official Timeline :
Investigation phase: 2021–2023 
Preparation phase: Nov 2023 – Oct 2025 (completed) 
Current phase: Technical readiness + legislative process 
Legislation: Trilogues between European Parliament, Council and Commission started mid-July 2026. 
Target = adoption by end of 2026. 

ECB formal decision window: Possible from 1 January 2027 
Pilot phase: Second half of 2027 → lasts 12 months 
Potential first issuance: 2029 (ECB’s working assumption if regulation is adopted in 2026)

Sources: ECB Progress Report (30 Oct 2025), ECB Press Release (14 July 2026), Reuters (13–14 July 2026). 

The Big Pilot (2027)On 14 July 2026 the ECB selected 36 payment service providers (out of >50 applicants) including major names like Deutsche Bank, UniCredit, Revolut, Adyen, BPCE, Banco Comercial Português and others.
The pilot will run at the ECB + 19 national central banks: Belgium, Germany, Estonia, Ireland, Greece, Spain, France, Croatia, Italy, Cyprus, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Netherlands, Austria, Portugal, Slovenia, Slovakia, Finland.They will test:

Person-to-person payments (online + offline)
Person-to-business (physical POS + e-commerce)
Real everyday use by central bank staff and selected merchants (cafeterias, shops, etc.)

This is a “beta” version — no legal tender status yet.

Key Design Features
Online + Offline capability 
Offline mode offers cash-like privacy: only payer and payee know the transaction details. No internet required. 

 Distributed by commercial banks and PSPs (you won’t have a direct account at the ECB) 

Holding limits under discussion: range tested by ECB was €500–€3,000 per person (to protect banks from deposit flight). Zero interest. 

“Waterfall” mechanism: excess money above the limit automatically moves to your regular bank account. 

Free for basic consumer use 
Planned legal tender status across the euro area 
Non-programmable (cannot be restricted to specific goods/services) 

Strong privacy design: Eurosystem cannot link payments to individuals. PSPs handle KYC/AML.

Potential ImpactBull case (ECB narrative):
Strategic autonomy — reduce dependence on Visa/Mastercard and US payment rails 
Digital cash that works even when the internet is down 
More competition in European payments 
Financial inclusion + free basic payments 
Keeps central bank money relevant in a digital world

Bear case / real concerns:

Holding limits make it a weak store of value 
Possible acceleration of the decline of physical cash 
Privacy trade-offs (even if offline is strong, online still involves intermediaries) 
Banks fear deposit outflows (though ECB studies claim impact is manageable under €3,000 limit) 
Cybersecurity and single point of failure risks 
Political risk: future governments could push for more surveillance features

Why this matters right nowCash usage is falling fast. Private digital payments are dominated by non-European players. China already has the e-CNY. The US is moving on stablecoin regulation. Europe is racing to keep the euro relevant in the digital age.The digital euro will not replace cash — the ECB repeatedly says both will coexist. But once it launches, the payment landscape in Europe will never be the same.Sources (most recent):
• ECB official pages (pilot, progress, privacy)
• ECB Press Release 14 July 2026
• Reuters 13–14 July 2026
• Bloomberg 14 July 2026
• European Commission & Parliament legislative texts 2026 What do you think — necessary tool for European sovereignty… or a step toward more control? 

rop your take below.  This is one of the biggest monetary shifts of our generation.

text:
No. Decentralisation does not require an earlier failure of centralisation. It requires people willing to resist the convenience of being governed.

That is the difficult part.

The American Revolution demonstrated that individuals can unite around liberty before every abuse has become unbearable. But such moments are rare, because freedom demands effort while authority offers administration.

Centralised power enjoys an institutional advantage. It is concentrated, organised and persistent. Those who possess it know exactly what they stand to lose.

The public is diffuse. People are busy, divided and easily persuaded that the next restriction is temporary, necessary or someone else’s problem. Each group waits for another to object, and complacency performs the work that coercion would otherwise require.

This is why liberty so often disappears gradually. Not through one magnificent act of tyranny, but through a long sequence of tolerable concessions.

Decentralisation does not emerge automatically from failed centralisation. It emerges when people recognise that power accumulates unless deliberately checked, and that rights unused eventually become permissions granted by others.

Centralised power rarely sleeps.

Freedom, unfortunately, often does.
