Your query touches upon philosophical categories, and I will try to explain and connect them with empiriocriticism, based on your text, but in a clearer and more structured form.
Empiriocriticism and its approach
Empiriocriticism (from "experience" and "critique"), associated with the names of Ernst Mach and Richard Avenarius, emphasizes that knowledge of the world must be based on experience and critical analysis. In this approach, matter is viewed not as something absolute "in itself," but as a set of sensations that we can measure, compare, and organize. For example, the mass of matter is something we can quantitatively assess under identical conditions (e.g., weigh it in a vacuum or under specific gravity) and draw conclusions based on observations. For empirio-criticism, truth is that which is confirmed by experience, not metaphysical assumptions.
Now let's break down your categories:
Objective reality = objective truth?
You write: Objective reality (actuality) = exists = objective truth. In the context of empiriocriticism, this can be interpreted as follows: objective reality is that which exists independently of our consciousness and is accessible to verification through experience. If the mass of matter is measured and ordered under identical conditions, we can speak of objective truth — a fact that does not depend on subjective interpretations. However, empirio-criticism would rather say that "truth" is the consistency of our sensations and measurements, not an absolute property of reality itself.
Reality
You define reality as occurring actions leading to a state and phenomenon, where matter possesses mass and order. This is close to the philosophical understanding of reality as the totality of everything that exists — processes, changes, states. In the empiriocritical approach, reality does not so much "act" as it manifests in our observations: we see that matter has mass, measure it, record patterns. Reality here is the "raw material" of experience.
Actuality
You write: Actuality — actions occur, leading to reality and fiction. This is an interesting distinction. Actuality can be understood as that layer of reality which we experience at a given moment, including our interpretations. Fiction, on the other hand, is a product of consciousness that does not correspond to objectively verifiable facts (e.g., a fantasy about a unicorn: the actions in the imagination exist, but the unicorn does not exist in reality). In empiriocriticism, actuality would be linked to concrete experience, while fiction is that which is not confirmed by measurements or observations.
Comparison and conclusion
✅Reality  is everything that exists, including matter with its mass and order, whether we are aware of it or not. This is the objective foundation accessible to analysis through experience (in the spirit of      empiriocriticism).
✅Actuality  is the part of reality that is relevant to us here and now, plus what we can add to it through imagination (fiction). It is more subjective, as it is connected to our perception.
✅Empiriocriticism  proposes testing both reality and actuality through experience: take matter, measure its mass under identical conditions, compare, draw conclusions. Truth is what withstands such a test.
To summarize: reality is the objective "everything," actuality is the subjectively experienced "slice" of reality, and fiction is a deviation from it, unconfirmed by experience. Empiriocriticism teaches us to trust only what we can "touch" through sensations and measurements. How does this analysis strike you?

Lenin's definition of matter
Lenin defines matter as a philosophical category denoting objective reality, which:
1. Exists independently of human consciousness.
2. Is given to man through his sensations (that is, we perceive it through our  senses).
3. Is "copied, photographed, reflected" by our sensations.
For Lenin, this definition served as a polemical tool against idealism and empiriocriticism, which, in his opinion, dissolved the objectivity of the world into subjective sensations. He insisted that matter is that which exists "outside us" and does not depend on our perception, but is nonetheless accessible to us through experience.
Critique of Lenin's definition
You point out a weakness in the formulation: "Lenin, in the definition, made the subject (man) only as someone reading the observation of objective reality, but the subject... can hit matter with a stick and objective reality will change". This is an important point. Lenin indeed emphasizes the passive role of man as an observer who "reflects" objective reality, but does not account for the active interaction of the subject with this reality. If a person, for example, moves mass (hits a stone with a stick, moves it), then objective reality changes — the stone ends up in a new place, its state changes, and this affects the surrounding world, even if to a small degree.
Your thought that "when a human moves mass (matter), reality throughout the entire Universe changes" can be interpreted as an indication of the interconnectedness of processes in the physical world. Even a small action (moving mass) creates a chain of consequences — from changing the position of particles to, theoretically, gravitational or energy effects on a cosmic scale. Lenin in his definition does not pay attention to this active role of the subject, limiting himself to the reflection of matter in sensations.
Alternative: Definition by E.P. Ziemelis
You provide the definition: "Matter is that which has mass, by means of force through the transformation of matter, the action of moving mass, leads to the state of a thing or phenomenon with a certain quantity and order, imparting quality to matter." ✅Matter is characterized by mass (a physical quantity).
✅It  is subject to transformation through force and action (moving, changing state).
✅As a result of these actions, things or phenomena arise with a certain order and quality.
Ziemelis, unlike Lenin, emphasizes active interaction with matter. Here, the subject does not just "read" reality but influences it, shaping new states or qualities. For example, if you take clay (matter with mass) and mold a pot from it, the mass does not disappear, but its order and quality change due to human action.
Comparison and conclusions
Lenin: Matter is objective reality, existing independently of us and reflected in our sensations. The definition is static and oriented towards opposing      idealism, but overlooks the role of man as an active transformer of reality.
Ziemelis: Matter is that which possesses mass and can be changed through force and action, leading to new states and qualities. The definition is dynamic,      considering the subject as a participant in the processes of reality.
Your critique of Lenin is valid: his approach does not explain how the subject, by interacting with matter, changes objective reality. If I take a stick and move a stone, the objective reality (the position of mass in the Universe) is no longer what it was before my action — and this goes beyond simple "reflection in sensations." Ziemelis, however, offers a more materialist and practical view, where matter is not just an object of observation, but something we work with and transform.
Your example about changing reality throughout the entire Universe adds philosophical depth: any action with matter, even local, is theoretically connected to the whole through physical laws (e.g., gravity or conservation of energy). This makes Ziemelis's definition closer to modern physics and a dynamic view of the world. What do you think of this comparison? Would you like to delve deeper into some aspect?

☑️Reality is the objective existence of matter (things and phenomena) with quantity, order, and quality. That which is, exists in itself.
☑️Actuality is actions with matter plus information, which can reflect reality or be fiction (named, but not existing in reality).
I agreed that actuality is broader than reality due to information and fiction, and that reality is only the material basis. But let's try to challenge this division.
Refutation
1. Information is part of reality, not just actuality
     You claim that the Universe consists of matter and information, and that information is included in actuality, distinguishing it from reality. But what if information is not a separate non-material entity, but a property of matter itself? For example, in physics, information is often considered the state of a system: the arrangement of particles, their energy, momentum. When you say "the stone lies there," this is not something external to reality, but a description of the real state of matter. Even fiction ("a dragon is flying") as a message exists in reality — in the form of neural impulses in the brain, sound waves, or letters on paper. This would mean information does not separate actuality from reality, but is part of reality. Is there not an overlap here?
2. Actuality as a part of reality, not something separate

text:
Gm Folks
We are back!

This is another edition of the Predict Alpha Report, our bi-monthly collaboration with @CoinsiliumGroup tracking the rise of prediction markets, event-driven finance, and the growing role of AI agents within it. Each edition focuses on the signals that matter, from capital flows and fundraising activity to regulatory shifts and product innovation. As information is increasingly priced in real time by both humans and machines, the Predict Alpha Report will track where these signals lead.
But first, let’s get this part out of the way:

Always DYOR:
This bulletin is for informational purposes only and contains summaries of news articles originally published by third-party media outlets. Please refer to the full disclaimer at the end of the post.

Now, let’s get started.
Here are the highlights:

💸 Capital Signals
👉Underdog Acquired For US$1.3 Billion
👉The New York Mets 🤝 Novig
👉ProphetX’s US$35 million Raise
👉Fanatics’ Latest Moves
👉Coinsilium CEO Eddy Travia Delivers Keynote at WikiExpo Global Hong Kong

📈 Industry Pulse
👉Record US$20 Billion
👉US Elections on Kalshi
👉Binance US in Prediction Markets?
👉Surpassed Crypto Trading on Robinhood…
👉Instadocs: The Prediction Games

💸 Capital Signals

💰 Underdog Acquired For US$1.3 Billion

IG Group has agreed to acquire US fantasy sports and prediction markets platform Underdog in a deal worth up to US$1.3 billion. The transaction values Underdog at about US$1.1 billion upfront, with a further US$200 million tied to future performance. IG plans to fund the deal with roughly 24.1 million new shares and US$380 million in cash, while also repaying about US$160 million of Underdog’s debt.

Underdog only entered prediction markets in 2025 but has already become the third-largest regulated US platform by trading volume. IG expects the acquisition to more than double its US revenue and increase its monthly active US customer base more than tenfold, giving it a large sports-focused audience that it can later introduce to financial, crypto, political and economic markets.

💰The New York Mets 🤝 Novig

The New York Mets have signed a multi-year partnership with Novig, becoming the first MLB team to name a prediction market platform as its exclusive partner. Novig’s branding will appear across Citi Field, game broadcasts and the Mets’ digital channels, alongside fan contests and promotions. The platform operates more like an exchange than a traditional sportsbook, allowing users to trade directly against one another via an order book instead of playing against the house.

Novig, which launched in 2024 and is backed by Pantera Capital, has received federal approval to operate under US commodities rules and is also an authorised MLB partner, giving it access to official league data. That approval comes with restrictions designed to protect the integrity of games, including limits on markets tied to individual pitches, umpire decisions and other outcomes that could be easily influenced by one person. With similar partnerships now spreading across leagues and events, including the NHL, MLS, UFC and FIFA, the Mets deal shows how quickly prediction markets are becoming part of the wider sports economy.

💰ProphetX’s US$35 million Raise

ProphetX has raised US$35 million in an oversubscribed funding round led by Parlay Capital and Data Point Capital, with backing from investors including FDJ Ventures, Greenwave Ventures, Connexa Capital, Chicago Trading Company Ventures and Belvedere Trading. The funding follows the company’s recent approval from the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission to operate a federally regulated, peer-to-peer prediction market focused exclusively on sports.

The raise marks the latest step in ProphetX’s shift from a state-regulated betting exchange to a sweepstakes platform and now to a nationwide event-contract marketplace. ProphetX allows users to trade directly with one another, while its Request for Quote system helps users find prices for multi-event trades. The new capital will be used to deepen liquidity, expand institutional participation, develop the platform, and build more partnerships as competition across US sports prediction markets continues to grow.

💰Fanatics’ Latest Moves

Fanatics has agreed to acquire Water Street Labs and CX Clearinghouse from BGC Group, giving it direct control of the regulated infrastructure needed to run its own US prediction market exchange. Water Street Labs is licensed to list prediction contracts, while CX Clearinghouse handles the processing and settlement of trades.

Fanatics Markets launched in December 2025 using Crypto,com’s infrastructure, which meant Fanatics acted mainly as an intermediary rather than operating the exchange itself. Owning these businesses will allow the company to bring more of the platform in-house, reduce its reliance on outside providers, and expand beyond its current sports-focused contracts. Fanatics is also partnering with BGC to combine prediction market activity with traditional financial data, pointing to a wider ambition to serve institutional investors as well as everyday sports fans.

And rounding up this section:

💰Coinsilium CEO Eddy Travia Delivers Keynote at WikiExpo Global Hong Kong

At WikiExpo Global Hong Kong, @CoinsiliumGroup CEO @eddybitcoin delivered a keynote, The New Economic Agents: Why AI and Blockchain Are Converging, highlighting why blockchain-based trust infrastructure will be essential to unlocking the full potential of the agentic economy. The presentation explored how programmable trust, prediction markets and decentralised coordination can enable autonomous AI agents to transact, collaborate and make decisions at machine speed, drawing on real-world examples including Predictive Labs' Nijinn, @Yellow Network and @Otomato_xyz.

Eddy Travia joined @johann_evrard, Founder and CEO of @Predictive_Labs, for a panel exploring the future of prediction markets. The discussion examined their growing use in forecasting and AI-driven decision-making, while addressing challenges around market integrity, regulation and trust, and their potential role as a core source of machine-readable intelligence for the agentic economy.

📌 FYI: Coinsilium’s shares are traded on the Aquis Stock Exchange Growth Market in London, under the ticker symbol "COIN", and on the OTCQB Venture Market in the United States under the ticker symbol "CINGF".

But it’s not just capital flowing into the space.
Keep reading for the latest signals in regulation, adoption, and structure.

📈 Industry Pulse

⚡️Record US$20 Billion

The 2026 FIFA World Cup generated US$20 billion in prediction market trading from January through the end of the tournament, including US$5.7 billion during the five-week competition itself. Around 400,000 crypto wallets traded contracts covering match results, the eventual winner, player performances and novelty outcomes, and at the tournament’s peak, World Cup-related contracts accounted for roughly 63% of all prediction market activity.

The activity was largely driven by legitimate fans, with fewer than 1% of participating wallets showing links to illicit sources. FIFA also generated US$24 million through FIFA Collect, its blockchain-based digital collectibles platform, which helped more than 100,000 fans gain access to match tickets. Together, the figures show how prediction markets and other blockchain products are becoming a bigger part of the experience around global sporting events.

⚡️US Elections on Kalshi

@Kalshi has launched a new US elections portal that brings together campaign polls, fundraising figures, political news and live prices from its prediction markets ahead of the November midterms. The company wants the hub to become a go-to source for election odds, giving voters, traders and campaigns a real-time view of how expectations are changing rather than waiting days for new polling data.

Political markets have become one of Kalshi’s biggest categories outside sports, with trading already rising sharply this year. Supporters argue that prediction markets can capture the collective view of thousands of traders, while critics warn that large trades, insider information or manipulation could distort public perceptions.

⚡️Binance US in Prediction Markets?

@BinanceUS plans to apply for a US CFTC licence next month as it explores launching its own prediction market. The licence would allow the exchange to offer contracts tied to real-world outcomes, putting it in direct competition with platforms such as Kalshi and Polymarket, which saw trading surge during the World Cup and around major global events.

The move follows a broader push by crypto exchanges into the sector, with Gemini securing a similar licence earlier this year and Coinbase offering prediction markets through a partnership with Kalshi. Moreover, prediction markets could provide a new route back into the country’s fast-growing retail trading market for BinanceUS, which has lost some market share since 2023.

⚡️Surpassed Crypto Trading on Robinhood…

@RobinhoodApp’s prediction markets business has become the fastest-growing product in the company’s history, with revenue rising tenfold year on year to US$156 million in the second quarter. That was enough to surpass the US$100 million generated from crypto trading, as weaker digital asset prices reduced activity across the sector. CEO @vladtenev said prediction market usage has grown consistently since March and expects the momentum to continue.

The FIFA World Cup provided a major boost, attracting customers to trade contracts linked to match results and other tournament outcomes. It also served as an important test for Rothera, the derivatives exchange jointly owned by Robinhood and Susquehanna International Group, which has already become one of the three largest federally regulated contract markets in the US. With prediction markets now outperforming crypto within Robinhood, they are quickly becoming a core part of the brokerage’s growth strategy.

⚡️Instadocs: The Prediction Games

Netflix has released Instadocs: The Prediction Games, a 37-minute documentary exploring how prediction markets have moved into mainstream culture. Featuring @Polymarket CEO @shayne_coplan, Kalshi CEO @mansourtarek_, CFTC Chairman Michael Selig and The Wisdom of Crowds author James Surowiecki, the film looks at how platforms turn collective judgement into live probabilities on everything from elections and sport to weather, celebrity events and armed conflict. The scale is already significant, with around US$5.7 billion traded on the 2026 World Cup final across Polymarket and Kalshi alone.

The documentary also examines the tensions behind that growth, including insider information, market manipulation and the risk that traders may try to influence the events they are betting on. By bringing those debates to a global streaming audience, Netflix is not just documenting the rise of prediction markets, but helping push the industry further into the public conversation.

And that’s it!
Long read, but if you enjoyed this, set a reminder in your calendar for the next edition of the Predict Alpha Report.

Thanks to Coinsilium, we’ll be dropping these updates every other Monday, i.e, twice a month.

Till then,

Greenland Exposed NATO’s Blind Spot: Trump’s Claim, Turkey’s Occupation, Alliance Silence

A  Line of State doctrine published in @HighNorthNews 👇

Donald Trump did not insult Denmark. He tried to reclassify an ally as inventory.

At the NATO summit in Ankara, beside Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Trump again claimed that the United States should control Greenland. The Alliance reaffirmed Ukraine’s sovereignty, celebrated its unity and erased Greenland. Mark Rutte answered with Russia, China and Arctic security.

He answered security and abandoned sovereignty.

Trump’s claim depends on imperial fiction. In 1941, Danish envoy Henrik Kauffmann authorised American defence facilities in Greenland after Nazi Germany occupied Denmark. He granted access, not title. Liberated Denmark ratified the agreement. Washington later tried to buy the island. Copenhagen refused.

America returned nothing. It owned nothing.

Military access is not sovereignty. Strategic value confers no title. Vulnerability is not consent.

NATO recognises sabotage, cyberattacks, economic pressure and weaponised migration as hybrid threats. Yet between Article 4 consultation and Article 5 defence lies ungoverned coercion: tariffs, obstruction, border tests, eroded guarantees and protection weaponised into leverage.

That is NATO’s blind spot.

It requires Article 4.5: a Coercion Defence Protocol.

Once sustained coercion against an ally’s territorial integrity, political independence or security is attributed, consultation must trigger intelligence fusion, infrastructure defence, deployments, sanctions, exclusion and decoupling. The coercer cannot invoke consensus to judge its own conduct or veto the response.

The NATO label may be blocked. Allied action may not.

Greenland’s constitutional order is layered, not ambiguous. It is an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark and the homeland of a people entitled to determine their future. Copenhagen holds constitutional responsibility. Nuuk holds democratic legitimacy. Neither can erase the other. Washington can erase neither.

The United States operates Pituffik Space Base by agreement. That presence may expand, contract or end by agreement.

Presence remains permission. It never ripens into possession.

Sovereignty, however, requires endurance. Greenland needs continuity in warning, command, logistics, cyber and critical infrastructure. American forces may remain. Dependency may not. Refusal is sovereign only when the system survives it.

The same blind spot shields Turkey in the Aegean. Ankara threatens war over a lawful Greek extension of territorial waters, challenges Greek sovereignty, obstructs surveys, cables and energy activity, and calibrates pressure below conflict.

These are not disputes. They are a coercive architecture designed to narrow Greek choices while exploiting NATO consensus as immunity.

Cyprus is the destination. Turkey has occupied its north since 1974. NATO did not recognise the occupation. It routinised it. Ankara remained useful, summits continued, privileges endured and the breach acquired procedure.

Administration accomplished what recognition could not: permanence without legitimacy.

In Ankara, Trump and Erdogan furnished each other with alibis. Turkey’s occupation offered Trump a precedent for coercion branded as protection. Trump’s Greenland claim gave Erdogan cover to repackage occupation as security.

Neither legitimises the other. Each launders the other.

Russia exploits the same grey zone through sabotage, border provocations, covert violence and deniable escalation. Article 4.5 treats the sequence as a campaign before ambiguity becomes immunity.

Europe needs Lisbon 2.0: not another treaty, but Lisbon put to work. Command, infrastructure, mobility, finance, energy, industry, sanctions and access must align before coercion isolates a state.

That doctrine prevents Turkish pressure on Greece from being quarantined as bilateral, Cyprus from being administered into permanence, Denmark from facing Washington alone and Russian operations from dissolving into disconnected national incidents.

Mutual defence must prevent isolation, not merely answer invasion.

Trump’s doctrine extends beyond Greenland. His “Trump Corollary” converts hemispheric security into an American veto over other states’ territory, alignments and strategic assets. Admit that principle in Greenland and it travels to French Guiana, European territory in South America and home to Europe’s spaceport.

A protector who demands control is a coercer.

Greenland exposed NATO’s blind spot: coercion from within. The Alliance cannot defend sovereignty against Russia while excusing its erosion by the United States and Turkey.

That is not unity. It is immunity for the powerful.

Article 4.5 sets the rule. Lisbon 2.0 preserves European action. Sovereign capacity gives refusal force.

Without them, access becomes authority, protection becomes leverage and sovereignty becomes permission.

text:
Middleweights Farid Salim and Wilbert McClure weigh in, on August 4, 1962, for their 10-round middleweight bout at Madison Square Garden. 

The undefeated (9-0-0) McLure, who won the Light Middleweight Gold Medal for the United States at the 1960 Olympics in Rome, Italy, defeating future Junior Middleweight Champion Carmelo Bossi in the final, will win a 10-round unanimous decision over the veteran Salim.

Salim, out of Argentina, would go 46-5-3 (18 KO's) during his career, losing to Rubin Carter, Joey Giambra, Joey Archer, Yama Bahama and McLure along the way and would never fight for a world title.
----------------------------------------------------------
From Mike Silver for Boxing Over Broadway (It is a long, but very worthwhile, read) following the passing of Wilbert McClure in 2020:

Dr. Wilbert “Skeeter” McClure, the former professional boxer, passed away last week at the age of 81. Between 1958 and 1960, Skeeter McClure won virtually every important national and international amateur boxing championship including Amateur Athletic Union (AAU), Golden Gloves (Chicago and Inter-City), Diamond Belt, Tournament of Champions, and Pan American Games. The crowning achievement to his brilliant amateur career was winning the Olympic Gold Medal in the light-middleweight divisionat the 1960 Olympics in Rome, Italy.
McClure’s roommate at the Olympics was another Gold Medal winner named Cassius Marcellus Clay. At that point, McClure was considered to be a more accomplished boxer than Clay. But whereas Clay, later known as Muhammad Ali, won the professional heavyweight championship in 1964 and became the most recognized face on the planet, McClure’s once promising professional career stagnated, never living up to expectations. One wonders how things might have turned out had McClure, like Clay, been guided by the savvy Angelo Dundee instead of the incompetents with whom he entrusted his professional boxing career. 
It is to McClure’s everlasting credit that he did not let the terrible mismanagement of his professional boxing career stop him from achieving great success in an entirely new profession. McClure had a college degree in literature and philosophy. After his pro career ended, he returned to school where he earned a master’s degree in counseling and, in 1973, a doctorate in psychology from Detroit’s Wayne State University. The Ohio native joined the teaching staff of Northeastern University in Boston, where he taught courses in counseling and psychology for five years. Over the next 20 years, McClure built a successful private clinical practice. In addition, he operated a consulting firm that provided corporations, non-profit foundations, and police departments with education and training in stress management, conflict resolution, team building, and performance evaluation.
Considering his post-boxing success, one might ask if it makes any difference that Skeeter did not win a professional boxing championship. I believe it absolutely does make a difference. McClure dedicated 17 years of his life to the sacrifice and discipline it takes to master the toughest of all sports. He had it within him not only to win a professional boxing title, but also to achieve all-time great status perhaps equal to or even exceeding that achieved by Muhammad Ali. Bad decisions made by the people he trusted to guide him to a title destroyed those dreams. The history of his pro boxing career serves as a primer for how to ruin a brilliant young prospect through appallingly careless matchmaking. 
As an Olympic gold medal winner, McClure would be a hot commodity if he were to turn pro today, especially considering that he was a college graduate. But the scenario in 1960 was quite different from today. An Olympic title, while desirable, did not automatically insure a megabuck promotional contract or a lucrative television deal. 
After considering several management offers, McClure signed on with a wealthy Ohio businessman whose hobby was managing professional fighters. This person hired a trainer who had been affiliated with Archie Moore, the great light heavyweight champion. Regrettably for McClure, both the businessman and the trainer proved to be clueless in the ability to make appropriate matches for the young phenom.  
McClure was drafted into the Army directly after the Olympics, but he was able to turn pro and fight several times while on leave. He won his ninth straight pro fight June 30, 1962 – a 6-round decision over Harold Richardson at Madison Square Garden. Teddy Brenner, the Garden’s matchmaker, was impressed with McClure’s performance and his sterling amateur background. Television was in need of new faces to fill a weekly schedule calling for almost fifty Garden main events per year. So, with a grand total of nine pro fights (5 KOs) and 39 rounds of professional experience, McClure was signed to fight the South American middleweight champion Farid Salim on August 4, 1962 at Madison Square Garden in front of a nationwide television audience. Salim, a rangy 6’ 2” middleweight had lost only two of forty professional fights. 
McClure was excited to be headlining at the world famous arena and wanted to be ready for his first major test as a pro.  I asked my trainer: ‘Is he a boxer? Does he have fast hands? What’s he got?’ And the answer I received was: ‘I don’t know.’   What the [expletive]! My first TV fight…10 rounds…and the son-of-a-gun doesn’t know anything about my opponent! No one [today] would do that to a fighter with a Gold Medal.”  McClure shook his head in disgust.  It was the same thing with everyone else I fought. I’d ask: ‘What has he got?’  Every first round was a surprise.
Despite the lack of advance knowledge, the former Olympian, a 12-to-5 underdog, was more than up to the task. He won a unanimous decision. His superlative boxing skills were a revelation to many who witnessed the bout. One reporter wrote:  McClure moves with the grace of a young Ray Robinson, hits with authority, and fights back furiously when hurt. Comparing a boxer with only ten pro bouts to Robinson, the greatest fighter who ever lived, was a huge compliment. More experience before taking on top contenders was all that McClure would have needed in order to realize his full potential.  
After four more fights, McClure was rated the eighth best middleweight in the world. But it was all happening too fast. There was little respite from one hard match to the next, all against top opposition. One didn’t have to be a boxing expert to know that McClure was being rushed into matches with fighters he should have avoided at that stage of his career.  At some point, the boxer must be tested against a quality opponent to see what he’s got, but the timing has to be right. Unfortunately, instead of being handled like a precious diamond in the rough that needed a master craftsman to cut and polish it, McClure was thrown to the lions while he was still learning the ropes as a pro. 
Considering his spectacular amateur accomplishments and the tremendous promise shown in his early professional bouts, the ruination of that great potential, through no fault of his own, makes Wilbert Skeeter McClure the most poorly managed fighter in the history of the sport. 
This is how it evolved: Six weeks after the bout with Farid Salim, McClure returned to his hometown of Toledo, Ohio and won a unanimous 10-round decision over tough Tony Montano, a 37-bout pro who’d competed with several world ranked boxers. Three weeks after the bout with Montano, McClure was back in the Garden meeting 63-bout veteran Gomeo Brennan. Once again displaying fighting spirit and superb boxing smarts, McClure won a hard-fought 10-round decision over a far more experienced opponent.  In early 1963, he returned to Toledo to outpoint former welterweight contender Ted Wright, a veteran of 60 professional bouts. 
Amazingly, despite his limited professional experience, he was good enough to be competitive with these seasoned veterans, even outpointing them, but every fight was tough. He certainly wasn’t being overprotected, that’s for sure. In fact, in his 33 professional fights, only five opponents had losing records.  As if to emphasize this point, in his next fight, on October 18, 1963, McClure was matched against the great former welterweight champion Luis Rodriguez in yet another nationally televised fight from Madison Square Garden. 
Rodriguez was a substitute for Jose Gonzales, a granite-chinned contender who six months earlier had withstood the bombs of “Hurricane” Carter and stopped the feared puncher on a cut in the sixth round. When Gonzales was injured in training, he pulled out of the scheduled bout with McClure; Luis replaced him. A bout with Gonzales would have meant another punishing contest for McClure, but taking on Rodriguez made even less sense. 
McClure didn’t have to ask about Rodriguez. The great Cuban boxer was a former welterweight champion and one of the ten best fighters in the world. His only losses in 55 bouts were against Emile Griffith and Curtis Cokes. Rodriguez was capable of beating the world’s top welterweights and middleweights. He had scored a stunning ninth-round knockout of middleweight contender Denny Moyer in his most recent fight. Luis had a total of 430 professional rounds compared to McClure’s mere 14 fights and 85 rounds. 
McClure knew that he was not ready for Rodriguez. He told his manager and trainer that he thought they were crazy for accepting him as an opponent at this stage of his career.  We argued for two days, said McClure. I was just so tired of all this crap. Isolated in a remote New Jersey training camp, the young fighter was fatigued and disgusted. But, his handlers eventually convinced him to accept the match, saying that his weight advantage of nine pounds would give him an edge. 
Meeting a fighter of Rodriguez’s stature in his 15th professional bout was both negligent and stupid. 
Compare it to the early career of future middleweight champion Marvin Hagler who turned pro after winning the National AAU light-middleweight championship in 1973. 
In Hagler’s 15th pro bout, he won a 10-round decision over Sugar Ray Seales, the 1968 Olympic gold medalist. It was Seale’s first defeat in 22 bouts. Hagler’s next two opponents had a combined record of 5-14-3.  
Another future middleweight champion, Roy Jones Jr., a light middleweight Silver medalist in the 1988 Olympics, had a spectacular amateur record similar to McClure’s.  In his 15th pro bout, Jones KO’d Lester Yarbrough who came into the ring with a 12-16-1 record and would win only one of his next 34 bouts. 
Neither of these future pro champions faced the type of brutal competition that McClure had to contend with during his first two years as a pro. 
Of course it was a forgone conclusion that Skeeter would lose. 
Once again displaying the heart and talent of a true champion, and despite being dropped for the first time, the overmatched Olympian actually gave Rodriguez a tough fight. The Cuban won a unanimous 10-round decision, but he had to work hard for the victory. Even Rodriguez was impressed. Give that kid another year, he said, and he’ll be champion.
After that fight, Skeeter should have taken a rest and then taken on a series of lesser opponents, while at the same time perfecting his professional skills. Instead, Brenner insisted on a rematch two months later. After all, their first televised fight was exciting and interesting so why not do it again? McClure’s management should have refused the rematch.  
It is a truism in the unforgiving world of professional boxing that a quick rematch between an inexperienced boxer and an old pro is just asking for trouble. The old pro will use his vast experience to figure out what to do in the rematch while the inexperienced boxer will be at a distinct disadvantage. 
And that is exactly what happened. Rodriguez adjusted his strategy and concentrated his attack on McClure’s body to slow him up and bring down his guard.  In Round 6, Rodriguez dropped McClure for an 8-count with a solid left hook to the jaw. Once again McClure got up and fought his heart out. He was able to win a few rounds but lost another unanimous decision in a punishing fight. Putting McClure into the ring with Luis Rodriguez for his 15th and 16 fight was not just bad matchmaking, it bordered on criminal negligence. 
A young boxer doesn’t walk away from a series of tough and punishing fights without paying a price. If it happens often enough there will come a time in the abused boxer’s professional life when something changes within him.  It can happen after one vicious beating, or it can take place over the course of several tough fights with too little time to rest between them. The change can be dramatic, or it can be subtle and unrecognizable except to an experienced trainer or someone close to the boxer. The damage is both physical and psychological. Eventually the law of diminishing returns takes effect as progress ends and potential is blunted. 
The boxing portion of this story could very well end here even though Skeeter went on to fight 14 more times over the next four years. 
Five months after the Rodriguez debacle, there was a 10-round decision loss to future light-heavyweight champion Jose Torres (another Garden fight McClure needed like a hole in the head); only two fights in 1965, and in 1966, a pair of back-to-back 10-rounders spaced two months apart with murderous-hitting middleweight contender Rubin “Hurricane” Carter. McClure lost a decision in the first bout and fought to a draw in the second. The cost of those two fights added to the erosion of this once brilliant prospect. 
The decline was underscored four months later when he lost a 10-round decision to unrated Harold Richardson, the same fighter he previously had beaten easily. It was McClure’s 24th professional fight and his fifth loss. 
Comparisons to Sugar Ray Robinson were long past. He had been put in too deep too early, and sunk.
Yet, it took a while for this proud and intelligent boxer to finally accept the inevitable, to acknowledge that the boxing part of his life was ended. 
In 1967, after being stopped for the first time in his career by Johnny Smith and then losing a lackluster 10-round decision to England’s Johnny Pritchett, McClure hung up his gloves. His record was 23-7-1 (11 KOs). Three years later, feeling the itch to give it one more try, he had two more fights and then retired for good. 
Although a large part of the blame for McClure’s failed boxing career goes to his managers, the person who was most responsible for ruining him was Teddy Brenner, the powerful Madison Square Garden matchmaker. 
Both Brenner and Harry Markson, the director of the Garden’s boxing department, were uninterested (or perhaps incapable) of using the resources, reputation, and influence of the world’s most famous arena to its fullest capacity. Developing and nurturing new talent was not a priority with them. 
There are people who mistakenly hail Brenner as a great matchmaker. 
The facts do not support that opinion. 
During his tenure at the Garden (1959 to 1977), Brenner made some good matches, but he did far more damage by destroying the careers of at least a score of very promising young fighters, including McClure, by overmatching them against superior opposition before they were ready. This pattern was repeated far too often. Brenner knew better but just didn’t care.  If the result of a match ended up ruining a prospect, so be it. It was of no concern to either Brenner or Markson. Their weekly paychecks arrived whether they put on a good show or not. They would also abuse their power by favoring certain “house fighters” handled by compliant managers who never argued with Brenner’s choice of opponent. Making matters worse, the marketing skills of Brenner and Markson were negligible. The great arena was running on its reputation and interest was dwindling. One time, near the end of their tenure, in a fit of pique they revoked the press privileges of a journalist who dared to criticize one of their awful matches in print. So much for freedom of the press.  
In those days the prestige of appearing in a main event at Madison Square Garden was second only to winning a world title. Even when matched against an opponent that was all wrong for their fighter, managers were reluctant to turn down a Garden main event.  
But it didn’t have to be that way. In Los Angeles, during the same period, promoters George Parnassus and Aileen Eaton were carefully developing and nurturing local talent and making the sport hugely popular without benefit of a national television sponsorship. 
But because this is an article in tribute to Wilbert McClure, I won’t go into further details about the destructive nature of Brenner and Markson’s arrogance and incompetence. Suffice it to say that boxing suffered as a result. 
McClure was not prone to self-pity, nor did he live in the past. His positive attitude helped him to start over in an entirely new field. But boxing was not totally out of his life. From 1995 to 1998, he served as chairman of the Massachusetts Boxing Commission where one of his chief priorities was the athletes’ safety. He especially was concerned about over-the hill-boxers who can no longer properly defend themselves yet still are allowed to fight. The boxing community, said McClure, especially the state commissions, ought to have more courage lifting the licenses of fighters who cannot and should not do it anymore. During my tenure as chairman, I was threatened with lawsuits by managers because we suspended those boxers who couldn’t fight anymore.
When asked to evaluate today’s fighters McClure’s response was precise. 
You cannot become skilled and polished if you are fighting two or three times a year. 
When you’ve got fighters challenging for a world title with 15 pro fights, you know you’ve got a problem. It makes it difficult to appraise the top boxers of today based on what they have accomplished. It is not scientifically sound, accurate, or fair. I feel sorry for Roy Jones Jr. because he hasn’t fought a great or even a very skillful opponent yet. So he cannot be placed in the pantheon of great middleweights because it takes great opponents to make great fighters.
McClure also said that welterweight champ Oscar de La Hoya, although still a work in progress, was lucky that there were no Kid Gavilans around to test him. 
Put Oscar in the ring with Gavilan when he was champion, or a Ray Robinson when he was champ or a Tony Zale. Those guys were tough, man. There isn’t any way in the damn world you’re going to hurt them…and they will hurt you badly. It is a lesson that Skeeter learned the hard way. 
Wilbert “Skeeter” McClure, a gracious and intelligent man, made his mark both inside and outside of the boxing ring. But most importantly, he lived his life with meaning and purpose.

text:
History is often hidden in the memories and belongings of those who lived through it.
The Army Institute of Military History hosted Major General Yasin (retd.) for an exclusive guest lecture on "East Pakistan 1971: War and Prison Camp Experiences." Drawing on his firsthand experiences as a prisoner of war, he offered interns a deeply personal perspective on one of the most defining chapters in the Subcontinent's military history.
The session explored the human dimensions of conflict, the importance of resilience, faith, and perseverance, and encouraged young participants to value knowledge, make meaningful use of their time, and dedicate themselves to a purpose greater than themselves.
Adding a rare personal dimension to the lecture, Major General Yasin shared personal belongings that accompanied him during his years as a prisoner of war, including a shaving mirror, a copy of “My Experiments with Truth” by Mahatma Gandhi, and a water bottle dating back to the Second World War.
Together, these objects served as tangible reminders that history is not only documented in records, but also carried through the lives and experiences of those who witnessed it.

text:
Not all heroes move mountains. Some just roll in the sand 🐿️❤️ :

In the Sri Vaishnava tradition, the lila of the squirrel during the construction of the Ram Setu is celebrated as one of the most profound examples of pure devotion, immortalized in the hymns of the Alvars. According to this narrative, specifically highlighted by Thondaradippodi Alvar in his sacred Tamil composition known as the Tirumaalai, Lord Rama's army of mighty Vanaras was engaged in the colossal task of building a bridge across the ocean to Lanka. The monkeys were uprooting massive trees, hauling gigantic boulders, and heaving entire mountains into the sea. Amidst this awe-inspiring display of physical strength, a tiny, unassuming squirrel felt an overwhelming, spontaneous urge to participate in the Lord’s mission and offer its own humble service.  

Unable to lift heavy stones or branches, the squirrel devised its own unique method of contributing to the bridge. It scurried down to the ocean to dip its little body in the waves, ran back to the beach to roll in the dry sand until its wet fur was completely coated, and then hurried to the dam site to vigorously shake the sand particles off into the water. It performed this repetitive task tirelessly, completely absorbed in its loving service. According to tradition, Lord Rama noticed this seemingly insignificant creature and was profoundly touched by its absolute dedication. He tenderly picked up the squirrel and stroked its back with his fingers, leaving behind the distinct stripes that Indian squirrels bear to this day as a permanent mark of divine grace.  

The Alvar draws deeply humbling spiritual lessons from this pastime, primarily emphasizing that the Divine does not measure devotion by the magnitude, scale, or material value of the offering, but entirely by the sincerity and purity of the devotee's heart. In his poetic verses, the Alvar laments his own spiritual state, expressing deep regret that his heart lacks the spontaneous, unquestioning eagerness to serve the Lord that the tiny squirrel possessed. The squirrel did not feel inadequate compared to the giant monkeys, nor did it let its physical limitations or the smallness of its contribution stop it from acting. It simply offered everything it had, teaching that true devotion and unconditional surrender (Saranagati) are entirely free from ego, self-consciousness, and the desire for recognition.  

Furthermore, the squirrel's lila embodies the core Vaishnava philosophy of kainkarya (joyful, selfless service to the Divine). It illustrates that every living being, regardless of their birth, status, power, or capacity, is fully qualified to serve the Supreme and can attain His grace. The squirrel’s handful of sand was accepted by Rama with the exact same love as the mountains moved by Hanuman and the other Vanaras. Through the Alvar’s profound reflections, the humble squirrel is elevated to the status of a great spiritual teacher, reminding devotees that even the most minuscule act of sincere love is cherished by the Lord, and that no service offered to the Divine with a pure heart is ever too small.

THEY TOOK THE CŘÝ OF NIGERIANS TO THE PRESIDENT. THEY RETURNED WITH AN ANSWER THAT SHOULD WORRY US ALL.

The Catholic Bishops didn't go to Aso Rock seeking contracts.

They didn't go lobbying for appointments.

They didn't go "standing on any mandate."

They went carrying the pain of millions of Nigerians.

They said Nigerians are hungřy.

The answer? "There has always been hunger before I was born."

They said the economy is crushing ordinary families.

The answer? "The economy is doing well."

They expressed concerns about public confidence in INEC.

The answer? "INEC is neutral."

They worried about whether the next election would offer a level playing field.

The answer? "Whoever wants power should be ready to wrestle for it."

And immediately, my mind went to Rehoboam.

The people begged him to reduce their suff£ring.

The elders pleaded with him: "Listen to your people."

His loyalists told him: "Show them who's boss."

He listened to the loyalists.

He ignored the people.

The result?

A kingdom that took generations to build split in a single day.

The people walked away shouting:

"To your tents, O Israel!" (1 Kings 12:16)

Every government should fear one thing more than criticism:

The day it stops listening.

The greatest threat to any president is not the opposition.

It is the army of professional cheerleaders who tell him that everything is working while the people are telling a different story.

A nation cannot be governed by applause.

Propaganda cannot fill empty stomachs.

Slogans cannot reduce the cost of living.

And praise-singers cannot rewrite reality.

History is littered with leaders who mistook loyalty for truth.

May President Tinubu never become another Rehoboam, surrounded by people who protect his ego while exposing his legacy.

Because when leaders stop listening, history starts speaking.

text:
A French candy maker spent 14 years boiling meat, milk, eggs, and vegetables inside sealed glass bottles.

He did not know bacteria existed.

But his strange experiment created the method behind canned food.

His name was Nicolas Appert.

In the late 1700s, France had a serious military problem.

Its soldiers could travel hundreds of miles.

Their food could not.

Fresh meat quickly spoiled. Milk turned sour. Fruits and vegetables rotted before they reached the soldiers.

Armies depended on food that was salted, smoked, or dried.

It lasted longer, but often tasted terrible and lacked the nutrition soldiers needed during long campaigns.

Hunger and disease could weaken an army before it even reached the battlefield.

So in 1795, the French government offered 12,000 francs to anyone who could find a reliable way to preserve large amounts of food.

It was a fortune.

Scientists and inventors had every reason to chase it.

But Appert approached the problem like a cook.

He had worked in kitchens, breweries, and confectionery shops. He understood how food reacted to heat, air, and different containers.

He began filling glass bottles with almost anything he could find.

Beef. Chicken. Eggs. Milk. Soup. Beans. Peas. Fruit.

He sealed the bottles with cork, wire, and wax.

Then he placed them in boiling water.

Afterward, he waited.

Some bottles broke under the heat.

Some seals leaked.

Some food still spoiled.

Appert changed the cooking time, temperature, bottle shape, and sealing method.

Then he tried again.

Year after year, he kept testing.

Eventually, he noticed a pattern.

If the food was heated properly and the bottle remained completely sealed, it could stay edible for months.

Appert had discovered the basic principle behind modern canning.

But he had no idea why it worked.

The science of microorganisms did not exist yet. Louis Pasteur would not prove the connection between microbes and food spoilage until decades later.

Appert was solving an invisible problem without knowing what the enemy was.

He only had observation, patience, and thousands of failed experiments.

The French navy tested his preserved food on long voyages.

Months later, the meat, vegetables, and milk were still safe to eat.

In 1810, the French government awarded Appert the 12,000 francs.

But the reward came with a condition.

He had to make his method public.

Appert accepted.

He published a book explaining how anyone could preserve meat, vegetables, fruit, milk, and prepared meals using heat and airtight containers.

Thousands of copies were printed.

His 14 years of work were no longer confined to his workshop.

Anyone could learn from them.

Appert originally used glass bottles, not metal cans.

Later, an English merchant named Peter Durand patented a similar process using tin containers.

Tin was stronger than glass, easier to transport, and far more useful aboard ships and military wagons.

That improvement gave us the can we recognize today.

But the method inside it came from Appert.

His discovery changed military supplies, ocean travel, disaster relief, and eventually everyday life.

Today, canned food feels ordinary.

We walk past entire supermarket aisles filled with it without thinking twice.

But behind every can is a confectioner who spent 14 years boiling food inside glass bottles.

Nicolas Appert never saw a bacterium.

He still found a way to defeat billions of them.

Connecting the Ptolemaic bloodline to Simon Magus involves overlapping real ancient history with fringe esoteric theories, Gnostic mythos, and occult traditions.
1. Who Was Simon Magus?Historical/Biblical Figure: Simon was a 1st-century Samaritan magician mentioned in [Acts 8:9]. He amazed people with sorcery, converted to Christianity, and tried to buy the power to bestow the Holy Spirit from the Apostles Peter and John.
The "Father of Heresies": Early Church writers (such as Irenaeus and Justin Martyr) labeled him as the founder of Gnosticism, a movement that taught salvation through secret knowledge.
Divine Partner: He traveled with a woman named Helena, a former prostitute from Tyre, whom he claimed was his divine female counterpart, the "Ennoia" or "First Thought" of God.
2. The Ptolemaic Connection: Fringe History & Esotericism
The Ptolemaic dynasty was the Greek royal family that ruled Egypt from 305 to 30 BCE, ending with Cleopatra VII. In academic history, there is no direct lineage linking Simon Magus to the Ptolemies. However, fringe and occult historians connect them through a few distinct channels:
Hellenistic Samaria: Samaria, where Simon Magus lived, was deeply influenced by Hellenistic culture and ruled by various Macedonian generals and Hellenized elites following Alexander the Great's conquests.
The "Ptolemaic Bloodline" Conspiracy: In alternative history circles (such as the theories proposed in Holy Blood, Holy Grail), the Ptolemaic dynasty is claimed to have intermingled with Jewish, Herodian, and even Davidic lineages. Theorists often claim this "sacred bloodline" (or the Desposyni) survived and merged with other Gnostic teachers, including Simon Magus.The Alexandria Link: Alexandria, the capital of the Ptolemaic Empire, was the birthplace of Western Gnosticism (e.g., the teacher Basilides). Many esoteric theorists argue that Simon Magus’s teachings were a blend of Samaritan magic and the mystical philosophy taught in Ptolemaic Alexandria.

Sako
Origin & Etymology: Sako operates on a few different historical tracks depending on the region:
In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.
In the Balkans: In Albania, it functions as a standalone occupational surname for a "church servant" or as a nickname for the Muslim name Isak (Isaac).

What was the Levitical priesthood?
Answer
The Levitical priesthood began with Aaron, the older brother of Moses (Exodus 28:1–3). Aaron’s descendants served as the priests in Israel, ministering in the tabernacle and, later, the temple, primarily as mediators between man and God. The Levitical priests bore the responsibility of offering the sacrifices required by the Mosaic Law. Some of the Levitical priests in the Bible are Ezra; Eli; and Zechariah, the father of John the Baptist.

The term Levitical is derived from the Israelite tribe of Levi. Levi was the third son of Leah and Jacob (Genesis 29:34) and the father of the tribe of Levi, the tribe of Moses and Aaron. Originally, it was the firstborn son of every family who was consecrated to God and inherited the birthright, leadership, authority, etc. (Exodus 13:2). We see this institution of “first” things being what God requires as far back as Genesis 4:4 when God was pleased with the firstborn of Abel’s flock that he offered to God (see Proverbs 3:9 and Romans 11:16). Later, when God made Israel into a nation, He called them His firstborn son (Exodus 4:22–23), and each individual Israelite was called to be holy, priestly, and royal (Exodus 19:5–6). And then out of the nation of Israel God chose the tribe of Levi to serve Him and the sons of Aaron to be the priests. Thus, all priests were Levites, but not every Levite was a priest.

Some Bible commentators have said God chose the tribe of Levi to be His priests because they were obedient to God after the infamous “golden calf” incident at the foot of Mt. Sinai (Exodus 32:26–29). However, God had made Levi’s tribe priestly before that time (Exodus 28:1–4). Furthermore, on his deathbed, Jacob had issued a stern malediction against his son Levi (Genesis 49:5–7). Patriarchal prophecies such as these were not taken lightly, and Jacob’s words must have dealt Levi a sharp blow.

Jacob’s prophecy that Levi’s descendants would be scattered throughout Israel (Genesis 49:7) was fulfilled when God appointed them as the priestly tribe who, unlike the other tribes, would receive no land inheritance. However, in God’s sovereign and mysterious way, Jacob’s prophecy turned into a blessing because Levi’s inheritance was better than land—it was God Himself (Numbers 18:20). And God promised to provide for the Levites from the abundance of all of the other tribes (Numbers 18:8–14).

The Levites who were not priests were given various duties in the caretaking of the tabernacle and its furnishings (Numbers 3:21–26). The priests among the Levites were given the immeasurable privilege of doing service in the tabernacle. The Levitical priests also served as judges (Deuteronomy 17:8–13) and teachers of God’s law (Deuteronomy 33:10).

The high priest could deliver edicts to guide the nation (Numbers 27:21). He was the only one permitted to enter the Most Holy Place (1 Chronicles 6:49; Leviticus 24:9), divided by a curtain from the rest of the tabernacle and containing the Ark of the Testimony (or Covenant), the symbol of God’s very presence (Hebrews 9:3; 1 Kings 8:6; Exodus 25:22). The high priest could only enter the Most Holy Place once a year on the Day of Atonement to offer sacrifices for all the people, including himself (Hebrews 9:7). There was only one high priest at a time.

God held the priests to the most stringent standards of behavior and ritual purity (Leviticus 21). Abihu and Nadab were sons of Aaron and two of the first priests. They disobeyed God, however, and were instantly struck down (Leviticus 10:1–2). Later, the sons of the high priest Eli “treated the offering of the Lord with contempt” and were also judged (1 Samuel 2:12–17).

In the time of Christ, the Sadducees comprised most of the priesthood and were known to be a wealthy class of people. The Sadducees did not believe in a resurrection (Matthew 22:23) or in any kind of spiritual realm such as angels and demons (see Acts 23:8). The chief priests Caiaphas and Annas were instrumental in having Jesus crucified (John 18:13).

The Levitical priesthood was never intended to be permanent (Hebrews 7:11). The death of Christ put an end to the Old Covenant and the Levitical priesthood, as evidenced by the rending of the temple veil (Matthew 27:51). Now Jesus Himself serves as the believer’s Great High Priest (Hebrews 4:14), called according to the order of Melchizedek, not of Levi (Hebrews 7:11–17). Through His death and resurrection, we have access to God’s presence, where we can freely enjoy Him forever (Hebrews 6:19–20).

🌍 Commodity Markets Daily: Energy Routes Are Being Redrawn | August 4, 2026
（📍Data From https://t.co/rtKhA53pFF Daily Report）

The global energy market is no longer asking only how much oil and gas exist. It is asking which refinery is still operating, which pipeline remains open and how many extra miles a tanker must travel before someone dares insure it.

Six Saudi supertankers are rerouting around Africa, Kazakhstan’s output has fallen 14%, a Russian refinery has stopped operating and the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve is back at its lowest level since 1983.

Meanwhile, politicians would still like cheaper gasoline immediately.

⚡ Energy

⛽ Trump Demands Lower Retail Fuel Prices

• President Trump called on major oil companies to reduce retail fuel prices immediately.

The political objective is obvious: gasoline is one of the most visible components of household inflation.

But retail prices are determined by more than crude oil:

• Refinery utilization.
• Regional inventories.
• Transportation costs.
• Taxes and blending requirements.
• Distribution margins.
• Geopolitical supply premiums.

Political pressure may encourage refiners and retailers to compress margins, but it cannot restore a damaged refinery or shorten a tanker’s voyage around Africa.
Washington wants lower pump prices. The physical market has apparently not subscribed to the presidential social-media feed.
🇿🇦 South Africa Cuts Gasoline Prices
• South Africa said gasoline prices would fall by 52 cents per liter in August.
The reduction should provide some relief to households and transportation businesses.
The final economic benefit will depend on global oil prices, refining costs and the rand’s exchange rate. A weaker currency could quickly offset the advantage of lower international fuel prices.

🇰🇼 Kuwait Raises Crude Production

• Kuwait’s July crude production rose to its highest level since the outbreak of the Middle East war.

The increase could partially compensate for disrupted supply elsewhere in the region.

However, additional production only helps if export terminals, tankers and shipping lanes remain available. In the current market, producing a barrel and delivering it have become two separate geopolitical achievements.

🇧🇪 Belgium Becomes Fully Dependent on Russian LNG

• The Iran war reportedly left Belgium entirely dependent on Russian liquefied natural gas during July.

The development illustrates how disruption in one energy corridor can increase reliance on politically sensitive suppliers elsewhere.

Europe spent years discussing energy diversification. A fresh crisis has demonstrated that “diversified” sometimes means purchasing from whichever supplier still has an available vessel.

The situation could increase pressure on European policymakers to expand:

• LNG storage.
• Alternative supply contracts.
• Regasification capacity.
• Pipeline flexibility.
• Strategic gas reserves.

🇰🇿 Kazakhstan Production Falls 14%

• Kazakhstan’s July oil and gas-condensate production declined 14% from June.
• The drop followed disruptions to exports through the Caspian Pipeline Consortium system.

The decline shows how pipeline bottlenecks can force producers to reduce output even when wells remain operational.

If the disruption persists, it could tighten supplies of CPC Blend crude and affect buyers across Europe and the Mediterranean.

For Kazakhstan, lower production also means reduced export revenue and greater pressure on fiscal and currency policy.

🇷🇺 TurkStream Gas Flows Decline
• Gazprom supplied an average of 48.8 million cubic meters of gas per day to Europe through TurkStream in July.
• Daily flows were 5.2% lower than one year earlier.
The decline adds another layer of uncertainty to Europe’s gas balance.
Key variables include:
• Storage levels.
• LNG arrivals.
• Asian LNG competition.
• Weather and electricity demand.
• Pipeline security.
• Further sanctions or payment restrictions.

Europe may enter the next winter with storage tanks. The uncomfortable question is what it will cost to refill them afterward.

🇮🇳 India Raises Fuel Export Taxes
• India increased the windfall tax on gasoline exports from ₹2.5 to ₹3.5 per liter from August 3.
• The diesel export tax was raised to ₹24 per liter.

The policy is designed to protect domestic supply and capture additional profits from exporters.

Higher taxes could reduce the incentive to export refined products, potentially tightening diesel and gasoline availability in regional markets while improving domestic supply.

Diesel matters particularly because it powers freight, agriculture, construction and industrial activity. A reduction in Indian exports could strengthen refining margins elsewhere.

🚢 Six Saudi VLCCs Reroute Around Africa

• Six empty Saudi-flagged very large crude carriers recently changed course in the Gulf of Aden.
• The vessels began traveling toward southern Africa instead of continuing through the higher-risk route.
• At least one tanker listed Gibraltar as its destination.
The coordinated rerouting suggests shipowners and charterers are actively reassessing Red Sea and Gulf of Aden risks.

Longer voyages around the Cape of Good Hope can:

• Increase freight rates.
• Reduce effective tanker availability.
• Increase fuel consumption.
• Delay cargo delivery.
• Raise insurance and financing costs.
• Tighten the physical oil market without removing a single barrel of production.

The oil still exists. It is simply taking the scenic route at several hundred thousand dollars per day.
🏭 Lukoil Refinery Halts Operations
• Lukoil’s Volgograd refinery reportedly suspended processing after a drone attack on July 31.
A prolonged shutdown could reduce Russian refined-product output and affect domestic or export availability.
The market impact will depend on:
• The scale of the damage.
• Available inventories.
• Repair duration.
• Utilization at alternative refineries.
• Government restrictions on fuel exports.

Crude production attracts the headlines, but refinery outages often determine what drivers and industrial users actually pay.

🇺🇸 US Strategic Reserve Hits a 43-Year Low

• US Strategic Petroleum Reserve inventories declined by approximately 2.85 million barrels last week.
• Stocks fell to 304.8 million barrels, the lowest level since 1983.
The decline reduces Washington’s emergency cushion at a time when Middle East supply routes and global refinery operations remain vulnerable.

A smaller reserve does not mean the US is about to run out of oil. It means policymakers have less room to respond to another major disruption without relying on domestic producers, imports or demand destruction.

The strategic reserve is intended for emergencies. The market is beginning to wonder how many emergencies remain included in the current subscription.

🇮🇶 Iraq Reports July Crude Sales

• Iraq sold 35.5 million barrels from southern ports during July.
• Another 7 million barrels were sold through the Ceyhan terminal.

The flows provide meaningful supply to global markets, but Iraq remains exposed to regional security conditions, infrastructure constraints and political disagreements over export revenue.
Any disruption to southern terminals or the Ceyhan route would have immediate implications for Mediterranean and Asian buyers.
🇻🇪 Venezuela’s Export Mix Shifts

• Venezuela exported approximately 1.16 million barrels per day in July, slightly below the previous month.
• Shipments to the US increased to around 786,000 barrels per day.
• Exports to Europe fell to approximately 82,200 barrels per day.
• Shipments to India declined to around 178,000 barrels per day.

The data show that total exports were relatively stable, but destination flows changed significantly.

Higher US purchases may influence Gulf Coast refinery supply, while lower shipments to Europe and India could force those buyers to seek replacement heavy crude elsewhere.
🌾 Agriculture and Mining
🌴 Indian Palm Oil Imports Surge 50%
• India imported approximately 733,000 tonnes of palm oil in July.
• Imports increased 50% from June and reached their highest level in five months.
The increase signals stronger restocking or improved palm oil competitiveness relative to soybean and sunflower oils.
Higher Indian demand could support benchmark palm oil prices, but the impact may be offset by rising Malaysian production and inventories.

🇲🇾 Malaysian Inventories Approach a Five-Month High

• Malaysia’s July palm oil inventories are expected to reach their highest level in five months as production increases.

This creates a direct contest between stronger Indian imports and expanding Malaysian supply.

If production grows faster than exports, inventories could continue rising and limit price gains.

Palm oil bulls have demand. Bears have warehouses. The monthly inventory report will decide who brought the larger number.

🌾 Thailand and Indonesia Expand Agricultural Trade
• Thailand plans to import 100,000 tonnes of urea annually from Indonesia.
• Thailand also offered to become a reliable rice supplier to Indonesia.
The arrangement could strengthen regional food and fertilizer security.
For agricultural markets, it reflects increasing government efforts to secure long-term bilateral supply instead of relying entirely on volatile spot markets.
⛏️ White House Plans Mining Executive Meeting

• President Trump is expected to attend a roundtable with mining executives on Friday.

Potential topics could include:

• Critical-mineral security.
• Domestic mining permits.
• Processing capacity.
• Strategic stockpiles.
• Foreign supply dependence.
• Investment incentives.
• Environmental regulations.
The meeting could be significant for copper, lithium, rare earths and other minerals linked to defense, energy infrastructure and AI data centers.

🇺🇦 Ukraine Adjusts Agricultural Export Prices

• Ukraine temporarily modified minimum export prices for certain agricultural products.
• The measure is intended to prevent disruptions to grain and oilseed exports during the stabilization period.

The policy could help maintain trade flows while limiting disorderly pricing or tax avoidance.

Global grain markets remain sensitive to Ukrainian logistics, Black Sea security and changes in export regulation.

⚠️ Strait of Hormuz: Negotiations Continue
🤝 Iran and Oman Approach a Navigation Agreement

• US and Iranian officials said Iran and Oman were close to an agreement governing navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

A workable agreement could reduce shipping risk premiums, improve tanker availability and pressure oil prices lower.

However, the details will determine whether the arrangement is commercially viable and politically acceptable.

🚫 Iran Rejects a Non-Iranian Route
• A senior Iranian official said the country would not allow the US to establish a route through the strait that avoids Iranian waters.
The statement shows that control and sovereignty remain central to negotiations.
Any arrangement that does not address Iran’s role may fail to produce durable shipping security.

⏳ Trump Calls Talks Iran’s “Final Chance”

• President Trump confirmed that negotiations with Iran were continuing.
• He described the talks as Iran’s final opportunity.

The rhetoric keeps military risk elevated even while negotiations progress.

Commodity markets must therefore price two conflicting possibilities:

• An agreement reopening safer shipping routes.
• A breakdown producing renewed attacks and supply disruption.
Diplomacy is currently bearish for oil. The phrase “final chance” is doing its best to keep the risk premium employed.

📌 Key Takeaways

• Energy flows are being reshaped by war, refinery outages and shipping risks.
• Saudi tanker rerouting could increase freight costs and reduce effective vessel supply.
• Kazakhstan’s output decline and the Russian refinery shutdown tighten regional availability.
• The US strategic reserve has fallen to its lowest level since 1983.
• India’s higher export taxes could reduce regional fuel supply.
• Strong Indian palm oil imports are competing with rising Malaysian inventories.
• Hormuz negotiations offer downside risk for oil, but failure could trigger another sharp price spike.

👀 What Commodity Traders Should Watch

• Confirmation of the Hormuz navigation agreement.
• Saudi tanker routes and VLCC freight rates.
• Repair timelines at the Volgograd refinery.
• CPC pipeline export operations.
• US strategic-reserve policy.
• Indian diesel export volumes after the tax increase.
• European LNG flows and storage levels.
• Malaysian palm oil inventories.
• Further attacks on energy infrastructure.
• Outcomes from the White House mining roundtable.

The world does not currently have one energy market. It has several regional markets connected by longer shipping routes, political negotiations and increasingly nervous insurers.

Supply has not disappeared. It has become slower, more expensive and much more selective about which direction it travels.

text:
On July 1, I had to put down my dog, Bruno.

I got Bruno during a season of my life when I needed protection more than I needed a pet. For the next ten years, he quietly filled that role. I rarely posted about him because that just wasn’t our relationship.

I wasn’t looking for another dog.

Then one day, I logged into Facebook, and the very first post in my feed was someone trying to rehome a white husky.

It wasn’t from a friend. It wasn’t from a page I followed. I hadn’t searched for dogs. To this day, I have no idea why Facebook decided to show me that post.

My first thought wasn’t, “I need a puppy.”

My mom runs Pippa’s Paws, a rescue, so I reached out and offered to foster her until we could find her the right home.

Well…

We all know how well that turned out. 😂

That little white fluffball with one cloudy blue eye is now Luna, and somewhere along the way she decided this was her home.

Since then, she’s learned how to open doors, carries her buffalo horn around like it’s the greatest treasure on earth, sighs dramatically when she’s annoyed with me, and has completely taken over my house.

Funny how life works. I wasn’t looking for another dog. I was just trying to help one.

It turns out… I was the one who actually needed rescuing. ❤️

text:
This is the sad reality: 60,000 to 70,000 travelers are impacted by the strike every single day. That number accumulates with each passing day, so the queue only gets longer without a resolution.
There are simply not that many seats available on short notice — especially domestically in Canada — at any time of year, but particularly during the summer peak and at the end of a long weekend.

Other airlines are not privy to WestJet’s data, so even if they could quickly add capacity (unrealistic), where would they deploy it without knowing exactly where travelers are stranded?

Unfortunately, for most travelers still at home, their plans have been vaporized. The only recourse is refunds and compensation, though it would be unrealistic to expect not to be out of pocket for some expenses.

For travelers already away from home, the journey back will likely be difficult and far more expensive than planned.

Outside of the Christmas peak, there are few other travel windows when a strike could have come at a worse time for rebooking.

My advice:

•  Forget about calling WestJet. Their call centres are overwhelmed. Waiting hours on hold only to be told there’s nothing that can be done is pointless — and while you’re on hold, any remaining seats are being snapped up by other impacted travelers.

•  First try to rebook yourself online with Air Canada. Its route network is similar to but larger than WestJet’s, so it offers the best chance of reconstructing your itinerary. Porter and Air Transat may also provide options. Keep in mind that during peak season these airlines are running full or near-full.

•  If the Canadian carriers can’t offer a suitable replacement, consider U.S. airlines, including flights from border airports such as Buffalo, Burlington, Bangor, or Bellingham. Watch out for codeshare flights operated by WestJet (especially when booking with WestJet’s partners). If the strike lasts longer, those codeshares will be impacted. Even after the strike ends, it will take upwards of a week for WestJet’s full schedule to be rebuilt.

• On short haul routes especially in the Quebec City-Windsor rail corridor, ViaRail may be a viable alternative especially to connect to airports such as YYZ, YUL, YOW and YQB BUT keep in mind ViaRail is notoriously delayed so allow for plenty of time to catch connecting flights.

•  Other non-U.S. foreign carriers may offer alternatives, especially if you’re traveling to or from the larger Canadian hubs (YYZ, YUL, YYC, YVR).

•  Keep all receipts. There is a good likelihood that reasonable expenses will be covered.

•  Finally, be kind. The WestJet employees you encounter are as stressed as you are, and staff at other airlines are also doing their best to get you where you’re going — safely and comfortably.
