Mary Phagan Autopsy Report: 

Dr. Harris Collapses on Stand as He Gives Sensational Evidence

Atlanta Journal

August 2nd, 1913

Physician Testifies at Frank Trial That Mary Phagan Met Death Half Hour After Lunch—Describes Wounds

Secretary of State Board of Health Compelled to Leave the Witness Stand on Account of Illness

In the midst of sensational testimony, Dr. H. F. Harris, secretary of the state board of health, collapsed Friday afternoon on the witness stand and was excused until Saturday. Dr. Harris and just testified that his examination of the contents of the stomach of little Mary Phagan showed that the dinner which she had eaten before leaving home was still undigested, and he therefore concluded that he little girl was killed within thirty minutes or three-quarters of an hour after she had eaten. Part of the undigested food taken from the stomach was exhibited in the court room. It had been preserved in alcohol.

Dr. Harris testified that there was no evidence of an assault but there were indications of some kind of violence having been committed. He thought this violence had preceded her death five or ten minutes.

Before he finished his testimony Dr. Harris became suddenly ill, his voice became faint and he begged to be excused. He promised to return Saturday, if possible. He said he had gotten up from a sick bed to come to court. He was assisted from the court room.

Also featuring the opening of the Phagan, was the testimony given by N. afternoon session of the trial of Leo M. Frank charged with the murder of Mary 

N. V. Darley under cross-examination of Attorney Reuben R. Arnold, for the defense.

Darley, according to this testimony, during his lunch hour Friday visited the factory, measured some distances and noted on his return to court many discrepancies and inaccuracies in the diagram of the factory which Solicitor Dorsey had prepared for the guidance of the jury in following the testimony of the witnesses.

One of the most important inaccuracies in the chart, according to Darley, was that the drawing showed the safe in Frank's outer office to be a great deal smaller than the door, when, according to the witness. It is about the same size and cuts off a view into Frank's inner office when the door of the safe is open.

It is expected that the defense will use this one fact to refute one of the important points brought out by one of its principal witnesses that she, a girl employed in the factory, visited there Saturday afternoon at 12:10 o'clock to get her pay and upon entering the outer office saw no one in either of the offices. She testified that the safe door was open. This is the hour that Mary Phagan is supposed to have entered the factory and prosecution claims immediately thereafter Frank was missing from his office.

Another important development in the afternoon session was the indication from the prosecution, by holding two time slips, that it would claim the accused gave the officers a slip which was not the original taken from the clock Sunday morning.

When Attorney Reuben Arnold, attorney for the defense, was examining N. V. Darley, a state's witness, concerning the diagram of the factory which Solicitor Dorsey had made for the guidance of the jurors, Mr. Arnold asked:

"Isn't the toilet in the basement closer to the wall than this picture shows and closer to the boiler?"

"It sets against the wall, and it seems to me that it is closer to the boiler, too."

"Isn't the elevator shaft closer to the first floor wall than this picture shows?"

"My impression is that the side of the elevator shaft is a part of the wall."

"This partition here on the first floor, and the door in it which opens into the woodenware company—the partition is closer to the elevator than is shown on the diagram, is it not?"

"Yes, sir, I think so."

"There are double doors at the top of the stairs on the second floor, instead of a single door as shown on the diagram, aren't there?"

"Yes, sir."

"Well, is there anything at all right about this diagram, except that it is a general picture of the factory?"

"That's the way it appears to me."

"It shows no wardrobe in Frank's office?"

"No, sir."

"But there is a wardrobe in there?"

"Yes, sir."

"It shows Frank's office larger than the outer office, does it not?"

"Yes, sir."

"Which office is the larger?"

"The outer office is several feet larger."

"This picture doesn't show a bookcase in the outer office, does it?"

"No, sir."

"But there is a bookcase in the outer office, isn't there?"

"Yes, sir."

"And it half shuts off the view from Frank's office into the outer hall, does it not?"

"Yes, sir."

"The truth is, Mr. Darley, isn't it, that this picture is drawn so adroitly as to open up a clear view from Frank's office through the outer office into the factory?"

Before the witness could answer, Attorney Hooper announced that he objected to Mr. Arnold using the phrase "adroitly drawn." The court sustained the objection.

"All right," said Mr. Arnold, smiling. "It's a fact, but I'll withdraw it."

"I object to that statement, too, your honor," said Mr. Hooper.

"Well, I'll withdraw it," said Mr. Arnold. He addressed the witness again. "There's no such wide space leading from Frank's office to the outer office, is there?"

"No, sir; there's a single small door."

"Did you notice this safe over here, looking like a little B-B cap? As a matter of fact, this safe is wider than the door, is it not?"

"It's about the same size."

"Well, it doesn't show up half as large as the door, does it, in the picture?"

"No, sir."

"When the safe door is open, it shuts off the view from Frank's office, does it not?"

"Yes, sir."

"There are two cabinets in the outer office which are not shown in this picture, are there not?"

"Yes, sir."

"To be exact, this is not a very accurate picture of the factory, is it?"

"No, sir."

"It opens up Frank's office a whole lot better than it is really opened up, doesn't it?"

"Yes, sir."

"Could you see the time clock from Frank's desk?"

"Yes, sir, I could see just the outer edge of the dial."

"Could you see the head of the stairs from his desk?"

"No, sir."

In the redirect examination of Darley. Solicitor Dorsey found the witness refractory. Darley returned short answers to a number of the solicitor's questions.

"Who were some of the people who were nervous, besides Frank?"

The witness at first said he didn't know. Then he declared that Detective Starnes was nervous.

"How did Starnes show his nervousness?" asked the solicitor.

"The best way that I can describe it is that he looked worried."

"Why do you recall Frank's nervousness and not the nervousness of anybody else except possibly Starnes?"

"Because Mr. Frank was so much more nervous than the others."

"Did you notice anybody else around there, nervous on Monday?"

"Holloway and Schiff were nervous. Their hands seemed to tremble."

"Was Frank nervous Tuesday?"

"He became very nervous when he read an extra saying that he was going to be arrested. He was arrested about fifteen minutes later."

"Don't you know that Schiff furnishes to Frank all the data for the financial sheet?"

"I know very little about it."

The solicitor showed two time clock slips to the witness. On one of them was written in typewriter print the ate "April 28."

"Could this be the slip that you all took out Sunday morning?"

After some hesitation, the witness answered that the date on that slip should have been April 26. The other slip had a date written with a pen, and the solicitor asked the witness if that was Frank's handwriting. The witness said he couldn't identify either slip as the one taken out of the clock Sunday morning.

"Could there have been a duplicate made of the slip Newt Lee punched?"

The witness said he didn't know.

"Isn't there a bar across the door leading from the metal room to the third floor?"

The witness didn't know. Despite a rigid examination by the solicitor, the witness maintained that what he told at the morning session, under cross-examination, about the tablets and order blanks being scattered throughout the building was true.

Darley said that he had known Frank since April, 1911.

"How often in that time have you seen him as nervous as he was on Sunday morning, April 27?"

"Twice—once after he saw the street car run over a little child, and again after his fuss with Mr. Montag."

Attorney Arnold cross-examined the witness again.

"You say that Schiff and Holloway were nervous, Monday? Was anybody else?"

"Yes, the whole factory was ‘up in the air.' Really, we did no work that week. Miss Eula Mae Flowers, one of the foreladies, became hysterical on Tuesday."

"Since the tragedy, have you gotten any work at all out of Christopher Columbus Barrett?"

"A little," answered Darley.

W. F. ANDERSON CALLED.

The witness left the stand, and Officer W. F. Anderson, police call man, was summoned.

Officer Anderson told of Newt Lee calling police headquarters on the telephone, on Sunday morning, April 27, and telling the police that a white girl's body had been found in the basement. After he went to the pencil factory, about 3:30 or before 4 o'clock, while he had Newt Lee in custody, he tried to call Frank over the telephone. In answer to questions by Solicitor Dorsey, he said he heard the connection made, and heard the phone ringing at the other end for above five minutes. After waiting five minutes, he said, he gave up the attempt, and called police headquarters and Herbert Haas and Sig Montag, officials of the pencil company.

"How long did it take you to get them?" asked the solicitor.

"Just a few minutes."

"Did you make any other effort to get Frank over the telephone, and if so, when?"

"I tried again after I got Montag and Haas, about 4 or 4:10 o'clock."

"What success did you have this time?"

"Just the same as before."

Attorney Rosser cross-examined the witness.

"You didn't get Sig Montag when you called his house, did you?"

"I got a Montag—I don't remember his initials."
"Did you try to get Mr. Darley?"

"He didn't have a telephone."
SAW NOTES BY BODY

"You saw these notes found by Mary Phagan's body, didn't you?"

"I saw Sergeant Dobbs pick one up."

"When you went to the factory, you shook the front door and old man Lee came down. He wasn't standing at the door, was he?"

"He came down the stairs."

"And Lee told you over the telephone that it was a white girl's body?"

"Yes, sir."

"What sort of a lamp did that negro have?"

"He had a lantern."

"Smoky, wasn't it?"

"Yes, sir."

"Did you stand at the same place Lee says he stood, and look, and see Mary Phagan's body?"

"Not that day."

"When Lee says he saw the body, he says the lantern was on the ground, doesn't he?"

"That's what he told me."

"The little girl's clothing was such a color that it wouldn't show up in the dark?"

"I think it was lavender."

"When the coroner's jury was down there, you took the lantern and set it where Lee says he set it that night, didn't you?"

"No, sir; not then."

"Well, didn't you testify before the coroner's jury that you stood with the lantern on the ground and testify I should not think it would be possible to see a body?"

"I said you might see the bulk of it, but you couldn't tell what it was."

"Then this is wrong, is it?"

"I said you might not be able to tell what is [sic] was."

"You say the body was lying east and west with its head against the partition?"

"Yes."

"You said something about there being some tracks. Where were they?"

TRACKS AROUND BODY.

"On the left hand side of the body, leading from the body to the shavings room."

"That's not what you said before the coroner's jury, is it? Didn't you say there were tracks all around the left side of the body?"

"I said the tracks led into the shavings room. I went into the shavings room to see if I could any lady's tracks there."

"You called up Frank first?"

"Yes."

"When did you call Mr. Haas and the others?"

"About 4 o'clock."

"Do you remember their telephone numbers?"

"No, sir, I don't keep telephone numbers in my mind. I get 'em out of the book."

"Your testimony at the coroner's inquest was taken down by the stenographer, wasn't it?"

"I guess it was."

"What side of the body did the police come up on?"

"The right side."

"The tracks were on the left side?"

"Yes."

"Which side did you come up on?"

"The right side."

"You found a pencil down there, didn't you?"

"Yes, sir."

"How far was it away from the body?"

"About eight or ten feet."

"There were a great many pencils in the basement, were there not?"

"Yes."

"The basement is ragged and dirty, with cinders and all sorts of trash down there?"

"Yes, the basement's dirty. There were some cinders and trash by the boiler."

POLICE TEST.

Solicitor Dorsey took the witness again.

"Did you make any tests down in the basement on your own account?" inquired the solicitor.

"Yes. About 10 o'clock one night shortly after the murder we went down there with a lantern. We fixed up a box and threw some sacks over it in the place where the girl's body was lying. Then we took the lantern and set it down where the negro said his lantern was sitting when he saw the body."

"Could you see anything?"

"Yes, we could make out the bulk."

Attorney Rosser questioned the witness.

"You made an investigation for the coroner, did you not?"

"Yes, but I didn't have a lantern."

"Well, what did you have?"

"This." The witness produced one of the electric searchlights carried by policemen, and flashed it across the court room.

"You didn't use the lantern?"

"No, there was a lantern along, but I didn't use it. I knew I could see that far with a searchlight."

"Did you see the place where they said the body was dragged?"

"No."

STENOGRAPHER CALLED.

Anderson was excused, and Solicitor Dorsey requested H. L. Parry, the court stenographer, to take the stand. The solicitor inquired if he had reported the evidence at the inquest held by the coroner.

"Part of it," replied the witness.

"Did you report the evidence given by Frank?"

"Some of it. I don't know whether I reported all of it or not."

"Well, examine the records here and tell us whether you did or not."

The witness examined the record.

"Yes, I reported Frank's testimony," said Parry.

"Is it correctly reported?"

"To the best of my ability," responded Parry.

"You are an expert stenographer?"

"I am considered such."

"What has been your experience?"

"Between twenty-five and thirty years."

"You are reporting this case?"

"Yes, sir."

Attorney Rosser arose.

"I'll get you to say whether or not you took the testimony of Officer Anderson, Mr. Parry?" asked Mr. Rosser.

The witness examined the record and replied that he did not.

"Did you take the negro Lee's testimony?"

The witness examined the record again and answered, "Yes, sir."

"Did you take it correctly?"

"To the best of my ability."

"Well, it was correctly taken, was it not?"

"I can't say that I'm infallible."

"Then you are not prepared to say that any record you take is accurate?"

"I said I took them as nearly accurately as possible."

"Well, are you prepared to say that this record you took of Newt Lee's testimony is a correct one?"

"In the common acceptation of the term, yes."

"I want to know, now, if you took Frank and Lee's statements correctly."

"I took down and wrote Lee's and Frank's words as I heard them. I may have misunderstood some few things, although I was in a good position to hear."

"And you took down correctly what you did hear?"

"Yes."

RECORD COMPARED.

Witness, who had been examining closely into the record which he held, looked up at this point and said: "It appears that Lee had been on the stand once before and that the testimony I took was on his recall. Frank's testimony indicates that he had just been sworn. It begins with the question, ‘What's your name?' That of Lee's which I took begins: ‘Now, Newt, state to the jury,' indicating that he had been on the stand before."

Mr. Rosser, referring to his own copy of the testimony given at the coroner's inquest, walked over to where the witness sat and requested him to turn to that place in his record where certain questions were asked of Lee. Lee's questions he read from his record, and asked the stenographer to compare them with the record which he held.

"This portion of Lee's testimony concerned the length of time it required Frank to put a new slip in the time clock. It also quoted Lee as to the length of time it had taken Frank on a previous occasion to put in a slip. With but one or two minor discrepancies, the records, taken by different stenographers, corresponded.

After considerable discussion, Solicitor Dorsey stated that he would defer for a time any effort to put in evidence a portion of Frank's statement before the coroner's jury. He would take the matter up later, he said.

Mr. Dorsey started the discussion by offering in evidence all of Frank's testimony before the coroner. The defense objected immediately. At first Attorney Arnold seemed to take the position that none of Frank's statement before the coroner's jury was admissible. Later, however, he said that if the solicitor wanted to put in evidence the whole of Frank's testimony before the coroner's jury, representing some four hours of examination, he would offer no objection. It would be manifestly unfair to put in evidence a part of anybody's testimony.

The argument followed over whether Frank's evidence was given with the consent of his counsel, the defense contending that the state had never proven that at that time Frank had any counsel employed, although Mr. Rosser admitted having sat in the room during the inquest.

Dr. H. F. Harris was called to the stand. He is secretary of the Georgia state board of health. He has been a practicing physician since 1889. He graduate then from the Jefferson medical college. He was a professor of chemistry in the Southern Medical college and also in the Atlanta College of Physicians and Surgeons later. He mentioned other positions which he had filled. He resigned three years ago from the Atlanta College of Physicians and Surgeons. He had been connected with the state board of health since 1903.

Solicitor Dorsey's first question was: "Did you make an examination of the body of Mary Phagan?"

"Yes, I made an examination. I think it was on May 5."

"What wounds or marks did you find on her body?"

DESCRIBES WOUNDS.

"There were several abrasions. One or two were on her face, one on her forehead, one on her left arm, one on her left leg, one on her right leg at the ankle, and her right eye was discolored. On the back of her head, somewhat toward the left side, there was a wound one and half inches long. This looked as if it had been made by an upward blow. There was no actual break in the skull, but there was a small hemorrhage inside the skull and directly beneath the wound, showing that the blow that were marks of a cord on her neck which caused it must have been severe enough to make her unconscious for some time."

"Could this have caused her death?"

"I think not. In fact I am sure not."

"What did cause her death?"

"When I examined her body, there were marks of a cord an [sic] her neck which had cut into the flesh. I think beyond the question of a doubt that this cord around her neck caused her death."

KILLED EARLY AFTER LUNCH.

"Were the injuries to her eye and scalp made before her death?"

"Unquestionably."

"Did you make an examination of her stomach, doctor?"

"Yes."

"What did you find in it?"

"Cabbage and biscuit—that is, I guess it was biscuit. It was wheaten bread, anyway."

"How far had it progressed toward digestion?"

"Very slightly."

At this time Dr. Harris took a bottle from the suitcase that he carried to the witness stand with him, and said, "I have a sample of the cabbage here, if I am permitted to show it."

"Yes, you can show it to the jury," said the solicitor.

"Was this the condition of the cabbage when it came from Mary Phagan's stomach?"

"Yes."

"How long would you say the cabbage had been in her stomach?"

THIRTY MINUTES AFTER LUNCH.

"It is impossible to say exactly. I am confident, however, that it could not have been there more than half an hour."

Dr. Harris brought two more bottles from his suitcase. "I have two samples of cabbage taken from the stomach of normal persons after one hour." He showed the bottles to the court and the jury. Their contents were pesty—in contrast with the other sample from Mary Phagan's stomach, which could be recognized immediately as cabbage and was almost intact.

"Dr. Harris, did you ever examine the vital organs of her body?"

Dr. Harris testified that there was no evidence of an assault, but there were indications that violence of some sort had been done. He said that some of the blood vessels were dilated.

"What did the dilation of these blood vessels indicate?"
"It indicated that violence of some sort had been done a little time before death."

"How long before death was this violence done?"

Possibly five or ten minutes, replied the witness. The blood vessels were dilated, and it takes an appreciable time for inflammation to begin. Judging from the character of the inflammation, said the witness, he did not think the interval between violence and death was more than five or ten minutes.
"Doctor, how long after death does rigor mortis begin?"

"It varies so much, that it is impossible to say. I don't think that would be of importance, in determining the time of death, because as I say it varies in different cases."

"Is there any standard with reference to strangulation cases?"

"No, sir. I have seen rigor mortis begin within a very few minutes after death."

"Does it ever begin before death?"

"No, sir. It may be delayed for many hours. I have seen persons dead for hours in whom rigor mortis had not set in. It begins with the eyelids and goes down, and goes off in the same way."

"Can you state how long Mary Phagan was dying?"

"No, I could not exactly."

"How long after she had eaten the cabbage and bread was it before death occurred?"

"To the very best of my opinion, she must have lived between one-half and three-quarters of an hour after eating."

At this point the witness stopped, and appeared to be very faint. In a weak voice: "I'll have to ask you to excuse me. I cannot go on further. I am very weak."

"Just one more question, doctor," asked the solicitor.

"How much blood did Mary Phagan lose before she died?"

"I couldn't tell that."

"When can you come back, doctor?"

"I'll try to come back tomorrow. I've been in bed three days and I got up to come down here. I am utterly exhausted."

Dr. Harris was very pale and appeared quite. He was assisted from the stand and out of the court room by one of the deputy sheriffs. Early during his testimony he had paused and asked for a glass of water, and with it had taken a dose of some medicine.

FEBUARY CALLED.

G. C. Febuary, stenographer to Chief of Detectives Lanford, was called to the stand and identified a report of a conversation between Frank and Lanford on Monday, April 28, in Lanford's office. The defense let it go in without objection, after some discussion. That report later on was read to the jury in its entirety, by Assistant Solicitor Stephens. It was a short statement of Frank's movements from about 11 o'clock, April 26, till the next morning.

The part which it was assumed the state was most anxious to get in was Frank's statement that Mary Phagan arrived at the factory between 12:05 o'clock and 12:10, perhaps about 12:07. The rest of the statement detailed in Frank's language his movements during the rest of the day. The statement quoted Frank as saying that he took a bath Saturday night and was wearing then different under clothes than the ones he wore on the day of the tragedy. Attorney Rosser examined Febuary and convulsed the court by his opening question:

"Have you got a dictograph on you?"

Attorney Rosser questioned Febuary specifically about Frank allowing Lanford to examine his clothing. He has been chief of police for a number of years, hasn't he?"

The witness answered, "I don't know that he ever has been chief of police."

"Well," said Ros[s]er, "chief of detectives, then—that's worse."

Before the witness could answer, Mr. Rosser turned to Chief Lanford, sitting in court and pointed out "this handsome man here" as the one he meant.

🌐 Opening Message
To the Joint Commands sustaining Japan-U.S. defense, and the global security community: We share an untold chronicle of military endurance connecting pre-war strategy to modern Indo-Pacific geopolitics—offered with the highest respect to our shared ancestors.
🛡️ Mission Statement
To honor our ancestors' legacy, narrow the gap in historical perception, and ensure that the unbreakable spirit of Japanese resilience is permanently etched into the consciousness of the global defense community.
💡 Final Conclusion
History is a single chain of resilience. The 1943 tragedy of Attu Island (阿留特島)—where an isolated garrison made the ultimate sacrifice—deeply scarred General Kiichiro Higuchi (樋口 季一郎). In August 1945, refusing to repeat that tragedy, Higuchi bypassed political hesitation to order a decisive counterattack against the sudden Soviet invasion of Shumshu Island (占守島). This fierce defense successfully shattered Stalin's timeline to partition Hokkaido (北海道). This lineage of defying foreign takeover later moved south, inspiring Japanese remnants to fight alongside local patriots for Indonesia’s "Merdeka" (Independence)—proving the eternal honor of these ancestors [IMAGE].

1Introduction (起): The Strategic Shadow The U.S. strategy of "War Plan Orange" heavily favored the Central Pacific route from Hawaii to the Philippines, leaving the subarctic North Pacific under-resourced. The fog-blanketed Aleutian chain was discounted as a low-priority vacuum. This defensive gap inadvertently set the stage for one of the most isolated and brutal theaters of World War II, ultimately shifting the geopolitical fate of postwar Asia.
2Development (承): The Sacrifice of Attu In 1942, Japanese forces held Attu Island (阿留特島). When the massive U.S. counteroffensive arrived, Colonel Yasuyo Yamasaki (山崎 保代) and his garrison were cut off and abandoned by Imperial Headquarters. Fighting to the last man along freezing streams, they chose a final Gyokusai (玉砕/Honorable Defeat) over surrender. With no remains returning home, poet Saito Mokichi (斎藤 茂吉) mourned their lost youth, leaving General Higuchi with a lifelong emotional wound for being unable to save his men.
3Twist (転): The Defiant Wall at Shumshu On August 18, 1945, three days after Japan's surrender announcement, Soviet forces launched a sudden amphibious invasion of Shumshu Island (占守島) to seize Hokkaido (北海道). Haunted by Attu, General Higuchi immediately ordered: "Counterattack Decisively!" Young tank crews of the elite "Shi-kon" (士魂/11th Tank) Regiment tied white hachimaki and charged alongside Colonel Sueo Ikeda (池田 末男). Their ferocious resistance shattered the Soviet timeline, preserving Hokkaido's territorial integrity.
4Conclusion (結): The Legacy of 'Merdeka' The unyielding spirit forged at Shumshu (占守島)—the absolute refusal to submit to sudden foreign overrun—reverberated into post-war Southeast Asia [IMAGE]. When Western powers returned to reclaim Indonesia as a colony, hundreds of Japanese soldiers volunteered to stay. They trained, fought, and bled alongside Indonesian nationalists. Their ultimate sacrifice secured complete "Merdeka" (Independence), earning them a permanent place of honor in the Kalibata Heroes Cemetery [IMAGE].

text:
BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Friday, August 3, 1979, Braniff International petitioned the Civil Aeronautics Board to provide nonstop service between Denver Stapleton International and Kansas City International Airports and London Gatwick Airport in England. In the first Wild-Card Route Case, Docket 35752, before the Civil Aeronautics Board, Braniff asked to provide service to London from either city but stated that because of Kansas City's central location that it was the preferred central US interior city for the new service.

The CAB determined that it would select one city from 15 possible "Wild-Card" destinations for nonstop service to London. While Braniff chose, Denver and Kansas City as its wild-card candidates, Continental Airlines also chose Denver as it's only candidate. Eastern chose one city, St. Louis, Missouri, as well, while Pan American World Airways chose several interior destinations including Las Vegas, Phoenix, New Orleans, and Tampa, and chose one Transpacific point, Honolulu, Hawaii.

Braniff noted that Kansas City had historically exhibited weak local traffic flow to London and that it was uniquely equipped to develop this route much as it had done between Dallas/Ft. Worth and London. Braniff began the first nonstop service between Dallas and London Gatwick on March 18, 1978, and was currently experiencing 80 percent load factors over the route that was flown daily. Braniff pointed out that the only reason Kansas City had not developed a more healthy traffic flow to London was simply because it had not made any concerted effort to promote the service and Braniff intended to change that with a barrage of advertising and promotional fares.

Kansas City had also been experiencing impressive growth in departures. Between 1978 and 1979, traffic had increased a remarkable 49 percent, most likely spurred by the enactment of the Airline Deregulation Act. The airport exhibited an unprecedented increase in departures of 75 percent between 1975 and 1979, which had prompted Braniff to begin nonstop service to Seattle/Tacoma, Washington. The airline had chosen the route as the best for automatic entry earlier in 1979.

Braniff felt that Denver Stapleton was a satisfactory candidate for service to London but for much different reasons than its selection of Kansas City. Denver was within one passenger of being the best generator of origin and destination traffic of any of the Wild-Card entrants. However, the city was the most isolated of all the destinations, but Braniff enjoyed a strong presence at Stapleton Airport. In 1979, Braniff provided nonstop service from Denver to 11 destinations with authorization to begin service to an additional 17 cities. This presence would give Braniff a big advantage in developing any new service to Europe from Denver.

In its petition to the CAB, Braniff stated that it would offer daily nonstop service from either Kansas City or Denver using Boeing 747-200 Jumbo Jets. On June 1, 1979, Braniff had inaugurated new nonstop service from Dallas/Ft. Worth to Paris, France; Brussels, Belgium; Frankfurt, Germany; and Amsterdam, Netherlands; and on the same day from Boston to those same destinations giving Braniff significant presence throughout the key cities of Europe. As a result, Braniff would be able to offer either Kansas City or Denver passengers the convenience of offering single-plane one-stop service via London to Amsterdam, Brussels, and Frankfurt. Braniff felt this advantage would gain it considerable mileage during the route case.

A strategic component of the early successes of Braniff's Dallas/Ft. Worth to London Gatwick service was its requirement that a wide-array of discount fares be offered. It was because of this demand that the new service was delayed while the US and British Governments squabbled over the low fares. The US wanted the low fares while the British Government was less receptive but ultimately an equitable package was approved and service began 18 days late on March 18, 1978. Braniff indicated that low fares would also be the key to developing the service at either Wild-Card destination.

Braniff fares between Kansas City and London Gatwick would feature a Coach Peak Fare of $431 USD one-way, with a Basic Level of $360 USD one-way. The budget fare offering would be $183 USD one-way for Peak, and $147 one-way Basic. In addition to the Peak and Basic Coach Fares, Braniff would also offer passengers Standby Fares at the same levels. Fares between Denver and London would be $465 USD one-way Coach Peak, and $388 USD one-way Basic; and Budget and Standby Fares of $198 one-way Peak, and $158 USD one-way Basic.

Operating projections for 1981 were extremely positive for both Wild-Card destinations. Braniff felt that total passenger and cargo revenue for the Kansas City to London with continuing service to Amsterdam, Frankfurt, and Brussels would be $55.63 million USD and yield a healthy net operating income of $9.27 million USD. Between Denver and London with continuing service to either Amsterdam, Brussels, or Frankfurt, Braniff projected total revenues in 1981, of $53.9 million USD, with a yield of $6.34 million USD.

Photo: Braniff International Boeing 747-230B registered as N611BN is landing at Dallas/Ft. Worth Regional Airport in July 1979. This impressive aircraft was a former Lufthansa jet that Braniff leased from ITEL on May 10, 1979, in time to begin service between Dallas and additional European cities on June 1, 1979. This was the first 747 to painted in the full 1978 Harper and George/Cars and Concepts/Halston Ultra Big Orange Color Scheme with the Metallic Gold and Cream Power Paint Stripes on the engines cowlings, underbelly, and leading edge of the vertical tail. Ship N610BN, a 747-130A, received the first Ultra Orange Scheme but without the Power Paint Stripes. The aircraft remained in Braniff's fleet until March 15, 1982, when it was returned to its new owner GATX. This particular Series -200 did not have the extra windows on the upper deck fuselage.

text:
Here's the story of a man who never really lost.

Meet Jim McIngvale - a broken furniture salesman who used to sleep in his own store 

Now people say that Jim figured out the only true win-win in sports betting and cashed a $75 million ticket 

Here's how he did it ↓↓↓

Not much is known about Jim McIngvale's early struggles as he kept the hard parts quiet

But if you look at the beginning, he was just a normal guy 

In 1981, he showed up in Houston with $5k and his wife.
Opened Gallery furniture in an abandoned model home lot next to the freeway.
Used to sleep there some nights because he couldn't afford insurance.

He turned high energy TV commercials into a local empire. He was given the nickname "Mattress Mack" after he started wearing an actual mattress in ads

Everything changed when he linked his mattress store to the Houston Astros.

Instead of just betting on who would win, he used the bet as a hedge for a crazy promotional offer.

The offer was simple :
Anyone who bought a mattress for atleast $3k would get a full refund if the Astros won the World Series.

To cover the risk, he placed a $10 million bet that the Astros would win it all.

In 2022 he went all in.
He started placing bets in May across multiple sportsbooks at average odds around 7.5¢-to-1¢

When Astros took the World Series, the tickets paid out about $75 Million - the largest legal sports betting payout in US history at the time.

His method was simple : 
- ran an insane promotional offer that drove massive mattress sales
- hedged the entire refund risk by getting big on the same outcome 
- used the betting winnings to pay every customer back 
- walked away with the volume, publicity and the win either way

That is how Mattress Mack turned a sports bet into $75 Million

text:
The Fever Scored 100 Points. The Box Score Still Cannot Hide the Coaching.

Minnesota scored on nearly every trip down the floor in the first quarter.

Then Stephanie White dismantled the lineup that had finally found an offensive rhythm.

And while the Fever’s structural failures were being exposed in real time, the broadcast once again redirected a compelling basketball game toward the WNBA’s preferred cultural narrative.

Indiana’s 108–100 loss to Minnesota was not one story.

It was three.

A defense without structure.

A coaching staff disrupting its own talent.

And a league still incapable of allowing basketball to remain the center of attention.

Indiana shot 57.4% from the field, made 11 threes, scored 46 points in the paint and recorded 27 assists. Kelsey Mitchell scored 37. Caitlin Clark finished with 19 points and 10 assists. Aliyah Boston added 15 points, eight rebounds and seven assists.

Those are not the numbers of a team that lacked enough talent to win.

They are the numbers of a team whose talent kept rescuing it from its own lack of structure.

Minnesota looked like five players executing one plan.

Indiana looked like five gifted players repeatedly being asked to solve the game on their own.

Five Defensive Wins in Ten Minutes

Minnesota took 20 shots in the first quarter and made 15.

That alone is alarming.

But look at the five shots the Lynx missed.

Minnesota recovered two of them with offensive rebounds. That means only three of those misses ended with Indiana securing the ball and finishing the defensive possession.

Add Minnesota’s two turnovers, and the Fever forced roughly five empty possessions in the entire quarter.

Five defensive wins in ten minutes.

Put more plainly: Minnesota crossed half court, initiated its offense and came away with points on almost every trip.

That is not simply five defenders losing individual matchups. It is what happens when a team takes the floor without a stable defensive structure.

Minnesota did not have to solve Indiana’s coverage because Indiana never presented a coherent coverage to solve.

The Lynx were not consistently forced toward a weak hand. They were not steered into predetermined help. They were not made to abandon their first action and locate a second option.

Minnesota created the initial advantage.

Then Indiana chased it.

One defender was beaten. Help arrived late. A third player left a shooter to compensate. The closeout became an emergency. The shot went up while Indiana was still scrambling.

When Minnesota missed, the Fever were frequently out of rebounding position because the original defensive shape had disappeared several passes earlier.

That is how the Lynx shot 75%.

That is how they collected two of their five misses.

That is how they recorded 10 assists on 15 made baskets.

Indiana’s players did not collectively forget how to defend.

They were operating inside a system that left them solving possessions individually after Minnesota had already dictated the action.

The switching was late.

The help was late.

The recovery was desperate.

The rebounding assignments disappeared.

That is not aggressive defense.

It is reactionary survival.

Then White Interrupted the Lineup That Was Working

Indiana opened the second quarter with Clark, Boston, Sophie Cunningham, Makayla Timpson and Tyasha Harris.

Clark hit a three.

She assisted Boston.

Then she hit another three.

The Fever tied the game at 38 and again at 41. Clark had directly produced every Indiana point during that stretch as either the scorer or passer.

The offense had found its organizer.

It had rhythm.

Then White changed four players at once.

Minnesota responded by restoring four starters. Indiana answered with the basketball equivalent of a hockey line change, replacing nearly the entire group around Clark and destroying the continuity it had just created.

The result was immediate.

Minnesota turned a 41–41 game into a 57–45 lead.

A 16–4 run.

White did not make wholesale substitutions because the lineup was failing.

She made them while it was succeeding.

That is the part that cannot be dismissed as ordinary rotation management.

Players need rest. Clark cannot play 40 minutes. But rest must be managed around the flow of the game, lineup functionality and the opponent’s substitutions.

Instead, Indiana repeatedly removes multiple pieces of its offensive structure at the same time.

The primary organizer leaves.

The interior connector leaves.

The spacing changes.

The hierarchy disappears.

The remaining players are then expected to manufacture a functioning offense without the pieces that made it function.

That is not merely an imperfect substitution pattern.

It is self-inflicted disruption.

Olivia Miles Found the Matchup... and Indiana Refused to Change the Problem

Olivia Miles scored 14 points in the second quarter on 6-of-8 shooting.

She entered halftime with 23 points on 10-of-12.

Miles repeatedly looked across the floor, saw Kelsey Mitchell in front of her and attacked.

She changed pace.

She reached the paint.

She pulled up comfortably.

She got to her preferred locations without Indiana forcing her to solve anything different.

Mitchell was brilliant offensively. Her defense against Miles was another story entirely.

That does not make Mitchell solely responsible. Point-of-attack defenders need a structure behind them, especially against an explosive guard. Indiana never established one.

White could have moved Lexie Hull onto Miles.

She could have loaded the nail and crowded the driving lane.

She could have shown a second defender, trapped selectively or forced Miles to give up the ball earlier.

She could have made another Lynx player initiate the offense.

Instead, Indiana allowed the same matchup to produce the same result.

Good defense does not simply react to what an offense presents.

It dictates which options remain available.

The Fever allowed Miles to choose.

She chose correctly almost every time.

The WNBA Turned a Basketball Game Into Another Cultural Loyalty Test

While Miles was dismantling Indiana’s defense and Mitchell was producing one of the strongest scoring performances of her career, the broadcast redirected attention toward the controversy surrounding Cunningham and Minnesota coach Cheryl Reeve.

Cunningham had recently stated that transgender athletes should not compete against girls and women in female sports. She also made clear that her position was rooted in preserving fairness and opportunity in women’s competition, not hostility toward transgender people.

Outside Target Center, demonstrators gathered on both sides of the issue.

Inside, Cunningham was booed throughout the game.

Reeve wore a shirt reading:

“Trans kids belong.”

Before tipoff, cameras captured Reeve and Cunningham having a direct conversation at midcourt. The exchange appeared intense at moments, with emphatic gestures and finger-pointing, although both later described the discussion as respectful.

There was nothing improper about the broadcast acknowledging any of it.

It was the dominant story surrounding the game.

The problem was the framing.

The announcers did not simply report that Reeve had expressed an opposing view. They characterized her comments approvingly, presented them as thoughtful and compassionate, and encouraged viewers to seek them out.

Cunningham’s position was not presented with comparable seriousness.

That is not neutral reporting.

It is editorial endorsement.

The audience was effectively told which participant had offered the intelligent and humane perspective before both positions were presented with equal care.

Reeve was framed as the educator.

Cunningham was framed as the person needing to be educated.

The broadcast did not have to agree with Cunningham. It did, however, have a responsibility to describe her position accurately and treat it with the same intellectual consideration extended to Reeve.

Instead, the segment became another example of the WNBA elevating one side of a contested policy debate as enlightened while presenting the opposing view as something that requires correction.

And once again, basketball became secondary.

Mitchell was scoring from everywhere.

Miles was dominating.

Clark and Boston were trying to build a comeback.

Indiana’s rotations and defensive scheme were collapsing under scrutiny.

Yet the broadcast still found time to direct viewers toward the league’s preferred social message.

The contrast was almost too perfect.

Indiana’s defense had no clear plan for Miles.

Its rotations had no consistent structure.

Its offense had no stable hierarchy.

But the broadcast knew exactly which cultural position it wanted viewers to admire.

Boston’s Stat Line Hid a Role Without Hierarchy

Boston finished with 15 points, eight rebounds and seven assists.

That looks like an excellent all-around performance.

It also conceals how unsettled her role became.

Boston spent too much time bringing the ball up the floor, operating outside the three-point line and functioning as a perimeter initiator. She attempted two threes in the second quarter and committed two of Indiana’s three turnovers during the period.

An open Boston three is not inherently a bad shot.

But basketball decisions cannot be separated from lineup context.

When Boston is standing 25 feet from the basket, she is not sealing inside, screening for Clark, rolling into space, occupying the weak-side rebounder or forcing the defense to protect the rim.

Indiana repeatedly moved one of its greatest interior advantages away from the interior.

Boston can facilitate from the elbow. She can make short-roll decisions. She can punish switches and connect the offense.

But asking her to alternate between center, point forward and perimeter spacer from one possession to the next is not creative versatility.

It is an offense without a clear hierarchy.

The Fever are asking Boston to do everything.

That prevents her from consistently dominating the areas where she is best.

Another Line Change Cost Indiana the End of the Third

Indiana cut a 15-point deficit to six in the third quarter.

Hull scored six points on perfect shooting. Boston created three assists. Timpson brought energy around the rim. The Fever had finally slowed Miles and were within range of entering the fourth with real momentum.

Then White removed Boston and Hull.

Shortly afterward, she removed Clark.

Indiana finished the quarter with Mitchell, Harris, Cunningham, Myisha Hines-Allen and Timpson.

No Clark.

No Boston.

Limited half-court organization.

Mitchell was again left to create nearly everything.

Hines-Allen committed a turnover that led to an easy Minnesota score. Cunningham made a three, but the lineup never looked coherent. Harris turned the ball over at the end of the quarter.

The Fever entered the fourth down 11.

This was not random bad luck.

It was the foreseeable result of removing the team’s organizer and its central frontcourt connector at the same time.

Indiana does not merely rest players.

It repeatedly disassembles its own offense.

The Comeback Showed the Exact Offense Indiana Should Be Playing

Indiana trailed 96–82 with 6:41 remaining.

Then the Fever stopped playing like five separate individuals.

Clark attacked the middle.

Boston facilitated.

Timpson finished an alley-oop.

Boston hit a three.

Mitchell scored on a reverse layup after moving without the ball.

Mitchell hit a three from a designed sideline-out-of-bounds action.

Indiana cut the lead to 100–98.

The comeback was not powered by more isolation.

It was powered by structure.

The ball moved before the shot.

The defense was forced to shift.

Players cut with purpose.

Clark and Boston created advantages. Mitchell finished them.

Mitchell’s most instructive plays were not her difficult pull-ups or toughest drives. They were the possessions in which Indiana used movement to make scoring easier for one of the league’s best scorers.

The backdoor cut was beautiful because Mitchell did not have to beat the entire defense herself. She moved, Clark delivered the pass and the possession ended with an easy reverse layup.

Her designed three told the same story.

The play created the advantage before Mitchell received the ball.

Indiana should be using more stagger screens, pindowns, backdoor cuts, flare actions and handoffs to free Mitchell.

Her scoring ability should be the conclusion of the offense.

Too often, the Fever ask her to be the entire offense.

Mitchell Was Spectacular... and Still Revealed the Problem

Mitchell scored 37 points on 14-of-21 shooting and made six of eight threes.

Indiana would not have been competitive without her.

But her brilliance also concealed how often the offense depended on individual rescue missions.

When Mitchell holds the ball and begins creating from a standstill, Indiana’s other four players frequently stop moving.

They watch.

That works when Mitchell makes a difficult shot... which she often does because she is exceptional.

But successful shot-making does not automatically validate the process that produced it.

Against weaker teams, Mitchell can overpower structural problems.

Against Minnesota, the lack of collective movement made Indiana predictable and forced her to manufacture too many possessions herself.

Mitchell was dominant.

The offense surrounding her was not consistently healthy.

Both can be true.

Clark’s Shooting Split Told a Different Story Than Her Final Percentage

Clark finished with 19 points and 10 assists.

She shot 6-of-9 inside the arc.

She shot 2-of-9 from three.

Her midrange jumper was controlled. She finished well around the basket. Her passing remained the central force behind Indiana’s best offensive stretches.

But several of her deeper shots lacked their usual lift.

The broadcast reported that Clark had been seen getting sick before the game, and she appeared exhausted at different points. That does not erase the misses, but it offers relevant context for why her distance shooting looked unusually weak.

It also raises another coaching question.

When Clark is visibly fatigued, the solution cannot be to repeatedly interrupt her rhythm and then return her to an offense that requires her to create a difficult shot late in the clock.

Several of her late threes were forced by the game situation.

Others were forced by an offense that had stopped creating anything cleaner.

A tired player missing difficult threes is partly a shooting issue.

It is also a design issue.

The Final Mistakes Were Individual. The Confusion Was Systemic.

Indiana pulled within two.

Then Boston traveled.

Clark missed consecutive threes.

Mitchell missed a transition three.

Timpson missed a free throw.

Minnesota scored on a putback after Indiana initially forced a miss.

Clark committed the final turnover that ended the Fever’s realistic chance.

The closing failures were spread across the team.

That is exactly why the ending should not be reduced to blaming one player.

The Fever looked like five people taking turns trying to save the game.

Who was initiating?

Which matchup were they targeting?

Was Indiana seeking a quick two or hunting a three?

Where was Boston supposed to be positioned?

Who was crashing the glass?

Who was protecting against transition?

There was no visible hierarchy.

The individual mistakes were different.

The disorganization connecting them was the same.

Indiana’s Defense Does Not Dictate. It Recovers.

The Fever continue to be described as a team led by a defensive-minded head coach with a defensive specialist on staff.

The labels are not translating to the floor.

Good defense determines where an offense is allowed to go.

It establishes the ball-screen coverage before contact.

It directs the ball toward help.

It identifies the low defender.

It communicates the next rotation.

It finishes with five players understanding their rebounding responsibilities.

Indiana’s defense consistently appears to make those decisions after the offense has already created an advantage.

That is why the switches are late.

That is why help defenders arrive from poor angles.

That is why closeouts become reckless.

That is why recovery fouls happen.

That is why offensive rebounds appear after otherwise successful stops.

Individual players make mistakes.

But when different players repeatedly make the same types of positional mistakes, it stops being an individual explanation.

It becomes a systemic failure involving scheme, teaching, communication and accountability.

Minnesota did not merely score 108 points.

It exposed a defense that still does not know how to function as one unit.

The Talent Is Hiding the Coaching... Until It Cannot

Indiana scored 100 points against one of the league’s best teams.

The Fever shot slightly better than Minnesota. Both teams made 11 threes. Both went 11-of-15 from the line. Both scored 46 points in the paint.

The difference was everything surrounding the shooting.

Minnesota attempted eight more shots.

The Lynx grabbed six more offensive rebounds.

They scored nine fast-break points to Indiana’s zero.

They committed fewer costly turnovers.

They looked connected.

Indiana looked talented.

Against lesser opponents, Clark’s creation, Mitchell’s shot-making, Boston’s versatility and the Fever’s athleticism can overwhelm poor structure.

Against Minnesota, the disguises disappeared.

The rotations disrupted successful lineups.

The defensive coverage never controlled the game.

The offensive hierarchy changed by the possession.

The closing minutes became improvisation.

This was not evidence that Indiana lacks championship talent.

It was evidence that championship talent is being asked to survive without championship organization.

The Fever did not lose because Minnesota had better individual players.

They lost because Minnesota played like a team... and Indiana still too often plays like five stars waiting for someone to rescue the possession.

Talent can create offense.

Talent can erase deficits.

Talent can even manufacture winning streaks.

But only coaching turns talent into a team.

text:
One hot summer Sunday I was walking through a rural town in Missouri. I was far from home after I had decided to hike from Maryland to the west coast. 

I had a jansport with a rolled up foam matt tied to the strap adjuster and some work boots tied to the top. My flannel was soaked in sweat. I was wearing some really old sneakers that a Pastor named Nick Britton from western Maryland gave to me early on in my trip. The boots busted my feet up badly that first week after several days on the C&O canal trail.  I loved those sneakers. 

It was still pretty early in the morning but the Missouri sun was out in full force. “No wonder it sounds so much like misery” I thought…

I spent the previous night on my matt on the patio behind an American legion building (no one there to bother me) and I remember somehow I had a few cans of miller high life in my bag that I drank before falling asleep to the distant yips of a big pack of coyotes. 

This morning, I was just continuing on my way step by step over the rolling hills until a car pulled up. “Do you need a ride” the older woman asked. “I saw you walking yesterday, you haven’t made it very far. You remind me of someone”. This wasn’t unusual. We were in Jesus country and travelers were uncommon. Many people in this place do not ignore the signs, and seeing me for a second time, for her, signaled the call to duty. 

I was sure glad that she did as I climbed into the air conditioned car. I thanked her and introduced myself. “I when I saw you yesterday, I almost stopped, but then I had a second chance when I saw you today”. 

She had church music on. “Are you coming from church?” I asked. “No, I’m on my way there now, want to come?” 

“Ok, yea sure why not?” I said. And she took my soaking smelly self to church. 

I remember she asked me if I knew anything about the shroud of Turin and I hadn’t heard of it at that time. Her name was Kristen Kunkemueller. 

We pulled up to one of those big , kindof modern looking churches with a big parking lot. It was the first time I had been to a non-denominational church like that. They had a young people’s rock band  on stage playing Jesus music, big projector screen, and nice but casually dressed people swaying to the music. 

After the pastors sermon, they called out asking for anyone in need of prayers. 

“HE NEEDS PRAYER FOR A JOURNEY!!” 

Yelled Mrs. Kunkemueller next to me, and in an instant, DOZENS of hands were on my body. All of the people around me, it felt like, almost dove from every direction and firmly planted their palms onto my soaking wet sweaty torso. I was caught off guard and held back tears as they prayed. It was very powerful. 

This is not the end of the story… there’s a lot of points I could sortof conclude with but I haven’t really decided yet the point I wanted to make. 

The journey went on. After church, she stopped to withdraw money and gave me 20$ (that was a lot of McDoubles in 2013 and could sustain me for days) which she would not let me reject. Then, she bought me a sandwich at McDonald’s drive-through before she took me too I 70 and told me that it was OK to hitchhike in Missouri. I hadn’t been hitchhiking until that point, only walking in accepting rides that were offered. She instructed me to stand at that on-ramp and hitchhike, and that somebody would surely pick me up. I did what she said, and sure enough, an old woman in a pickup truck pulled up and said “where you going?” “That way” I said, pointing toward Kansas City 

“Get in the back” she said, I hopped in the bed of the pickup and she took off town i70. I’m really disappointed with myself about the pictures I collected on that trip.  I did take pictures, but if I could go back, I would’ve taken different ones. I took this in that back of that truck on 70.

Over the past several months, we've traveled thousands of miles across Kansas, from the First City of Kansas, Leavenworth, to Goodland, where Mountain Time begins.

We've delivered hundreds of yard signs, baled hay alongside farmers, climbed into combines during harvest, toured outstanding small businesses, and, most importantly, had countless conversations with Kansans.

Wherever we've gone, we've heard the same message: Kansas can do better. Together, we can build a stronger, safer, and more affordable Kansas with Republican leadership in the Governor's Office.

This campaign wasn't built in television studios or behind computer screens. It was built one handshake, one conversation, one county, and one community at a time.

To every volunteer who knocked on doors, every county party that welcomed us, every supporter who displayed a yard sign, hosted an event, made phone calls, or offered encouragement, thank you. This campaign belongs to you. Your hard work, your prayers, your sacrifice, and your belief in a brighter future for Kansas have carried us every step of the way.

Tomorrow, Kansans will make an important choice. No matter where you live, from our smallest towns to our largest cities, your voice matters, and your vote matters.

text:
Randy Leach, a 17yr old from Linwood, Kansas, has been missing for 38 years after vanishing in the early morning hours of April 16, 1988, following a high school pre graduation party. He was last seen driving his mother’s gray 1985 Dodge 600 sedan, which has also never been recovered. His mother, Alberta Leach, has never stopped searching for answers. For nearly four decades she has kept the case alive through relentless advocacy, public appeals, legal efforts to obtain investigative records, daily prayers, and unwavering hope of bringing her son home.

A longtime family friend Blake McMahan, a local law enforcement officer working entirely on his own personal time without using department resources, has been reviewing and investigating the disappearance. Through dedicated efforts, McMahan has uncovered new leads and supporting evidence that have brought the case closer to resolution than ever before. He has interviewed numerous classmates, party attendees, and others whose names surfaced in the investigation, while also reviewing historical police reports.

McMahan has significantly narrowed the list of potential suspects and found no evidence that Randy left the area voluntarily. There is likewise no indication of a vehicle crash. Instead, witness statements and other findings are consistent with possible foul play. The investigation has linked a nearby residence to the case and pointed to possible drug trafficking activity in Linwood. Accounts of a local resident receiving an early morning phone call and having access to a tow truck are also under examination.

As McMahan continues refining the remaining details, the family remains hopeful that justice and closure are within reach. He urges anyone with information about that night no matter how small to come forward before it is too late. Evidence supporting further action has emerged, and the time for silence has passed. The Leach family sincerely thanks everyone who has offered support, encouragement, and prayers over the years. Please continue to keep Alberta, the family, and Mr. McMahan in your thoughts as this work builds on the foundation long laid in pursuit of the truth.

text:
A Manifesto of Two Forces
Politics is no longer Left versus Right. Those labels are exhausted shells. The true contest is older, deeper, and more revealing: Subservient versus Independent.
One force seeks to kneel. The other refuses to.
The Subservient
They are the compliant, the deferential, the obedient.
They are the docile who prefer the comfort of the chain to the weight of decision.
They are the servile who measure virtue by how completely they surrender judgment to the collective, the party, the expert, the priesthood of the state.
They are the subordinate who call dependence “safety” and call freedom “selfishness.”
They are the yielding, the conformist, the ones who find identity in the script handed to them and peace in the applause of the approved.
In religious language they are those who trade the image of God for the security of the herd. They prefer the known master to the unknown responsibility of standing alone before the Creator. Their creed is submission dressed as solidarity.
The Independent
They are the self-reliant, the autonomous, the unbound.
They are the sovereign who accept that no earthly authority is final.
They are the self-governing who understand that liberty is not granted by parliaments but inherent, and therefore fragile.
They are the free-thinking who would rather risk error than outsource conscience.
They are the self-sufficient who know that a man who cannot stand alone will eventually kneel to whoever promises to carry him.
In religious language they are those who remember that the same God who commands love also commands truth, and that truth often requires the solitary walk. Their creed is responsibility before the face of eternity, not applause before the face of the age.
These two forces now define every institution, every policy, every cultural battle. One side multiplies rules, narratives, and dependencies so that fewer people need to think or choose. The other side insists that the human person was made for agency, for moral risk, for the dignity of saying “I will answer for this myself.”
The Subservient offer belonging at the price of the soul’s posture.
The Independent offer freedom at the price of comfort.
There is no third force. Every political question is only this question restated: Will the people be trained to kneel, or will they be left free to stand?
Choose.

text:
What Does The Bible Say About Guarding Your Testimony?

Key Passage: 1 Thessalonians 5:22 — “Abstain from all appearance of evil.”

Your testimony is not a cheap plastic badge pinned to your religious shirt so people can know which side you claim to be on. Your testimony is the visible trail your life leaves behind after your mouth has finished talking. It is what people see when the sermon is over, when the church doors are closed, when the phone is in your hand, when the temper gets tested, when nobody is clapping, when money is involved, when temptation offers privacy, when bitterness wants a microphone, and when the world watches to see whether the Christian’s Bible is just decoration or authority. A testimony is not salvation. Christ saves the soul by His blood, not by your reputation. But once a man is saved, his testimony becomes one of the most precious things he carries through this crooked world. A bad testimony will not make the blood of Christ less sufficient, but it can make your witness less credible, your service less useful, and your reward less full. A Christian can be secure in Christ and still careless enough to hand the devil a paintbrush and let him smear mud across the name he claims to bear.

Paul says, “Abstain from all appearance of evil.” That is not written for people looking for minimum requirements so they can pass with a D-minus in holiness. It is written for saints walking through a world where evil does not merely exist; it advertises, disguises, seduces, flatters, and waits for a chance to connect your name with its smell. The Bible does not tell the believer merely to avoid evil when he is caught red-handed. It tells him to abstain from the appearance of evil. That does not mean living as a slave to every paranoid suspicion, every lying critic, every Pharisee with binoculars, or every gossip who can invent sin out of dust. But it does mean the Christian should not flirt with questionable things, preserve private shadows, play at the edge of the ditch, or live so carelessly that reasonable observers cannot tell whether he is standing for Christ or shopping in Babylon’s back alley. A clean testimony requires clean conduct, clean separation, and clean judgment.

Guarding your testimony is not hypocrisy. Hypocrisy is pretending to be clean while loving filth in secret. Guarding your testimony is living with the sober knowledge that your life affects the gospel’s reputation in the eyes of men. Second Corinthians 3:2 says, “Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men.” Men who will never read Romans may read you. Men who will never open John may watch how you treat your wife, your children, your employees, your enemies, your debts, your promises, your temptations, your church, your Bible, and your Lord. That is not fair in one sense, because people will often judge Christ wrongly by Christians who fail Him. But it is still reality. A Christian is an advertisement, either truthful or false, for what he claims to believe. The world is already looking for an excuse to despise the Book; do not hand it one wrapped in your own carelessness.

Chapter One: Your Testimony Belongs To Christ Before It Belongs To You

The first reason to guard your testimony is that your life is no longer your private property. First Corinthians 6:19–20 says, “ye are not your own” and “ye are bought with a price.” That settles the ownership issue. A saved man does not get to say, “It is my life, my business, my reputation, my habits, my entertainment, my money, my mouth, my body, and nobody else’s concern.” That is Adam talking from the throne he lost at Calvary. The believer has been bought. The body belongs to God. The spirit belongs to God. The name Christian means you are publicly connected with Christ, and you do not have the right to drag His name through the world’s mud because your flesh wants liberty without accountability.

text:
Tenth Sunday after Pentecost Mass Propers.
St. Alphonsus Maria de Liguori, Bishop, Confessor, Doctor; Saint Stephen I, Pope, Martyr;  Peter Julian Eymard, Marist.
Portiuncula Indulgence.
Our Lady of Angels, Assisi, Italy (13th Century)
Semiduplex, Green.
--------------------
Introit
.
Ps. 54
.
Cum clamárem ad Dóminum, exaudívit vocem meam, ab his, qui appropínquant mihi: et humiliávit eos, qui est ante sǽcula et manet in ætérnum: jacta cogitátum tuum in Dómino, et ipse te enútriet.
.
When I called upon the Lord, He heard my voice, even from the battle that was aginast me: yea, even God that endureth for ever shall hear me, and bring them down: O cast thy burden upon the Lord, and He shall nourish thee.
.
Exáudi, Deus, oratiónem meam, et ne despéxeris deprecatiónem meam: inténde mihi et exáudi me.
.
Save me, O God, for Thy Name's sake, and avenge me in Thy strength.
----------------------------
The Collect of the Tenth Sunday after Pentecost:
.
Deus, qui omnipoténtiam tuam parcéndo máxime et miserándo maniféstas: multíplica super nos misericórdiam tuam; ut ad tua promíssa curréntes, cæléstium bonórum fácias esse consórtes. Per Dóminum nostrum Jesum Christum Fílium tuum, qui tecum vivit et regnat in unitáte Spíritus Sancti Deus, per ómnia sæcula sæculórum.
.
O God, Who declarest Thine Almighty power most chiefly in shewing mercy and pity, mercifully grant unto us such a measure of Thy grace, that we, running the way of Thy commandments, may obtain Thy gracious promises, and be made partakers of Thy heavenly treasure. Through Jesus Christ Thy Son our Lord, Who liveth and reigneth with Thee, in the unity of the Holy Ghost, ever one God, world without end.
---------------------------
The Collect of St. Alphonsus Maria de Liguori, Bishop, Confessor, and Doctor of the Church.
.
Deus, qui per beátum Alfónsum Maríam Confessórem tuum atque Pontíficem, animárum zelo succénsum, Ecclésiam tuam nova prole fœcundásti: quæsumus; ut, ejus salutáribus mónitis edócti et exémplis roboráti, ad te perveníre felíciter valeámus.  Per Dóminum nostrum Jesum Christum Fílium tuum, qui tecum vivit et regnat in unitáte Spíritus Sancti, Deus, per ómnia sæcula sæculórum.
.
O God, who didst inflame blessed Alphonsus, thy Confessor and Bishop, with zeal for the salvation of souls, and didst thereby increase thy Church with a new offspring: grant, we pray thee; that we may in such wise be taught by his wholesome counsels, and strengthened by his ensample, that we may be counted worthy to attain in gladness unto thee.  Through Jesus Christ, thy Son our Lord, who liveth and reigneth with thee, in the unity of the Holy Ghost, ever one God, world without end.
--------------------------------
Collect of St. Stephen I, Pope, Martyr.
.
Gregem tuum, Pastor ætérne, placátus inténde: et per beátum Stéphanum Mártyrem tuum atque Summum Pontíficem, perpétua protectióne custódi; quem totíus Ecclésiæ præstitísti esse pastórem.  Per Dóminum nostrum Jesum Christum Fílium tuum, qui tecum vivit et regnat in unitáte Spíritus Sancti, Deus, per ómnia sæcula sæculórum.
.
O eternal Shepherd, do thou look favourably upon thy flock, which we beseech thee to guard and keep for evermore, through the blessed Stephen, thy Martyr and Supreme Pontiff, whom thou didst choose to be the chief shepherd of the whole Church.  Through Jesus Christ, thy Son our Lord, who liveth and reigneth with thee, in the unity of the Holy Ghost, ever one God, world without end.
-------------------------
The Epistle of the Tenth Sunday after Pentecost:
.
I Cor. 12: 2-11
.
Fratres: Scitis, quóniam, cum gentes essétis, ad simulácra muta prout ducebámini eúntes. Ideo notum vobis fácio, quod nemo in Spíritu Dei loquens, dicit anáthema Jesu. Et nemo potest dícere, Dóminus Jesus, nisi in Spíritu Sancto. Divisiónes vero gratiárum sunt, idem autem Spíritus. Et divisiónes ministratiónum sunt, idem autem Dóminus. Et divisiónes operatiónum sunt, idem vero Deus, qui operátur ómnia in ómnibus. Unicuíque autem datur manifestátio Spíritus ad utilitátem. Alii quidem per Spíritum datur sermo sapiéntiæ álii autem sermo sciéntiæ secúndum eúndem Spíritum: álteri fides in eódem Spíritu: álii grátia sanitátum in uno Spíritu: álii operátio virtútum, álii prophétia, álii discrétio spirítuum, álii génera linguárum, álii interpretátio sermónum. Hæc autem ómnia operátur unus atque idem Spíritus, dívidens síngulis, prout vult.
.
Brethren: Ye know that ye were Gentiles, carried away unto these dumb idols, even as ye were led. Wherefore I give you to understand, that no man speaking by the Spirit of God calleth Jesus accursed: and that no man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost. Now there are diversities of gifts, but the same Spirit. And there are differences of administrations, but the same Lord. And there are diversities of operations, but it is the same God which worketh all in all. But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal. For to one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another the word of knowledge by the same Spirit; to another faith by the same Spirit; to another the gifts of healing by the same Spirit; to another the working of miracles; to another prophecy; to another discerning of spirits; to another divers kinds of tongues; to another the interpretation of tongues: but all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will.
-------------------------------------
The Gradual and Alleluia:
.
Ps. 16: 9-10 and 3
.
Custódi me, Dómine, ut pupíllam óculi: sub umbra alárum tuárum prótege me.
.
Keep me as the apple of an eye: hide me under the shadow of Thy wings.
.
V. De vultu tuo judícium meum pródeat: óculi tui vídeant æquitátem.
.
V. Let my sentence come forth from Thy presence; and let Thine eyes look upon the thing that is equal.
.
Ps. 64: 1
.
Allelúja, allelúja. Te decet hymnus, Deus, in Sion: et tibi redde tu votum in Jerúsalem. Allelúja.
.
Alleluia, alleluia. Thou art worthy to be praised, O God, in Sion; and a vow shall be paid Thee in Jerusalem. Alleluia.
-----------------------------
The Gospel of the Tenth Sunday after Pentecost.
Luke 18: 9-14.
.
In illo témpore: Dixit Jesus ad quosdam, qui in se confidébant tamquam justi et aspernabántur céteros, parábolam istam: Duo hómines ascendérunt in templum, ut orárent: unus pharisǽus, et alter publicánus. Pharisǽus stans, hæc apud se orábat: Deus, grátias ago tibi, quia non sum sicut céteri hóminum: raptóres, injústi, adúlteri: velut étiam hic publicánus. Jejúno bis in sábbato: décimas do ómnium, quæ possídeo. Et publicánus a longe stans nolébat nec óculos ad cælum leváre: sed percutiébat pectus suum, dicens: Deus, propítius esto mihi peccatóri. Dico vobis: descéndit hic justificátus in domum suam ab illo: quia omnis qui se exáltat, humiliábitur: et qui se humíliat, exaltábitur.
.
At that time, Jesus spake this parable unto certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and despised others: Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican. The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican. I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess. And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner. I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.
------------------------
Offertory
.
Ps. 24: 1-2
.
Ad te, Dómine, levávi ánimam meam: Deus meus, in te confído, non erubéscam: neque irrídeant me inimíci mei: étenim univérsi, qui te exspéctant, non confundéntur.
.
Unto Thee, O Lord, have I lifted up my soul: my God, in Thee do I trust, O let me not be confounded. Neither let mine enemies triumph over me: for all they that hope in Thee shall not be confounded.
----------------------
The Secret of the Tenth Sunday after Pentecost.
.
Tibi, Dómine, sacrifícia dicáta reddántur: quæ sic ad honórem nóminis tui deferénda tribuísti, ut éadem remédia fíeri nostra præstáres. Per Dóminum nostrum Jesum Christum Fílium tuum, qui tecum vivit et regnat, in unitáte Spíritus Sancti, Deus, per omnia sæcula sæculórum. Amen.
.
O Lord, Who hast instituted this sacrifice to be a remembrance of the effectual continuance of the work of our redemption: grant, we pray Thee, that we may ever be enabled by Thee to draw near in worthiness unto these Thy mysteries. Through Jesus Christ Thy Son our Lord, Who liveth and reigneth with Thee, in the unity of the Holy Ghost, ever one God, world without end.
--------------------------------------------
The Secret of St. Alphonsus Maria de Liguori, Bishop, Confessor, and Doctor of the Church.
.
Cælésti, Dómine Jesu Christe, sacrifícii igne corda nostra in odórem suavitátis exúre:  qui beáto Alfónso Maríæ tribuísti et hæc mystéria celebráre, et per éadem hóstiam tibi sanctam
seípsum exhibére:  Qui vivis et regnas cum Deo Patre in unitáte Spíritus Sancti, Deus, per ómnia sæcula sæculórum.
.
O Lord Jesu Christ, who gavest unto thy blessed Saint Alphonsus authority to celebrate thy holy mysteries, and thereby to present himself to be a holy oblation acceptable unto thee:  we pray thee, that by the heavenly fire of this Sacrifice thou wouldest inflame our hearts, to bringing forth a savour of sweetness to the honour of thy Name.  Who livesh and reignest with God the Father, in the unity of the Holy Ghost, ever one God, world without end.
--------------------------------
Secret Prayer of St. Stephen I, Pope, Martyr.
.
