text:
Investors, ROI, and the Environment.
An entrepreneur friend of mine texted me today with a video of Borys Musielak (an early-stage startup investor) talking about his investment in Shen AI - a medical deep-tech startup that essentially measures blood pressure from a smartphone face scan.

He said he decided to invest only because he knew the founder personally and because the founder already had a prior exit (even though it was in an entirely different industry - gaming). Without that personal connection, he would have passed.
He mentioned that it was tough at the beginning - lots of research, hard to build client trust, etc. - but once they entered the market, their revenue went from 0 to $200k in year one, and jumped from $200k to $2M the following year.

When I see things like this, to be completely honest, I’m not even sure what I feel...
On one hand, it validates everything I think about DeepTech and HealthTech - it’s brutal to break into, but once you’re in, it’s practically impossible to displace 😅
On the other hand - they got funded at the idea stage, on pure concept. They had the backing and support to make it happen. Connections and the right ecosystem are simply everything.
Meanwhile, I have to reach that exact same milestone - credibility, validation studies, and market entry - completely on my own, without any safety net or funding. Working at my dad’s vegetable stall just to pay for tokens, recruiting a team on pure vision and technical documentation with zero payroll budget, and being forced to learn how to code and build the entire system single-handedly once I realized that without an MVP, no one would give me a single cent... 😑

Life isn’t fair. But then again, nobody ever promised it would be, so no surprises there.

On the flip side, I'm realizing I don't even need the grace of investors right now 😅 I recruited an exceptional team that is already advising and helping me, I mastered coding and built far more than just a basic MVP - and if you don't believe me, just go to https://t.co/AEbHWxv9Kk and open DevTools (more than one Stanford CS student would envy what I built completely on my own without a CS background in Replit in just two months 😉). On top of that, a professor offered me a PhD track, I’m currently writing our first scientific paper, and I’ve mapped out a full validation roadmap under the affiliation of the Wrocław University of Health and Sport Sciences - which, by the way, doesn’t cost me a single cent 😅 
So I guess I'm not doing too bad. 

Where others need a check for a few hundred thousand dollars just to get started, I deliver through pure determination and raw execution 😎
My ROI is going to be astronomical in a few years 😂

text:
The video repeatedly tells us what repentance is not. It is not guilt. It is not sorrow. It is not an emotional weight. It is not moral scolding. It is not God standing as an angry Judge waiting for a sinner to feel badly enough. By the end of the presentation, repentance has been protected from so many biblical realities that it is left sitting in an empty room with nothing but a new perspective. But Scripture does not present the sinner merely as misinformed. It presents him as guilty. “All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” “There is none righteous, no, not one.” “That every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God.” Man’s trouble is not simply that he sees reality from an inadequate angle. His trouble is that he has rebelled against the God who made him, loved darkness rather than light, suppressed truth, served the creature, and refused the testimony of God concerning His Son. Repentance must include a changed mind because the sinner’s mind is hostile to God, but it is not a therapeutic reframing exercise. It is a moral reversal beneath divine authority. A sinner can acquire a new worldview, read philosophy, change political parties, attend therapy, travel the world, embrace a new identity, and still die in his sins. Biblical repentance is not merely seeing differently. It is agreeing with God against yourself.

Chapter Three

Judas Was Not Destroyed by a Missing Vocabulary Word

The video’s portrait of Judas is emotionally powerful because it emphasizes his remorse. He sees that Christ has been condemned. He returns the silver. He confesses, “I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood.” The religious leaders coldly answer, “What is that to us? see thou to that.” Judas throws down the money and leaves. The video then presents him as a man trapped inside regret, unable to imagine what God might still do, and offered no road toward restoration by the religious authorities. His sorrow folds inward. His mind never receives the renovated perception necessary to move beyond what he has done. The whole scene is arranged to make Judas look almost like the tragic victim of an inadequate theology of repentance. He had the remorse, the confession, the restitution, and the anguish, but he lacked the decisive inner shift. He could see his sin but not see beyond it.

There is a grain of truth here: Judas despaired instead of seeking mercy. But the presentation relocates the center of his guilt. Judas was not a poor confused man whose main problem was that no one gave him the proper Greek distinction between remorse and repentance. Judas had walked with Jesus Christ for years. He heard the Sermon on the Mount. He watched devils flee, storms stop, blind eyes open, lepers cleansed, dead bodies rise, and multitudes fed. He travelled with the apostles. He preached. He was entrusted with the bag. He heard Christ warn that one of the twelve was a devil. He heard the Lord announce that one of them would betray Him. He sat close enough at supper to receive the sop from Christ’s own hand. He went out into the night. He guided armed men to the garden. He identified the Lord with a kiss. Judas did not perish because the church had not given him sufficient vocabulary for emotional transformation. He perished as the son of perdition after deliberately rejecting more light than almost any lost man who ever lived.

His confession did not equal faith. Scripture contains several men who said, “I have sinned,” without possessing the repentance God required. Pharaoh said it and hardened his heart again. Saul said it but cared more about being honoured before the elders than obeying the Lord. Balaam said it while loving the wages of unrighteousness. Judas said it and went away from Christ. The mouth can confess a fact while the heart remains alienated from God. The return of money could not erase the betrayal. The chief priests could not absorb his guilt. The temple could not cleanse him.

Take time for yourself.  

Seek out real nourishment, especially if you’re constantly surrounded by people who take from you without pouring anything back.

There’s nothing wrong with giving.  
In fact, most cultures rightfully advocate for generosity.

But remember: not everyone lives by those teachings.

You can be generous and still protect your energy.  
You can serve others and still honor your own needs.  
You can lead with an open heart without letting yourself be drained dry.

Your "Connection Pillar" is strongest when it includes healthy boundaries.  
Your "Self-Worth Pillar" grows when you treat yourself with the same care you offer everyone else.

Rest is not selfish.  
Nourishment is not optional.  
And protecting your Inner Temple is one of the most responsible things you can do, for yourself and for the people who depend on you.

Give freely where it is mutual.  
But don’t abandon yourself in the process.

You matter too.

Aspire Higher. Build Firmer.

With care,

text:
Are the K3 Sisters Curating Secrets of Ancient Muses?
By Gino Balducci

The word curate comes from an old Latin word that means "to take care of,” but to Kaylen, Kelsey and Kristen Kassab and their 17 year old K3 Sisters Band (K3SB) it means systematically picking their best creative works to tell special stories, help fans understand relevant topics better, and counter the postmodern zeitgeist. In the process, they offer truths, healing and encouragement to millions of fans who are struggling to overcome current dystopian and demoralizing world conditions. And their counter culture effort syncs up with age old beliefs.

Historians know the nine mythological female Greek Muses embraced their roles as divine sources of inspiration that bridged the gap between human creativity and the minds of the gods. They were not just patrons of the arts, but keepers of a profound secrets: the power to channel universal truth, heal human suffering, and grant a form of immortality through fame. It is intriguing to view the evolution of the K3SB through this ancient historical prism.

The original figures in Greek mythology were daughters of Zeus and Mnemosyne. They were goddesses of art, music and literature. Many believe their “divine sparks” still inhabit and inspire select creators. And these contemporary muses are not all females. Together these celebs and prominent musical artists perpetuate the same sociological functions that those ancient muses represented.

The K3 Sisters admit to being influenced and inspired by past and contemporary muses that dabbled actively in the arts, philosophy, music and dance. A study of the K3 Sisters’ impressive catalogue of original works reveals their forays into all of these disciplines. Their efforts are resonating with fans as their staggering international viewership confirms.

Kaylen (27), Kelsey (25) and Kristen (22) started their creative journeys two decades ago. They
each began their lifelong creative pursuits at three to four years old. In our instant gratification society this fact is often overlooked. On the surface it might appear they are an overnight sensation when one sees their dazzling numbers of musical works and performance skills that are hitting “chords of encouragement,” optimism and healing to millions of fans in over eighty countries with a cumulative social media reach approaching 3.5 billion views. But, their successes didn’t happen overnight. 

Before forming the K3SB in 2009 the sisters began serious vocal and instrumental studies that which quickly led to hundreds of public recitals, and “novelty performances” for non-profits, citywide festivals, theme parks and institutions such as Six Flags, Great Wolf Lodge the State Fair of Texas and the Smithsonian Museum. They were tireless in building their brand and reach little by little. In those early years they were viewed as a flash in the pan novelty act, but that did not deter their determination and work ethic.

Their relentless study of various musical instruments, vocals, performance and stagecraft was catalyzed by the fact that they were free from the constraints of a public school education. From the beginning they were homeschooled by parents who were both degreed educators as well as decorated performers and music producers. Being enabled to travel freely to perform fueled their stage presence, creativity and awareness of diverse cultures.

Along the way they were approached and evaluated by several major record labels and national talent show producers, but they were advised to turn down each offer due to the suffocating creative and financial controls embedded in the contracts that in some cases exceeded three dozen pages of legalese.

When they decided to form their K3SB on a plane ride back to Texas from Disney World in 2009 they were already exploring numerous genres of music, expanding their study of multiple instruments and perfecting intricate three part harmonies. FULL article at https://t.co/Li20mzKAWz

This agreement underscores Clearway’s commitment to drive investment in American manufacturing, while maintaining industry-leading traceability, quality, and domestic content standards.

“Contracts with top-tier manufacturers like T1 help ensure that Clearway can deliver on our ambitious development pipeline with competitive and reliable projects,” said Frances Cook, Vice President of Procurement at Clearway Energy. “With this deal, we are especially excited to bring domestic cells into future construction, generating American-made power with American-made parts.”

T1 continues to increase the domestic content of its modules, as domestic modules with domestic cells are highly valued given rising uncertainty around trade and tariff policy. text:
Elon Musk went to Russia in 2002 to buy a rocket. They wanted $8 million per unit. Back home, American aerospace quoted over $65 million. He turned down both offers and pulled out a spreadsheet on the plane.

Line by line, he priced the raw ingredients. Aerospace-grade aluminum. Titanium. Copper. Carbon fiber. Commodity market rates, nothing exotic.

The materials added up to roughly 2% of the asking price.

That gap is what first principles thinking actually produces. Not "how do we negotiate a better deal." Not "who else sells rockets." Just the most basic question: what is this thing made of, and what should it actually cost?

The answer was structural. Overhead, legacy processes, contractors billing subcontractors, and margin stacked on margin at every layer. Nobody challenged the price because nobody had looked underneath it.

He built it himself.

The first Falcon 1 exploded 33 seconds in. The second failed to reach orbit. The third exploded. Three rockets gone, and the company was nearly out of money.

Musk wired in his last $35 million. The fourth launch would decide everything.

September 28, 2008. Flight 4 made orbit. First privately developed liquid fuel rocket in history to do so.

Seven years on, they were landing boosters back on Earth. Now it is routine. Launch costs fell from $65 million to under $3 million on a reused Falcon 9.

The rest of the industry reasoned by analogy: rockets cost this much because they always have.

Musk reasoned from atoms: they cost this much because nobody had rebuilt the system from the ground up.

text:
In November 2017, 43 year old Elmer Alvarez was walking through the streets of New Haven, Connecticut, when he noticed an envelope lying on the ground. Inside was a check worth 10,000 United States dollars, 10,000 USD, made out to local real estate broker Roberta Hoskie.

Elmer had been homeless for more than a year. He had very little to his name and could have walked away with the check or ignored it completely. Instead, he searched for its owner and made sure it was returned safely.

When Roberta met the man who had found it, she learned he was sleeping outside and trying to rebuild his life after overcoming addiction. His honesty meant even more to her because she had once experienced homelessness herself before becoming a successful business owner.

Rather than handing him a simple reward, Roberta chose to invest in his future. She arranged a place for him to live, helped him find employment, enrolled him in English classes, offered him a scholarship to her real estate school, and continued mentoring him as he got back on his feet.

Within a year, Elmer's life had changed completely. He joined the board of directors of Roberta's Outreach Foundation, where he began helping others facing the same struggles he had once lived through.

A single check found on a sidewalk became the beginning of a new chapter, not because of its value, but because one man refused to compromise his honesty when no one was watching.

text:
He Moved to Escape the Civil War. The War Found Him.

When Confederate General P.G.T. Beauregard arrived at Wilmer McLean's estate near Manassas, Virginia in July 1861 and commandeered it as his headquarters, a Union cannonball interrupted his dinner by dropping through the kitchen fireplace. McLean — a retired militia officer — cooperated. Then a second battle was fought on his property. That was enough. He packed up his pregnant wife and moved his family as far from the front as he could get.

He chose a quiet hamlet in southern Virginia, more than 100 miles from any active fighting. It was called Appomattox Court House.

Two years passed peacefully. Then, on April 8, 1865, a Confederate aide knocked on McLean's door. General Robert E. Lee needed a suitable place to meet Ulysses S. Grant and discuss surrender. McLean suggested a derelict building. The aide rejected it. McLean, reluctantly, offered his own parlor.

The next day, Lee surrendered in Wilmer McLean's living room. Grant allowed Lee's men to keep their horses. Officers of both sides shook hands. And then, before the ink was dry, Union officers began stripping McLean's house of furniture as souvenirs. Sheridan paid $20 in gold for a small table. Custer took one without paying at all. The children's rag doll vanished. McLean spent years petitioning Congress to buy the property. Congress declined, every time.

A promoter eventually bought the house in the 1890s and dismantled it to move it to Washington D.C. as a tourist attraction. He never raised the money. The ruins sat in Appomattox for half a century before the National Park Service rebuilt the house in 1949. McLean himself died in 1882, never having profited from the peace.

He fled the war. The war followed him 120 miles and moved into his parlor.

text:
Why KAST Earn Feels Like the Next Step for Stablecoins

The crypto industry has spent years building better ways to trade, stake, and farm yields. Yet when I look at how most people actually use their money every day, I realize there has always been a missing piece.

Most users don't wake up thinking about APY or DeFi strategies. They simply want their money to be safe, accessible, and productive instead of sitting idle.

That's why KAST Earn caught my attention.

What makes it interesting isn't that it promises yield. There are already countless protocols that do that. The difference is where the experience begins.

Instead of asking users to bridge assets, connect multiple wallets, approve endless transactions, or constantly monitor changing protocols, KAST brings earning directly into an application that many people are already using for payments, transfers, and spending. Deposits are allocated into professionally managed on chain vaults while users retain control of their funds, with no lockups and no additional platform fees. It feels much closer to how a modern financial app should work than how traditional DeFi products have worked for years.

When comparing this direction with other projects, the difference becomes even more obvious.

Projects like Aave and Morpho have built some of the strongest decentralized lending infrastructure in crypto. They are trusted by experienced DeFi users because of their transparency and efficiency. But they still expect users to understand wallets, collateral, lending markets, and protocol mechanics before earning anything.

Ethena introduced another model through synthetic dollars and yield generation, while Pendle created an entirely different market around trading future yield itself. These are impressive financial innovations, but they naturally appeal to users who are already comfortable navigating advanced DeFi concepts.

KAST seems to be targeting a different audience.

Instead of building another protocol for crypto natives, it feels like they're building a financial application for people who simply want stablecoins to work like everyday money.

That distinction matters.

If you think about where the market is heading, stablecoins are gradually becoming less of a trading asset and more of a payment layer.

We're already seeing companies like Stripe integrate stablecoin infrastructure for global payments. Circle continues expanding USDC into more payment networks and financial institutions. PayPal launched PYUSD to bring stablecoins into mainstream consumer finance. Even traditional banks across different regions have started exploring tokenized deposits and digital dollars because cross border settlements are becoming increasingly important. The conversation has clearly shifted from "Can stablecoins work?" to "How do we make them useful for everyone?"

That is why products combining saving, earning, transferring, and spending inside one ecosystem may have a stronger long term advantage than products focusing on only one feature.

Looking at KAST today, I don't see it competing directly with Aave, Morpho, or Pendle.

I see it sitting one layer above them.

Infrastructure projects continue building the financial engine underneath, while applications like KAST focus on making that engine invisible to everyday users.

That reminds me of how the internet evolved.

Most people don't know how TCP/IP works, but everyone knows how to open an app and send a message.

I think stablecoins are beginning to follow the same path.

The winning products may not necessarily offer the highest yield or the most sophisticated financial strategies.

Instead, they'll probably be the ones that make digital dollars feel as simple as opening a banking app.

KAST Earn feels like a step in that direction.

Not because it reinvents DeFi, but because it quietly removes much of the complexity that has kept DeFi from reaching everyday users for so many years. @KASTxyz

Good morning, friends. As the first hints of light appear on this August 3, 2026, I find myself reflecting on the quiet strength we all need to carry into the day. At this early hour, before the rush begins, many of us wake already feeling the weight of what lies ahead.

The verse for today speaks right into those moments: "...I am not afraid; what can mortals do against me?" from Psalm 118:6. It is a gentle yet powerful reminder that the fears pressing on our hearts often come from things beyond our control—rising costs that stretch family budgets thinner each month, news of conflicts and divisions around the world, or personal worries about health, jobs, and relationships that keep us up at night.

We live in a time when uncertainty seems to multiply. Perhaps you are facing an unexpected bill, a difficult conversation with a loved one, or the quiet ache of wondering how things will turn out. These are real struggles, and it is okay to name them. Yet the psalmist invites us to look beyond what people or circumstances can do to us.

God stands as our sure foundation. No human threat, no economic shift, and no headline holds ultimate power over the peace He offers. This morning, let that truth settle into your spirit like the sunrise itself—steady, warm, and full of promise. You do not walk through these challenges alone.

In the Catholic tradition we are blessed with the sacraments and the prayers of the saints who faced their own trials with the same trust. Bring your cares to the Lord in simple prayer today. Let His presence turn anxiety into quiet confidence and fear into hope.

As you step into the hours ahead, carry this verse with you. Choose one small act of courage, one moment of kindness, and remember that mortals can only do so much. Our God can do infinitely more. You are held, you are loved, and there is light waiting for you today.

text:
Students are anxious – and it’s no surprise, since we are teaching them to be that way | Erin Clabough, The Conversation

Temporary anxiety can often surface before the first day of school. Sometimes, that can help kids get in the right mindset for a big day. But when anxiety becomes a constant feature of children’s and teenagers’ days, that stress doesn’t switch off when they leave the classroom or finish an exam. It can become the body’s normal, staying with learners long after graduation.

I teach biology and neuroscience to undergraduates, and I believe that the way we educate our children – prioritizing performance and grades over curiosity and well-being – is producing a society full of anxiety-ridden adults.

A recent survey of over 84,000 college students found that one-third of them self-reported moderate or severe anxiety, and roughly the same share self-reported depression.

I’ve seen this unfold in ways I am only just starting to understand. A few years ago, one of my neuroscience students, whom I will call Hannah to protect her privacy, described how she experienced high school only as a way to get a scholarship to attend college. She became, in her words, a “complete robot.”

“I developed extreme anxiety; it like completely took over my life,” she said. “There was no excitement to learn.”

Learning Can Be Fun, But Isn’t Always

Learning, as experienced by young children, is normally very rewarding. When organic, it is delightful, immersive, timeless and fun.

Curiosity itself triggers a dopamine response in children’s brains. Researchers describe it as a “curiosity loop,” in which the brain predicts something, runs into something new or unexpected, releases dopamine, and the child is hooked, chasing the answer because it feels good to find it.

As kids grow, they take on more homework and more exams, and have more evaluation tied to specific benchmarks, like grades, which can inadvertently cut off the curiosity loop.

Some educators argue that grades help keep students accountable, push them to work harder even on material they wouldn’t otherwise prioritize, and give teachers a shared standard, however imperfect, for tracking whether learning is happening.

Others argue, meanwhile, that grades are not actually an accurate representation of what students are learning. They can also cause students to experience academic pressure.

Research shows that a high degree of academic pressure stems from fear of failure, chronic stress about workload and exams, worry about parental expectations and competition with peers for grades.

Though many things impact well-being, academic pressure is related to kids’ mental health in a well-documented way. A 2026 study, for example, found that academic pressure to achieve at age 15 can predict depressive symptoms that persist into adulthood.

Grades aren’t the only source of pressure that students experience. Social comparison plays a role, too, along with the pressure to only answer questions when they’re already sure, to never seem confused and to stay constantly productive.

Based on my experience and research, kids pick up on the message that they should keep their curiosity at a 5 out of 10 scale, instead of a 10 out of 10, especially if it strays outside the curriculum.

Learning To Avoid Fear And Pain

A theory dating back more than 100 years suggested that there is an optimal amount of stress for good performance, based on a study that had nothing to do with humans.

Researchers ran mice through a maze, using electric shocks to punish wrong choices. On harder tasks, moderate shocks produced the fastest learning, while stronger shocks made it worse. Over the years, this got reinterpreted into claims about punishment, reward, motivation and stress in humans.

But the original study was about how animals learn to avoid fear and pain, not about optimal learning at all. Once a mouse learns to avoid a shock, escape itself triggers dopamine release; in other words, the escape – not the discovery – is the reward.

How Stress Shapes The Brain

In 1855, engineers coined the word “stress,” from the word “distress,” to describe a beam pulled, pushed or twisted from multiple directions until the strain shows as a deformation.

Apply distress to a young brain, and the deformation isn’t just in the education process, but in the neurodevelopment of people’s minds.

Over time, chronic stress reshapes the hippocampus, a part of the brain where memories get encoded, making learning itself harder. Chronic stress blunts people’s dopamine response, so nothing feels quite as rewarding, which can look like depression.

Chronic stress also reshapes the prefrontal cortex, impairing our ability to manage stress overall. Each stressor lowers the bar for the next one, until anxiety becomes less a reaction than a preset that follows a student long after they’ve left the classroom.

Chronic stress has implications for general health too, and can cause inflammatory and autoimmune symptoms. I see conditions like chronic pain and panic disorders in my students every semester.

Unlearning Old Habits

In college, Hannah shared that she is still healing from some of that anxiety and has worked to “unlearn the study habits” she developed in high school.

“I was that person always in the library, like you’re going to study, study, study. Wake up at 5:30, do this. Check every box perfectly and not halfway,” Hannah said.

Through journaling and reading, Hannah began noticing the subconscious patterns she’d been repeating since childhood. That process, along with years of talk therapy, let her separate real learning from what she calls “programming,” so she no longer needs that rigidity to feel like she was learning.

I interviewed Hannah this past spring as part of a book I am writing about how people actually experience learning, and what a living systems approach to education could offer them instead. Living systems theory says the goal of a system is what it actually produces, not what it intends – an idea I’m applying directly to education.

This plays out in our current educational environment in the United States. In my view, even if educators, parents and policymakers say their intent is to build lifelong learners, they are reliably producing anxious, burnt-out students. Anxiety, then, is functionally what our education system’s goal is.

It’s not what the system says it does, it’s what it does.

A Different Approach

Since I’ve learned that at least a third of students in my college classrooms are struggling with mental health, I’ve changed the way I teach. I have altered my courses to seek out pockets of wonder, simultaneously supporting learning and well-being.

In my 300-person course with pre-med students, I no longer only teach through lecturing. Instead, I emphasize our humanity and curiosity, while also teaching very difficult content. I provide a solid structure, emphasize that everyone belongs and ask them to teach each other. I use real-world situations and games, give students choice within their assignments and offer opportunities for reflection.

And yes, I use a traditional grading system.

Learning can require persistence and struggle, and no one benefits from a classroom without challenge. But struggle and dread aren’t the same thing.

Does stress belong in learning? Maybe, maybe not.

The first step is recognizing that the U.S. built an education system that runs on stress – not because we meant to, but because most people did not notice.

Ten countries, twelve defense companies, one premise: Europe can no longer rent its missile defense. The FREYJA program, launched in Paris with Ukraine, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden, and the UK, is the institutional answer to a number I wrote about last week, the American interceptor ledger that does not replenish until 2029.

The design choices tell you what lesson was learned. A Ukrainian company, @FirePointUA , is the technical integrator and builds the interceptor, formalizing Ukraine's shift from recipient of air defense to architect of it. The stated target is a cost per intercept four to ten times below current systems, because the Iran war proved that exquisite interceptors lose the exchange ratio war against cheap ballistic mass. And the architecture is deliberately modular and distributed across member states, so that no single nation, and no single supplier, is a point of failure. That last clause is written with Washington in mind without naming it.

The membership rule is the most revealing detail. Zelensky's offer to countries without production capacity: invest your existing Patriot interceptors into the coalition and join. Scarce American munitions have become the entry currency of a European alliance. When your stockpile is your membership fee, the magazine is no longer logistics. It is diplomacy.

text:
The most dangerous development is not simply that Iran has denied Trump’s announcement of new negotiations. It is that the financial market is repeatedly pricing diplomatic progress while the physical oil market remains constrained.

Iran says it is negotiating only with Oman over a temporary shipping corridor, not with Washington, and that any new route would remain under Iranian control rather than restore normal freedom of navigation. That is not a reopening of Hormuz in the conventional sense. It is an attempt to replace an internationally accessible chokepoint with an Iranian-administered permission system in which Tehran decides which ships pass, under what conditions and potentially at what cost. 

This distinction matters because Trump’s announcements can lower paper oil prices immediately, but they cannot move physical barrels. Brent fell roughly 5% after he cancelled planned strikes and announced negotiations, yet Iran subsequently denied that such talks existed. The market is therefore pricing de-escalation before tankers, insurers and refiners have evidence that normal flows are returning. 

Paradoxically, these repeated false dawns may accelerate the inventory problem. Lower oil prices reduce the incentive for consumers to conserve fuel and delay demand destruction, while the actual supply routes remain impaired. Consumption continues, refineries draw available crude and products, but replacement barrels cannot arrive at the normal rate. The longer diplomacy suppresses prices without restoring physical flows, the larger the hidden stock draw can become.

The inventory data already show how fragile the system is. Since the conflict began, global observed oil stocks have been drawing at an average rate of approximately 3.8 million barrels per day. May alone recorded a 143 million-barrel decline, while OECD government reserves fell to their lowest level since 1990 as emergency releases accelerated. 

June initially looked better because global observed inventories increased. However, that headline was misleading. Oil on water rose by 117 million barrels as stranded tankers finally departed, while onshore inventories continued falling by approximately 96 million barrels and OECD governments released another 44 million barrels. The system did not genuinely rebuild its buffer; it moved emergency barrels from storage onto ships. 

The product market is even more vulnerable than crude. Gulf crude exports recovered to nearly three-quarters of pre-war levels during June, but exports of refined products and LPG remained below half their previous rates. Gasoline and diesel cracks consequently rose sharply even when crude prices declined. A temporary route capable of moving selected tankers does not automatically restart refineries, normalize product exports or repair the logistical network. 

Iran’s proposed corridor therefore appears designed to maximize leverage rather than normalize trade. Tehran could permit enough traffic to prevent a complete global economic breakdown while retaining the ability to slow, inspect or deny individual vessels. This would allow Iran to continuously calibrate pressure on oil prices, inflation and Western bond yields without formally declaring the strait reopened.

For Trump, that is politically uncomfortable. Each announcement of imminent negotiations temporarily lowers oil prices and Treasury yields, but every Iranian denial damages credibility. If Washington repeatedly postpones military action while Tehran preserves control of the strait, Iran can portray the pause as evidence that energy pressure is constraining the United States.

The risk is that the market becomes desensitized to diplomatic announcements. Once traders stop believing that another Trump statement means physical reopening, oil will respond only to tanker movements, insurance availability and verified export volumes. At that point, verbal intervention loses its effectiveness and prices may need to rise sharply enough to destroy demand.

OPEC+ production announcements offer little immediate relief when producers cannot move the barrels. The group’s planned September increase is largely irrelevant while Hormuz remains impaired, especially because several Gulf producers are already operating far below quotas due to export constraints. 

The sharpest conclusion is that time is not neutral. Every additional week of political theatre consumes physical inventory, weakens emergency buffers and increases dependence on an eventual agreement. The apparent calm created by diplomatic headlines can actually make the final adjustment more violent because consumers behave as though supply is returning while storage continues to empty.

Trump controls the headlines. Iran still controls the chokepoint. Until tanker traffic, refinery operations and onshore inventories normalize, the oil market is not experiencing peace. It is financing the negotiations with barrels taken out of storage.

text:
Jeff Bezos explains the heavy-eater test behind Amazon Prime.

The finance model said the idea looked "horrifying."

Amazon would offer "unlimited shipping."

No minimum order threshold.

A customer could buy "a single $20 item" or "a single $10 item" and still get "free two-day shipping."

Then Bezos names the part most models miss:

"Shipping is expensive, and customers love free shipping."

"When we modeled this, it didn't look pretty."

"What happens when you offer a free, all-you-can-eat buffet? Who shows up to the buffet first? The heavy eaters."

I like this as an operator test.

A scary early cohort can mean the product is broken. It can also mean the people with the most acute pain found it first.

The question is whether the heavy users are abusing the system, or proving where the market has been under-served.

Prime worked because the expensive users were not a rounding error. They were the demand signal.

Jeff Bezos at The Economic Club of Washington, D.C.

text:
Here’s a summary of what Bigelow revealed in the interview:

Biggest news is that Bigelow described meeting President Trump in the Oval Office on or around January or February 6 (with staff secretary William Sharf also present). Bigelow had prepared seven reports on various topics over several months to brief the President.

One report focused on UAPs, extraterrestrial intelligence, and disclosure. He briefed Trump for roughly 75–80 minutes total and left the full briefing papers on the Resolute Desk.

Bigelow said he urged Trump to deliver a short, carefully worded statement—ideally in a casual setting such as boarding Air Force One rather than from a formal podium. The exact wording he proposed was:
 “A non-human intelligent presence has been on Earth for a very long time using spacecraft and with performances completely beyond our capabilities and our human physics.”
 Bigelow stressed that this would constitute both confirmation and the start of disclosure, ending roughly 80 years of denial, speculation, and noise. 

He argued that presidents are generally not briefed on the most sensitive unacknowledged special access programs (SAPs) and that official confirmation is the essential first step before deeper revelations.

He also discussed “gatekeepers” — individuals in government and private aerospace and defense contractors who hold physical materials, hardware, and detailed knowledge of the phenomenon. (Bigelow Aerospace has long been rumored to have downed UAP materials.)

Bigelow described these gatekeepers as possessing information “more [valuable] than diamonds in a coal mine,” living in isolation (unable to tell even family), and taking secrets to the grave. He called them “heroes of a different kind” and suggested the government should offer preemptive pardons or immunity so they can come forward without fear of prosecution.

Additional points included:

•Belief that the U.S. (and other nations, including Russia/China) has recovered craft and materials that were handed to contractors for study.

•Examples of strong historical cases (Phoenix Lights, Belgian triangle wave, the 1952 White House/Capitol sightings) that he included in the materials given to Trump.

•The need for careful, non-alarming disclosure that does not hand technological advantages to adversaries, followed eventually by attempts at dialogue with non-human intelligence.

•Brief mentions of related topics he also briefed on (such as survival of consciousness after death — another major Bigelow interest) and also clarifications about anomalous events at Skinwalker Ranch.

New information revealed?
 The most notable new public details are Bigelow’s firsthand account of the specific Oval Office meeting (timing, attendees, duration, reports left on the desk) and the precise short statement he drafted for Trump to deliver as the opening act of disclosure.

Also the explicit call for preemptive pardons is important, since Bigelow himself would need one of those to reveal more, from what I’ve been told.

My work over the years has brought me in contact with many of the people who have worked with and for Bigelow. The long briefing and the call for presidential preemptive pardons freeing people to speak are *highly* significant.

I know that @elonmusk has said he’s seen no evidence of aliens. I’m personally curious if Elon would also be in favor of preemptive pardons so that people previously prevented from talking about UAP and related subjects could go on the record.

➖ليست المعركة بالسلاح فقط.. بل بمن يستطيع إنتاجه وتعويضه

تُظهر إحصائيات التصديات الروسية للمسيّرات الأوكرانية بعيدة المدى حجم الاستنزاف الذي تفرضه هذه الحرب. وحتى الآن، لا توجد إحصائية دقيقة لعدد الصواريخ التي اعترضتها روسيا، لكن متابعتنا تشير إلى أنها تُقدَّر بالمئات.

كان الرئيس فلاديمير بوتين قد قال عام 2023 إن روسيا تنتج من صواريخ الدفاع الجوي أكثر مما ينتجه بقية العالم مجتمعًا.

و تقول صحيفة كوميرسانت الاقتصادية الروسية إن روسيا أسقطت 54,500 طائرة مسيرة خلال الأشهر السبعة الأولى من عام 2026.

قبل عام 2022، كانت أوكرانيا تمتلك نحو 145 منظومة دفاع جوي بعيدة ومتوسطة المدى، وأكثر من 100 منظومة قصيرة المدى، إضافة إلى آلاف صواريخ الدفاع الجوي، ما جعلها تمتلك إحدى أكبر شبكات الدفاع الجوي الأرضية في أوروبا بعد روسيا.

كما أن معظم عمليات إسقاط الطائرات الروسية، وجزءًا كبيرًا من اعتراض الصواريخ، نُفِّذت بمنظومات ذات أصل سوفيتي أو روسي كانت موجودة لدى أوكرانيا قبل الحرب.

كما أظهرت الحرب مع إيران حجم الاستنزاف الكبير لمنظومات وصواريخ الدفاع الجوي الأمريكية، ما أعاد تسليط الضوء على تحديات تعويض المخزونات بسرعة، خاصة مع استمرار دعم أوكرانيا على مدى السنوات الماضية، واستنزاف ذخائر الدفاع الجوي في الحروب التي خاضتها إسرائيل في المنطقة.

وبالموازاة مع ذلك، برزت مؤشرات على محدودية مخزونات بعض الأسلحة الهجومية بعيدة المدى، وهو ما يعكس أن القدرة الصناعية أصبحت عنصرًا حاسمًا في الحروب الحديثة.

قوة الجيوش تقاس بقدرة الدولة على مواصلة الإنتاج وتعويض الخسائر والاستمرار في القتال لسنوات. وهذا ما جعل القدرة الصناعية والعسكرية الروسية تصمد أمام حرب استنزاف غير مسبوقة، في حين كشفت هذه الحروب تحديات كبيرة أمام القدرة الأمريكية على مجاراة صراع طويل وعالي الكثافة.

How much does Congressman Chuck Edwards love Western North Carolina’s Veterans?

Here’s the answer.

On December 15, 2024, Chuck messaged one of the young female staffers he was sexually harassing and offered to skip votes on the House floor the next day to help her decorate her Christmas tree.

She responded and asked if he was sure about skipping votes and he responded: “And yes, I’m sure about skipping votes — so you’ll get to enjoy your tree a little longer.”

On December 16, 2024, the House voted to approve the Senator Elizabeth Dole 21st Century Veterans Healthcare and Benefits Improvement Act. The bill passed 382-12 (the 12 nays were all Republicans). Next to Chuck Edwards name in the vote tally it says “Not Voting.”

The Military Officers Association of America said this about the bill: “This landmark bipartisan bill, representing more than 90 pieces of legislation developed throughout the 118th Congress, provides significant relief to veterans and their families by expanding benefits, enhancing services, and improving long-term care solutions.”

But Chuck skipped the vote on a milestone piece of Veterans legislation so that he could decorate a young woman’s Christmas tree!

As Veterans know, in the military we call that AWOL and dereliction of duty.

text:
A local witness reported seeing Reuben go underneath a gate to enter a wooded area on the private hunting property immediately after leaving the gas station. 

Based on investigations by the Calera Police Department and statements from his family, after hitchhiking out of his son's neighborhood, Reuben had asked a DoorDash driver for a ride "to town". When he was dropped off at the highway gas station, his confused mind likely perceived the surrounding landscape through the lens of his rural property in Kiambu County, Kenya.

Individuals experiencing severe dementia-related disorientation frequently mistake unfamiliar environments for their past homes. Reuben likely viewed the open, unpaved terrain behind the gate of the private hunting property as a familiar walking path or shortcut back to his own land, completely unaware of the dense, industrial nature of the Alabama wilderness.

His confusion gave him a singular focus to continue moving forward, which drove him to physically crawl underneath the gate structure to keep walking in the direction he thought would lead him home. 

The Calera Police Department, alongside state and federal partners, immediately saturated the hunting club grounds and surrounding forest. They deployed ATVs, helicopters, and grid search teams to clear the heavy undergrowth. 

Both tracking dogs and cadaver dogs scoured the woods trying to catch his scent, but the dogs were unable to establish a definitive path forward. 

Investigators tracking Waithaka's cell phone data noted a puzzling digital ping originating in Frankfurt, Germany. Police deduced this was not due to travel, but rather a technical glitch. This type of digital ping occurs because of how mobile networks route data when a phone loses its primary connection.

Mobile data often routes through a carrier's core servers, many of which are hosted in major international telecom hubs located in Frankfurt. When a device suddenly disconnects or loses its local connection, it can briefly register a Frankfurt IP address, making the phone appear to be in Germany while it is physically elsewhere.

Tracking Waithaka's footprint digitally or physically proved impossible because he left the house without his passport, any U.S. currency, or active credit cards. 

To date, Reuben Waithaka remains missing. Marking the anniversary of his disappearance, Calera Police Chief David Hyche and Alabama Cold Case Advocacy launched a renewed public billboard campaign along major Alabama corridors. The Calera Police Foundation continues to offer a $13,000 (approx. 1.7M shillings) reward for any actionable tips that would lead to his location.

text:
Can't Recall What He Said.

Q. After Mr. Holloway left, who was the next person you saw come in? Who did you tell the police?—A. I think Quinn came in.

Q. Did you tell the police that?—A. I can't recall.

Q. Did you tell them a lady in green came up after Mr. Holloway?—A. I don't know.

Q. You didn't tell them?—A. I might have.

Q. Was that right or a lie?—A. It wasn't true.

Q. When did you explain it to the police?—A. After I left the jail.

Q. When did you say Quinn went in?—A. I think I told them he was the last one.

Q. Didn't you tell the officers you saw Mr. Holloway come in and right after him a lady in green?—A. Yes, I think so.

Q. Why did you tell that?—A. I must have been mistaken.

Q. Did you tell the officers she remained there five or six minutes?—A. I might have, but I was mistaken.

Q. How many mistakes did you make?—A. I don't know.

Q. Who did you correct them with?—A. I don't know. I don't think they asked me about it.

Q. After the lady in green came down, how long was it before anybody else came up?—A. I can't think.

Q. All the people you told the officers you saw go up were Darley. Mattie Smith, Holloway and the woman in green?—A. Yes, I reckon so.

Q. You told them that four people were there.

Wasn't there four witnesses against you—couldn't they connect you with the crime?

"I object to that question, your Honor," interrupted Solicitor Dorsey. "It is a question for argument."

Rosser: "Can't I show that people saw him or didn't see him, to show some object in his being there."

Judge Roan: "I think so."

Dorsey: "Do I understand Your […]

SWEEPER CUNNINGLY WITHSTANDS ROSSER'S FIERCE ATTACK
Admits Previous Falsehoods, but His Main Story Stands Unyielding
CONLEY GLIBLY EXPLAINS DISCREPANCIES IN STORY OR BLAMES BAD MEMORY
[…] Honor rules that question is admissible?"

Judge Roan: "Ask your question, Mr. Rosser."

Dorsey sat down smiling.

During Mr. Rosser's questioning a number of the members of the jury were inattentive. It was obvious that Mr. Rosser was postponing the climax of his cross-examination for some time ahead.

More and more it was apparent that he was endeavoring to weary the negro down before making a real effort to impeach him.

The strategy with which he preserved his own strength was undisguised. He kept his seat and asked most of his questions in an even, natural voice. The Rosser who had fired the lightning questions at Newt Lee and the Rosser who had crushed John Black was not yet in action.

Q. You did know that four other people had gone up and down the steps who could have seen you?—A. Yes, sir; they could have seen me.

Q. And you wouldn't tell the others because you were afraid they might have told on you?—A. Yes, sir.

Didn't Think of Them.

Q. What did you think about the four who had seen you?—A. I didn't think about them.

Rosser—That is just what I thought.

Q. When did you correct your statement about whom you saw?—A. At the police station to Mr. Starnes and Mr. Campbell and Mr. Black and Mr. Dorsey.

Q. How many times did Mr. Dorsey see you in jail?—A. About three times.

Q. How many times did he see you at the police station?—A. About four times.

Q. Then it took Mr. Dorsey seven visits to get your story straight? Why didn't you tell it all before he had been to see you seven times?—A. I didn't want to tell it all at first.

Q. You had already told so much that what you were holding back could not help Mr. Frank?—A. I don't know so.

Q. Well, why didn't you tell it?—A. I just wanted to keep back a little all the time. I didn't want to tell it all at once.

Q. You had a whole lot of other stories to take back and correct didn't you?—A. No, sir; I didn't have no other stories to take back.

Admits He Corrected Story.

Q. What about telling the police about buying whisky at 11 o'clock when you bought it at 8, and about seeing various people at times you didn't see them?—A. Yes, sir; I had to correct them.

Q. To whom did you correct them? A. Mr. Starnes, Mr. Campbell and Mr. Dorsey.

At this point the jury went out for a breathing spell.

Q. You told the officers that when you left the factory that day that you went to a moving picture show?—A. No, sir.

Q. But didn't you say that in an affidavit?

Dorsey objected to the point of questioning and was sustained.

Q. On the 28th of May, in the presence of Scott, Black and other detectives in the city of Atlanta, Fulton County, Georgia, didn't you make the statement that you had gone to a moving picture show?—A. I guess so, if it's down there.

Fails to Remember.

Q. Didn't you tell the officers you went back to Peters street?—A. Yes.

Q. How long did you stay there?—A. About ten or fifteen minutes.

Q. How many beers did you take?—A. I don't know.

Q. Didn't you supplement your statement of May 28 or May 29?—A. I don't know.

Q. Was that the truth?—A. All except the time.

Q. You didn't tell about moving the girl?—A. I don't know.

Q. When was the first time you told about watching Mr. Frank?—A. I don't know.

Q. Was it before or after you left the jail?—A. I don't know.

Q. Were Detectives Black and Scott there?—A. I don't know. There were two men there.

Q. You don't know when you told Mr. Dorsey that?—A. I forget.

Q. Now, Jim, you can't tell me anything about these additions you made to these statements?—A. No.

Knew It Was Before 2 o'Clock.

Q. Well, you saw Mr. Dorsey six or seven times?—A. Yes.

Q. Now you say that when Mr. Frank spoke to you Miss Willis heard him?—A. I don't know that she heard him.

Q. Well, what time was that?—A. About 2 o'clock.

Q. How do you know?—A. It was after Mr. Frank had come back from dinner.

Q. How do you know he had come back from dinner?—A. I was looking out of the window and saw him coming from Alabama street.

Q. Well, this Saturday you and Mr. Frank got to the factory at the same time—you met at the door?—A. Yes, sir, he got there just a little before me.

Q. Didn't you go in together?—A. Yes, sir, he went in ahead.

Q. Where did he go.—A. He went on upstairs.

Q. What time was it you locked the door?—A. I don't know.

Q. Give your best estimate.—A. I don't know.

Q. Was it 1 o'clock?—A. I know it was earlier than that, because I heard the screaming and stamping before that.

Q. You locked the door before he stamped?—A. When he stamped I locked the door.

Left Door Unlocked.

Q. When did you unlock it?—A. When he whistled.

Q. Was that before he went upstairs?—A. Yes, sir.

Q. The door was unlocked while you were upstairs, then?—A. Yes.

Q. Anybody could have come in and gone out, couldn't they?—A. Yes.

Q. Don't you know you locked that door and left it locked?—A. No, sir.

Q. You say that when you met Mr. Frank at the factory he went in ahead of you. Didn't you say yesterday that you went in together?—A. I expect I did say something like that.

Q. Whey do you change to-day?—A. Well, we were right there together. He went in ahead of me.

Q. What did he say to you about you wanting to go to the laundry?—A. He didn't say that to me right then. He said when I met him at the factory that I was a little early for what he wanted me to do and said he did not want me to let Mr. Darley know about it.

Q. Now, Jim, didn't you say that yesterday?—A. I disremember.

Hooper Strenuously Objects.

Q. Now, Jim, I want to know just what you said to me yesterday. You know that you didn't say that. I want to know what you said next—"

Attorney Hooper interrupted with a strenuous objection.

"We object to him questioning the witness as to what he said next," said Hooper. "Such questions can only be for the purpose of impeaching the witness. In the eyes of the law what he said yesterday is written testimony. The stenographer took it down and the stenographer can read the notes to him. It is not fair to the witness, especially a witness who has been on the stand for a day to make him give the logical sequence to his testimony. In a matter of cross-examination like this when a witness is questioned rapidly it is neither fair to him nor right in the eyes of common fairness to attempt to thus impeach him. The law makes it plain that the questions and answers of the day before should be read to him and left to him to either qualify, affirm or deny."

Rosser replied: "Your honor, we are simply trying to test this witness' memory. We are attempting to find out if he can tell the truth twice, or if he can lie twice. He has already lied. We want to test his memory of his parrot-like story of yesterday, and we have the right to test his memory."

Judge Roan overruled the objection, declaring that the defense had the right to test the witness' memory by asking if he had said those things.

Tells of Meeting Frank.

Q. Jim, you told the officers first that you met Mr. Frank accidentally on Forsyth street.—A. I disremember.

Q. You were at Nelson and Forsyth streets at 10:30?—A. Between 10 and 10:30.

Q. You saw Mr. Frank going to Montag's and how long he stayed? You don't know you said about an hour?—A. Yes, sir, about that.

Q. When you started back to the factory, then, it was about 11:30?—A. I guess so.

Q. When Mr. Frank saw you what did he say?—A. "Ha, ha, you are here, are you?"

Q. How many times did? Say it again.—A. Ha, ha, ha, ha.

Q. That makes four times.—A. The way I say it it seems like twice.

Q. What else did he say?—A. He said: "Ha, ha, ha, ha, I see you are here, are you. I will see you as soon as I go to Sid Montag's."

Q. He didn't give you any new instructions? Just told you to wait?—A. That was all. I didn't know what he wanted.

Q. What was it he wanted with you at Nelson street? Got no idea?—A. No, sir, I don't know.

Q. Just had you go up there for no reason in the world? He told you he was going to move a body—to come and chat with him a while?—A. Yes, sir; he told me that, and then in a little while he told me again.

Told to Shut Door.

Q. He repeated it to you? You didn't say anything about this yesterday, did you?—A. Yes, sir; I did.

Q. What else did he say?—A. He said for me to shut the door and nobody could get in unless they had a key.

Q. You did not say anything about a key yesterday?—A. Yes, sir; if I didn't, you cut me off.

Q. Mr. Dorsey was questioning you. He didn't cut you off, did he?—A. If I didn't tell him that, he cut me off.

Q. Now, you got back to Montag Brothers. Who was the first person you saw go upstairs?—A. The first one was a lady in a green dress who worked upstairs. I don't know her name.

Q. Was that before you saw Mr. Holloway and that peg-leg nigger drayman?—A. Yes, sir.

Q. What time was it?—A. I don't know, sir.

Q. How long was it after you got back?—A. About five minutes.

Q. How long did she stay?—A. I don't know.

Q. About how long?—A. I don't know; a pretty good while.

Q. How long after the woman went up did the peg-leg nigger come?—A. I don't know, sir.

Q. How long did he stay?—A. He didn't stay no time.

Q. How long after that did Mr. Holloway come?—A. Not long.

Q. Give me your best estimate?—A. I don't know.

Q. What else happened?—A. Mr. Darley come down then; Mr. Holloway come down and then the lady in green come down, and then Lemmie Quinn come down.

Saw Persons Enter Factory.

Q. Lemmie Quinn came up and went down before Monteen Stover?—A. Yes.

Q. You are sure of that?—A. No, the dead girl came up before she did, and the lady in green, too.

Q. You didn't see the office boy?—A. No.

Q. Miss Hall?—A. No.

Q. The office boy?—A. No.

Q. May Barrett?—A. No.

Q. You didn't see any of those folks I just named?—A. No.

Q. What did you do while you waited?—A. I got water.

Q. Where?—A. Near the elevator door.

Q. Q. You say when Monteen Stover came in you just went to sleep?—A. No.

Q. You locked the door, then?—A. No; when the girl left.

Q. When did you go to sleep?—A. After she left.

Q. When was it you heard those screams—before or after Monteen Stover went up there?—A. It was before.

Q. Was it before you went to sleep that you heard those footsteps going back there?—A. It was right after the little girl went in.

Q. When was it you first told the detectives about those footsteps?—A. I don't know.

Q. When did you tell them about the scream?—A. I don't know.

Q. Whom did you tell?—A. Detective Starnes, Campbell and Lanford.

Q. Was it before or after you left the jail?—A. I think it was after.

Q. Were you asleep when you heard those screams?—A. No; that was just before Monteen came in, then a-running on tiptoe.

Q. You didn't wake up until you heard the stamping?—A. No.

Q. Was he stamping when you woke?—A. I don't know. I heard the knocking when I woke.

Q. What did you do?—A. I kicked on the elevator door.

Q. Why didn't you tell the detectives that?—A. I did tell one of them.

Q. What kind of shoes did the woman in green have on?—A. I don't know.

Q. You didn't notice?—A. No.

Q. Isn't it a fact that you didn't notice anybody's shoes but the Stover girl's?—A. Yes.

Q. Why do you know about her?—A. I couldn't hear her walk and noticed her shoes.

Saw Frank Trembling.

Q. How long did the girl in green stay up there?—A. About fifteen minutes.

Q. I thought you told me yesterday you couldn't tell?—A. Yes; I am only guessing at that now.

Q. How long did the Stover girl stay up there?—A. It seemed about like five minutes.

Q. After Frank stamped, he whistled, and you went on upstairs?—A. Yes.

Q. When did you tell the detectives that?—A. I don't know.

Q. It wasn't very long between the time you heard him stamp and heard him whistle?—A. It didn't seem very long.

Q. You went upstairs, and what did you see?—A. I saw Mr. Frank standing there trembling.

Q. Now, when did you tell this? You didn't say anything about it when you first told about helping carry the body?—A. I don't know whether I told it then or not; I did tell it, I know.

Q. To whom?—A. Mr. Starnes, Mr. Campbell and Mr. Dorsey, too.

Q. Did you tell all the truth then?—A. I intended to tell it all.

Q. You told all you know, did you?—A. I tried to tell all I remembered.

Frank Told Him to Hurry.

Q. You said Frank had a cord in his hand. What did he do?—A. He told me to hurry, and he threw the cord toward his office.

Q. Was that the first thing he said?—A. He asked me if I saw that little girl go out. I told him I saw on go out, but I saw one go up who ain't come back down. He said, "Um humph."

Q. Those very words?—A. That's what I said.

Q. Well, what else did he say?—A. He said: "Yes, I wanted to be with the little girl, and she refused me." He said: "I struck the little girl and struck her too hard."

Q. Jim, when did you get this revelation? When you said you told the whole truth, why didn't you tell it?—A. I meant to tell it.

Q. You said all of that yesterday?—A. Yes.

Q. You are certain of that?—A. I don't know if I did, I intended to.

Q. You didn't say anything about money yesterday, don't you know that?—A. No, I don't remember.

Q. When did you tell the officers?—A. I don't know.

Q. What did he strike her with?—A. I don't know. He just said he struck her too hard.

Q. Why didn't you tell the police that on May 29?—A. I think I told one of them.

Q. Didn't you say this (reading from the affidavit of May 29): "He there"?—A. I reckon so, but I told picked up a girl and dropped her back also about striking her.

Q. Did Frank say anything about the girl being dead when he told you to go back there and get her?—A. No.

Q. What did he say?—A. He just told me to go back there and get her and "bring her up here."

Q. That was all he said?—A. No, he said: "We will have to get her out of here."

Q. What did you do?—A. I went back there.

Q. You found her near the toilet in the dressing room?—A. Yes.

Q. You know where the ladies' toilet is?—A. Yes.

Q. Now you went back there and found a cord around her neck? And a part of her underclothes?—A. Yes, sir; I found her with a knot back of her head, like her head had been raised up off the floor and a cord put around it.

Q. You just know that knot was at the back of her head?—A. No, sir; I looked at it close.

Q. Why didn't you tell the detectives this?—A. I think I did.

Q. You said he told you to bring her "up here." Didn't you tell the detectives he told you to bring her up to the elevator?—A. Not about that time. When Mr. Frank dropped her feet. I told them he said to take her to the elevator.

Q. Jim, you went back there and hollered to Mr. Frank, you told the detectives.—A. I didn't holler. I went outside the door and told him she was dead.

Q. Now, when Mr. Frank whistled for you, you looked at the clock?—A. No, sir, not then.

Q. When did you look at the clock?—A. Well, when I saw the little girl was dead, he told me to bring her up there and I asked him, "How was I to move her." He said to go back and get a cloth by the clock-box.

Q. Don't tell me all that, just answer […]

Conley Admits Lying, but Claims to Tell Truth Now
[…] swer my question.—A. Well, I was trying to explain.

Q. I don't want you to go off on an explaining excursion. You looked at the clock when you went to get the cloth to move the body?—A. Yes, sir.

Q. What time was it?—A. Four minutes to 1 o'clock.

Q. Jim, when you talked to the detectives that time, you were telling all that you knew. You didn't say anything about getting that cloth?—A. I intended to.

Q. What sort of a cloth was it? Like that burlap you had up here the other day?—A. No, sir, it wasn't like that. It was striped.

Q. How wide was it?—A. I don't know exactly.

Q. Was it two feet?—A. Yes, sir, I guess it was two foot.

Q. What is two feet?—A. Like these. (Conley pointed to his feet.)

Q. What then did you do with the body?—A. I turned it on to the cloth and wrapped it up.

Q. Now, when you were talking to Black and Scott, you didn't say anything about coming up to Frank before you went and got the cloth to wrap the little girl in?—A. No, sir, I don't remember saying that.

At this time court adjourned until 2 o'clock.

Asks Ruling Out of Testimony.

When the court was resumed Reuben Arnold asked that the jury be excluded while he made a motion. When the jurors had left, he asked that all the testimony relating to Frank's alleged degeneracy be ruled out.

"We move to exclude all evidence about this negro watching for Frank on other occasions," said Arnold. "We propose to withdraw all cross-examination on this subject.

"Your Honor, the stuff is too vile to be read before these women. I'll show it to Your Honor and to the attorneys for the prosecution.

"Our motion is to exclude this testimony on the ground that it is irrelevant."

"Now, I want to bring to the attention of the court," continued Arnold, "that this was not brought out on cross-examination. It was put in for nothing in the world but to prejudice the jury against this man, and we propose to rule out our cross-examination on those questions. We want to rule out the fact that he watched and what he claims he saw."

Attorney Hooper said that when the defense did not object when that question was put and answered it seemed to him they were too late.

"There is every reason why it should be admitted," he said. "They have had the full benefit of the cross-examination. I am almost positive they forfeited the right to get this ruled out when they didn't ask for it at the time they were admitted."

Before ruling, the Judge called for authorities.

"We appeal to your honor," continued the Solicitor, "that such a motion is unfair and we submit this evidence as admissible as an original proposition."

"That's the authority we want to hear," said Rosser.

"The defense has offered no authority and I daresay they won't," retorted Dorsey.

"When one of the prosecution," said Rosser, "admits in the beginning that it was inadmissible originally, I think we at least are entitled to an authority from his assoc[i]ate."

Dorsey proceeded to read authorities. The argument was that the evidence established a course of conduct and established intent and motive.

Leo Frank kept his eyes fixed on Dorsey during the argument. His expression was the same enigma as always.

Judge Ends Argument.

Dorsey said:

"I submit that as an original proposition this evidence is admissible."

Judge Roan: "Well, that ends the argument."

Dorsey adds that there was also the proposition of being too late. He asked the defense to cite their authority.

Rosser said: "I have too much respect for the court to trot out the authorities."

Dorsey retorted: "Run them out, anyway, just so you get them out."

Rosser replied: "No matter how I brought them out you wouldn't understand them."

"Your honor," said Dorsey, "as a commonsense proposition, it is not fair for the defense to remain silent when this evidence was first submitted, then cross-question this witness for two days and get all the benefit they can possibly hope to get and then to move to withdraw the evidence."

Fixed Trap for State.

"They would withdraw this evidence and make the impression on the jury that we are unable to support this witness. I'll tell the court that we expect to introduce witnesses and back them up. When they see how powerful ti is after a vain effort to derive a benefit from it for two days they would withdraw it all to leave the State high and dry."

Mrs. Frank, the prisoner's wife, was absent for the first time since the trial opened. She left the room when Dorsey started his accusations in the course of his argument. The mother kept her seat by the side of her son.

"The course of conduct sworn to by this witness will be amply corroborated. It is a powerful thing to show that this man killed little Mary Phagan as will be shown later on. Your honor, we ask that you go slow before deciding to rule out this evidence. The courts are to show justice and I defy the mto [sic] cite an authority from the textbooks written in the last five years that sustains their motion," said Dorsey.

When Solicitor Dorsey concluded and Reuben Arnold arose to speak Mrs. Frank returned to her seat beside her husband, her eyes wet with tears.

Arnold said:

"It is not any use to get excited over this proposition. Now the person who is hurt by this poisonous evidence is this defendant here. In a criminal case you can't try a man for but one crime. It is a simple question of law. I sympathize with that poor little girl and think the man who throttled her life out should punished. We came here to try a case of murder and this miserable wretch on the stand comes here and charges capital crime. Any white man should be ashamed to believe it. Now, we don't want to come here and try this other disgusting and vile charge. It is absolutely irrelevant. They put him on the stand and it is up to them to bolster up his tale. Why, we would have to stay, trying this case, and investigating other cases."

Judge Roan intervened:

"The first of your motion was to rule out what he said about watching. The second about his conduct."

Arnold answered in the affirmative. Then he continued:

"If you don't call it a crime on those other occasions it would be a distinct transaction. How much harm might it do? How much would it confuse the jury? It would be eminently unfair to this man. We could cross-examine even to determining the illegality. If it is unfair to the State to rule it out it is a thousand times more harmful to permit this creature to poison a jury's mind against this innocent man."

Court Ruling Withheld.

Judge Roan: "Colonel Arnold, if the evidence on the day he watched and the murder occurred is admissible, why isn't the watching on the other days admissible?"

"Why isn't any other murder admissible?" replied Arnold. "My friend, Mr. Leonard Haas, has handed me another authority."

Attorney Arnold then read the authirity [sic]. Judge Roan hesitated for a moment, then said:

"There is no doubt in my mind that it was inadmissible as an original proposition. I am inclined to think it should all be ruled out, except his watching on the day of the crime."

Attorney Hooper interrupted: "Your honor," he said, "will you withhold your ruling until in the morning, in order that we may cite you more authorities?"

"I would reverse myself at any time, if I found I was wrong," Judge Roan replied. "I will refrain from saying anything to the jury until I have received your authority."

The jury was then recalled.

Examination Continues.

Tulane Green Wave 

Class of 2026 Spotlight

LB
 Chan Lumpkin
6-4/220
Butler, GA
 Chandarin “Chan” Lumpkin is a versatile linebacker prospect from the Class of 2026, known for his athleticism and multi-positional capabilities. 
 He played primarily as a middle linebacker (MLB) and wide receiver (WR) during his high school career, but projects best as an outside linebacker with coverage ability or could be a bandit at the collegiate level. 
 Lumpkin signed with Tulane University on December 3, 2025, after committing on June 24, 2025, choosing the Green Wave over offers from programs like Memphis, East Carolina, Rice, South Florida, Appalachian State, and others. 
 He hails from Taylor County High School in Butler, Georgia (with earlier time at Rockdale County High School in Conyers, Georgia), where he also competed in basketball.
 Scouting Report:
 Versatility and Position Flexibility: Excelled at both linebacker and wide receiver in high school, with potential to play strong safety in college due to his coverage skills. Described as a “do-it-all defensive player” who can line up anywhere in the secondary or at edge.
 Coverage Skills: 
Excels in open space, with the ability to cover receivers on the perimeter. Good feet, hips, and instincts allow him to drop into coverage effectively, break on the ball, and play tight man coverage. Has good hands for interceptions.
 Tackling and Physicality: 
A punishing hitter who “knows how to hit and can lay the boom.” Strong tackler who supports the run well, delivers big hits to ball carriers, and isn’t afraid to come up and lay a hit. Effective at setting the edge against the run as an edge prospect.
 Instincts and Football IQ: 
Smart player with excellent read-and-react ability. Good instincts help him diagnose plays quickly, cause turnovers (forced fumbles and interceptions), and make plays on the ball. Tracks the ball well in the air and has hops to high-point it.
 Athleticism: 
Plays fast and aggressive, with good speed for his size. Versatile enough to contribute in the run-stopping game and create chaos.

text:
🚨WOW: Eight year old Zayin Berry was at a skate park in Somerton, Arizona, when he saw a group of older children throwing a tiny kitten between them like a football.

He knew they were bigger than him. Arguing wasn't going to stop them.

So Zayin went and got the one thing he valued most. His skateboard.

He walked over and offered it to the boys in exchange for the kitten. They took the skateboard, left with it, and dropped the frightened little cat behind.

The kitten was covered in dirt, struggling to breathe, and suffering from a severe eye infection. Zayin carried him straight to his mother, and together they rushed him to the Humane Society of Yuma. Veterinarians managed to save the kitten's life, but one eye could not be saved.

The family named him Peaches and gave him a permanent home.

When Zayin was told Peaches would lose an eye, he had only one concern.

"I don't care as long as he lives, because he's my best friend."

For giving up something he loved to save a life that couldn't save itself, the ASPCA named Zayin Berry its 2025 Kid of the Year. Peaches still sleeps beside him every night, a quiet reminder that one child's kindness changed everything.

text:
CLARITY Act odds decline to 23%

Bernstein & Bernstein’s skepticism is supported by prediction market traders who are betting against the passage of the CLARITY Act before the end of 2026.

Odds of the legislation’s passage before the end of the year are now at 23%, down 11ppt in the past week and down 13ppt in the past month, according to Polymarket, which shows about $3.7 million has been wagered on that prediction.

Meanwhile, White House officials are reportedly weighing a bipartisan ethics counterproposal received on Thursday, following weeks of negotiations between Republican Senator Thom Tillis and Arizona Democrat Ruben Gallego.

The proposal would enable state attorneys general to sue the Department of Justice if it fails to enforce ethics laws against federal officials, three sources familiar with the matter told crypto journalist Eleanor Terrett.

The CLARITY Act aims to establish the first regulatory framework for digital assets in the US, but it has been met with massive pushback from the banking industry and Democratic lawmakers, which argued that the current draft would allow crypto firms to offer yields on stablecoins without facing the same requirements as traditional financial institutions.

On June 26, Galaxy Digital cut its odds of the CLARITY Act becoming law in 2026 to 50%, warning that the US Senate is running out of time to move the crypto market structure bill before its August recess.

Indian-origin Canadian trucker caught hiding millions in cocaine on cross-continent run 🇨🇦

Newly released bodycam footage shows the moment an Arizona trooper stops the trucker and finds bricks of cocaine hidden throughout his rig.

Bodycam footage from an Arizona state trooper on January 6, 2025, shows just how casually certain truck drivers engage in fraud and high-stakes smuggling.

It also shows how easily this kind of criminality rides alongside ordinary traffic on North American highways.

On Interstate 40 near Holbrook, a Volvo tractor-trailer drew a state trooper's attention when its hazard lights began flashing, then leaving a turn signal flashing. When questioned, the driver claimed there was a switch problem and said he was heading to a Love’s mechanic — after already passing both a Love’s and a TA truck stop. The driver quickly pivoted his story, claiming he was heading to an “Indian mechanic,” when the trooper flagged his response as suspicious.

While examining the electronic logging device, the trooper quickly became aware of a concerning driving pattern.

There were multiple stretches of “unidentified drive time” appearing from Michigan through Ohio into New York, and again just before the stop.

The driver invented a co-driver named “Uncle” — someone who never logged in or out yet somehow erased hours when convenient. He claimed to be in the sleeper berth when the records showed he was driving. This is textbook hours-of-service fraud designed to push past the federal 11-hour driving limit.

What began as a traffic stop escalated when the trooper checked the sleeper berth. Tightly wrapped bricks of cocaine were found hidden underneath. More packages appeared on the opposite side. Officers then found kilo after kilo concealed throughout the produce load itself, turning out to be one of the larger commercial-truck seizures in recent memory.

The driver, 31-year-old Amarjeet Singh Matharu, had allegedly made the run multiple times before. For moving cocaine valued in the tens of millions of dollars range, he received just under three years in prison.

This bodycam footage finally offers a clear window into the kind of culture that has taken root in commercial trucking.

Ontario’s Auditor General reported in May that private career colleges routinely cut the required 103.5-hour Entry Level Training to as little as 59 or 81 hours, with some skipping emergency stops and left turns at major intersections altogether.

Unregistered schools were handing out certificates, dozens of colleges were never even inspected, and nearly 100 trucking companies with serious safety violations were still being approved to bring in temporary foreign workers; putting them behind the wheel of these increasingly deadly trucks.

“Driver Inc.” has become widely known as a model that misclassifies drivers as independent contractors, allowing companies to dodge overtime, proper wages, and hours-of-service rules. The result is financial pressure that keeps exhausted drivers on the road, compromising road safety at large.

Transport trucks represent about 3% of vehicles on Ontario roads yet are involved in 12% of fatal crashes. It should be common sense that one cannot flood the highways with drivers from a broken training system, questionable hiring practices, and a culture that treats logbooks as optional, then act surprised when the roads become death traps.

Ultimately, this bodycam puts the lies, the technical fraud, and the willingness to risk everything for the extra load on full display.

The next truck sharing the highway with your family may be running the same playbook, and the only difference is whether the cargo is legal produce… or tens of millions of dollars in cocaine.
