text:
Canada’s Victims of Communism monument included proposed honorees from the Waffen-SS, the Ustaša, and the Ukrainian Insurgent Army. The charity that supplied the names is still helping shape the memorial’s next phase. Internal government records show that the charity behind the fiasco is still at the center of the publicly funded project.

The Canadian government scuttled plans to display hundreds of names on Ottawa’s controversial “victims of communism” monument, after officials concluded that individuals listed for commemoration, in the bloodless vernacular of bureaucratese, did not “align with Canadian values.”

“After a thorough review, it has been determined that the names (both donor and commemorative) will not be displayed on the Wall,” the briefing, obtained through Access to Information, read in part.

“The Memorial to the Victims of Communism – Canada, a Land of Refuge” has faced considerable scrutiny since it was revealed that the names of Nazis and suspected war criminals had been proposed for commemoration. A list of names was provided to the Department of Canadian Heritage when it took over the project from a charitable organization, Tribute to Liberty (TTL).

Despite this, the same documents reveal Canadian Heritage plans to continue working with Tribute to Liberty to develop new, yet-to-be defined commemorative elements for the memorial’s Dedication Wall (also referred to as the Wall of Remembrance). The Wall of Remembrance was supposed to contain the names of hundreds of alleged victims of communism, though when the monument was unveiled to the public on December 12, 2024, no names had been affixed to it. The wall was instead covered up during the unveiling ceremony and remains unfinished.

As reported by the Ottawa Citizen in October 2024, an internal assessment of the names revealed more than half of the 553 names listed for commemoration should be dropped. According to a 2023 internal report, between fifty and sixty were directly linked to the Nazis, while hundreds more were either suspected of such links, lacked sufficient information to determine one way or the other, or had no connection to Canada whatsoever.

Tribute to the Waffen-SS

A February 2025 article published by Ricochet revealed that the name of a Nazi collaborator who participated in the massacre of Latvian Jews was found attached to the dedication wall by a Canadian Heritage official during a site visit in early November 2023. Ricochet further reported that, although Canadian Heritage had not completed its vetting of the names slated for commemoration, the National Capital Commission (which oversees monuments in Canada’s capital city of Ottawa and the surrounding region) had nonetheless gone ahead with engraving nameplates to be affixed to the memorial. The unredacted sections of the documents obtained by Jacobin specify that the nameplates are “approximately the size of a business card, and could be removed or replaced.”

The memorial’s planned public unveiling, originally scheduled for November of 2023, was canceled and postponed for over a year after the Yaroslav Hunka scandal. Hunka, then a ninety-eight-year-old veteran of World War II, was honored by Canada’s parliament during a state visit by Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky in September of 2023. Hunka was praised as a “Ukrainian and Canadian hero” for fighting the Soviet Union in World War II.

The Wall of Remembrance was supposed to contain the names of hundreds of alleged victims of communism, though when the monument was unveiled to the public, no names had been affixed to it.

Reporting soon revealed that Hunka had volunteered for the Waffen-SS, the combat arm of the Nazi Party. Veterans of the 14th Waffen Grenadier Division of the SS, such as Hunka, were among thousands of suspected and alleged war criminals who immigrated to Canada after the war. The government of Canada created the Deschênes Commission to investigate some of these cases in the mid-1980s. The commission’s two-part final report contained a list of those investigated in its second half, though this remains a state secret and is not available to the public.

In December 2025, Jacobin asked Canadian Heritage if they had been granted access to the Deschênes Commission’s final report to compare against the names slated for commemoration. Ines Akué, a Canadian Heritage spokesperson, said the final report’s second part was not made available to their staff. Canadian Heritage asked two historians — Michael Petrou and Roman Krakovsky — to review the names, whose reports were submitted in 2021 and 2023, respectively.

Among his recommendations, Krakovsky proposed changing the monument’s name to be more inclusive and reflective of the refugee experience in general. As the Ottawa Citizen reported, Canadian Heritage officials told him the recommendation was “not required,” even though it was consistent with a separate and earlier suggestion made by the National Capital Commission (NCC).

Michael Petrou’s recommendations offered Canadian Heritage three options: remove only the names of the individuals whose histories are conclusively known; establish criteria for assessing the submitted names and evaluate each individually; or only list the names of donors, rather than those submitted as “victims of communism.”

“No Banderites, No Nazis”

Why Steven Guilbeault, then heritage minister, ultimately rejected these options isn’t clear. The heavily censored documents submitted for Guilbeault’s decision on the matter appear to list three possible options, of which only the second is unredacted. It reads: “Replacing the rear face of the Dedication Wall with other thematic content or design elements.” This is preceded and followed by page-length redactions, presumably the two other options. Guilbeault signed the document on September 2, 2025.

“Canadian Heritage undertook a due diligence process to ensure the Memorial aligns with Canadian values and principles of democracy and human rights,” said Caroline Czajkowski, a Canadian Heritage spokesperson, in a statement to Jacobin. “To that end, the Wall of Remembrance will not feature any names. Instead, it will present thematic content that conveys the broader commemorative and educational intent of the Memorial.”

Some of those listed as ‘victims of communism’ were in fact suspected war criminals, Nazi collaborators, and other assorted fascists.

The documents somewhat contradict Czajkowski’s statement, which indicate that Guilbeault actually opted to nix including the names of specific individuals because their backgrounds couldn’t be conclusively verified. “Including names without complete verification would create a significant risk to the credibility and purpose of the Memorial. Not displaying any names is the only approach that ensures no controversial names are included or associated with the site” read, in part, the briefing notes prepared by Canadian Heritage in advance of a meeting with Paul Raff, the architect who designed the memorial.

Elsewhere in the released documents, Canadian Heritage notes that the monument was vandalized in April 2025, a fact not previously made public. Signs and fencing surrounding the memorial’s construction were vandalized in 2020 with the slogan “Communism will win.” At the memorial’s public unveiling in December of 2024 — an event that no federal politicians or members of the government attended — protesters shouted “No Banderites, no Nazis” during a speech by Tribute to Liberty Chairman Ludwik Klimkowski.

The uncensored sections of the documents also reveal that Klimkowski requested — and Guilbeault provided — a signed letter explaining his decision. Klimkowski had requested such a letter so that he could show it to the other members of Tribute to Liberty’s board.

“I understand that this outcome may be disappointing and would like to express my sincere appreciation for your valuable contributions throughout this process,” reads the letter. “Your input has played a key role in shaping the vision for the monument.”

“Buy a Brick” for Nazis

As chairman of Tribute to Liberty’s board, Klimkowski played an integral role in raising $1.5 million CAD to develop the monument. Donations were made initially as part of a virtual “buy a brick” campaign for a memorial element called “Pathways to Liberty,” wherein donors purchased bricks at a set price and could dedicate the bricks to commemorate alleged victims of communism. Ultimately, this component was shelved in favor of the Dedication Wall, which was to feature a list of donors who had contributed over $25,000 to the project (called the Donor Recognition Element), as well as a Wall of Remembrance featuring up to one thousand business-card-sized plaques, listing the names of alleged victims of communism. These nameplates represented donors who had provided between $1,000 and $24,999 to Tribute to Liberty.

According to a 2021 CBC News report, some of the donors include former Canadian Prime Minister Stephen Harper, and former Alberta Premier Jason Kenney. Kenney championed the project while he was a cabinet minister in Harper’s government. Senator Linda Frum, sister of Iraq War propagandist and Atlantic Senior Editor David Frum, is among the project’s legacy donors, having committed over $100,000 CAD.

The uncensored sections of the documents confirm Canadian Heritage knew hundreds of donors contributed with the understanding that their money would cover specific commemorative elements. Although Guilbeault decided to abandon the specific recognitions, there was no indication Canadian Heritage intended to refund the money to the project’s donors. When asked about this, Czajkowski told Jacobin that TTL transferred the money they collected to the NCC, not Canadian Heritage. She referred to all questions concerning refunds — including whether TTL had asked for one — back to the charity.

While hundreds of private donors may have contributed to the monument’s price tag, taxpayers nevertheless were on the hook for the lion’s share of the cost, covering about $6 million of the $7.5 million total.

As reported by CBC News in 2021, some of those listed as “victims of communism” were in fact suspected war criminals, Nazi collaborators, and other assorted fascists. Names listed for commemoration on TTL’s website included Roman Shukhevych, Ante Pavelić, and the Order of Vitéz. Shukhevych led the wartime Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which was responsible for the deaths of tens of thousands of Belarusians, Jews, Poles, and Ukrainians. Pavelić led the Ustaša, the fascist movement that ran the Independent State of Croatia, a Nazi puppet state chiefly responsible for the Holocaust in the Balkans. Vitéz members organized and benefited from the Holocaust in Hungary and then became leaders of the Hungarian Nazi puppet state late in the war.

Of Redactions and Evasions

Though some of these names were removed from TTL’s website shortly after being contacted by CBC News, the names of other collaborators, fascists, and Holocaust perpetrators remained. Asked at the time whether donations had been returned, Klimkowski told CBC News it would be “premature to comment.” He also said at the time that questions about the individuals listed for commemoration were “premature,” as Canadian Heritage and TTL were still reviewing the names, and that this would be completed by December of 2021.

By then, however, the list of names to be commemorated on the memorial had already been submitted to Canadian Heritage.

Jacobin sent Canadian Heritage detailed questions about its review of the names with TTL, including what aspects of the names submitted to Canadian Heritage “wasn’t aligned” with Canadian values. Further questions included whether TTL conducted their own independent review of the names prior to their submission, and whether they challenged the assessment of the names by historians hired by the government.

When asked why the monument came close to not being built, Klimkowski explained that this was because some members of Canada’s federal government inclined toward ‘Marxist-Leninist ideology.’

Canadian Heritage did not respond to these questions. Instead, David Larose, another spokesperson for the government department, replied: “As the review was an iterative process involving multiple parties, PCH [Canadian Heritage] cannot identify specific dates marking the completion of one party’s review and the start of another’s.”

Canadian Heritage also didn’t respond to questions concerning TTL’s continued involvement in the project. Per Guilbeault’s letter to Klimkowski, Canadian Heritage remains committed to working with the charitable organization to “collaboratively develop thematic content” and to explore “alternative design elements for the Wall of Remembrance that foster remembrance, commemoration, and reflection for all visitors.”

Questions about what this might entail were not answered, as Canadian Heritage insisted that any questions regarding TTL’s involvement were best handled by the charitable organization.

However, briefing notes that appear to date to November of 2025 indicate Canadian Heritage “will be responsible for developing the thematic content, which remains to be defined.”

Neither Tribute to Liberty nor Ludwik Klimkowski responded to Jacobin’s questions.

The Politics of Commemoration

A2015 letter written by Klimkowski and published by the Ottawa Citizen indicated Klimkowski believes in the conspiracy theory that communism killed 100 million people. The figure comes from the 1997 book The Black Book of Communism, edited by Stéphane Courtois. Historians and other experts dispute both the figure and the book’s content; in order for it to be accurate, it would have to count all the Nazis killed during World War II, among others, as “victims of communism.”

Klimkowski reiterated this view last year during an interview on American Thought Leaders with host Jan Jekielek, a senior editor with the Epoch Times and a donor to the monument. During the interview, Jekielek stated that communism was responsible for the deaths of hundreds of millions, while Klimkowski stated that Ernesto “Che” Guevara was “personally responsible for the slaughter of thousands of innocents.”

When asked similar questions in 1997, investigative reporter and Guevara biographer Jon Lee Anderson told PBS News Hour there was no evidence Guevara had ever murdered an innocent, and that the people executed by his order were “condemned for the usual crimes punishable by death at times of war or in its aftermath: desertion, treason or crimes such as rape, torture or murder.”

In answering a question from Jekielek about why the monument came close to not being built, Klimkowski explained that this was because some members of Canada’s federal government inclined toward “Marxist-Leninist ideology.”

Canadian Heritage could not provide details about the thematic elements that would be incorporated into the memorial, or whether any academics or other experts would be involved in developing them. It also could not say when the project might be completed.

Jacobin, 26 July 2026. 

Taylor C. Noakes is an independent journalist and public historian.

Full Transcript: 硅谷101 Interview with Ying Sheng (盛颖)

Introduction
Host (陈茜): Hello everyone, welcome to Silicon Valley 101. I'm Chen Qian. Our guest for this video podcast is Ying Sheng — former head of inference systems at xAI and creator of the open-source inference engine SGLang. Ying graduated from Shanghai Jiao Tong University's ACM Honors Class, received her Master's in Computer Science from Columbia University, and her PhD in Computer Science from Stanford. Her research spans algorithms, formal verification, and large model systems. After the large model wave began, she became a core member of the LMSYS open-source community, helped drive several industry-influential projects, and founded the inference engine SGLang. She then joined xAI and co-led Grok's inference team, bringing open-source research into cutting-edge large model engineering. Now she's incubated RadixArk from the SGLang open-source ecosystem, aiming to make frontier AI infrastructure — previously only available to a few tech giants — accessible to the entire industry. RadixArk completed a $100M seed round at inception, with investors representing nearly all of Silicon Valley's compute giants and tech leaders.

Part 1: Early Life & Education
----------
Q: You were at Shanghai Jiao Tong University's ACM Honors Class, then came to Columbia University in 2017 for your Master's. Why did you choose to go abroad?

A: Many people were going abroad at the time. But I actually learned about the concept of going abroad quite late. Coming from Jiangxi to Shanghai for undergrad was already a strong culture shock — people around me understood career development and life planning better. I was in a state of ignorance. When I first graduated, I hadn't gotten into the US universities I applied to. I accepted a PhD offer from Chinese University of Hong Kong. Then, the day after the "gentleman's agreement" April 15th deadline, I suddenly received a regular Master's admission from Columbia. It was a very ordinary offer, but I wanted to see something new. The academic center was still in the US. I called my dad to ask about breaking the previous commitment. He said yes within one minute. We paid the penalty fee.

Q: From Shanghai to America — did you experience another culture shock?

A: Yes, but New York is very inclusive. Nobody stared at me, nobody cared what I wore, thought, or did. The shock in New York was going from a constrained state to a completely free state — not needing to be judged, not needing to judge others. It was actually a more relaxing process.

Part 2: Columbia & Theoretical Research
----------
Q: At Columbia, your papers were quite theoretical — testing functions, mathematical properties of linear regression. Did that research influence your later work?

A: I didn't plan to do research when I started grad school. But I took a computational complexity course in my first semester and found it fascinating. I made some PhD student friends doing theory, found it interesting, produced results, and naturally went to Stanford.

Q: Did you consider working versus applying for a PhD?

A: I wasn't fixated on a PhD, but I kept the option open. I found the theoretical problems very interesting. I thought I wanted to "stay poor" and find a place with no one. I visited Princeton for a workshop and was immediately enveloped by that environment — a feeling of being disconnected from worldly concerns. Nothing mattered except truth. Mathematics felt particularly beautiful in that setting — it's certainty, it's absolute. You can enter a flow state with nothing else to think about.

Part 3: Stanford PhD & Formal Verification
----------
Q: Why didn't you become a mathematician?

A: I wanted to! But life had its various interferences. At Stanford, the feeling wasn't the same. The West Coast has more "noise" about success. I started feeling connected to the world again.

Q: What is formal verification?

A: We take human-written code, decompose and map it to underlying mathematical logic — like first-order logic — and then mathematically prove whether the code satisfies certain properties. My research was mainly on SMT solver optimization — efficiency, correctness, and semantic design.

Q: You won the IJCAR Best Paper Award in 2020. What was your research state like?

A: The real process is much more barren than what the CV shows. My first year finding an advisor wasn't smooth. I passively entered formal verification. The first best paper was completely unexpected — I was a blank slate in the field. But after that paper, I entered a very low period. During COVID, I had nearly a year of depression where I didn't do anything. My advisor Clark was incredibly supportive — he only cared about my mental health and never pressured me to produce papers. He never cut my funding. He's truly an exceptional mentor.

Q: How did you come back?

A: After about a year, I slowly emerged and worked on the Sequence paper. The proof was 20+ pages, rewritten from scratch 4-5 times. When it was done, both Clark and I felt enormously accomplished. Clark said that proof was his highlight of the past year.

Part 4: ADHD, Flow States & The 甄嬛传 Moment
----------
Q: Are you someone who needs intensity?

A: I'm someone who must have intensity. Even when sleeping, I'm always dreaming. I can't stop.

Q: When you were doing theoretical research, how did you find inspiration?

A: I was watching TV when the idea came. I had read a paper before watching, and midway through the show, something from that paper suddenly echoed back. I realized that might be the breakthrough point. The problem was solved in that instant — a phase transition.

Q: Do you remember what TV show?

A: 《甄嬛传》(Erta of the Palace). I genuinely remember.

Q: Are you ADHD?

A: I am. But it's not a disease — it's a characteristic. Learning about it was like finding a manual for how to use myself. I suddenly understood: I shouldn't fight against my nature; I should work with it. Once you realize that, many things become solvable. I can't focus when things don't grip me, but when they do, I'm extremely focused — I won't hear my name being called, I'll miss meetings, I won't know what time it is.

Part 5: Transition to AI & SGLang
----------
Q: How did you transition to AI?

A: I saw formal verification's limitations — too expensive to verify real programs, too narrow in practical application. I wanted to be closer to the real world. I did a Google internship in AI for code (2022). There I saw that large models had already covered everything traditional program analysis could do. That convinced me to fully commit to large models.

Q: Why make SGLang when vLLM already existed?

A: I was actually working on similar ideas. I was "merged" into the vLLM project because our ideas overlapped. But SGLang was where I wanted to push my own vision forward — a comprehensive system collecting all my previous research into one product-ready engine. From the start, it was designed to be widely deployable.

Q: What's the core difference between SGLang and vLLM?

A: If you don't put time into the equation, they converge because they learn from each other. But at any given moment, they have different focuses. SGLang advanced earlier into scale-up — thousand-GPU, million-GPU serving. vLLM focused more on community coverage and long-tail model support.

Part 6: xAI Experience
----------
Q: Why did you join xAI in October 2024?

A: xAI offered both support and freedom — the only place that gave me both simultaneously. I could build the entire inference stack with my husband Lianmin.

Q: What was xAI like?

A: xAI is the most beautiful period in my work memories. Everyone was talented, supportive, humble, grateful. There was zero office politics — at least what I could see. I could focus purely on doing things. The intensity brought growth that might take years elsewhere. Elon set a culture of "no boundaries" — you could access anything, everything was transparent.

Q: Why did you leave?

A: SGLang's open-source community needs were growing beyond what volunteer effort could sustain. By July, my anxiety reached a point where I couldn't be productive at xAI anymore. I left 2 months before my one-year cliff vested. Even two months felt too long to wait.

Part 7: RadixArk Vision
----------
Q: What is RadixArk's ultimate mission?

A: RadixArk's ultimate mission is to build next-generation AI — something that doesn't currently exist in the world. Inference is a starting point, not our long-term core. We want to give everyone the ability to create the best AI for themselves. We're not competing with other inference companies — we want to be their allies.

Q: What does "infrastructure beauty" mean to you?

A: In most model-focused companies, infrastructure aesthetics are compromised. Infrastructure people are in a supporting role. But to me, infrastructure is the product. It's not just about function — it should be elegant, well-designed. I have a "romantic relationship" with infrastructure. RadixArk's culture is: meticulous, humble, focused, and demanding of ourselves.

Part 8: Open Source Philosophy
----------
Q: Why are you so committed to open source?

A: It's not that I'm deliberately committed — it's natural to me. Growing up in Jiangxi without many programming resources, I learned everything from the internet — random posts, online judge systems, CSDN. Unknown people raised me through their shared code. Sharing feels like air — it would be strange not to share.

Part 9: Gender in Tech
----------
Q: Have you experienced gender bias in research?

A: It's everywhere, in very subtle ways. When I won competitions as a girl, people would say "she's hardworking" or "she's lucky" — never "she's talented." Every win needed to be explained. "Her opponents were in bad form," "She'd seen this problem before." If a boy won, it was simply accepted. These tiny things happen constantly — you can't escape them. The only solution is for women to truly gain power at the top 0.001%. Everything else — education, awareness — isn't enough.

Part 10: Life Philosophy
----------
Q: You're so logical, but the world is messy. How do you reconcile that?

A: I'm actually very emotional. Tiny things affect me greatly. But I separate emotional impact from my value system. I see things I don't want to see, but they don't make me think those things are normal. I still believe in what I haven't yet seen. My past experiences give me positive feedback loops — I wait, and things are eventually verified. First months, then years, then decades. I know it will always be verified eventually.

Q: What if some people wait and never find it?

A: You need to find that self-consistency. Even if my entire life is split between my internal logic and external reality, I won't compromise. That split is actually fine — people are just afraid of it. The key is whether you're acting according to your own will or being led by others.

Closing
----------
Ying Sheng: I want to say — all good things exist. Good mentors exist. Good investors exist. Good interviewers exist. They're not made up. But you have to believe in them intensely — believe even when there's no one like that around you. And one day, the person who believes the same way will cross your path.

text:
The Continuing Relevance of Emmanuel Mounier’s Thought — Moloda Ukraina magazine, 1952 (second picture linked - in Ukrainian)

Emmanuel Mounier was one of the founders of the French nonconformist movement of the 1930s and of its “personalist” current — a “third way” between radical individualism and radical collectivism.

“The moment someone, in striking at communism, also strikes at the hard-won rights of the working class, we stand with the working class.” — Emmanuel Mounier

This was how Mounier was presented in the revived Moloda Ukraina (Young Ukraine). Both the name and the magazine itself have a long history — from Mykhailo Pavlyk and Ivan Franko, through the student organization of Social Democrats, radicals, and anarchists in Galicia, to its revival in 1951 by the youth organization of the Ukrainian Revolutionary Democratic Party (URDP), associated with Ivan Bahrianyi.

In general, the revolutionary democrats (Bagryanists) quite often quoted nonconformists-personalists, translated and published them in Ukrainian. Here, for example, Denis de Rougemont in quoting M. Dalnyi:

"“…Bourgeois morality is no longer of any help; it can no longer provide the best guidance in life.

Neither customs nor principles nor religious faith continue, in practice, to govern the lives of a great many of our contemporaries. The young person of today is left exposed to painful anxiety and to moral and material insecurity. Where can they find a human community that will offer them protection and defend their interests? And how can one live without a purpose, without any source of inspiration?

Mussolini and Hitler, strongly influenced by Lenin’s example, were the first to understand that the modern individual had been brought to a state in which they wished to be delivered from a freedom devoid of meaning… The individual seeks a leader — a ‘Duce,’ a ‘Führer,’ a ‘Caudillo,’ a ‘Father of Nations’ — who would prescribe a course of conduct and justify it beyond question, relieving them of the fear of error, the burden of free choice, and remorse over that choice.

It was not out of malice or moral corruption that so many people became fascists and communists. They did so because, with their entire being, they vaguely felt a need for unity, commitment, and security — things that only dictatorships promised to provide. Until the Western democracies recognize their fundamental weakness in this respect, they will not understand the nature of the totalitarian temptation. Their polemics against dictatorships and their freedom-loving rhetoric will remain ineffective—or will produce the opposite effect — unless the Western democracies can offer the individual a reassuring order…”

"Let our democrats of the old school not be horrified by this “heretical” quotation. It comes not from some opponent of democracy but from one of the finest representatives of revolutionary democracy — a thinker who reflected more deeply than most upon the causes of the prolonged crisis of liberal and socialist ideology and who had the courage to voice his criticism openly."

text:
What Is the Opposite of Anxiety?

I asked myself this question first, and then I shared it here because the answer surprised me.

From a psychoanalytic perspective, anxiety is a state of alertness - a signal that something, within or outside of us, is telling us we are not safe.

Perhaps that's why peace feels so precious, and why calm can feel like a hug for the soul. It's why we long for tranquility and why faith has the power to transform us. At the root of all of them is the same thing.

Safety.

Not the false sense of safety that comes from trying to control everything, but the deeper safety of knowing that even when we can't control the road ahead, we can still find solid ground beneath our feet.

Learning to look at ourselves with kindness - to seek what makes us feel at peace with who we are, both in our essence and in our own skin. That should be non-negotiable.

We live in a time when insecurity seems to be everywhere. The news never stops. Crises keep piling up. Fear travels more freely than we do. At different moments in history, fear has also been exploited for political, economic, or social purposes, because people who feel unsafe are more likely to react before they have the chance to reflect.

Still, I believe there is a way forward.

The Christian faith has never promised a life without storms. It offers something deeper: the assurance that God remains present in the middle of them.

That's why Jesus so often said, "Do not be afraid."

Not because everything was okay.

But because even when everything seemed to be falling apart, God was still worthy of our trust.

Perhaps that's why peace, calm, tranquility, and faith are so closely connected.

Because they all blossom when the heart finally finds safety.

And perhaps that is one of the deepest longings of the human soul: not a life without hardship, but a place where the soul can finally rest—secure in the knowledge that, up to this moment, we have done the best we could.

Thank you to everyone who answered, this is why I am here - because the real ones always show up.

text:
On February 12, 1946, Isaac Woodard Jr. was traveling home after serving in the United States Army during World War II when an encounter with police changed his life forever. Woodard, a decorated Black veteran who had been honorably discharged only hours earlier, was still wearing his uniform when he was removed from a bus in Batesburg, South Carolina, arrested and brutally beaten by local police. The attack was so severe that Woodard permanently lost his sight. He was 26 years old.

Woodard had served his country in the Pacific, earning a battle star and rising to the rank of sergeant, yet returning home offered no protection from the racial violence Black Americans continued to face. The incident reportedly began after Woodard asked the bus driver if he could use a restroom during the journey. Although the disagreement initially appeared to be resolved, the driver later contacted police. Batesburg police chief Lynwood Shull arrested Woodard and struck him repeatedly with a blackjack. By the following morning, Woodard could not see. Doctors later determined that the damage was permanent.

The case became national news after the NAACP took up Woodard's cause, and figures including Orson Welles publicly drew attention to what had happened. President Harry Truman was reportedly deeply disturbed by the case. After meeting with NAACP leaders in September 1946, Truman established the President's Committee on Civil Rights later that year. In 1948, he issued Executive Order 9981, directing equality of treatment and opportunity in the United States armed forces and accelerating the process of military desegregation.

There was still the question of justice for Woodard himself. Because South Carolina authorities did not prosecute Shull, the federal government brought a civil rights case against him. An all-white jury acquitted the police chief in November 1946. The acquittal demonstrated just how difficult it was for Black Americans to obtain justice through the courts when racial violence was committed by white officials.

Yet the case had another consequence. Federal judge J. Waties Waring, who presided over Shull's trial, was disturbed by what he witnessed and increasingly challenged segregation in subsequent years. Waring later issued important civil rights rulings and, in Briggs v. Elliott, argued that segregated public schools were inherently unequal. That case became one of the cases incorporated into the Supreme Court's landmark 1954 decision in Brown v. Board of Education.

Isaac Woodard lived for decades after the attack, carrying injuries inflicted on him shortly after he returned from defending a country that still denied millions of Black citizens equal protection under its laws. His story is an important reminder that the struggle for civil rights was shaped not only by the famous marches and speeches of the 1950s and 1960s, but also by individual cases of injustice that forced Americans to confront the contradiction between the nation's democratic ideals and the reality experienced by Black people.

text:
The Army Recruiting Boom Is A Warning About the Civilian Economy

The Army is reportedly experiencing one of its strongest recruiting rebounds in years, with enlistment up nearly 38% from its fiscal 2022 low. Better recruiting, higher pay, expanded preparatory programs, advertising and enlistment incentives all matter. But those explanations only tell part of the story.

Military recruiting often improves when the opportunity cost of civilian life falls. The Army becomes more attractive when private sector hiring weakens, entry level jobs disappear and young adults no longer believe that following the traditional path will lead to independence.

That appears to be happening now.

Youth unemployment is around 9.2%, more than twice the overall unemployment rate. Recent college graduates face unemployment near 5.6%, while the rate for younger degree holders is closer to 8.9%. Roughly 42% of recent graduates are underemployed, meaning they are working in positions that do not require the degrees they spent years and often significant debt obtaining.

The problem is not simply that young people cannot find any work. It is that the work available increasingly fails to provide a path forward.

Working Without Moving Ahead

A record 25.2 million Americans under 35 now live with their parents, representing roughly one third of that age group. Among adults aged 18 to 29, the share is close to 50%.

The most revealing statistic is that about 70% of 25 to 34 year olds living at home are employed. These are not primarily people who refuse to work. Many have jobs but still cannot afford rent, purchase a home, repay student debt and build an independent life.

They are employed, but economically stranded.

The civilian economy is offering many young adults wages without security, degrees without professional entry points and work without upward mobility. At the same time, the military offers a structured alternative that combines several things increasingly difficult to obtain elsewhere.

•    Reliable income and housing support
•    Health care, education and technical training
•    A defined career ladder and long term benefits

What The Recruiting Surge Is Really Signaling 

This does not mean everyone joining the Army is acting out of economic desperation. Patriotism, family tradition, education and a desire for purpose remain important motivations.

But the scale of the rebound matters. It suggests that the military’s employment package has become more competitive because the civilian bargain has deteriorated.

For years, strong private hiring made military recruitment harder because young adults had more attractive alternatives. Now the process may be reversing. Entry level professional hiring is weakening, housing costs remain elevated and employers increasingly want experience without being willing to train inexperienced workers.

The Army is benefiting from that mismatch.

The recruiting boom should therefore be understood as both a military success and a macroeconomic signal. It reflects better execution by the Army, but it also reveals how difficult civilian adulthood has become for younger Americans.

When a generation is working, educated and still unable to leave home, build savings or see a credible future, military service becomes more than a calling. It becomes one of the few remaining institutions offering a complete path into adulthood.

text:
Paying Dearly

The Atlanta Campaign Continues — July 29–August 7, 1864

[Author's Note: Posting this one a few days ahead of the anniversary — Utoy Creek runs the 5th through the 7th of August, and the coming week won't leave much time for writing. Didn't want it to wait.]

Hardee's verdict on Ezra Church — serious, he had called it, and left the word to do its own work — did not end the fighting around Atlanta. It only changed its shape.

Sherman had spent eleven days and something over ten thousand men, Union and Confederate combined, learning what Joseph Johnston could have told him without losing a man to teach it: that the works ringing Atlanta, whoever occupied them, were not going to be carried by walking men into them. Peachtree Creek had failed to prove otherwise. The Battle of Atlanta, four days later, had failed to prove it too, though it cost McPherson his life in the trying. Ezra Church, on the 28th, proved it a third time, this time at Confederate expense — Hood's men going forward four separate times into works Union soldiers had thrown up that same morning, and finding, four separate times, that entrenched infantry with a clear field of fire did not much care which side wore the blue. Sherman was a methodical man, whatever else could be said of him, and methodical men do not generally require a fourth demonstration of a lesson three battles have already taught. He would find another way into Atlanta, or around it. In the last days of July, he turned to the cavalry.

The plan had a certain elegance on paper, which should perhaps have been the first warning. Major General George Stoneman would take his horsemen — the mounted arm of Schofield's Army of the Ohio — east and south around the city toward Macon, tearing up the Macon & Western Railroad as he rode. Brigadier General Edward McCook would swing wide in the opposite direction with a second column and do the same kind of damage from below, the two commands meeting near Lovejoy's Station once they had, between them, cut every rail line still feeding Hood's army from the south. Kenner Garrard's cavalry would screen the movement and hold the Union right in the meantime. It was the sort of maneuver that looked, on a headquarters map, like it might end a siege in a week.

Stoneman had asked Sherman for something more than the railroad. Forty miles below Macon lay the stockade at Andersonville, where something on the order of thirty thousand Union prisoners were dying of exposure and dysentery and plain starvation at a rate already reaching the Northern papers, and Stoneman wanted to free them. Sherman, not entirely easy with the request but unwilling to refuse it outright, granted it conditionally — Stoneman could try for Andersonville once the railroad work with McCook was finished, and not before. It was the kind of conditional permission a commander grants when he suspects, correctly, that the condition will not entirely hold.

It did not. Loose from Sherman's direct supervision, Stoneman put Macon and the prison camp ahead of the rendezvous with McCook, and the joint operation meant to sever Atlanta's supply lines from two directions at once became, in practice, two separate raids that Joseph Wheeler's Confederate cavalry could handle one at a time.

McCook went first. Wheeler's troopers caught his column at Brown's Mill, south of Newnan, on the 30th of July, and broke it. McCook got clear with what remained of his command, but the raid was finished as a fighting force before it had done more than minor damage to the railroad. Stoneman fared worse. With McCook no longer dividing Confederate attention, Wheeler's cavalry ran him to ground the following day at Sunshine Church, north of Macon, and surrounded what was left of his column. Stoneman split his force a last time — Adams's brigade and Capron's brigade would try to cut their way clear while Stoneman himself, with Biddle's brigade, held the rear and bought them the time to do it.

It worked, after a fashion, for two brigades out of three. Adams broke free and reached Union lines on the 4th of August, his men scattered but alive. Capron's command made it as far as King's Tanyard, near Winder, before Confederate cavalry caught up with them on the 3rd and tore the column apart — most of his troopers were captured in the running fight that followed, though Capron himself, separated from his men, somehow rode clear and found his own way back to Federal lines. Stoneman did not. He surrendered with Biddle and roughly six hundred troopers still under arms — the highest-ranking Union officer captured in the whole of the war, a distinction he had not ridden out that July to earn.

The arithmetic, once the stragglers finished finding their way home, was brutal in its plainness. Of the forty-seven hundred Union cavalrymen who had set out in the last days of July to cut Atlanta's lifelines, sixteen hundred came back. The rest were dead, wounded, captured, or simply lost in the Georgia countryside, working their way north the way Capron had, alone or in twos and threes. The Macon & Western remained open and running the whole while. Sherman had spent nearly a third of his mounted arm and had nothing to show for it but casualty rolls and one major general behind Confederate wire.

If the Confederacy could claim a single clean success in the days after Ezra Church, this was it. Wheeler's cavalry had done in a week what Hood's infantry had failed to do in eleven days of far bloodier fighting. It had beaten Sherman outright, and cost him something he could not simply order more of from Washington: time.

Sherman did not sit with the failure long. If cavalry alone could not cut the Macon & Western, infantry would help do it, and by the first days of August he had settled on the same basic maneuver Howard's men had already bled for at Ezra Church — swing right, extend the line, reach for the railroad — except this time the flanking hand belonged to Schofield.

Garrard's cavalry took over the trenches east of the city that Schofield's infantry had been holding, freeing the Army of the Ohio to march, and by August 2nd Schofield's men had worked their way around to a position along Utoy Creek, southwest of Atlanta, within reach of East Point and the junction where the Macon & Western met the Atlanta & West Point road. Take that junction and Hood lost both railroads in a single stroke.

Hood saw it coming. He had learned, if nothing else in his three weeks of command, to watch for a threatened flank, and he moved to cover this one — Major General William B. Bate's division, pulled out of Hardee's corps, marched to extend the Confederate left down to South Utoy Creek, stretching Hood's line better than four miles beyond his main works around the city, thin enough in places to worry any engineer who studied it closely. Confederate work parties went in behind Bate's infantry, and what they raised over the following days earned its own name in the reports — a railway defense line, abatis in overlapping bands, rifle pits sited for interlocking fire, head-logs for overhead cover, gun positions on whatever high ground the terrain offered. It was a gamble, thinning the line that far from the rest of the army to hold ground nobody expected to need holding for long. It very nearly did not get the time it needed to pay off. Then it got more time than anyone on the Confederate side had any right to expect, and the reason had nothing to do with Bate, or Hood, or anything the Confederate army did. It came from inside Schofield's own lines.

Sherman had reinforced Schofield's advance with Major General John M. Palmer's XIV Corps, on loan from Thomas's Army of the Cumberland, and it was here the campaign very nearly stopped — not on account of anything Hood did, but because two Union major generals could not agree on which of them outranked the other.

The dispute turned on a technicality narrow enough to be almost comic, if it had not been costing the Confederates exactly the time they needed. Palmer and Schofield held the same date of commission as major general. Army custom settled such ties by whichever officer had worn his previous grade — brigadier general — the longer, and Schofield had worn that star before Palmer had. Sherman ruled accordingly: Schofield ranked, and Palmer's corps would take his orders.

Palmer would not have it. He believed himself senior, said so, and refused to place his corps under Schofield's tactical direction — not mutiny exactly, nothing so dramatic as that, but a flat refusal all the same, delivered by a corps commander to the officer coordinating his movements, with Confederate infantry entrenching in plain sight less than a mile off. Messages ran back and forth for days between Palmer, Thomas, Schofield, and Sherman, each side trying to talk the other into moving, and neither did. Palmer, finding no other way to hold his position, tendered his resignation. Sherman turned it down at first — he had not wanted the distraction, and did not relish losing an experienced corps commander over a matter of commission dates — but the standoff would not resolve itself any other way, and in the end Sherman accepted what he had first refused.

It made Palmer, so far as the record shows, the only corps commander of the war, on either side, to resign in the middle of active field operations. That was a small and almost absurd distinction to have earned — a general choosing to go home rather than serve a single day under a man he considered his junior, in a war that had already asked infinitely larger sacrifices of men who never got asked their opinion on who ranked whom. Small did not mean cheap, though. Palmer left for Illinois on the 6th of August. Brigadier General Richard W. Johnson took the corps in his place. And Sherman did his own arithmetic on what the standoff had cost him, in the same blunt currency he measured everything else in: a delay, he reckoned, "equal to the loss of 2,000 men." Bate's Confederates, given days instead of hours to dig, had used every one of them.

By the morning of August 5th, with the command question settled if not exactly healed, Schofield's combined force went forward to feel out Bate's new line. Baird's division, on the Union left, struck first — Turchin's brigade rolling up a Confederate skirmish line held by pickets from Anderson's division and taking a hundred forty prisoners for eighty-three casualties of its own, a lopsided exchange that told Schofield the real Confederate position still lay somewhere ahead, not yet found. Armstrong's Confederate cavalry, screening in front of Bate's infantry, fought a series of delaying actions through the morning that cost Bate's engineers nothing and bought them everything — more hours to finish the abatis and gun pits that would matter far more the next day.

Somewhere in that skirmishing, near a place called Cascade Springs, the 11th Kentucky — Union men, part of Cameron's brigade — came up against the 4th Kentucky, one of five regiments in Joseph H. Lewis's brigade, the outfit every soldier on both sides of the line still called the Orphan Brigade. No border state had sent sons into both armies in the numbers Kentucky had, and on that particular stretch of Georgia pine outside Atlanta, the war's oldest cruelty played itself out again in miniature — men who might have grown up on adjoining farms, now trading fire across a few hundred yards of open ground. Private Johnny Green, in Lewis's brigade, thought it worth setting down afterward in his diary: Kentuckian against Kentuckian, in a war three years past the point where anyone still believed it would end quickly, or end clean.

The full weight of the attack came the next morning, the 6th, at ten o'clock, the Georgia heat already thick enough by then to make wool uniforms miserable before a shot was fired. Jacob Cox's division went in against Bate's left, James Reilly's brigade — borrowed from Hascall's division for the occasion — leading the assault against a ridge south of the Sandtown Road, open ground the whole way. Bate watched them come from behind everything his men had spent the intervening days building: abatis in overlapping bands, rifle pits sited for crossing fire, the kind of position that turned open ground into a killing floor no measure of individual courage could cross by main force alone. He had perhaps thirty-five hundred infantry and dismounted cavalry to hold better than four miles of line. He did not need all of it in front of Reilly. He only needed enough of it aimed the right way, and after days of steady digging, it was.

They came on anyway. A Confederate defender, watching the Federal line advance, wrote afterward that the attackers "swept past…not knowing that they were about to encounter breastworks…but they were plucky fellows and charged to within a few yards of our works, paying dearly for their temerity." Paying dearly undersells it by a considerable margin. Reilly's brigade went in twelve hundred strong and came out the other side of it with three hundred six casualties — seventy-six dead, a hundred ninety-nine wounded, thirty-one more taken prisoner in the confusion in front of the Confederate line. One man in four who went forward that morning did not come back whole. Some did not come back at all.

While Cox's men bled in front of Bate's infantry, Hascall tried the flank, pushing his division across South Utoy Creek toward the ground where Lawrence Ross's Texas cavalry, dismounted and fighting as infantry and spread thin enough along the position to look like a considerably larger force than it was, held the Confederate left — the same troopers who, less than a week before, had helped run Stoneman's raid to ground at Sunshine Church, now doing on foot what they had already proven they could do from the saddle. Hascall's attack found early success. Ross's Texans gave ground under the pressure, and Union soldiers overran enough of the position to take several stands of Confederate colors — though the exchange cut both directions, the 25th Michigan losing its own flag in the same confused fighting before recapturing it later the same day, an action that earned Private Benjamin Van Raalte a nomination for the Medal of Honor. Ross's men bent but did not break, and South Utoy Creek itself — swollen enough to slow a man down, not deep enough to stop him, the worst kind of obstacle for troops already taking fire — combined with Confederate rifles and artillery to stall Hascall's momentum before it could become a breakthrough. Further down the line, Private Samuel Grimshaw of the 105th Ohio helped carry a Confederate battery position along the Sandtown Road, and earned his own Medal of Honor for it. It was, in the end, the kind of day that produced a great many individual acts of the sort men wrote citations for, and very little ground that stayed won. Johnson's corps — Richard Johnson's corps now, not Palmer's — came up in support, but came up late, and whatever gap Hascall had opened never widened enough to matter before the day ran out.

Bate did not wait to find out whether the Federals would try the same ground twice. During the night his division fell back to the main Confederate line covering the railroads directly, leaving the Utoy Creek position empty behind him — not abandoned in defeat, but given up on his own schedule, once it had done its work of buying Hood's engineers the time they needed on the inner works. When Union skirmishers probed forward on the morning of the 7th, they found the ground in front of them empty and the Confederates dug in somewhere stronger still. Johnson's corps, Baird's division leading, tried the new position anyway, and got the same answer the previous two days should have already taught them: roughly two hundred more casualties, and nothing gained that the Federals did not already hold simply by walking into trenches the Confederates had chosen to leave.

Thirty-five hundred Confederate infantry and dismounted cavalry, dug into a position four miles from any support, had absorbed everything two full Union divisions could throw at them across three days of fighting, and had given up the ground only when they chose to, in the dark, on their own schedule. By the final tally, Sherman's three days at Utoy Creek had cost him somewhere between eight hundred fifty and a thousand men. Bate's Confederates, fighting the whole engagement from prepared positions with the advantage of the ground, lost somewhere between two and three hundred — the same lopsided arithmetic that had held at Ezra Church nine days before, except this time it was Union blood paying the bill instead of Confederate. Hood's army, badly used as it had been in the fighting around the city that month, had not forgotten how to punish an attacker who came at it across open ground into a fixed position. If anything, it had gotten better at the business, out of necessity.

Sherman had spent two weeks now trying to take Atlanta without paying Atlanta's full price — infantry against the works, then cavalry around them, then infantry again by a wider road — and each time the bill had come due anyway, in a different currency: dead and wounded at Ezra Church, captured troopers scattered across middle Georgia after Sunshine Church, three hundred six men of Reilly's brigade left in the grass in front of Bate's abatis. By the 7th of August he had run out of maneuvers that did not cost him what he was trying not to pay. He had not run out of artillery.

The order went to Chattanooga within days: send the siege guns. They would not be aimed at Bate's trenches, or at any other line of Confederate infantry. Atlanta itself — the depot, the foundries, the houses, the people still living in them, Mary Rawson Mallard among them, keeping her own diary through what came next — would be the target now, at whatever hour the guns were ready to fire, for as long as it took. Sherman had tried maneuver. Now he would make the city itself unbearable to hold, and see if that worked where three infantry assaults and two ruined cavalry columns had not.

It would take three more weeks and one more flanking march, to Jonesborough at the end of August, before Hood evacuated the city on the 2nd of September. But something had already changed by the second week of August, and it had changed at Utoy Creek as much as anywhere else that summer. Sherman had stopped trying to spare his army the cost of this campaign. He had only started looking for cheaper ways to spend it.

I've long admired Andrew Lambert: when I was a PhD student he convinced me over a formal departmental dinner that the Battle of Britain was guff/Churchillian propaganda to lure the Americans into the war, and that the RAF should be abolished and turned into air arms of the navy and army.

However, this piece is a mixed bag - on the one hand he is very clear about how NATO membership distorted Britain's national interests away from the historic importance of the sea, to defending the Fulda Gap.

On the other hand, he offers no new strategic concept for our current world order, and looks no higher than catching Russia's shadow fleet as the great task of the day - effectively recreating the Cold War era he criticises: locked in forever war with Russia and with Britain acting as an adjunct to another NATO conflict.

Under the Green Pakistan Initiative (GPI) Phase I, following the successful transformation of 2,460 acres of barren land into cultivable farmland, a Green Agri Mall has been established in Mirani, Dasht to provide modern agricultural support to local farmers.

Syria just moved to Level C alert. Nationwide.

August 4, 2026. Multiple reports -including Al Arabiya confirm the Syrian Army, the force built by the transitional government under President Ahmed al-Sharaa, has raised its readiness across the entire country.
Every soldier and officer recalled from leave. Ordered to report to their units immediately.

Units moving toward the Syrian-Iraqi border.
Damascus has offered no explanation. It doesn't need to. Watch the last few days and the picture is clear.
Syrian officials already warned Baghdad: Iran-backed militias have been detected moving near the shared border. The message was blunt - any attack launched from Iraqi territory will get a response.

That border runs roughly 600 km. Three crossings matter most: al-Yarubiyah–Rabia, al-Bukamal–al-Qaim, al-Tanf–al-Waleed. All exposed. All being watched now.

This isn't happening in a vacuum. Jordan. Saudi Arabia. Kuwait. All leaning on Baghdad over the same problem - Iranian-aligned groups operating freely on Iraqi soil, threatening neighbors who never asked for this fight.

Remember what this army actually is. Not Assad's army. A reconstituted force, built from former opposition factions after his fall in December 2024, still finding its footing inside a transitional Ministry of Defense.

Now it's on alert.

Iraq keeps insisting it isn't a battlefield. Syria just signaled it's preparing for the chance that it is.

Robert Jeffress is senior pastor of the 14,000-member First Baptist Church in Dallas, a Fox News contributor, and host of Pathway to Victory. He holds a B.S. from Baylor University, a Th.M. from Dallas Theological Seminary, and a D.Min. from Southwestern Baptist Theological Seminary; zero medical degrees, zero scientific training, zero epidemiological credentials, and zero public-health qualifications of any kind.

In 2021 he got vaccinated early, hosted vaccine clinics at his megachurch, called the shots a “gift from God” and “present from God,” urged members to take them so the church could fully reopen, and flatly refused to issue or encourage religious exemptions - telling the Associated Press his staff would neither offer nor support them while dismissing fetal-cell objections as inconsistent with everyday medicines.

A high-profile Trump-aligned evangelical who spent years railing against government overreach and defending religious liberty suddenly declared there was no biblical case against the jab, equated refusal with spiritual danger, and leveraged “pro-life” language to shame holdouts. 

Elite media platforms and early access for the pastor; “no credible argument” and no exemption letters for the congregation. He framed isolation from church as the greater risk while the real risk of institutional pressure went unexamined.

When the only degrees you hold are in theology, the only mandate you’re qualified to enforce is the one that keeps the pews - and the compliance - full.

$ASTS (2W) — One hell of a bullish candle since touching down between support and the momentum cloud, and bulls have taken this one from $55 toward $70 in a matter of days.

Right now we are barreling toward the blue zone, which is a cluster we need to breach and fight our way back into.

text:
Colorful Songs: The Red Telephone

1967 was known as the Summer of Love, but maybe it wasn't for the band Love. After the release and commercial failure of their second album, Da Capo, Tjay Cantrelli and "Snoopy" Pfisterer left the band, and Arthur Lee left the Castle. Instead, he rented a house on Blue Heights Drive near Laurel Canyon where Roger Corman shot the film The Trip starring Peter Fonda, Dennis Hopper and Bruce Dern. The house had a pool that went from the outside into the living room. The script for The Trip was written by some guy named Jack Nicholson. Maybe you've heard of him? 

But for Love, 1967 was turning into a bad trip. Some of the band members were dealing with drug habits, there was friction between Bryan MacLean and Arthur Lee over songwriting, and Lee was convinced he wasn't going to live to see 1968. So, Lee wrote a series of songs dealing with his fears, as well as the political turmoil engulfing America with race riots and the Vietnam War. Soon, he had an album's worth of tunes, but a band that didn't seem interested in recording them. So, the decision was made to record a double album called Gethsemane. Two sides would be for the songs written by Lee, the third side would be songs written by MacLean, and the fourth side would feature songs written by lead guitarist Johnny Echols. However, when Love approached Elektra president Jac Holzman with this idea, he rejected it. Instead, the new album would feature the songs written by Lee with two from MacLean. 

Having abandoned Gethsemane, Love chose a different title, Forever Changes. This was inspired by something Arthur Lee said to a girlfriend when they broke up. She said "I thought you told me you'd love me forever." Lee replied, "Yeah, well, 'forever' changes." Bruce Botnick, who engineered the first two Love albums, was brought in as producer, and he brought along his friend Neil Young to act as co-producer. Young had recently left Buffalo Springfield and needed money to help launch a solo career. He worked a day helping arrange the song The Daily Planet, was paid, and then left the album.

When the band got together to record, the members MacLean, Echols, bassist Ken Forssi, and drummer Michael Stuart were having trouble with Lee's complex tunes. So, Botnick did something that was common for bands at the time, but had never been done with Love: he brought in session musicians from the Wrecking Crew.

Now, before I continue, I want to point out something that many folks don't know. Back in the 60s, recording an album could be an expensive proposition. So, record labels would often bring in session musicians to play the instruments while the band just sang the songs. This was the case with the Byrds first album, where only Roger McGuinn played an instrument. The same with the Association, Simon & Garfunkel, the Mamas & the Papas, the Beach Boys, Paul Revere & the Raiders, Gary Puckett and the Union Gap, and Herb Alpert & the Tijuana Brass. But it was not the case with Elektra artists like Paul Butterfield Blues Band, The Doors, and Love.

The members of the Wrecking Crew who played on Forever Changes were Carol Kaye on bass, Hal Blaine on drums, Don Randi on keyboards, and Billy Strange on guitar. They can be heard on the songs The Daily Planet and Andmoreagain, which were recorded in just three hours. This worked as it lit a fire under the other members of Love, who went on to record the remaining songs in about two weeks. Only Randi remained from the Wrecking Crew to play the keyboard parts on various songs. Afterwards, Lee got together with arranger David Angel to work on adding horns and strings to most of the songs. Lee would sing and play the parts he wanted for the different instruments, and then Angel would use this add the orchestration. 

The Red Telephone is a standout track on Forever Changes. Some thing it had to do with the red telephone that was at the Castle. It may have been Lee remembering his childhood in Memphis, where he sang a song about a red telephone in nursery school. The song may also have to do with the hotline between the White House and the Kremlin. The lyrics themselves are truly haunting, opening with the line: "Sitting on a hillside/Watching all the people die/I'll feel much better on the other side/I'll thumb a ride."

Lee was obsessed with his own mortality at the time, and he'd often sit in the pool at his house, looking down on LA, hearing the sirens from ambulances and police cars. The song itself is deceptively pretty, with MacLean fingerpicking chords on a twelve-string guitar while Don Randi plays an eerie harpsichord melody. The strings and horns add to the growing ominous feeling of the song. Its interesting because the harpsichord had usually been used to brighten psychedelic songs, like Fixing a Hole by the Beatles.

Another influence on Lee was the film version of Peter Weiss's play "The Persecution and Assassination of Jean-Paul Marat as Performed by the Inmates of the Asylum of Charenton Under the Direction of the Marquis de Sade" aka Marat/Sade. Lee went to see it numerous times. The Red Telephone features a nursery rhyme at the end: 
"They're locking them up today
They're throwing away the key
I wonder who it'll be tomorrow, you or me?"
It then goes into a line taken from Marat/Sade: "We're all normal and we want our freedom"

Forever Changes was released to general indifference in 1967. Everyone was into the happy sounds of Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band. They weren't ready for an album that showed the dark side of the psychedelic period. It also didn't help that Love did not tour behind the album, and even turned down a chance to play at the Monterrey Pop Festival. 

This led the classic lineup of Love to breakup. Bryan MacLean was the first to leave. He wasn't happy that his writing contributions to Forever Changes had been limited to Alone Again Or and Old Man. Making matters worse, his original title of Alone Again had been changed by Lee without his permission, and the final mix moved Lee's backing vocals into the foreground and turned MacLean into a backing singer on his own song. The decision to release it as the first single off of Forever Changes didn't mollify MacLean, who left to pursue a solo career. Echols and Forssi fell into drug addiction, while Stuart turned down an offer to tour with Neil Diamond and retired from music. 

Fortunately, Lee's prediction of his own early death proved false. He continued to put together different incarnations of Love, and lived to see Forever Changes become the success he always knew the album would be. He passed away in 2006 at the age of 61. MacLean became a successful Contemporary Christian musical artist until his death in 1998. Forssi also died that year. Echols kicked his drug addiction and became a successful session musician. He continues to tour today as Love Revised with Rusty Squeezebox on lead vocals, Mike Randle on rhythm guitar, Daddy O Green on drums, and James Nolte on bass.

text:
High Elevation Wine Farming Works without chemicals
(while most other regions depend on them)

If it's not cold, and it's not dry, you're going to have pest, disease or fungus problems. Most U.S. wine regions don't offer both which is why farming organically is nearly impossible.

On the extreme difficulty end of the spectrum, Virginia (2% of US wine production) is too hot and too humid. Summer rain fuels black rot, downy mildew, powdery mildew, and botrytis. Only three vineyards in the entire state are certified organic.

The Finger Lakes (0.5%) are cold, but still humid. Same diseases.

California (81%) is dry, but pest pressure is extreme. They fight Pierce's disease, phylloxera, and leafroll virus with a mix of chemicals and integrated pest strategies.

Fighting all of these issues is while remaining organic can be like fighting against inflation by holding treasury bonds. Its just not affective enough and is the main reason why only 0.4% of the wine grapes grown in the USA are produced organically.

The best way to avoid these issues is to find a place that is just cold enough to kills pest and just dry enough to stave off infection while also not being too cold and too dry to be able to actually farm.

Only small pockets of these zipper zones exist around the USA and they do come with their own challenges, but Colorado's West Elks AVA is one of them.

Here we farm at knifes edge between the Rocky Mountains and the Utah Desert. At 6,000+ feet, the winters kill off most threats and the arid summers prevent mildew.

The tradeoff? Most vines can't survive here and even the ones that do get frozen back to the ground (destroying an entire vintage) every few years.

Despite being known as a finicky grape, Pinot Noir thrives here. Chardonnay, Gewurztraminer and Riesling do too.

Our Wine Region is small, but this climate allows us to punch above our weight.

text:
In the vast, restless embrace of the California seas, a majestic humpback whale lay imprisoned—bound by cruel tangles of fishing lines that tethered its mighty form to the ocean floor. What first appeared to the returning fishermen as a mere floating buoy revealed itself, upon closer approach, as a soul of the deep in desperate peril, its vast body hopelessly entangled and weary from the struggle.

When cries for aid met only silence, these ordinary men refused to abandon the giant. For nearly three hours they labored with unwavering resolve, hearts pounding against the weight of time and tide. One final rope still held the exhausted creature captive, moments from a fatal dive into darkness.

Then came an act of pure, selfless courage: one fisherman plunged into the cold waters, climbed upon the whale’s broad back, and with steady hands severed the last cruel line—just as the great beast prepared to vanish beneath the waves.

As the rope slipped free, the humpback surged into liberation. In that sacred instant, the crew sensed something profound—the whale had understood. It remained calm, trusting the very hands that sought its freedom.

What unfolded was no ordinary rescue, but a living testament to courage, compassion, and the quiet gratitude that binds all living hearts. To these fishermen we offer our deepest thanks: for risking everything, for choosing mercy over ease, and for granting one of the ocean’s most magnificent souls a second chance at the open, boundless sea.

Immigration and naturalization are federal powers for a reason. One country. One people under one body of law at the border. The moment you hand fifty legislatures their own guest-worker machines, you do not get “federalism.” You get a bidding war.

California will not run the same program as Indiana. New York will not run the same program as Texas. Labor contractors, statehouse lobbies, and industries that prefer cheaper imported workers will write the real rules. Some states will maximize inflow. Others will try to resist and then get sued, boycotted, or outflanked by neighbors in a compact. The national immigration system becomes a patchwork of local HR departments with flags.

National immigration law exists so the United States remains one jurisdiction at the gate. Fifty competing import programs shred that. Birthright citizenship turns every multi-year “guest” household into a potential permanent expansion of the electorate and the welfare footprint, whether or not the original visa said temporary. Curtis can walk 250 miles across Utah talking about values. Values are not the same thing as a border. What Curtis and Kelly offered is local patronage immigration, bipartisan cover, and a demographic time fuse the Court just refused to snuff out.

America does not need fifty little immigration departments. It needs one government that remembers what a country is.
